  1. Calico in policy-only mode: Calico can be deployed without its network overlay (policy-only mode). If the overlay CNI doesn't support policies, Calico's policies are silently ignored. Verify: kubectl get ippools — should show Calico-managed IP pools.
  2. NetworkPolicy order/priority conflict: Multiple policies select the same pod. Policies are ADDITIVE — a more permissive policy that also selects the pod can override the deny-all. Check ALL policies: kubectl get networkpolicy -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 podSelector.
  3. hostNetwork: true bypasses all NetworkPolicies: Pods with hostNetwork: true use the node's network namespace — NetworkPolicies do NOT apply to them. Check: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostNetwork==true) | .metadata.name'.
  4. NetworkPolicy CRD not registered: In very old or custom clusters, the networking.k8s.io/v1 CRD may be missing. kubectl api-resources | grep networkpolicies — if missing, the API server won't reject the YAML but the CNI won't receive it.
  5. Calico Felix not running or misconfigured: Felix is Calico's policy enforcement agent. If the felix daemonset pods are CrashLoopBackOff or not running, policies aren't enforced. Check: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep felix.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default-allow all traffic: A newly installed CNI often defaults to ALLOW-ALL until the first NetworkPolicy is created. But some CNIs (like default Flannel) NEVER enforce policies regardless. Verify CNI capabilities before relying on NetworkPolicy.
  2. CNI not configured with policy engine: Calico requires the CALICO_NETWORKING_BACKEND set correctly. Cilium requires --enable-policy=enforcement. A fresh install may have policy disabled by default. Check CNI configmap.
  3. kube-proxy iptables mode vs IPVS mode: Some CNI/policy combinations behave differently depending on kube-proxy mode. IPVS mode may bypass certain policy chains. Check: kubectl get cm kube-proxy -n kube-system -o yaml | grep mode.
  4. IPv6-only cluster with IPv4 NetworkPolicies: NetworkPolicies must match the IP family of the cluster. An IPv4 CIDR block in a policy won't match IPv6 traffic. Check cluster IP family: kubectl get svc kubernetes -o yaml | grep ipFamily.
  5. CNI installation order: If NetworkPolicy CRD was installed AFTER pods were created, existing pod-to-pod connections may persist. Restart affected pods: kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave" Confirms CNI policy support — if none found, your NetworkPolicy YAML is dead code.
kubectl get networkpolicy -A Shows all policies across all namespaces — verify yours is in the right namespace.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide --show-labels Verify pod labels match the policy's podSelector. A mismatch = policy selects ZERO pods.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: CNI plugin doesn't support NetworkPolicy enforcement. Flannel (default mode) and some minimal CNIs silently IGNORE NetworkPolicy resources — the YAML is accepted but never enforced.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify CNI supports NetworkPolicy kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave" If none found, install Calico: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28/manifests/calico.yaml
2. Verify pod labels match the podSelector kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels Ensure the NetworkPolicy's podSelector matches exact pod labels. A mismatch = policy selects ZERO pods.
3. Add Egress rules with DNS allow policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] A deny-all without egress DNS (UDP 53 to kube-dns) breaks ALL pod-to-service communication. Always whitelist DNS.
4. Test isolation kubectl exec anihpj-web -- curl --connect-timeout 3 anihpj-api:8000 Connection should TIME OUT (not return 200). If it succeeds, the policy isn't enforcing.
5. Apply anihpj/jobpost baseline Default-deny + explicit allows: web→api:8000, api→db:5432, api→redis:6379, all→kube-dns:53/UDP. This implements least-privilege networking.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always verify the CNI first. The #1 CKS exam trap: a cluster running Flannel where NetworkPolicy YAML is accepted but silently ignored. Run kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep calico before writing any policy.
Deny-all without DNS = broken cluster. If you block all egress without allowing UDP 53 to kube-dns, pods can't resolve service names. Every deny-all policy MUST include a DNS egress rule.
Policies are additive, not exclusive. A single "allow" policy that selects the same pod can punch a hole through your deny-all. Audit ALL policies in the namespace before assuming isolation.
Test, don't assume. kubectl exec anihpj-web -- curl --connect-timeout 3 anihpj-api:8000 NetworkPolicies that "look right" on paper often fail because of label mismatches or CNI gaps. Trust only the curl test.
CS2
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS2
Ingress TLS Not Working — ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID

🔍 Symptom: Browser shows ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID when accessing https://anihpj.jobpost.com. The TLS Secret exists (kubectl get secret anihpj-tls shows it), the Ingress references it correctly, but HTTPS connections fail with certificate errors. openssl s_client -connect anihpj.jobpost.com:443 shows the certificate is self-signed or issued by an untrusted CA.

  curl -v https://anihpj.jobpost.com
  * SSL certificate problem: self signed certificate
  * SSL certificate verify failed
  curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate

  kubectl get secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj
  NAME         TYPE                DATA   AGE
  anihpj-tls   kubernetes.io/tls   2      10m

  kubectl describe ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj
  TLS:
    anihpj-tls terminates anihpj.jobpost.com
  Rules: Host=anihpj.jobpost.com → Service=anihpj-web:80
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Self-signed certificate in the TLS Secret: The most common cause. Someone generated a self-signed cert with openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -days 365. Browsers and clients REJECT self-signed certs unless explicitly trusted. Fix: Use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt or a trusted CA.
  2. TLS Secret contains wrong certificate or key: The Secret's tls.crt and tls.key don't match (key doesn't correspond to cert), or the cert is for a DIFFERENT hostname. Verify: openssl x509 -in <(kubectl get secret anihpj-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d) -text -noout | grep DNS.
  3. Intermediate certificate chain missing: The TLS Secret only contains the server certificate but NOT the intermediate CA certificate(s). Clients can't build the trust chain to a trusted root. The tls.crt field must contain the FULL chain (server cert + intermediate(s)). Use kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem.
  4. Ingress controller not configured for TLS passthrough or termination: Some Ingress controllers (especially nginx) require specific annotations to properly handle TLS. Missing nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true" or nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS" can cause TLS negotiation failures.
  5. Host mismatch between certificate SAN and Ingress host: The TLS certificate was issued for api.jobpost.com but the Ingress rule specifies anihpj.jobpost.com. Certificate Subject Alternative Names (SANs) must EXACTLY match the Ingress host. Check: kubectl get ingress -o yaml | grep host vs openssl x509 -text -noout | grep -A1 "Subject Alternative".
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Ingress class not set or wrong controller: Multiple Ingress controllers installed (nginx + traefik) and the wrong one picks up the Ingress resource. Set spec.ingressClassName: nginx explicitly.
  2. TLS Secret in wrong namespace: The Ingress references anihpj-tls but the Secret exists in the default namespace. Ingress can ONLY reference Secrets in the SAME namespace. kubectl get secret -A | grep anihpj-tls.
  3. Certificate expired: The TLS certificate's notAfter date has passed. Check: openssl x509 -enddate -noout. cert-manager auto-renews, but manually created certs don't.
  4. Let's Encrypt rate limit exceeded: Too many certificate requests for the same domain. Let's Encrypt has strict rate limits (50 certs per domain per week). cert-manager shows 429 Too Many Requests in the Certificate resource events.
  5. Firewall blocking ACME challenge: Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 challenge requires port 80 to be publicly accessible. DNS-01 challenge requires API access to DNS provider. NetworkPolicy or cloud firewall blocking the challenge path.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. cert-manager not installed: Fresh cluster, no cert-manager. TLS Secrets must be created manually or cert-manager CRDs won't exist. Install: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml.
  2. ClusterIssuer not configured: cert-manager is installed but no ClusterIssuer (Let's Encrypt staging/production) exists. Without it, Certificate resources stay Pending. kubectl get clusterissuer — should show at least one READY issuer.
  3. Ingress controller not installed or pending: Fresh kubeadm cluster has no Ingress controller. kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx — if namespace doesn't exist, install nginx-ingress.
  4. DNS not pointing to Ingress controller: Domain's A record doesn't point to the Ingress controller's external IP (LoadBalancer or NodePort). kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx — check EXTERNAL-IP.
  5. Default TLS Secret in kube-system missing: Some Ingress controllers look for a default TLS certificate for unmatched hosts. If missing, HTTPS on undefined hosts returns connection errors.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get certificate -A Check cert-manager Certificate resources — are they Ready: True? Events show the ACME challenge status.
openssl s_client -connect anihpj.jobpost.com:443 -servername anihpj.jobpost.com Inspect the actual certificate served — check issuer, SANs, and expiry date.
kubectl describe ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj Verify TLS section references the correct Secret name and the host matches the certificate SAN.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Self-signed or mismatched TLS certificate. The TLS Secret contains a certificate that clients cannot verify — either self-signed, missing intermediate chain, wrong hostname, or issued by an untrusted CA. Use cert-manager + Let's Encrypt to automate trusted certificate issuance and renewal.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify the current certificate kubectl get secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -text -noout Check Issuer, Subject, SANs, and Validity dates. A self-signed cert shows Issuer = Subject.
2. Install and configure cert-manager kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml Then create a ClusterIssuer for Let's Encrypt (use staging first to avoid rate limits).
3. Create a Certificate resource kubectl apply -f anihpj-certificate.yaml cert-manager will handle ACME challenge, obtain the cert, and store it in the Secret automatically.
4. Verify the Ingress references the correct Secret kubectl describe ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj | grep -A3 TLS Ensure the Secret name matches and the host exactly matches the certificate SAN.
5. Test with curl curl -vI https://anihpj.jobpost.com Should show "SSL certificate verify ok" and return HTTP 200. No certificate warnings.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never use self-signed certs in production. Self-signed certs train your team to click "Accept Risk" in browsers — making them blind to real MITM attacks. Always use cert-manager + Let's Encrypt or your organization's internal CA.
Always use Let's Encrypt staging first. The production LE endpoint has strict rate limits. Test your cert-manager configuration against the staging endpoint before switching to production.
The TLS Secret must be in the SAME namespace as the Ingress. This is a Kubernetes security boundary — Ingresses cannot reference Secrets across namespaces. This prevents namespace-A from stealing namespace-B's TLS certificates.
Monitor certificate expiry. kubectl get certificates -A cert-manager auto-renews 30 days before expiry, but monitor it. An expired TLS cert = production outage. Set up Prometheus alerts on certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds.
CS3
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS3
cert-manager Certificate Stuck Pending — No TLS Cert Issued

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get certificate -n anihpj shows READY: False indefinitely. The Certificate resource exists and references a valid ClusterIssuer, but no TLS Secret is created. kubectl describe certificate anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj shows events like "Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation" or "ACME authorization failed." The Let's Encrypt certificate for anihpj-api.jobpost.com is never issued.

  kubectl get certificate -n anihpj
  NAME               READY   SECRET             AGE
  anihpj-tls-cert    False   anihpj-tls         30m

  kubectl describe certificate anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj
  Status:
    Conditions:
      Type: Ready   Status: False   Reason: Pending
  Events:
    Warning  Failed  The HTTP-01 challenge failed —
      connection refused to anihpj-api.jobpost.com:80

  kubectl get order,challenge -n anihpj
  NAME                                    STATE     AGE
  order.acme.cert-manager.io/anihpj-...   pending   30m
  challenge.acme.cert-manager.io/...       pending   30m
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. HTTP-01 challenge path not reachable: Let's Encrypt's validation server must be able to reach http://anihpj-api.jobpost.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>. If port 80 is not exposed, blocked by firewall, or the Ingress isn't routing correctly, the challenge FAILS. curl http://anihpj-api.jobpost.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/test from outside the cluster must return something.
  2. DNS not pointing to the Ingress controller: The domain's A/AAAA record doesn't resolve to the Ingress controller's external IP. Let's Encrypt resolves the domain to find the challenge endpoint. Check: nslookup anihpj-api.jobpost.com — must return the Ingress controller's LoadBalancer IP.
  3. ClusterIssuer misconfigured: The ClusterIssuer references the wrong ACME server (staging vs production), has an invalid email, or uses an unsupported private key algorithm. cert-manager silently retries but never succeeds. Check: kubectl describe clusterissuer letsencrypt-prod — Status should show "ACME account registered."
  4. Ingress not created or not matching Certificate: The Certificate resource references an Ingress via issuerRef, but the Ingress doesn't exist or has a different hostname. cert-manager creates the challenge Ingress but can't complete validation. Verify: kubectl get ingress -A | grep anihpj.
  5. NetworkPolicy blocking ACME challenge traffic: A default-deny NetworkPolicy blocks inbound port 80 traffic to the Ingress controller or the solver pod. Let's Encrypt validation requests never reach the challenge endpoint. Temporarily allow port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 during certificate issuance.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. DNS-01 challenge with misconfigured credentials: Using DNS-01 instead of HTTP-01, but the cloud DNS provider credentials (AWS Route53, Cloudflare) are wrong or lack permissions. Check the Issuer's solvers.dns01 configuration and verify the Secret containing API keys exists.
  2. ACME rate limit hit: Let's Encrypt enforces rate limits: 5 duplicate certificates per week, 50 certificates per registered domain per week, 5 failures per account per hour. cert-manager retries exhausted the limit. Check Order status for rate limit errors.
  3. cert-manager webhook not reachable: The cert-manager webhook service validates Certificate resources. If the webhook pod is down or network issues prevent API server → webhook communication, Certificate resources can't be processed.
  4. Multiple Ingress controllers conflicting: Two Ingress controllers (e.g., nginx and traefik) respond to the same host. The ACME challenge request goes to the WRONG controller. Set spec.ingressClassName explicitly on the Certificate's solver Ingress template.
  5. Private IP / intranet domain: Let's Encrypt CANNOT validate certificates for domains that resolve to private IPs (RFC 1918) or internal-only domains. The domain must be publicly resolvable. For internal domains, use a private CA or cert-manager's self-signed issuer.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. cert-manager CRDs not installed: The custom resource definitions (Certificate, Issuer, ClusterIssuer) are missing. kubectl api-resources | grep cert-manager — if empty, apply the cert-manager CRDs first.
  2. No ClusterIssuer exists: cert-manager is installed but no ClusterIssuer is configured. Certificates reference a non-existent issuer. kubectl get clusterissuer — must have at least one with READY: True.
  3. ACME registration not complete: The ClusterIssuer shows "ACME account not registered." The initial ACME account creation with Let's Encrypt hasn't completed. Wait or check for errors in the cert-manager controller logs.
  4. Ingress controller not installed: New cluster, no Ingress controller. HTTP-01 challenges require an Ingress controller to serve the challenge files. Install nginx-ingress or similar.
  5. DNS propagation delay on first issuance: Newly created DNS records may take minutes to hours to propagate (depending on TTL). The first certificate issuance fails because Let's Encrypt can't resolve the domain yet.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe certificate anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj Check Conditions and Events — the exact failure reason is always in the Certificate status.
kubectl get order,challenge -n anihpj Orders represent a certificate request. Challenges represent individual domain validations. Both must reach "valid" state.
kubectl logs -n cert-manager deployment/cert-manager | grep anihpj cert-manager controller logs show the detailed ACME interaction — authorization attempts, errors, and retries.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: HTTP-01 challenge path unreachable. Let's Encrypt's validation servers cannot reach http://anihpj-api.jobpost.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/... — either DNS doesn't resolve, port 80 is blocked by firewall/NetworkPolicy, or the Ingress controller isn't routing traffic to the solver pod.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify DNS resolution nslookup anihpj-api.jobpost.com Must return the Ingress controller's external IP. If using NodePort, ensure the port mapping is correct.
2. Test HTTP reachability from outside curl -v http://anihpj-api.jobpost.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/test Should return HTTP 404 (not connection refused). If connection refused, check firewall/NetworkPolicy allowing port 80.
3. Check ClusterIssuer status kubectl describe clusterissuer letsencrypt-prod Status must show "ACME account registered" and Ready: True. If not, check server URL and email.
4. Temporarily allow ACME challenge traffic kubectl apply -f allow-acme-netpol.yaml Apply a NetworkPolicy that allows inbound port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. Remove after certificate is issued.
5. Use Let's Encrypt staging first server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory Test the entire flow against staging. Once it works, switch to production ACME URL. This avoids rate limit lockouts.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always test with Let's Encrypt staging first. Rate limits on production Let's Encrypt are harsh — you can lock yourself out for a week. The staging environment has MUCH higher limits and issues untrusted certs (perfect for testing).
HTTP-01 is simplest but requires public port 80. If your cluster is behind a corporate firewall that blocks inbound port 80, switch to DNS-01 challenges. DNS-01 requires API access to your DNS provider but works entirely behind firewalls.
Monitor Certificate resources proactively. kubectl get certificates -A -w Certificates stuck in False state for more than a few minutes indicate a configuration problem. Set up alerts on certmanager_certificate_ready_status in Prometheus.
Keep cert-manager updated. cert-manager follows Let's Encrypt API changes closely. Running an old version can break when Let's Encrypt deprecates API endpoints. Update cert-manager quarterly.

📌 CS4–CS6: Exposed Endpoints & Controller Misconfigurations

CS4
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS4
NodePort Exposed to Public Internet — Unauthorized External Access

🔍 Symptom: Redis (anihpj-redis:6379) is accidentally accessible from the public internet. A security scan reveals port 30001 open on the node's public IP, giving anyone direct access to the Redis instance without authentication. kubectl get svc anihpj-redis -n anihpj shows TYPE: NodePort with no authentication configured. An attacker can redis-cli -h <node-public-ip> -p 30001 and access all cached session data.

  kubectl get svc anihpj-redis -n anihpj
  NAME           TYPE       CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)          AGE
  anihpj-redis   NodePort   10.96.100.45   <none>        6379:30001/TCP   2d

  redis-cli -h 54.123.45.67 -p 30001
  54.123.45.67:30001> KEYS *
  1) "session:abc123"
  2) "cache:job-listings"
  3) "celery:task-queue"  ← UNATHORIZED ACCESS!

  kubectl describe svc anihpj-redis -n anihpj
  Type: NodePort
  NodePort: redis  30001/TCP  ← Exposed on ALL node IPs!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. NodePort service created for convenience without firewall: Developer used kubectl expose deployment anihpj-redis --type=NodePort for quick debugging and never changed it. NodePort opens the port on EVERY node's public IP. kubectl get svc --all-namespaces | grep NodePort — audit all NodePort services.
  2. No cloud firewall / security group restricting node ports: Cloud provider's security group or firewall allows 0.0.0.0/0 on all ports. NodePort range (30000-32767) is wide open. Restrict node security groups to only necessary ports (443, 80, 22 from trusted IPs).
  3. Database/cache service exposed directly instead of through API: Redis, PostgreSQL, or MongoDB exposed via NodePort instead of being accessed internally via ClusterIP + application layer. Backend services should NEVER have external endpoints — they should be reachable only via the API tier.
  4. No authentication on the backend service: Redis has no password (requirepass not set), MongoDB has no auth, PostgreSQL trusts all local connections. Even if NodePort is intentional, the service itself should require authentication.
  5. Default NodePort allocation without review: kubectl expose auto-assigns a NodePort in the 30000-32767 range without asking. Teams create services and forget about the external exposure. Regular audit: kubectl get svc -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.type=="NodePort")'.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. LoadBalancer service with externalTrafficPolicy: Local exposing node IPs: LoadBalancer services with externalTrafficPolicy: Local also open NodePorts on every node. Traffic to nodes without the pod gets dropped, but the port is still exposed.
  2. hostPort in pod spec: Pod directly binds to the node's port via hostPort: 6379. This bypasses kube-proxy entirely and is invisible to kubectl get svc. Check: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].ports[]?.hostPort)'.
  3. Ingress controller NodePort exposed directly: Ingress controller installed as NodePort (ports 30080/30443) with no cloud load balancer in front. The controller itself handles TLS termination, but the NodePort is open to the world.
  4. kubectl proxy with --address=0.0.0.0 left running: Developer ran kubectl proxy --address=0.0.0.0 --port=8001 for debugging and left it running. The Kubernetes API is now accessible without authentication.
  5. MetalLB/NodePort LB in BGP mode advertising node IPs: MetalLB or similar on-prem LB advertises node IPs via BGP without firewall rules. All NodePorts become accessible from the entire network.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No NetworkPolicy blocking external traffic: New cluster with no default-deny NetworkPolicy on NodePort services. kubectl get networkpolicy -A — empty or only internal policies.
  2. Cloud provider default security group too permissive: AWS/EC2 default security group allows all outbound and inbound from same security group. If nodes are in the default SG, all NodePorts are open between nodes.
  3. --service-node-port-range not restricted: kube-apiserver flag --service-node-port-range defaults to 30000-32767. A smaller range or disabling NodePorts entirely (--service-node-port-range=0-0) prevents accidental exposure.
  4. No OPA/Gatekeeper policy blocking NodePort: New cluster without admission controller policies. OPA can reject Services with type: NodePort in production namespaces.
  5. Firewall/security group not yet configured: Fresh cloud deployment — security groups haven't been hardened yet. Node ports are open pending firewall review.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get svc -A | grep NodePort Audit ALL NodePort services across all namespaces. Every one is a potential exposure point.
nmap -p 30000-32767 <node-public-ip> External port scan of the NodePort range. Any open port = exposed service. Automate this scan weekly.
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].ports[]?.hostPort)' Check for pods using hostPort — these bind directly to node interfaces and bypass Services entirely.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: NodePort service created for debugging convenience and never changed to ClusterIP. Combined with no cloud firewall restricting the NodePort range, backend services become directly accessible from the public internet — bypassing all application-layer authentication and authorization.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Convert NodePort to ClusterIP kubectl patch svc anihpj-redis -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"type":"ClusterIP"}}' This removes the NodePort allocation. The service remains accessible internally via ClusterIP. External access is cut off.
2. Add cloud firewall rules Restrict node security groups to only necessary ports. Block the entire NodePort range (30000-32767) from 0.0.0.0/0. Allow only from trusted IPs or internal VPC CIDRs.
3. Add authentication to backend services kubectl create secret generic redis-auth -n anihpj --from-literal=password=$(openssl rand -base64 32) Redis: set requirepass. PostgreSQL: use md5 or scram-sha-256. MongoDB: enable authentication. Never run backend services without auth even internally.
4. Enforce via OPA/Kyverno admission policy Create a policy that rejects Services with type: NodePort in production namespaces. Developers must use ClusterIP (internal) or LoadBalancer (controlled external entry).
5. Apply NetworkPolicy for defense-in-depth kubectl apply -f default-deny-netpol.yaml Even if a NodePort is accidentally created, a default-deny NetworkPolicy on the namespace prevents external traffic from reaching pods.
💡 Personal Advice:
NodePort is for DEVELOPMENT only. In production, use ClusterIP for internal services and Ingress/LoadBalancer for external access. NodePort exposes your internal architecture to anyone who scans your node IPs. Regular NodePort audits should be part of your security routine.
Cloud firewall is your last line of defense. Even with all Kubernetes controls in place, a misconfigured service can expose ports. Cloud security groups that block the NodePort range (30000-32767) from the internet prevent accidental exposure.
hostPort is worse than NodePort. Pods with hostPort bypass kube-proxy, Services, and NetworkPolicies entirely. They're invisible to kubectl get svc. Audit for hostPort usage and block it with admission controllers.
The NodePort range is a known attack surface. Attackers scan 30000-32767 looking for exposed databases, caches, and admin panels. If your NodePorts are open, they WILL be found. Shodan indexes them.
CS5
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS5
Ingress Controller Override — Wrong Controller Handling Traffic

🔍 Symptom: Two Ingress controllers (nginx-ingress and traefik) are installed. The anihpj Ingress resource is picked up by the WRONG controller, causing routing to fail or TLS to break. kubectl describe ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj shows the wrong controller in events. Traffic goes to traefik which doesn't have the TLS configuration, while nginx-ingress (which has the correct TLS Secret) never receives the request.

  kubectl get ingressClass
  NAME     CONTROLLER                      PARAMETERS   AGE
  nginx    nginx.org/ingress-controller     <none>       30d
  traefik  traefik.io/ingress-controller    <none>       5d

  kubectl get ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -o yaml | grep ingressClass
  <none>  ← No ingressClassName specified!

  kubectl describe ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj
  Events:
    Normal  Sync   traefik-ingress-controller  ← Wrong controller!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No ingressClassName specified: The Ingress resource doesn't have spec.ingressClassName set. When multiple Ingress controllers exist, the DEFAULT controller (or the first one to claim the Ingress) takes over. Always explicitly set ingressClassName: nginx.
  2. Multiple IngressClass resources with no default annotation: Two IngressClass resources exist, neither marked as default. The ingress controller that processes the Ingress first "wins." This is non-deterministic — the controller handling may change on restart.
  3. Old Ingress controller not fully uninstalled: Previous traefik installation wasn't fully cleaned up. The traefik controller pods are still running and processing Ingress resources. kubectl get pods -A | grep traefik — should return nothing if uninstalled.
  4. IngressClass annotation used instead of spec field: Using deprecated kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "nginx" annotation instead of spec.ingressClassName: nginx. Multiple controllers may respect the annotation differently, leading to conflicts.
  5. Controller watching all namespaces without scope restriction: Both controllers are configured to watch ALL namespaces. A controller can be scoped to specific namespaces with --watch-namespace flag, preventing conflicts.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm chart installed second controller without --set controller.ingressClass: Installing traefik via Helm with default values creates a default IngressClass that conflicts with nginx. Always customize ingressClass during installation.
  2. Ingress controller in kube-system vs application namespace: nginx-ingress in ingress-nginx namespace, traefik in kube-system. Controller scope differs, causing one to miss the Ingress and the other to claim it.
  3. Controller health checks interfering: Both controllers try to update the Ingress status field. The status subresource conflict causes one controller to stop processing. Check Ingress status for multiple controller entries.
  4. TLS Secret referenced by Ingress exists in wrong namespace: nginx-ingress can't read the TLS Secret because it's in a different namespace than the Ingress. traefik silently ignores the TLS section and serves HTTP.
  5. Ingress controller version incompatibility: Very old nginx-ingress doesn't support spec.ingressClassName (v1+ feature). Controller ignores the field and processes all Ingresses regardless.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default IngressClass created by Helm on first install: Running helm install traefik traefik/traefik creates a default IngressClass that captures all Ingresses without explicit className.
  2. No IngressClass resource exists: Very old cluster — Ingress controllers use only annotations. The spec.ingressClassName field is silently ignored, and annotation-based routing is unpredictable.
  3. Two controllers installed as part of "platform" Helm chart: A platform team installed a "standard tooling" chart that includes traefik, not realizing nginx-ingress was already installed.
  4. Testing controller left over from evaluation: Team tested both nginx and traefik, chose nginx, but never uninstalled traefik.
  5. No NetworkPolicy restricting Ingress controller communication: Both controllers can reach all pods, so either one "works" superficially, masking the conflict until TLS or advanced routing breaks.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get ingressClass -A List all IngressClasses. Check which one has the ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" annotation.
kubectl get pods -A | grep -E "ingress|traefik|nginx|haproxy|contour" Find ALL running Ingress controller pods. You might have more than you think.
kubectl describe ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj | grep -A5 Events The Events section shows WHICH controller picked up the Ingress. The wrong controller name = override problem.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Ingress created without spec.ingressClassName, allowing ANY controller to claim it. With multiple Ingress controllers installed, the traffic goes to the wrong one — breaking TLS termination, routing rules, and security configurations.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Identify all Ingress controllers kubectl get pods -A | grep -E "ingress|controller" List every running controller. Decide which ONE should handle anihpj traffic.
2. Set ingressClassName explicitly kubectl patch ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"ingressClassName":"nginx"}}' This binds the Ingress to ONLY the nginx controller. Other controllers will ignore it.
3. Remove the unwanted controller helm uninstall traefik -n traefik If traefik is not needed, uninstall it completely. One Ingress controller is simpler and safer.
4. Set default IngressClass kubectl annotate ingressClass nginx ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true This makes nginx the default for Ingresses without explicit className — but always set it explicitly anyway.
5. Verify TLS and routing curl -v https://anihpj.jobpost.com Ensure the correct controller handles TLS and routes traffic to the right backend service.
💡 Personal Advice:
One Ingress controller is the simplest security posture. Multiple controllers multiply your attack surface — each one has its own CVEs, configuration nuances, and TLS handling. Standardize on one.
Always set ingressClassName explicitly. Never rely on the default controller. An explicit ingressClassName prevents silent takeovers by newly installed controllers.
Audit for orphaned controllers periodically. kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress Controllers from past experiments or platform charts often linger. Include Ingress controller audit in your monthly security review.
CS6
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS6
NetworkPolicy Selector Not Matching — Pods Not Isolated

🔍 Symptom: A NetworkPolicy is created with podSelector: {app: anihpj-api} but the backend pods are labeled tier: api. The policy selects ZERO pods — traffic flows unrestricted as if no policy exists. kubectl get networkpolicy deny-api -n anihpj shows the policy exists, but kubectl exec anihpj-web -- curl anihpj-api:8000 succeeds despite the policy supposedly denying it.

  kubectl get networkpolicy deny-api -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: anihpj-api    ← Policy selects THIS label
    policyTypes: [Ingress]
    ingress: []            ← Deny all ingress

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels
  NAME               LABELS
  anihpj-api-7d8     tier=api,component=backend  ← ACTUAL labels
  anihpj-web-3f2     tier=web,component=frontend

  ❌ Policy selects {app: anihpj-api} — no pods have this label!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Label key mismatch: Policy uses app: anihpj-api but pods use tier: api or component: backend. NetworkPolicy label matching is EXACT — different key names = no match. Always verify with kubectl get pods --show-labels.
  2. Label value mismatch: Policy uses app: api but pods use app: anihpj-api. Both use the same key but different values. Case sensitivity matters: app: API ≠ app: api.
  3. Policy in wrong namespace: NetworkPolicy created in default namespace but pods run in anihpj. kubectl get networkpolicy -A — policies only affect pods in their own namespace.
  4. Pod was labeled AFTER NetworkPolicy was created:
    5. Policy created first, then pod deployed with different labels. The policy doesn't auto-update — it only selects pods with matching labels at evaluation time.
  5. Selector is empty {}: Policy has podSelector: {} (selects ALL pods in the namespace) but was intended to select only specific pods. An empty selector with deny-all ingress blocks ALL pods including system pods.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. namespaceSelector combined with podSelector incorrectly:
    2. Policy has BOTH namespaceSelector and podSelector in an ingress rule. Both must match for the rule to apply. A namespaceSelector mismatch blocks the entire rule.
  2. matchExpressions syntax error:
    3. Using matchExpressions with operator: In but forgetting the values array. The policy YAML is valid but the expression matches nothing.
  3. Policy selects pods by label that's added by a mutating webhook:
    4. The label security: enforced is added by Kyverno after pod creation. NetworkPolicy evaluation order — the policy may evaluate before the label is added.
  4. Policy applies to pod IPs that changed after restart:
    5. NetworkPolicy uses ipBlock with a specific pod IP. Pod restart changes IP, breaking the policy.
  5. Pod selected but egress rules don't cover DNS:
    6. Policy correctly selects the pod, but egress block-all also blocks DNS. Pod appears "not isolated" because DNS failures cascade into other errors, masking the actual isolation.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Labels not standardized: New cluster, no labeling convention. Different teams use different label keys (app vs tier vs component). NetworkPolicies are inconsistent because labels are inconsistent.
  2. First NetworkPolicy created incorrectly: Team new to NetworkPolicy copies a template without understanding podSelector. Policy looks correct but doesn't match any pods.
  3. Default-deny applied before understanding pod labels:
    4. Team applies a default-deny as "security hardening" but the podSelector is wrong. All traffic still flows, giving a false sense of security.
  4. Test pod with different labels:
    5. Manual test pod created with kubectl run test --image=busybox has auto-generated labels that don't match any policy. Testing "seems" to show policy doesn't work.
  5. CI/CD pipeline adds labels not in NetworkPolicy:
    6. Deployment pipeline adds version: v2 and commit: abc123 labels. NetworkPolicy was written for labels that exist only in staging, not production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels Compare actual pod labels against the NetworkPolicy's podSelector. Every key-value pair must match exactly.
kubectl get networkpolicy -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 podSelector Verify the podSelector in ALL policies affecting the namespace. Multiple policies may select the same pods.
kubectl describe networkpolicy deny-api -n anihpj The description shows which pods are selected — if empty, the selector doesn't match any pods.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Label mismatch between the NetworkPolicy's podSelector and the actual pod labels. The policy's selector key or value doesn't match any running pods, so the policy silently selects ZERO pods — all traffic flows unrestricted, creating a false sense of security.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Identify actual pod labels kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels Note the exact key-value pairs. The NetworkPolicy podSelector must match these.
2. Fix the podSelector kubectl edit networkpolicy deny-api -n anihpj Change app: anihpj-api to match the actual pod labels (e.g., tier: api).
3. Standardize labels across deployments Use recommended labels: app.kubernetes.io/name, app.kubernetes.io/component, app.kubernetes.io/part-of. Enforce with Kyverno.
4. Test the policy kubectl exec anihpj-web -- curl --connect-timeout 3 anihpj-api:8000 Should time out if policy is working. Test both ingress and egress directions.
5. Use kubectl describe to verify selection kubectl describe networkpolicy deny-api -n anihpj | grep "PodSelector" After fixing labels, verify the policy actually selects pods before assuming it works.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always verify with --show-labels before writing a NetworkPolicy. The most common NetworkPolicy failure is a label mismatch. One minute of checking labels saves hours of debugging phantom traffic flows.
Standardize your label schema early. Use the Kubernetes recommended labels or define your own standard. Enforce them with admission controllers. Without standard labels, NetworkPolicies become impossible to manage at scale.
A policy selecting zero pods is a SILENT failure. Kubernetes won't warn you that your NetworkPolicy matches nothing. It just... does nothing. Always test after applying.

📌 CS7–CS9: DNS, CIS Benchmarks & Gateway API

CS7
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS7
Egress DNS Blocked — Pods Can't Resolve External Names

🔍 Symptom: After applying a deny-all egress NetworkPolicy, anihpj-api can no longer reach the external payment API at api.payment-provider.com. nslookup api.payment-provider.com hangs and times out. All external connectivity is broken — even internal service names fail to resolve. The application logs show connection refused or name resolution failed for every external endpoint.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-7d8 -- nslookup api.payment-provider.com
  ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
  command terminated with exit code 1

  kubectl get networkpolicy -n anihpj
  NAME        POD-SELECTOR    AGE
  deny-egress <none>          10m   ← Blocks ALL egress!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Deny-all egress blocks DNS (UDP 53): The most common mistake. A deny-all egress policy blocks ALL outbound traffic, including DNS queries to CoreDNS (kube-dns). Pods can't resolve ANY names — internal or external. Always add an egress rule allowing UDP port 53 to CoreDNS.
  2. DNS rule allows TCP but not UDP: DNS primarily uses UDP port 53. An egress rule that only allows TCP 53 won't work for standard DNS resolution. CoreDNS uses UDP for most queries.
  3. DNS rule targets wrong namespace or pod selector: The DNS allow rule targets kube-system namespace but CoreDNS pods are labeled incorrectly. The egress rule doesn't match any CoreDNS pods.
  4. CoreDNS service IP not in allowed CIDR: The egress rule allows only specific IP blocks but CoreDNS's ClusterIP (e.g., 10.96.0.10) falls outside the allowed range. Use kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns to check the IP.
  5. NetworkPolicy also blocks CoreDNS from reaching upstream DNS: If CoreDNS itself has a NetworkPolicy blocking its egress, forwarded queries to upstream resolvers (8.8.8.8) fail. The pod's DNS query reaches CoreDNS, but CoreDNS can't forward it.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CoreDNS not running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns — if CoreDNS pods are down, no DNS resolution works regardless of NetworkPolicy.
  2. Pod's /etc/resolv.conf misconfigured: The pod's DNS config points to a wrong nameserver. kubectl exec anihpj-api -- cat /etc/resolv.conf should show CoreDNS service IP.
  3. Custom DNS policy in pod spec: Pod has dnsPolicy: None with custom nameservers that don't include CoreDNS. NetworkPolicy rules for CoreDNS are irrelevant because the pod doesn't use CoreDNS.
  4. CoreDNS cache poisoning or stale entries: CoreDNS returns stale NXDOMAIN for recently blocked domains. Flush CoreDNS cache: kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system.
  5. IPv6/IPv4 mismatch: Cluster uses IPv6 but the egress rule uses IPv4 CIDR blocks. CoreDNS IPv6 address not allowed in the policy.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default-deny applied without DNS allow rule: Security team applies cluster-wide deny-all egress first, DNS second. Between these two operations, all pods lose DNS.
  2. CoreDNS not yet deployed: Fresh cluster without CoreDNS installed. DNS doesn't work at all — not a NetworkPolicy issue.
  3. NetworkPolicy CNI not enforcing: New cluster uses Flannel which doesn't enforce NetworkPolicy. DNS works despite deny-all — masking the fact that ALL NetworkPolicies are silently ignored.
  4. kube-dns service IP changed from default:
    5. Custom --service-cluster-ip-range on kube-apiserver. The standard 10.96.0.10 CoreDNS IP is different.
  5. Node-local DNS cache not configured:
    6. NodeLocal DNSCache not set up. All DNS traffic goes through CoreDNS service IP, which is blocked by NetworkPolicy if not explicitly allowed.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec anihpj-api -- nslookup kubernetes.default If internal service names also fail, DNS itself is blocked. If only external names fail, it's an upstream DNS forwarding issue.
kubectl describe networkpolicy -n anihpj | grep -A10 egress Check every egress rule. DNS needs UDP port 53 to CoreDNS service IP or CoreDNS pod labels.
kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns Note the ClusterIP. The egress rule must allow traffic to this IP on UDP 53.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Deny-all egress NetworkPolicy blocks UDP port 53 to CoreDNS. Pods cannot resolve any domain names — internal or external. Every deny-all egress policy MUST include an explicit DNS allow rule as the FIRST egress rule.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add DNS egress rule kubectl apply -f allow-dns-egress.yaml Allow UDP 53 to CoreDNS: to: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}, podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}}] ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]
2. Verify DNS resolution kubectl exec anihpj-api -- nslookup api.payment-provider.com Should return IP addresses. Test both internal (kubernetes.default) and external domains.
3. Check CoreDNS pod health kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns All CoreDNS pods must be Running. If not, DNS won't work regardless of NetworkPolicy.
4. Allow CoreDNS egress to upstream resolvers If using external DNS forwarding, CoreDNS needs its own egress to 8.8.8.8:53 or your upstream DNS servers. Don't forget this.
5. DNS rule should be FIRST in every policy Make DNS the first egress allow rule. Without it, nothing works — pods can't even connect to other internal services by name.
💡 Personal Advice:
Every deny-all egress policy MUST start with DNS. This is the #1 NetworkPolicy mistake. DNS is the foundation of all service communication. Block it, and your cluster stops working. DNS allow rules should be the first thing in every egress policy.
Use a standard "allow-dns" NetworkPolicy in every namespace. Create a reusable NetworkPolicy that allows DNS egress and apply it to every namespace before any deny-all. This prevents accidental DNS blocks.
Test DNS after every NetworkPolicy change. kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup kubernetes.default If this fails, your latest NetworkPolicy broke DNS. Roll back immediately.
CS8
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS8
CIS Benchmark Failures — kubelet Anonymous Auth Enabled

🔍 Symptom: kube-bench reports multiple FAIL results against CIS benchmarks for the kubelet configuration. Specifically: anonymous authentication is enabled (--anonymous-auth=true), the kubelet's read-only port (10255) is open, and authorization mode is set to AlwaysAllow. An attacker with network access to the node can query the kubelet API without any credentials and enumerate running pods, retrieve logs, and execute commands.

  kube-bench run --targets node
  [FAIL] 2.1.1 Ensure anonymous-auth is set to false
  [FAIL] 2.1.2 Ensure --authorization-mode is not AlwaysAllow
  [FAIL] 2.1.3 Ensure read-only port is disabled (0)

  curl -k https://node-ip:10250/pods
  {
    "kind": "PodList",
    "items": [...]  ← Full pod listing WITHOUT authentication!
  }
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. kubelet installed with defaults: kubeadm init uses safe defaults for kubelet, but manual kubelet installation often leaves --anonymous-auth=true (the upstream default). Check: ps aux | grep kubelet | grep anonymous-auth.
  2. Read-only port 10255 still enabled: The kubelet's read-only port provides unauthenticated access to pod info and metrics. It should be disabled with --read-only-port=0. curl node-ip:10255/pods — if it returns data, the port is open.
  3. Authorization mode is AlwaysAllow: --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow means ANY request to the kubelet is authorized. This should be Webhook to enforce RBAC via the API server's SubjectAccessReview.
  4. kubelet config file not used:
    5. Kubelet flags on the command line override the config file. Even if /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml has anonymous: false, a command-line --anonymous-auth=true takes precedence. Check both.
  5. kubeadm upgrade didn't update kubelet config:
    6. After a kubeadm upgrade, the kubelet config file is updated but kubelet wasn't restarted. Old kubelet runs with old insecure flags.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. kubelet serving certificate not rotated:
    2. The kubelet's serving cert has expired. kubeadm auto-rotates these, but manual clusters need manual rotation. Expired certs cause authorization failures.
  2. Webhook authorization misconfigured:
    3. --authorization-webhook-cache-authorized-ttl and --authorization-webhook-cache-unauthorized-ttl too long. Recently revoked permissions still cached.
  3. kubelet API exposed via NodePort accidentally:
    4. A Service with externalIP maps to kubelet port 10250. The kubelet API is now accessible from outside the cluster.
  4. Cloud metadata endpoint accessible from kubelet:
    5. kubelet's cloud provider configuration exposes cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) to pods. Combined with anonymous auth, metadata can be queried.
  5. CIS benchmark version mismatch:
    6. Running kube-bench for K8s 1.28 against a 1.32 cluster. Some checks have different IDs or remediation steps have changed.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kube-bench never run before: Fresh cluster, first security scan. Multiple CIS failures expected. Prioritize: anonymous-auth → authorization-mode → read-only-port → TLS certs.
  2. kubelet flags in /var/lib/kubelet/kubeadm-flags.env:
    3. kubeadm stores kubelet flags in this file. New cluster may have permissive defaults before hardening.
  3. KubeletConfiguration not applied:
    4. The KubeletConfiguration CRD is available but no instance exists. Kubelet uses compiled-in defaults (insecure).
  4. NodeRestriction admission plugin not enabled:
    5. Without NodeRestriction, kubelets can modify labels on ANY node, not just their own. Check kube-apiserver --enable-admission-plugins.
  5. No NetworkPolicy between nodes and control plane:
    6. New cluster allows all node-to-node traffic. Until kubelet is hardened, limit access to kubelet port 10250 via NetworkPolicy or firewall.
🔍 What to Look At:
kube-bench run --targets node --check 2.1.1,2.1.2,2.1.3 Run targeted CIS checks for kubelet authentication. Focus on the FAIL items first.
ps aux | grep kubelet | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E 'anonymous|authorization|read-only' Check actual kubelet process flags. These override the config file.
cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep -E 'anonymous|authorization|readOnly' Check the kubelet config file. Both flags and config must be hardened.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: kubelet running with upstream defaults: --anonymous-auth=true, --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow, and the read-only port (10255) still enabled. This allows unauthenticated access to pod information, logs, and metrics from anyone who can reach the node's IP.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Disable anonymous authentication sed -i 's/anonymous-auth=true/anonymous-auth=false/' /var/lib/kubelet/kubeadm-flags.env Set authentication.anonymous.enabled: false in kubelet config. Restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet.
2. Set authorization mode to Webhook --authorization-mode=Webhook This delegates authorization decisions to the API server. RBAC rules apply to kubelet API access. Restart kubelet after change.
3. Disable read-only port --read-only-port=0 Set readOnlyPort: 0 in kubelet config. The read-only port has NO authentication and should always be disabled in production.
4. Re-run kube-bench kube-bench run --targets node --check 2.1 Verify all 2.1 checks pass. Remediate any remaining FAIL items.
5. Apply consistently across all nodes ansible-playbook -i inventory hardening-kubelet.yml Use Ansible or a DaemonSet to apply kubelet hardening across ALL nodes. Manual per-node fixes drift over time.
💡 Personal Advice:
CIS benchmarks are your minimum security baseline. The CKS exam expects you to know how to run kube-bench and fix common failures. Focus on section 2 (etcd), 1 (master), and 2 (worker). Section 2.1 (kubelet) is the most commonly tested.
kubelet hardening is critical — it runs on every node. With anonymous auth enabled, a compromised pod with hostNetwork can access ANY node's kubelet API. This is how attackers enumerate your entire cluster.
Automate kube-bench scans. kubectl apply -f kube-bench-job.yaml Run kube-bench as a weekly CronJob and pipe results to your SIEM. Configurations drift — regular scanning catches regressions.
CS9
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS9
Gateway API HTTPRoute Not Routing — BackendRef Not Found

🔍 Symptom: An HTTPRoute is configured to route 10% of traffic to anihpj-api-v2 (canary deployment), but all traffic still goes to v1. kubectl describe httproute anihpj-canary -n anihpj shows BackendRefNotFound — the referenced backend Service doesn't exist or is in a different namespace. Traffic silently falls through to the default backend.

  kubectl describe httproute anihpj-canary -n anihpj
  Status:
    Parents: gateway/anihpj-gateway
    Conditions: ResolvedRefs: False (BackendRefNotFound)

  kubectl get svc -n anihpj | grep v2
  <none>  ← Service "anihpj-api-v2" does NOT exist!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Backend Service doesn't exist: HTTPRoute references backendRefs: [{name: anihpj-api-v2, port: 8000}] but kubectl get svc anihpj-api-v2 returns "not found." The Service was never created or was deleted.
  2. Backend Service in wrong namespace: HTTPRoute can ONLY reference Services in the SAME namespace by default. Cross-namespace routing requires a ReferenceGrant.
  3. Gateway not programmed: The Gateway resource shows Programmed: False. The Gateway controller hasn't provisioned the infrastructure. No traffic routes at all.
  4. HTTPRoute not accepted by Gateway: The Gateway's allowedRoutes.namespaces policy restricts which namespaces can attach routes. The HTTPRoute's namespace is not in the allowed list.
  5. Listener TLS mismatch: HTTPRoute attached to an HTTPS listener but the route doesn't specify TLS. The Gateway can't match the route to the listener.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ReferenceGrant not created for cross-namespace: HTTPRoute references a Service in another namespace, but no ReferenceGrant exists. Gateways require explicit cross-namespace grants for security.
  2. Gateway controller not installed: The Gateway API CRDs are installed but no controller (e.g., nginx-gateway, istio, envoy-gateway) is running. Resources are accepted but never processed.
  3. Port mismatch: HTTPRoute references port 8000 but the Service listens on port 80. The port must match the Service's targetPort.
  4. Weight sum invalid: Canary route weights don't sum to 100 (e.g., forwardTo v1:90 + v2:5 = 95). The Gateway controller handles the discrepancy unpredictably.
  5. Multiple Gateways with same listener:
    6. Two Gateways listen on the same host:port. The HTTPRoute attaches to the wrong one. Use spec.parentRefs to specify the exact Gateway.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Gateway API CRDs not installed:
    2. kubectl get crd | grep gateway.networking.k8s.io — if empty, Gateway API resources won't work.
  2. GatewayClass not created:
    3. The GatewayClass is the cluster-scoped template for Gateways. Without it, no Gateway can be provisioned.
  3. Gateway controller deployed but no GatewayClass parameters:
    4. Controller running but GatewayClass references non-existent parameters. Gateways stay in Pending state.
  4. Experimental channel CRDs conflict with stable:
    5. Both v1beta1 and v1 CRDs installed. Controllers may only support one version.
  5. No IngressClass to GatewayClass migration:
    6. Team migrating from Ingress to Gateway API but keeping both. Routing conflicts between Ingress and Gateway controllers.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe httproute -n anihpj | grep -A10 Status The Status section tells you exactly why the route isn't working. ResolvedRefs, Accepted, or Programmed conditions.
kubectl get gateway -A Check that the Gateway is Programmed and has listeners. An unprogrammed Gateway routes nothing.
kubectl get svc -n anihpj | grep api Verify all backend Services exist and their ports match the HTTPRoute's backendRefs.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Backend Service referenced in the HTTPRoute's backendRefs doesn't exist or is in a different namespace without a ReferenceGrant. The Gateway controller can't resolve the backend and the route silently fails.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create missing Service kubectl expose deployment anihpj-api-v2 -n anihpj --port=8000 If the Service doesn't exist, the HTTPRoute has nothing to route to. Deploy the backend first.
2. Verify port mapping kubectl get svc anihpj-api-v2 -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 ports Ensure the Service port matches the HTTPRoute's backendRef port exactly.
3. Create ReferenceGrant for cross-namespace routing kubectl apply -f reference-grant.yaml Required when the HTTPRoute and backend Service are in different namespaces. This is a deliberate security boundary.
4. Check Gateway allowedRoutes kubectl describe gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj | grep -A10 Allowed If the HTTPRoute's namespace isn't in the allowed list, the Gateway rejects the route.
5. Verify with curl after fix curl -H "Host: anihpj.jobpost.com" http://gateway-ip/canary Should route traffic according to the HTTPRoute rules. Check canary weight distribution.
💡 Personal Advice:
Gateway API is the future of K8s ingress — learn it now. The CKS exam may include Gateway API concepts. It replaces Ingress with a more expressive, role-oriented model. The ReferenceGrant is a deliberate security improvement over Ingress.
Always check the Status conditions. Gateway API resources report detailed status. ResolvedRefs: False is a clear signal. Don't guess — the Status tells you exactly what's wrong.
CS10
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS10
Wildcard Ingress TLS — Subdomain Certificate Issues

🔍 Symptom: A wildcard TLS certificate (*.jobpost.com) is installed for api.jobpost.com and works correctly, but db.jobpost.com and admin.internal.jobpost.com fail with certificate errors. The wildcard *.jobpost.com only matches ONE level of subdomain — it covers api.jobpost.com but NOT db.admin.jobpost.com (two levels deep). cert-manager Certificate resources for deeper subdomains remain Pending.

  openssl s_client -connect db.jobpost.com:443 -servername db.jobpost.com
  SSL certificate verify failed
  Certificate: *.jobpost.com
  SAN: DNS:*.jobpost.com, DNS:jobpost.com

  curl -v https://admin.internal.jobpost.com
  SSL: certificate subject name '*.jobpost.com' does not
  match target host name 'admin.internal.jobpost.com'
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wildcard only covers one subdomain level: *.jobpost.com matches api.jobpost.com but NOT api.internal.jobpost.com. RFC 2818: wildcards only match ONE label. For multi-level subdomains, use individual certs or SAN entries.
  2. Certificate SAN doesn't include bare domain: *.jobpost.com doesn't match jobpost.com (bare domain). Add both *.jobpost.com and jobpost.com as SANs.
  3. Let's Encrypt rate limit on wildcard certs: Let's Encrypt only issues wildcards via DNS-01 challenge. HTTP-01 validation CANNOT issue wildcard certs. cert-manager Certificate request stuck because the wrong solver is configured.
  4. Separate Ingress resources using the same wildcard Secret: Multiple Ingresses in different namespaces all reference the same wildcard TLS Secret. If the Secret is in namespace-A, Ingresses in namespace-B can't access it.
  5. cert-manager generating individual certs instead of wildcard: Certificate resource specifies anihpj-api.jobpost.com instead of *.anihpj.jobpost.com. Individual certs only cover the exact hostname.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. International domain name (IDN) wildcard issues: Wildcard certs for IDN domains require punycode encoding. *.münchen.de needs special handling.
  2. TLS client SNI not sent: Client doesn't send SNI, server returns default certificate (which may be the wrong one for the requested host).
  3. CAA record blocking wildcard issuance: DNS Certification Authority Authorization record restricts which CAs can issue wildcards. The CA refuses to issue.
  4. Browser HSTS pinning: Browser previously pinned a specific certificate for the domain. The new wildcard cert is valid but the browser rejects it due to HPKP/HSTS pinning.
  5. OCSP stapling failure: The certificate is valid but the OCSP responder is unreachable. Some clients fail closed and reject the cert.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Wildcard cert issued via HTTP-01 (should be DNS-01): cert-manager default solver is HTTP-01 which can't issue wildcards. Switch to DNS-01: configure solvers: [{dns01: {...}}].
  2. DNS provider credentials not configured:
    3. DNS-01 requires API access to your DNS provider (Route53, Cloudflare). First-time setup: create IAM policy, store credentials in Secret, reference in ClusterIssuer.
  3. Wildcard domain not owned:
    4. New organization, wildcard cert requested for *.example.com but the ACME account doesn't control the domain. DNS-01 validation will fail.
  4. Shared wildcard cert across teams causing confusion:
    5. Platform team issues *.cluster.local, app teams expect *.anihpj.cluster.local to work. It doesn't — one level deep only.
  5. cert-manager not configured for DNS-01:
    6. New cert-manager installation with default HTTP-01 solver. Wildcard certificate requests silently fail because the wrong solver is used.
🔍 What to Look At:
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host | openssl x509 -text -noout | grep DNS Check the actual SANs on the certificate. *.domain.com only matches one level.
kubectl get certificate -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 dnsNames Verify the Certificate resource requests the correct DNS names (wildcard or individual).
kubectl describe clusterissuer letsencrypt-prod | grep -A5 Solvers Check which solver (HTTP-01 or DNS-01) is configured. Wildcards require DNS-01.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: DNS wildcard (*.domain.com) only matches exactly ONE subdomain level per RFC 2818. Multi-level subdomains like api.internal.domain.com require individual certificates or SAN entries covering each level explicitly.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Use individual certs for multi-level subdomains For admin.internal.jobpost.com, create a separate Certificate resource with that exact DNS name. Wildcards can't cover it.
2. Configure DNS-01 solver for wildcard certs kubectl patch clusterissuer letsencrypt-prod --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"solvers":[{"dns01":{"route53":{"region":"us-east-1"}}}]}}' Wildcard certs can ONLY be issued via DNS-01 challenge, not HTTP-01.
3. Add bare domain to SANs When requesting *.jobpost.com, also include jobpost.com in the dnsNames list. The wildcard doesn't cover the bare domain.
4. Use separate wildcard certs per subdomain level *.jobpost.com for single-level, *.internal.jobpost.com for internal. Two wildcard certs instead of hoping one covers everything.
5. Copy TLS Secret across namespaces if needed kubectl get secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj -o yaml | sed 's/namespace: anihpj/namespace: anihpj-db/' | kubectl apply -f - Ingress can only reference Secrets in its own namespace. Copy the wildcard Secret as needed.
💡 Personal Advice:
Wildcard certs are a convenience, not a security feature. If a wildcard cert's private key is compromised, ALL subdomains are exposed. Use individual certs when possible — cert-manager makes this easy with automatic issuance.
DNS-01 is required for wildcards. Plan for it. DNS-01 requires API credentials to your DNS provider. Set this up early — switching from HTTP-01 to DNS-01 later means reissuing all certificates.

📌 CS11–CS15: Advanced Security — Metadata, Binary Integrity, etcd, Profiling & DNS

CS11
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS11
Node Metadata Endpoint Exposed — Cloud IAM Credential Theft

🔍 Symptom: A pod can curl the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) and retrieve IAM credentials. kubectl exec anihpj-api -- curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ returns AWS IAM role credentials. An attacker who compromises ANY pod can steal the node's IAM role and access cloud resources (S3 buckets, RDS databases, SQS queues) with the node's permissions.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -- curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
  ami-id  hostname  iam/  instance-id  public-ipv4  ...

  kubectl exec anihpj-api -- curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/node-role
  {"AccessKeyId":"AKIA...","SecretAccessKey":"...","Token":"..."}
  ← FULL IAM CREDENTIALS STOLEN!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. IMDSv2 not enforced (IMDSv1 still allowed): AWS Instance Metadata Service v1 requires no token — any process can query. IMDSv2 requires a session token. Set http-put-response-hop-limit=1 and http-tokens=required in instance metadata options.
  2. Node IAM role has excessive permissions: The node's IAM role grants broad access (S3:*, RDS:*). A compromised pod inherits all these permissions. Use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) to give pods their OWN limited roles.
  3. No NetworkPolicy blocking metadata endpoint: Pods have unrestricted egress. A NetworkPolicy should block traffic to 169.254.169.254/32 for pods that don't need cloud API access.
  4. iptables rule to block metadata not applied:
    5. EKS and some cloud providers recommend iptables rules that block pod traffic to the metadata endpoint except for specific processes (like kubelet).
  5. hostNetwork pods bypass pod-level controls: Pods with hostNetwork: true bypass NetworkPolicies and can directly access the metadata endpoint via the node's network.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. GCP/Azure equivalent endpoints also exposed: GCP: metadata.google.internal, Azure: 169.254.169.254. Same attack, different clouds. All cloud metadata services are sensitive.
  2. Metadata proxy not deployed: Some cloud providers offer a metadata proxy (e.g., kube2iam, kiam) that filters access. If not deployed, direct metadata access is unfiltered.
  3. Hop limit set too high:
    4. IMDSv2 hop limit controls how many network hops the token can traverse. Default is 1 (same node). Setting it to 2+ allows token passing between nodes.
  4. Container runtime leaking metadata:
    5. containerd or CRI-O may proxy metadata requests. Even if the pod is blocked, the runtime itself may still serve metadata requests.
  5. DNS rebinding attack via metadata IP:
    6. An external attacker uses DNS rebinding to make the pod's DNS resolution point to 169.254.169.254, bypassing IP-based blocks.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. IMDSv2 not enabled at launch: New EC2 instances with defaults. IMDSv1 is the default. Must be explicitly configured at launch or via instance metadata options.
  2. IRSA not yet configured: Cluster uses node IAM roles because IRSA (pod identity) hasn't been set up yet. All pods share the node's IAM permissions.
  3. Default NetworkPolicy allows all egress:
    4. No NetworkPolicies applied yet. Metadata endpoint is reachable by default.
  4. EKS cluster with default node group:
    5. Default EKS node group has broad IAM permissions for cluster operations. These permissions are inherited by all pods.
  5. No kube2iam or metadata proxy installed:
    6. Fresh cluster, no metadata filtering. Direct access to cloud credentials from any pod.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec anihpj-api -- curl -s --connect-timeout 2 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ If this returns data, the metadata endpoint is accessible from pods. This is a critical security gap.
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-id i-xxx --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].MetadataOptions' Check IMDSv2 configuration. HttpTokens: required means IMDSv2 is enforced.
kubectl get networkpolicy -A | grep 169.254 Check if any NetworkPolicy blocks the metadata IP. If none exist, all pods can reach it.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: IMDSv1 still enabled on cloud nodes, allowing any process to curl 169.254.169.254 and retrieve IAM credentials without authentication. Combined with overly permissive node IAM roles, a single compromised pod can access all cloud resources the node can access.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enforce IMDSv2 on all nodes aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id i-xxx --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1 This blocks IMDSv1 requests. Pods must use a PUT request with a token to access metadata.
2. Use IRSA for pod-level IAM Annotate ServiceAccounts with IAM roles. Pods get their own limited credentials instead of inheriting the node's broad IAM role.
3. Block metadata endpoint via NetworkPolicy kubectl apply -f block-metadata-netpol.yaml Egress rule blocking 169.254.169.254/32 for all pods that don't explicitly need cloud API access.
4. Apply iptables rules on nodes Add iptables rules that DROP traffic to 169.254.169.254 from pod CIDRs, except for specific privileged containers (kubelet, CNI).
5. Minimize node IAM roles Node IAM role should have MINIMAL permissions — only what kubelet and CSI drivers need. No S3, no RDS, no SQS. Pods use IRSA for those.
💡 Personal Advice:
Metadata endpoint access = cloud credential theft. This is the #1 cloud-specific attack vector in Kubernetes. A compromised pod + accessible metadata endpoint + broad node IAM role = full cloud account compromise. The CKS exam may test your knowledge of cloud metadata protection.
Defense in depth: IMDSv2 + IRSA + NetworkPolicy + iptables. No single control is enough. Combine all four: IMDSv2 (instance level), IRSA (pod identity), NetworkPolicy (cluster level), iptables (node level).
CS12
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS12
Platform Binary Verification Failure — Tampered kubelet Binary

🔍 Symptom: sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet doesn't match the official Kubernetes release hash. The kubelet binary has been replaced with a backdoored version. The cluster appears to function normally — pods start, services work — but the compromised kubelet exfiltrates Secret data, injects sidecar containers, and reports false node status to the API server.

  sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet
  a1b2c3d4e5f6...  /usr/bin/kubelet

  curl -sL https://dl.k8s.io/v1.32.13/bin/linux/amd64/kubelet.sha256
  x1y2z3w4v5u6...  kubelet  ← OFFICIAL hash — MISMATCH!

  ❌ Binary has been TAMPERED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Node compromise via unpatched vulnerability: Attacker exploited a kernel or container runtime vulnerability to gain root on the node, then replaced kubelet binary to maintain persistence and intercept Secrets.
  2. Supply chain attack on installation source: kubelet was installed from an unofficial mirror or a compromised package repository. The binary was backdoored before it reached the node.
  3. Insider threat with node access: A team member with SSH access replaced the binary manually. Binary verification would have detected this immediately if it was checked regularly.
  4. CI/CD pipeline for node provisioning compromised: The Ansible/Puppet/Chef script that installs kubelet was modified to download from a malicious URL. All newly provisioned nodes get the backdoored binary.
  5. kubelet auto-update mechanism exploited: A custom auto-update script or systemd timer that updates kubelet was hijacked to pull from an attacker-controlled server.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Filesystem mounted with noexec, attacker used LD_PRELOAD:
    2. Binary itself isn't modified, but LD_PRELOAD injects malicious library that intercepts kubelet syscalls. Hash check passes but behavior is altered.
  2. Container breakout modified host binary:
    3. Privileged container with hostPath mount to /usr/bin modified kubelet from within the container. readOnlyRootFilesystem: false on a privileged pod = game over.
  3. kubelet running from a container (kubeadm in Docker):
    4. The kubelet binary on the host is fine, but the actual running kubelet is in a container that was replaced with a malicious image.
  4. Memory-only modification:
    5. Binary on disk hashes correctly, but the running kubelet process in memory was patched via ptrace or /proc/PID/mem. Disk hash verification passes.
  5. Signed binary with compromised signing key:
    6. The binary's signature is valid because the attacker stole the Kubernetes signing key. Hash matches "official" because the attacker published fake hashes.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Nodes provisioned from unverified AMI/golden image:
    2. The base image used for node provisioning contains a backdoored kubelet. All nodes from this image are compromised.
  2. No file integrity monitoring configured:
    3. New cluster, no AIDE, Tripwire, or Falco rules watching /usr/bin. Binary modification goes undetected.
  3. SSH keys shared across team without audit:
    4. Multiple people have SSH access to nodes. No audit trail for who executed which commands. Binary replacement is untraceable.
  4. kubelet downloaded via curl | bash in provisioning script:
    5. Common in quick-start guides. No hash verification step in the script.
  5. No periodic integrity scans configured:
    6. Fresh cluster, no CronJob that verifies binary hashes against official releases daily. Tampering could go unnoticed for months.
🔍 What to Look At:
sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet && curl -sL https://dl.k8s.io/v1.32.13/bin/linux/amd64/kubelet.sha256 Compare the local hash with the official Kubernetes release hash. Any mismatch = tampering.
which kubelet && ls -la /usr/bin/kubelet Check modification time. If the file was recently modified but no planned upgrade occurred, investigate.
kubectl get nodes -o wide Check if any nodes show unexpected behavior — false Ready status, missing labels, or unknown taints from the compromised kubelet.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Compromised node with root access. The attacker replaced /usr/bin/kubelet with a backdoored version that intercepts Secrets, injects malicious containers, and reports false status. Without file integrity monitoring and regular hash verification, this goes undetected.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Isolate the compromised node immediately kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --delete-emptydir --ignore-daemonsets Prevent new pods from scheduling. Evacuate existing pods to clean nodes. The node is untrusted.
2. Replace kubelet with verified binary Download from official dl.k8s.io, verify hash, replace binary, restart kubelet. Or terminate the instance and launch a fresh one from a trusted AMI.
3. Audit all Secrets accessed during compromise window kubectl get secrets -A -o yaml Rotate ALL Secrets that the compromised kubelet could have accessed. The attacker may have exfiltrated them.
4. Implement file integrity monitoring kubectl apply -f falco-fim-rules.yaml Set up Falco rules or AIDE to monitor /usr/bin/kubelet, /usr/bin/kubeadm, and /etc/kubernetes/. Alert on ANY modification.
5. Run periodic integrity checks Create a DaemonSet or CronJob that verifies hashes of all Kubernetes binaries against official releases daily.
💡 Personal Advice:
Binary verification is a CKS exam topic. The exam may ask you to verify the hash of kubelet, kubeadm, or kubectl against published hashes. Know: sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet and where to find official hashes (dl.k8s.io).
File integrity monitoring is not optional in production. Any modification to Kubernetes binaries is a security incident. Set up FIM before you go to production — retroactive detection means you've already been compromised for an unknown period.
CS13
🔐 CATEGORY 1: CLUSTER SETUP — Issue CS13
etcd Certificate Expired — Control Plane Unavailable

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get nodes returns Unable to connect to the server: net/http: TLS handshake timeout. kubeadm certs check-expiration shows etcd peer and server certificates EXPIRED. The API server cannot communicate with etcd — the entire control plane is down. RAFT consensus is broken because etcd nodes can't establish TLS connections to each other.

  kubeadm certs check-expiration
  CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME
  etcd-peer                  Jan 01, 2025 00:00 UTC  EXPIRED!
  etcd-server                Jan 01, 2025 00:00 UTC  EXPIRED!
  etcd-healthcheck-client    Jan 01, 2025 00:00 UTC  EXPIRED!

  kubectl get nodes
  Unable to connect to the server: net/http: TLS handshake timeout
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. etcd certificates not renewed before expiry: kubeadm certificates (including etcd) have a 1-year expiry. If not renewed with kubeadm certs renew, the cluster becomes inoperable after expiry.
  2. kubeadm upgrade didn't renew certificates: kubeadm upgrade apply upgrades the cluster but may not renew certificates that are close to expiry. Manual renewal required: kubeadm certs renew all.
  3. System clock skew between etcd nodes: NTP not configured or clock drifted significantly. TLS certificates appear expired or not-yet-valid due to time mismatch between etcd peers.
  4. Certificate renewal command ran but kubelet didn't pick up new certs:
    5. kubeadm certs renew regenerated certs but etcd/kube-apiserver weren't restarted. Old expired certs still loaded in memory.
  5. etcd cluster not using TLS (insecure):
    6. etcd was configured without TLS initially. Certificates were added later but the etcd configuration still references HTTP endpoints. TLS setup incomplete.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Incorrect CA used for certificate renewal:
    2. The CA certificate changed (cluster rebuilt, new CA generated). New certs signed by new CA aren't trusted by old peers still using old CA.
  2. etcd quorum lost during certificate rotation:
    3. Certificates were rotated one node at a time, but during rotation etcd lost quorum. The cluster can't recover without manual intervention.
  3. Disk full on etcd node:
    4. Certificates exist but etcd can't write to its data directory. RAFT consensus breaks, TLS errors appear as secondary symptom.
  4. Firewall rule changed blocking etcd peer port (2380):
    5. A firewall update blocked inter-etcd communication. TLS handshake timeout is the symptom, but the root cause is network, not certificates.
  5. etcd data corruption:
    6. WAL or snapshot corruption causes etcd to fail during startup. TLS errors appear because etcd never reaches the point of serving requests.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Cluster created 1+ year ago, certificates never rotated:
    2. First anniversary of cluster creation. All 1-year certs expire simultaneously. This is the most predictable outage in Kubernetes.
  2. kubeadm init with default 1-year expiry:
    3. New cluster, no custom certificate duration set. Certificates will expire in exactly 1 year.
  3. No certificate monitoring configured:
    4. Fresh cluster, no Prometheus alerts on cert_exporter metrics. Certificate expiry will be discovered when the cluster goes down.
  4. Backup etcd not configured:
    5. If etcd data is corrupted during the certificate expiry event, there's no snapshot to restore from.
  5. Manual kubeadm cluster without renewal automation:
    6. kubeadm doesn't auto-renew certificates. New users unaware of this, cluster goes down 365 days later.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubeadm certs check-expiration The first command to run. Shows ALL certificate expiry dates. Focus on etcd certs — they're the ones that break the control plane.
journalctl -u etcd -n 50 etcd logs will show TLS errors like "remote error: tls: bad certificate" or "certificate has expired."
crictl ps | grep etcd && crictl logs <etcd-container-id> If kubeadm-managed, etcd runs as a static pod. Use crictl (not docker) to inspect it.
