  4. Signature stored in wrong registry: Cosign signs the image and stores the signature in the SAME registry. If the registry is changed (migration, replication), signatures are left behind — images appear unsigned in the new registry.
  5. Private key expired or rotated without re-signing: The Cosign private key was rotated but all existing images were not re-signed. Admission controller with the new public key rejects all existing images as "unsigned."
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Cosign/Kyverno not in initial cluster setup: Image signing infrastructure is not part of the default toolchain. It's a manual addition that's never prioritized.
  2. No supply chain security policy: No organizational requirement for signed images. The security baseline doesn't include image integrity verification.
  3. Registry allows push without signature: Harbor/ECR/GCR doesn't enforce that images must be signed before push — or that signatures must be present before pull. The registry is a dumb blob store with no policy enforcement.
  4. No SBOM to correlate with signatures: Signatures prove WHO built the image. SBOMs prove WHAT is inside. Without both, you have identity but no物料清单 (bill of materials).
  5. Developers unaware of Sigstore/Cosign: Image signing tools are not part of developer onboarding or security training. The concept is foreign to the team.
🔍 What to Look At:
cosign verify --key cosign.pub anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 If this returns "no signatures found," the image is unsigned. Every production image should have at least one valid signature.
kubectl get clusterpolicy -A -o yaml | grep -i "cosign\|verifyImages" Check if Kyverno has a policy verifying image signatures. Absence means unsigned images are admitted without question.
kubectl get deployment -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[].spec.template.spec.containers[].image' List all images running in production. Every one should be verifiable with cosign verify against your trusted public key.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The CI pipeline does not sign images with Cosign before pushing to the registry. No admission controller verifies signatures at deploy time. Images are trusted solely by their name:tag — an attacker with registry push access can replace any image and the cluster will run it blindly.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Sign images in CI pipeline with Cosign cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj/jobpost-api:${TAG} Add signing as the last step in your CI pipeline after build and push. The signature is stored in the same registry alongside the image.
2. Deploy Kyverno policy to verify signatures at admission ClusterPolicy with verifyImages rule: check Cosign signatures for all images in anihpj/* repos. Reject pods with unsigned images or images signed with unknown keys.
3. Use keyless signing with OIDC (Fulcio) Instead of managing long-lived keys, use cosign sign --fulcio-url=https://fulcio.sigstore.dev --rekor-url=https://rekor.sigstore.dev <image>. The OIDC token from CI proves identity — no private key to store or rotate.
4. Enforce signing at the registry level Harbor: enable "cosign signature" policy — reject unsigned images. AWS ECR: use ECR Basic scanning + IAM policy requiring signatures. Registry is the enforcement point before images are pullable.
5. Block manual pushes — only CI can push Registry IAM: only the CI ServiceAccount has push access. Developers have pull-only access. This ensures all images go through the CI pipeline where signing happens.
💡 Personal Advice:
Unsigned images are supply chain blind spots. Without signatures, you can't distinguish between "the CI pipeline built this" and "an attacker pushed this." Image signing is NOT optional in a security-conscious organization — it's the foundation of supply chain integrity. Start with Cosign keyless signing — it takes 5 minutes to set up in CI.
Admission-time verification is your last line of defense. Even if an attacker compromises the registry and pushes a malicious image, a Kyverno policy verifying Cosign signatures will REJECT the pod at admission. The attack fails before the container starts. This is why admission control matters.
SC2
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC2
SBOM Not Generated — Zero Visibility Into Image Contents

🔍 Symptom: syft anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 shows 347 packages including log4j-2.14.1, openssl-1.1.1n, and curl-7.74.0 — but there's no SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) stored with the image. When CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) was disclosed, the team spent 4 days manually checking every running container to determine which ones had Log4j. Without an SBOM, vulnerability response is SLOW — you don't know what's in your images without scanning each one individually. An SBOM answers "do we have this vulnerable package?" in seconds.

  syft anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 -o spdx-json | wc -l
  # No SBOM attached to image — must scan from scratch every time

  cosign verify-attestation --type spdxjson anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2
  Error: no attestations found   ← NO SBOM ATTESTATION!

  grype db search log4j | head -5
  # Manually searching for Log4j across all images — hours of work
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No SBOM generation in CI pipeline: The pipeline builds and pushes images but never runs syft, trivy, or bom to generate an SBOM. The image goes to the registry with zero transparency about its contents.
  2. SBOM generated but not attached to image: The pipeline generates an SBOM (.spdx.json file) but stores it as a CI artifact — NOT attached to the image via Cosign attestation. The SBOM exists but is disconnected from the image it describes.
  3. No SBOM registry or storage: Even if SBOMs are generated, there's no central registry to store and query them. Each team stores SBOMs in different places (S3, CI artifacts, local disks) — no organization-wide visibility.
  4. SBOM not in standard format (SPDX/CycloneDX): The "SBOM" is a text file listing pip freeze output — not a machine-readable SPDX or CycloneDX document. Vulnerability scanners can't parse it, and it doesn't include transitive dependencies.
  5. Vulnerability scanners not integrated with SBOM: Tools like Grype, Trivy, and Dependency-Track can consume SBOMs for vulnerability matching. Without SBOMs, each scan starts from zero — analyzing the image layer by layer every time.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. SBOM outdated — doesn't match running image: The SBOM was generated for :v1.1 but the running image is :v1.2. The SBOM doesn't reflect the actual packages in production — false negatives during vulnerability response.
  2. SBOM only covers application dependencies, not OS packages: The SBOM lists pip packages but not apt/deb packages. The OS-level Log4j library (installed via apt-get) is missing from the SBOM — invisible to vulnerability scanners.
  3. SBOM too large to query efficiently: A full Debian image SBOM has 10,000+ entries. Without a proper SBOM database (Dependency-Track, Anchore), querying for a specific package is slow and manual.
  4. No policy requiring SBOM for production deployment: The security team wants SBOMs but there's no enforcement. Images without SBOMs are deployed to production without blocking.
  5. SBOM generated but not signed: An unsigned SBOM could have been generated by anyone — it's not cryptographically bound to the image. Attackers can swap the SBOM to hide malicious packages.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. SBOM not part of initial toolchain: syft/grype/trivy not installed in CI. SBOM generation is not in the pipeline template — every team must add it manually.
  2. No vulnerability management platform (Dependency-Track): No centralized system to ingest SBOMs, match against CVE databases, and alert on vulnerable packages. SBOMs are generated but never used.
  3. SBOM not required by compliance framework: The organization doesn't require SBOMs for compliance (no Executive Order 14028 mandate, no customer requirement). SBOMs are "nice to have" — never prioritized.
  4. Developers unaware of SBOM concept: The term "SBOM" is unfamiliar to the development team. They associate it with "security bureaucracy" rather than a practical tool for fast vulnerability response.
  5. No SBOM attestation with Cosign in pipeline docs: The CI/CD documentation covers build, test, push — but doesn't mention generating and attaching an SBOM. It's invisible in the workflow.
🔍 What to Look At:
cosign verify-attestation --type spdxjson anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 If no attestations are found, the image has no SBOM. Every production image should have an SPDX or CycloneDX SBOM attestation.
syft anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 -o spdx-json | grype Generate SBOM on-the-fly and scan for vulnerabilities. Compare with the attached SBOM (if any) to see if they match.
kubectl get deployment -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[].spec.template.spec.containers[].image' | while read img; do cosign verify-attestation --type spdxjson "$img" 2>&1; done Check SBOM attestations for all running images. Each "no attestations found" is a visibility gap in your supply chain.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No SBOM is generated during the CI build or attached to the image via Cosign attestation. When a critical CVE is disclosed, the team has no way to answer "which of our running containers has this vulnerable package?" without manually scanning every image — delaying response by hours or days.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Generate SBOM in CI pipeline syft anihpj/jobpost-api:${TAG} -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json Run syft after the image build. SBOM includes all OS packages, language dependencies, and transitive dependencies in SPDX format.
2. Attach SBOM as Cosign attestation to the image cosign attest --type spdxjson --predicate sbom.spdx.json anihpj/jobpost-api:${TAG} The SBOM is cryptographically bound to the image and stored in the registry. Anyone with the public key can verify it.
3. Deploy Dependency-Track for SBOM management Dependency-Track ingests SBOMs, matches packages against NVD/GitHub Advisory Database, and provides a dashboard of vulnerabilities per application. It answers "which apps have Log4j?" in seconds.
4. Scan SBOM for vulnerabilities at build time grype sbom:sbom.spdx.json --fail-on critical Fail the CI build if the SBOM contains packages with CRITICAL CVEs. The vulnerability check happens at build time — before the image reaches the registry.
5. Require SBOM attestation for production admission Kyverno policy: verify that the image has a valid SBOM attestation (Cosign) before admitting the pod. Reject images without SBOMs — no SBOM, no production deployment.
💡 Personal Advice:
SBOMs turn "days of panic" into "seconds of clarity." When the next Log4Shell hits, you don't want to be the team scanning images manually at 3 AM. SBOMs give you INSTANT visibility: search for log4j across all applications in seconds. Generate SBOMs. Store them. Query them. This is not optional in 2026.
An SBOM without attestation is just a file. Attestation binds it to the image cryptographically. Cosign attestation signs the SBOM and links it to the image digest. You can verify: "this SBOM describes THIS exact image, and it was generated by the CI pipeline." Without attestation, the SBOM could be swapped by an attacker.
SC3
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC3
CI/CD Pipeline Uses Cluster-Admin ServiceAccount — Full Cluster Control

🔍 Symptom: The CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions / GitLab CI) uses a ServiceAccount with cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding — granted during initial setup "so the pipeline can deploy anything." kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:anihpj-deployer shows [*] [*] [*]. Every commit to any branch can delete namespaces, exfiltrate Secrets, create backdoor ClusterRoleBindings, and deploy privileged pods. A single compromised CI token means complete cluster takeover. If a developer includes the kubeconfig in a public repo, anyone with the token has cluster-admin.

  kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:anihpj-deployer
  Resources   Non-Resource URLs   Resource Names   Verbs
  *.*         []                   []               [*]
  []          [*]                  []               [*]   ← CLUSTER-ADMIN IN CI!

  kubectl get clusterrolebinding ci-deployer -o yaml
  roleRef: {kind: ClusterRole, name: cluster-admin}   ← WRONG!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CI ServiceAccount bound to cluster-admin: During initial setup, the admin ran kubectl create clusterrolebinding ci-deployer --clusterrole=cluster-admin --serviceaccount=ci:anihpj-deployer. It "worked" but granted full cluster control to every CI pipeline job.
  2. No least-privilege RBAC for CI: The CI SA needs: create/update Deployments, get Secrets (for specific SAs), and nothing else. Instead it has * on *. The YAML was copy-pasted from a tutorial that used cluster-admin for simplicity.
  3. CI kubeconfig committed to Git repository: The kubeconfig with the CI ServiceAccount token is in the repo — either in .github/workflows/ or a kubeconfig.yaml file. Anyone with repo access (all developers, former employees, anyone who clones it) can extract the token.
  4. One CI ServiceAccount for all environments: The same SA deploys to dev, staging, AND production. A compromise in the dev pipeline (which may have looser security) grants production cluster-admin access. CI SAs must be per-environment with escalating permissions.
  5. CI token is a long-lived ServiceAccount token: The CI uses a legacy non-expiring SA token Secret — not a projected token with short TTL. If the token leaks, it's valid forever with no rotation.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CI pipeline uses certificate-based auth with system:masters: The CI kubeconfig has a client certificate with O=system:masters — bypassing RBAC entirely. This is even more powerful than cluster-admin because it's hardcoded in the API server.
  2. CI SA has impersonate verb: The CI SA can impersonate ANY user: kubectl --as=system:admin. Even if the SA itself has limited permissions, impersonation grants unlimited cluster-admin access.
  3. CI pipeline logs print the kubeconfig token: The CI script does echo "$KUBECONFIG" | base64 -d for debugging. The token is captured in CI logs — visible to anyone with CI log access (usually the entire engineering team).
  4. CI SA token stored in CI/CD platform secrets with broad access: GitHub Actions repository secrets with the kubeconfig are accessible from ANY workflow in the repo — including PRs from forked repos. An attacker can submit a malicious PR that exfiltrates the kubeconfig.
  5. No RBAC audit for CI ServiceAccounts: No regular review of what CI SAs can actually do. The assumption is "the pipeline works" — no one checks if it has excessive permissions.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Quick-start guide recommends cluster-admin for CI: Many CI/CD integration guides use cluster-admin as the quickest path. The team never replaced it with least-privilege RBAC.
  2. No CI/CD security review: CI/CD pipeline security is not in the threat model. The focus is on runtime security — the pipeline's RBAC is invisible.
  3. Developers create CI tokens manually: Each developer creates their own CI token with cluster-admin "so it works." No centralized CI token management or approval process.
  4. No pipeline isolation between teams: Same CI namespace and SA for all teams. The frontend team's CI token can delete the backend team's Deployments. No namespace isolation or per-team SAs.
  5. No OPA policy restricting CI SA permissions: No admission policy limiting what CI SAs can deploy. They can create privileged pods, hostPath volumes, and ClusterRoleBindings — all from the CI pipeline.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:anihpj-deployer If this shows *.* [*], the CI SA has cluster-admin. It should only show specific resources in specific namespaces with limited verbs.
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B10 "cluster-admin\|system:masters" Find all bindings to cluster-admin. Each one that's not a human admin account is a potential over-privileged service account.
kubectl get secrets -n ci -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.type=="kubernetes.io/service-account-token") | .metadata.name' Find legacy SA tokens in the CI namespace. Each one is a non-expiring credential that should be replaced with projected tokens.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The CI/CD ServiceAccount is bound to cluster-admin ClusterRole. Every pipeline execution has unrestricted control over the entire cluster — delete namespaces, exfiltrate Secrets, create backdoors. A single leaked CI token means total cluster compromise.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create least-privilege Role for CI pipeline kubectl create role anihpj-deployer -n anihpj --verb=get,list,create,update,patch --resource=deployments,services,configmaps,secrets Only grant the verbs and resources needed for deployment. Never *. Never cluster-wide. CI should only access its specific namespaces.
2. Delete cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding for CI kubectl delete clusterrolebinding ci-deployer Immediately revoke cluster-admin. The CI pipeline will fail — fix it with the least-privilege role. The temporary outage is worth the permanent security gain.
3. Use separate ServiceAccounts per environment anihpj-deployer-dev can deploy to dev namespace. anihpj-deployer-prod can deploy to prod namespace. Dev SA has no access to prod. Compromising dev doesn't compromise production.
4. Use projected tokens with short TTL for CI Generate CI tokens with kubectl create token anihpj-deployer --duration=1h. The token expires after the pipeline run. Even if leaked, it's useless after 1 hour.
5. Scan CI configs for committed kubeconfig/tokens Run trufflehog on your entire Git history. Look for kubeconfig, token:, client-certificate-data:. Rotate every token found in Git.
💡 Personal Advice:
Your CI pipeline is your most powerful "user" — and your biggest risk. CI has automated, programmatic access to deploy anything. If the CI token has cluster-admin, every source code commit is a potential cluster takeover. Least-privilege RBAC for CI is not optional — it's the difference between "someone pushed bad code" and "someone deleted the entire cluster."
Per-environment SAs + short-lived tokens = blast radius containment. Dev CI token can only break dev. Prod CI token expires in 1 hour. Even if both are compromised, the attacker's window is limited and contained. This is supply chain security 101.
SC4
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC4
Container Registry Allows Anonymous Pulls — Anyone Can Download Images

🔍 Symptom: docker pull anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 succeeds WITHOUT any authentication — from any machine, anywhere in the world. The container registry (Docker Hub / ECR / Harbor) allows anonymous pulls. Anyone can download all anihpj images, extract proprietary code, reverse-engineer the application, scan for vulnerabilities, and discover hardcoded secrets in image layers. Competitors can pull your entire application stack. Attackers can analyze your images offline — finding every CVE, every exposed port, and every misconfiguration before launching an attack.

  docker pull anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2   # From a random external machine
  v1.2: Pulling from anihpj/jobpost-api
  Digest: sha256:abc123...   ← ANONYMOUS PULL SUCCEEDED!

  docker run --rm anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 env
  DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...   ← Config extracted from public image!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Registry configured with public/anonymous pull access: Docker Hub repositories default to public. ECR repositories can be set to "Allow public pulls." Harbor projects can allow anonymous access. The registry is open to the world.
  2. No imagePullSecrets configured in Pod specs: Even if the registry requires auth, the pod doesn't have imagePullSecrets configured. The registry was made public because "pods couldn't pull images" — instead of configuring pull Secrets correctly.
  3. Registry credentials in plaintext in imagePullSecrets: The Docker config credentials are stored in a Kubernetes Secret. If RBAC allows reading Secrets in the namespace, any compromised pod can extract registry credentials and pull images.
  4. No IP-based access control on registry: The registry doesn't restrict pulls by IP range. Even if auth is required, there's no network-level restriction — the registry is reachable from the entire internet.
  5. Registry token with pull-only scope leaked: A "read-only" registry token was shared for CI/CD or monitoring. The token was committed to Git or exposed in logs. Anyone with the token can pull all images.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Registry behind CDN or mirror that caches anonymously: A registry mirror (e.g., docker.io proxy cache) caches images and serves them without auth. The main registry is protected but the mirror is open.
  2. Cloud provider registry with broad IAM policy: ECR repository policy has Principal: "*" with Action: ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer. The wildcard principal allows any AWS account to pull images.
  3. Registry accessible via public LoadBalancer: The registry is deployed in the cluster with type: LoadBalancer — exposing it directly to the internet with a public IP. Even with auth, it's reachable from anywhere.
  4. Image layers cached on public Docker Hub: Even after making your registry private, old image layers may still be cached on Docker Hub or public mirrors. The proprietary code is still accessible via layer hashes.
  5. Registry has no audit logging for pulls: Anonymous pulls go undetected. You can't answer "who pulled our images?" or "was our proprietary code exfiltrated?" No pull audit trail exists.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Docker Hub used as primary registry (default public): New projects push to Docker Hub which defaults to public repositories. The team never changed the visibility to private.
  2. Private registry not deployed (Harbor/ECR): No private registry infrastructure. Docker Hub is the only registry — and public repos are free. Private repos cost money — the team chose public.
  3. No registry access policy defined: No decision on who can push, who can pull, and from which networks. Registry access is undefined — defaulting to permissive.
  4. imagePullSecrets not templated in Helm charts: The Helm chart doesn't include imagePullSecrets. To make the chart "work out of the box," the registry was made public instead of adding pull Secret support.
  5. No image confidentiality policy: The team doesn't consider container images as intellectual property. The assumption is "images are just wrappers around open-source code" — ignoring proprietary business logic baked into layers.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker pull anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 Run from OUTSIDE your network without any Docker login. If it succeeds, your registry allows anonymous pulls — anyone with internet access can download your images.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 imagePullSecrets Check if pods use imagePullSecrets. If absent, the registry is either public or the node has registry credentials baked in.
docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 --no-trunc Check what's in each image layer. If ENV vars, config files, or source code are visible, anyone who pulls the image can extract them.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The container registry allows anonymous/public pulls. Anyone on the internet can download all anihpj container images — extracting proprietary code, scanning for vulnerabilities, discovering hardcoded configuration, and reverse-engineering the application without any authentication or audit trail.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Make the registry private — require authentication for pulls Docker Hub: set repository visibility to Private. ECR: set repository policy to require IAM auth. Harbor: set project to non-public. No anonymous pulls — every pull request must authenticate.
2. Configure imagePullSecrets in every namespace kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n anihpj --docker-server=<registry> --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<token> Add imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}] to every Pod spec or ServiceAccount. Pods authenticate to the registry using this Secret.
3. Restrict registry access by IP range (VPC endpoints) Only allow pulls from the cluster's VPC/subnet IP range. Use AWS VPC Endpoint for ECR, or GCP Private Google Access for GCR. Registry is unreachable from the public internet.
4. Deploy a private registry (Harbor) inside the cluster Run Harbor within your VPC. Images never leave your network. Use RBAC for project-level push/pull access. Enable vulnerability scanning and image signing policies.
5. Scan public registries for your organization's images Periodically search Docker Hub, GHCR, and public ECR for images tagged with your org name. If found, they may be public repos that need to be locked down or removed.
💡 Personal Advice:
Public registry = public intellectual property. Every image layer in a public registry is downloadable by anyone — competitors, attackers, researchers. They can extract your code, your configs, your secrets baked into layers. Your container images contain your entire application — treat them as proprietary intellectual property. Keep them private.
imagePullSecrets are not optional for private registries. Every pod, every namespace, every cluster that pulls from a private registry needs imagePullSecrets. Automate this in your Helm charts, Kustomize overlays, and infrastructure code. A pod that can't pull from a private registry shouldn't make the registry public — it should get the right credentials.

📌 SC5–SC8: Latest Tags, Provenance, Dependency Pinning & Git Secrets

SC5
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC5
Dockerfile Uses :latest Base Image — Non-Reproducible Builds

🔍 Symptom: FROM python:3.9 (effectively python:3.9:latest) means the base image is DIFFERENT every time the Dockerfile is built. A build today uses python:3.9 with OpenSSL 1.1.1n. Tomorrow's build uses python:3.9 with OpenSSL 3.0.8 — breaking TLS compatibility. Worse: an attacker who compromises Docker Hub can push a malicious python:3.9 and every rebuild of anihpj-api pulls and runs the compromised base. Floating tags make builds non-reproducible and vulnerable to upstream compromise.

  docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.3 .   # Today
  ---> Using cache for python:3.9   ← Pulled whatever :latest was TODAY

  docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.3 .   # Tomorrow (same Dockerfile)
  ---> Pulling python:3.9   ← DIFFERENT base image!
  # Different OS packages, different OpenSSL, different glibc!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. FROM uses floating tag (implicit :latest): FROM python:3.9 resolves to python:3.9:latest — a MOVING target controlled by the image maintainer. Every build may get a different base image with different packages. Use digest pinning: FROM python:3.9@sha256:abc123....
  2. No digest pinning in Dockerfile: The SHA256 digest is the ONLY way to guarantee you're using the exact same base image every build. Without @sha256:... after the tag, the base image is mutable.
  3. --pull flag forces re-download every build: docker build --pull always pulls the latest tag — ignoring the local cache. Combined with floating tags, every build gets a potentially different base image even within the same day.
  4. Build cache invalidated by upstream base change: When the base image changes (new layer digest), all cached layers are invalidated. The entire image rebuilds from scratch — doubling build time and changing the final image unpredictably.
  5. No image layer diffing between builds: The team doesn't compare image layers between build N and build N+1. They assume "same Dockerfile = same image" — which is FALSE with floating tags. A supply chain compromise via base image is invisible.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. apt-get update in Dockerfile pulls latest packages: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl installs whatever version of curl is latest at build time. Two builds days apart get different curl versions — one might have a new CVE.
  2. pip install without requirements.txt hash pinning: RUN pip install django installs the latest Django version. Tomorrow's build may get Django 5.0 with breaking changes or a new vulnerability.
  3. Base image tag deleted upstream: Docker Hub removes python:3.9-old tag. Your build that referenced it now fails. Even valid tags can disappear when the maintainer cleans up old images.
  4. Base image rebuilt with same tag but compromised: The python:3.9 tag was pushed by an attacker who compromised the Python Docker Hub account. Everyone pulling python:3.9 gets the backdoored image — no tag change, no alert.
  5. Different architectures get different base images: FROM python:3.9 resolves to different digests on amd64 vs arm64. Multi-arch builds with floating tags produce inconsistent images across architectures.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Dockerfile templates from tutorials use floating tags: Every Dockerfile tutorial uses FROM python:3.9. No tutorial shows FROM python:3.9@sha256:... — so teams never learn digest pinning.
  2. No Dependabot/Renovate for base image updates: No automated tool updating base image digests. The team pins a digest once and never updates it — running an image from 2 years ago with known CVEs.
  3. Digest pinning considered "too much work": Updating pinned digests requires a PR every time the base image is updated. The team views this as unnecessary overhead compared to "just use :latest."
  4. No reproducibility requirement: The organization doesn't require reproducible builds. "It works on my machine" is accepted — despite the build producing different artifacts each run.
  5. No image diffing in CI: CI doesn't compare the current build's layers with the previous build. A silent upstream change in the base image goes undetected.
🔍 What to Look At:
grep "^FROM" Dockerfile Check if FROM lines have @sha256: digests. If only tags (:3.9, :latest) are used, the build is non-reproducible.
docker inspect anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.[0].Config.Image' Check the base image digest that was actually used. If it shows a tag (not a digest), the image was built from a floating reference.
docker build --no-cache -t test-build . ; docker build --no-cache -t test-build-2 . ; diff <(docker history test-build) <(docker history test-build-2) See if two consecutive builds with the same Dockerfile produce different layers. If they differ, floating tags are causing non-reproducibility.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Dockerfile FROM lines use floating tags (python:3.9, node:18) without digest pinning (@sha256:...). Every build may pull a different base image — breaking reproducibility, introducing unexpected CVEs, and enabling upstream supply chain attacks via compromised base images.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Pin all base images by SHA256 digest FROM python:3.9@sha256:abc123def456789... Replace FROM python:3.9 with the pinned digest. Every build uses the EXACT same base image — guaranteed reproducible. Find the digest with docker pull python:3.9 && docker inspect python:3.9 | jq '.[0].RepoDigests'.
2. Pin apt/pip dependencies with hash verification pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt requirements.txt must include package hashes. apt packages pinned to specific versions. Every dependency is locked to an exact version+hash.
3. Use Renovate/Dependabot to update pinned digests Configure Renovate to automatically open PRs when base image digests are updated. This keeps images current with security patches while maintaining reproducibility.
4. Compare image layers between builds in CI syft diff image1 image2 CI step: compare this build's SBOM with the previous build's SBOM. Flag any unexpected package changes — catch upstream compromises before deployment.
5. Sign base images in your private registry Mirror trusted base images to your private registry. Sign them with Cosign. Dockerfiles reference your signed, pinned base images — not Docker Hub's mutable tags.
💡 Personal Advice:
:latest is a moving target. @sha256 is a fingerprint. A tag like python:3.9 promises "Python 3.9" — but the actual image changes every time the maintainer pushes. A digest @sha256:abc... is the exact image hash — it CANNOT change. Pin to digests. Every time. No exceptions.
Reproducible builds are the foundation of supply chain trust. If you can't rebuild the same image from the same Dockerfile twice, you can't verify that what's running in production matches what was built in CI. Floating tags make audits impossible — "which base image was used for build #457?" becomes unanswerable.
SC6
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC6
No Image Provenance — Can't Verify Who Built the Image or How

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 image is running in production, but there's no record of WHO built it, WHAT source code was used, WHICH CI pipeline produced it, or WHAT parameters were passed. No SLSA provenance attestation exists. If a security incident occurs (e.g., data exfiltration from the API), you cannot answer: "Was this image built by our CI pipeline? Was it built from the main branch? Was the build process tampered with?" Without provenance, every image is Schrödinger's container — trusted and untrusted simultaneously until proven otherwise.

  cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2
  Error: no attestations found   ← NO PROVENANCE!

  docker inspect anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.[0].Config.Labels'
  null   ← No build metadata labels (git commit, CI run ID, timestamp)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No SLSA provenance generated during build: The CI pipeline doesn't generate a SLSA provenance attestation. Tools like slsa-github-generator or cosign attest with provenance predicate are not in the pipeline. The image is a black box.
  2. No build metadata labels in Dockerfile: LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost" and LABEL org.opencontainers.image.revision="${GIT_SHA}" are missing. The image doesn't carry its own origin story.
  3. CI pipeline build logs deleted/expired: CI logs showing who triggered the build, which branch was used, and what parameters were set are in short-lived CI storage (90-day retention). For an image built 6 months ago, the build logs are gone — no way to reconstruct provenance.
  4. Developer pushed image manually from laptop: The image was built on a developer's machine and pushed to the registry with docker push. No CI pipeline involvement — no audit trail, no reproducibility, no provenance possible.
  5. No attestation verification at admission time: Even if provenance IS generated, there's no Kyverno policy requiring it. Images without provenance are admitted to production without question.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Provenance generated but not attached to image: The CI pipeline generates a provenance file but stores it as a CI artifact — not as a Cosign attestation in the registry. The provenance exists but is disconnected from the image.
  2. Provenance attestation signed with wrong key: The provenance is signed with a key that the admission controller doesn't trust. Verification fails — but the pod is still admitted because the policy is in audit mode (not enforce).
  3. Provenance doesn't include build parameters: The SLSA provenance has materials: [] (empty) — it doesn't record the source repo, commit SHA, or build parameters. The provenance exists but is useless for forensics.
  4. Multiple registries — provenance only in one: The image is replicated across ECR, GCR, and Harbor. The provenance attestation was only pushed to ECR. Images pulled from GCR appear to have no provenance.
  5. Provenance chain broken by image re-tagging: The image was signed with provenance at @sha256:abc, then re-tagged as :v1.2. The provenance follows the digest, but tools checking tags miss it.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. SLSA framework unknown to the team: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) is a relatively new framework. The team hasn't heard of it or doesn't know how to implement it.
  2. No provenance requirement in compliance: The organization's compliance framework doesn't require build provenance. There's no external pressure to implement it.
  3. Provenance tools not in CI pipeline template: The standard CI pipeline template has build, test, push — but no provenance generation step. Teams must add it manually, and most don't.
  4. No incident response dependency on provenance: The IR team doesn't ask provenance questions during incidents. Without this demand, provenance generation is never prioritized.
  5. Provenance considered "security theater": The engineering team views provenance as paperwork without practical benefit. They don't see how it helps during a real security incident.
🔍 What to Look At:
cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.payload | @base64d | fromjson' If no attestation exists, the image has no provenance. If it exists, check: source repo, commit SHA, builder ID, and build parameters.
docker inspect anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.[0].ContainerConfig.Labels' Check OCI labels: org.opencontainers.image.source, org.opencontainers.image.revision, org.opencontainers.image.created. Missing labels = missing metadata.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].image' | while read img; do echo "=== $img ==="; cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance "$img" 2>&1 | head -3; done Audit all running images for provenance. Each "no attestations found" is a supply chain blind spot.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No SLSA provenance attestation is generated during the CI build or attached to the image. When a security incident occurs, there's no way to determine who built the image, from which source code, using which pipeline — making forensic investigation and supply chain compromise detection impossible.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Generate SLSA provenance in CI pipeline GitHub Actions: use slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator. GitLab CI: use cosign attest --type slsaprovenance with predicate. The provenance records: source repo, commit SHA, builder ID, build parameters.
2. Attach provenance as Cosign attestation cosign attest --type slsaprovenance --predicate provenance.json anihpj/jobpost-api:${TAG} The provenance is signed and stored in the registry alongside the image. Anyone with the public key can verify it.
3. Add OCI labels to Dockerfile LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost" LABEL org.opencontainers.image.revision="${GIT_SHA}" LABEL org.opencontainers.image.created="${BUILD_TIMESTAMP}" Standard OCI labels make basic provenance queryable without Cosign verification — useful for quick checks.
4. Require provenance attestation at admission Kyverno policy: verify SLSA provenance attestation for all images. Require at minimum the source repo and builder ID. Reject images without provenance.
5. Store provenance in an immutable transparency log Use Rekor (Sigstore's transparency log) to store provenance attestations. This provides an immutable, append-only record that can be audited even if the registry is compromised.
💡 Personal Advice:
Provenance is your supply chain audit trail. When a CVE is discovered in a library, provenance tells you "which of our images were built after this CVE was patched?" When a security incident happens, provenance tells you "was this image built from a protected branch or a feature branch?" Without it, every investigation starts from zero.
SLSA is the framework. Cosign is the tool. Rekor is the proof. SLSA defines what to record (builder, source, parameters). Cosign signs and attaches it to the image. Rekor stores it immutably. These three together form a complete provenance chain from source code to running container.
SC7
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC7
Pip Dependencies Without Hash Pinning — Dependency Confusion Attack

🔍 Symptom: requirements.txt has django==4.2.7 and requests==2.31.0 — version-pinned but WITHOUT hash verification. An attacker who compromises PyPI (or typosquats a private package name) can publish a malicious django==4.2.7 with a backdoor. Pip installs it because the version matches and there's no hash to verify integrity. Additionally, a private internal package anihpj-common is listed without --index-url — an attacker can publish anihpj-common on public PyPI with a higher version number. Pip installs the malicious public package instead of the internal one.

  cat requirements.txt
  django==4.2.7
  requests==2.31.0
  anihpj-common>=1.0   ← No hash, no private index!

  pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt
  ERROR: Hashes are required but not provided   ← CAN'T VERIFY INTEGRITY!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No --require-hashes in pip install: pip install -r requirements.txt without --require-hashes. Pip trusts the package index implicitly — any package with the matching name and version is accepted, regardless of content.
  2. requirements.txt has no hashes: The file has django==4.2.7 but not django==4.2.7 --hash=sha256:abc123.... Without hashes, pip cannot verify that the downloaded package matches the expected content.
  3. Private packages without --index-url: anihpj-common is a private package published to a private PyPI server. But requirements.txt has no --index-url https://pypi.internal.anihpj.com/simple/. Pip searches PyPI first and may find a malicious public package with the same name.
  4. Dependency confusion via public package with higher version: The attacker publishes anihpj-common==999.0.0 on public PyPI. pip install anihpj-common>=1.0 resolves to 999.0.0 — the malicious public package. Dependency confusion is a well-known attack vector.
  5. pip install without --no-deps verification: Django depends on sqlparse. Pip installs whatever version of sqlparse satisfies Django's requirement — without verifying hashes for transitive dependencies. A compromised transitive dependency is invisible.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Package mirror/proxy compromised: The organization uses a PyPI proxy cache (DevPI, Artifactory). If the proxy is compromised, it can serve malicious packages — and pip has no way to detect this without hashes.
  2. Typosquatted package name: requiremnts.txt has djanjo==4.2.7 (typo). Pip installs the typosquatted package which may be malicious. Hash pinning would fail because the hash doesn't match the legitimate package.
  3. Package maintainer account compromised: The legitimate Django PyPI maintainer account is compromised. Attackers publish django==4.2.7 with a backdoor. Everyone who installs without hash verification gets the backdoored version.
  4. pip install from URL without hash: pip install https://github.com/user/repo/archive/v1.0.tar.gz — downloading from a URL without --hash. If the GitHub repo is compromised, pip installs the malicious code.
  5. Hash algorithm collision: Using MD5 or SHA1 hashes (weak). An attacker can craft a malicious package with the same MD5 hash as the legitimate package. Use SHA256 or SHA512.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. requirements.txt generated by pip freeze without --hash: pip freeze > requirements.txt outputs versions without hashes. The team uses this as the source of truth — never adding hashes manually.
  2. No dependency review tool in CI: No pip-audit, safety, or dependabot checking dependencies for known vulnerabilities or hash mismatches in CI.
  3. Private PyPI not deployed: No internal package registry (DevPI, Artifactory, Nexus). All packages — internal and external — come from public PyPI. Dependency confusion is easy.
  4. Developers add packages manually without hashes: pip install new-package && pip freeze > requirements.txt. Hashes are never generated because developers don't use pip-compile --generate-hashes.
  5. No policy on hash verification: The organization has no requirement for --require-hashes. Dependency integrity is assumed, not verified.
🔍 What to Look At:
pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt --dry-run 2>&1 | head -5 If it errors with "Hashes are required," your requirements.txt has no hashes. Pip cannot verify dependency integrity.
grep -E "^[^#]" requirements.txt | grep -v -- "--hash" Check if every package has at least one --hash=sha256: line. Any package without a hash is a dependency you're trusting blindly.
pip list --format=json | jq '.[] | {name, version}' | while read pkg; do pip show "$pkg" | grep -i "location\|source"; done Check where each installed package came from. Internal packages should come from your private index, not public PyPI.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: requirements.txt has version-pinned packages WITHOUT hash verification (--hash=sha256:). Pip trusts the package index implicitly — a compromised index, typosquatted package, or dependency confusion attack can inject malicious code without detection.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Generate requirements.txt with hashes pip-compile --generate-hashes requirements.in -o requirements.txt Use pip-tools to compile pinned dependencies WITH SHA256 hashes. Every package gets at least one hash entry.
2. Install with --require-hashes pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt Pip verifies the hash of every downloaded package. If the hash doesn't match, pip REFUSES to install — catching compromised or tampered packages.
3. Use --index-url for private packages --index-url https://pypi.internal.anihpj.com/simple/ --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ Private packages resolve from your private index FIRST. Public packages fall back to PyPI. This prevents dependency confusion — your private anihpj-common is never confused with a public package.
4. Deploy a private package registry Use AWS CodeArtifact, GCP Artifact Registry, or JFrog Artifactory. All packages — internal and cached external — are served from your controlled registry. Audit all package downloads.
5. Add pip-audit/safety to CI pipeline pip-audit --require-hashes -r requirements.txt CI step: scan dependencies for known CVEs AND verify hashes. Fail the build on critical vulnerabilities or hash mismatches.
💡 Personal Advice:
Version pinning ≠ integrity verification. django==4.2.7 tells pip WHICH version to install — but not THAT the downloaded package is the REAL Django 4.2.7. Hashes answer the second question. Without them, you're trusting the network connection between pip and PyPI. That's not security — that's hope.
Dependency confusion is the easiest supply chain attack. If your private package names aren't protected, an attacker can register them on public PyPI and your CI pipeline will happily install the malicious version. Always use --index-url pointing to your private registry FIRST.
SC8
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC8
Git Repository Contains Hardcoded Credentials — Secrets in Source Code

🔍 Symptom: git log -p | grep -i "password\|secret\|token\|api.key" returns 23 matches across 8 commits. AWS access keys, database passwords, and JWT signing secrets were committed to the anihpj/jobpost Git repository over the past 2 years. Some were "removed in the next commit" — but they're still in Git history. Every developer with repo access, every CI pipeline that clones the repo, and every former employee with a local clone has access to these credentials. Git is an append-only ledger — once a secret is committed, it's there forever unless you rewrite history.

  git log -p --all | grep -iE "password|secret|token|api.key|BEGIN.*PRIVATE KEY"
  -DATABASE_PASSWORD=SuperSecretP@ss123!
  +AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
  -JWT_SECRET=my-super-secret-jwt-key-do-not-share   ← 3 CREDENTIALS IN GIT!

  git show abc123:config/settings.py | grep PASSWORD
  DATABASE_PASSWORD = "SuperSecretP@ss123!"   ← STILL ACCESSIBLE IN GIT!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. .env file committed to Git: The project's .env file was committed during initial setup — with real credentials. Even though it was deleted 3 commits later, git checkout <old-commit> still retrieves it. .env must be in .gitignore from the FIRST commit.
  2. No pre-commit scanning for secrets: No git-secrets, trufflehog, or detect-secrets pre-commit hook. Developers commit secrets accidentally — and there's no automated gate to stop them.
  3. Credentials in config files instead of environment variables: config/settings.py has hardcoded DATABASE_PASSWORD = "...". The config file is version-controlled. Secrets should be injected at runtime via environment variables, Secrets, or external secret stores — never in source files.
  4. "Temporary" credentials for testing committed permanently: A developer added test credentials "just to get it working" and committed them. The commit was pushed before the credentials were replaced with placeholders. "I'll fix it later" never happens — the secret is now in Git forever.
  5. No .gitignore excluding sensitive file patterns: .gitignore doesn't include *.pem, *.key, .env, *.env.*, credentials.json, or secrets/. Any file matching these patterns can be committed accidentally.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Credentials in commit messages: A developer wrote git commit -m "Updated DB password to SuperSecretP@ss123!". The commit message itself contains the secret — visible in git log without even looking at diffs.
  2. Credentials in CI pipeline config: .github/workflows/deploy.yml has KUBECONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }} — but someone committed a version with the actual base64 value instead of the variable reference. The real kubeconfig is in Git.
  3. Credentials in Docker image layers committed to Git LFS: The repo uses Git LFS for Docker images. An image with baked-in credentials is stored in Git LFS — anyone who pulls the LFS objects has the credentials from the image layers.
  4. Git submodule with secrets: The main repo references a submodule that contains secrets. Cloning with --recursive pulls the submodule and its secret-filled Git history.
  5. Forked repository retains secrets from upstream: The repo was forked from a template that had secrets. Those secrets are still in the fork's Git history — accessible to all fork contributors.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No pre-commit hook installed by default: New repository, no .pre-commit-config.yaml or .git/hooks/pre-commit with secret scanning. Developers push secrets on their first commit.
  2. No secret scanning in CI: CI pipeline doesn't run trufflehog or ggshield on push/PR. Secrets committed to branches are only discovered manually — or never.
  3. Repository is public: The anihpj/jobpost repository is public on GitHub. Every committed secret is visible to the ENTIRE INTERNET. Public repos amplify the impact of secret leakage by 1000×.
  4. No incident response plan for leaked secrets: When a secret is discovered in Git, there's no process for rotating it. The team deletes the file and moves on — the exposed secret remains valid and exploitable.
  5. No developer training on secret management: Developers are not trained on what constitutes a secret, how to store them, or the risks of committing them to Git. The incident is treated as "oops" not "security breach."
🔍 What to Look At:
trufflehog git https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost --only-verified Scan the entire Git history for secrets. Trufflehog automatically verifies if found credentials are still valid by testing them against the service.
git log -p --all | grep -iE "password=|secret=|token=|api.key|BEGIN.*PRIVATE" Quick scan of Git diffs for common secret patterns. Each match is a potential exposed credential that needs immediate rotation.
cat .gitignore | grep -E "\.env|\.key|\.pem|credentials|secrets" Verify .gitignore covers all sensitive file patterns. Missing patterns mean developers can accidentally commit these files.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Credentials (.env files, API keys, database passwords) were committed to the Git repository. Even if "removed" in a later commit, Git history retains them permanently. Every developer with repo access, every CI pipeline, and anyone who clones the repo can extract these credentials.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Rotate ALL credentials found in Git IMMEDIATELY Every password, key, and token found in Git is COMPROMISED. Rotate them NOW. Generate new credentials. Update all services. This is priority #1 — before cleaning Git history.
2. Clean Git history with BFG Repo-Cleaner or git filter-repo bfg --replace-text passwords.txt --delete-files .env repo.git Rewrite Git history to remove secrets from ALL commits. Force push. All clones must be re-cloned. This is a destructive operation — coordinate with all contributors.
3. Add pre-commit hook for secret scanning pre-commit install; cat > .pre-commit-config.yaml <<EOF repos: - repo: https://github.com/Yelp/detect-secrets hooks: [{id: detect-secrets}] EOF Blocks commits containing secret patterns. Developers get immediate feedback — secrets never enter Git history.
4. Add CI secret scanning on every push GitHub Actions: run trufflehog or ggshield on every push. Alert if new secrets are detected. Block PRs that introduce secrets.
5. Use external secret management — never in source code HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, External Secrets Operator. Secrets live OUTSIDE the codebase. Code reads secrets at runtime — they are never written in files, never committed to Git, and never appear in diffs.
💡 Personal Advice:
Git is an append-only ledger. Secrets committed are secrets forever. Deleting a secret in a new commit doesn't remove it from history. Anyone with git clone can git checkout the old commit and see it. The ONLY fix is: (1) rotate the secret, (2) rewrite Git history with BFG/git filter-repo, (3) force push. In that order.
Pre-commit hooks prevent secrets. CI scanning detects leaks. Both are mandatory. Pre-commit stops secrets at the developer's keyboard. CI scanning catches what pre-commit misses (or what a developer bypasses with --no-verify). Two layers of defense — zero secrets in Git.

📌 SC9–SC12: SAST, Laptop Builds, Admission Control & Cache Poisoning

SC9
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC9
No Static Analysis in CI Pipeline — SAST Tools Not Integrated

🔍 Symptom: The CI pipeline builds, tests, and pushes the anihpj-api Django application — but NEVER runs static analysis (SAST). bandit -r anihpj/ would flag: B301: pickle deserialization (RCE vector), B602: subprocess call with shell=True (command injection), B108: hardcoded temporary file (race condition). These vulnerabilities have been in production for months. SAST tools would have caught them BEFORE deployment — but they're not in the pipeline. The first time anyone sees these issues is after a security incident.

  bandit -r anihpj/ -f json | python3 -m json.tool | head -20
  {
    "results": [
      {"test_name": "B301", "issue_severity": "MEDIUM", "issue_text": "Use of pickle"},
      {"test_name": "B602", "issue_severity": "MEDIUM", "issue_text": "subprocess call shell=True"},
      {"test_name": "B108", "issue_severity": "LOW", "issue_text": "hardcoded_tmp_directory"}
    ]
  }   ← SAST WOULD HAVE CAUGHT THESE — BUT IT WAS NEVER RUN!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No SAST tool in CI pipeline: bandit, semgrep, snyk code, or sonarqube is not part of the CI workflow. The pipeline only runs unit tests — it doesn't scan for security anti-patterns in source code.
  2. SAST run manually but never in CI: A developer ran bandit once on their laptop. The results were in a terminal that was closed. The findings were never recorded, never triaged, and never fixed. Manual SAST doesn't scale — it must be automated in CI.
  3. SAST configured but exit code ignored: CI runs bandit -r . but continues regardless of results. continue-on-error: true or missing --exit-zero means SAST findings are reported but never BLOCK the pipeline.
  4. SAST results not reviewed or triaged: The CI pipeline generates a SAST report artifact, but no one looks at it. The report sits in CI artifacts storage — findings accumulate without action.
  5. SAST tool not configured for the right language/framework: bandit is configured for Python but the project also has JavaScript and shell scripts. Those are unscanned — XSS vulnerabilities and command injection in JS go undetected.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. High false positive rate leads to alert fatigue: Bandit flags 200 findings per scan — 180 are false positives. The team disabled SAST because "it's too noisy." Tune rules or use a more precise tool (semgrep) instead of disabling entirely.
  2. SAST takes too long and slows CI: Full-project SAST takes 10 minutes. The team removed it to speed up CI. Instead, run SAST in parallel with other checks or use incremental scanning of changed files only.
  3. SAST findings in third-party code not differentiated: Bandit scans venv/ and node_modules/, flagging vulnerabilities in third-party code. The report is 90% third-party issues — burying the real application findings.
  4. No security champion to own SAST: No one on the team is responsible for SAST configuration, rule tuning, or finding triage. Without ownership, SAST rots — rules become outdated and findings ignored.
  5. SAST unable to detect business logic vulnerabilities: SAST finds code patterns (SQL injection, XSS) but can't detect: auth bypass, IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference), or rate limit bypass. These require manual review or DAST.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. SAST tools not in CI pipeline template: The standard CI template has lint, test, build — but no security scanning stage. SAST requires manual pipeline customization.
  2. Security scanning considered "Phase 2": The plan was to add SAST after MVP launch. The MVP launched 2 years ago — SAST is still "Phase 2."
  3. No SAST tooling budget or approval: Snyk Code and SonarQube (enterprise) require licensing. The free tools (bandit, semgrep OSS) are unknown or considered inferior without evaluation.
  4. Developers not trained on secure coding: SAST finds vulnerabilities — but developers don't understand them. "What is insecure deserialization?" Findings are ignored because they're not understood.
  5. No baseline file to suppress existing findings: Running SAST on an existing codebase produces 500 findings. Without a baseline, all are new — overwhelming the team. SAST should baseline existing issues and alert only on NEW findings.
🔍 What to Look At:
bandit -r anihpj/ -ll Run SAST on your codebase. If the output shows findings with confidence HIGH/MEDIUM, these are vulnerabilities that have been in your code since the feature was written.
cat .github/workflows/ci.yml | grep -iE "bandit|semgrep|snyk|sonarqube|codeql" Check if any SAST tool is in your CI pipeline. If not, your pipeline has a gap between "unit tests pass" and "code is secure."
semgrep --config=auto anihpj/ Run semgrep with auto-detection of applicable rules. It uses pattern matching to find security anti-patterns specific to your frameworks.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool is integrated into the CI pipeline. Vulnerabilities like insecure deserialization, command injection, and hardcoded secrets remain in production code for months — undetected because no automated security scanning exists in the build process.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add SAST to CI pipeline bandit -r anihpj/ -ll -f json -o bandit-report.json; semgrep --config=auto --error anihpj/ Run bandit (Python) + semgrep (multi-language) on every push. Fail the build on HIGH/CONFIDENCE findings.
2. Create a baseline of existing findings bandit -r anihpj/ -f json -o baseline.json Accept existing LOW/MEDIUM findings as a baseline. Only alert on NEW findings introduced in the current PR. This prevents alert fatigue while stopping new vulnerabilities.
3. Tune SAST rules for your project Disable rules with high false positives. Increase severity thresholds. Exclude venv/, node_modules/, and migrations/. A tuned SAST is 10× more actionable than a raw scan.
4. Add PR comments with SAST findings Integrate SAST with GitHub/GitLab PR interface. Findings appear as inline comments on the affected lines. Developers see security issues in the same workflow as code review.
5. Pair SAST with secure coding training Each SAST finding links to an explanation: "What is pickle deserialization? Why is it dangerous? How do I fix it?" Developers learn while they fix. Over time, they stop writing these patterns.
💡 Personal Advice:
SAST finds bugs that unit tests miss. Unit tests verify that code works. SAST verifies that code is safe. pickle.loads(user_input) passes all unit tests — but SAST flags it as a critical RCE vector. You need both. SAST in CI is not optional in 2026.
Start with semgrep — free, fast, multi-language. semgrep --config=auto detects 100+ security patterns across 30+ languages. It runs in seconds and has community rulesets for Django, Flask, React, and more. Add it to CI today — it takes 3 lines in your pipeline config.
SC10
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC10
Image Built on Developer Laptop and Pushed — No CI/CD Pipeline

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 image was built on a developer's laptop with docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 . && docker push anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2. There's no CI pipeline involvement — no provenance attestation, no vulnerability scan, no SBOM, no signature. The image could contain anything: uncommitted code, local config changes, developer's SSH keys, or malware from the developer's machine. There's no audit trail of who built it, what source code was used, or whether tests passed. Every image pushed from a laptop is a supply chain blind spot.

  docker inspect anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | jq '.[0].Config.Labels'
  null   ← No CI run ID, no build number, no pipeline metadata

  cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2
  Error: no attestations found   ← Manual build — no provenance possible

  docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.2 | head -3
  IMAGE          CREATED BY
  <missing>       /bin/sh -c pip install -r requirements.txt   ← Local build!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No CI/CD pipeline for image builds: The team never set up automated image builds. Developers build and push images manually from their laptops. This is the pre-DevOps anti-pattern that bypasses every security control.
  2. CI pipeline exists but developers bypass it for "hotfixes": The CI pipeline is for "normal deployments." Emergency hotfixes are built and pushed directly from laptops — bypassing SAST, vulnerability scanning, signing, and provenance generation.
  3. Registry allows push from any authenticated user: The registry IAM policy allows ANY developer with credentials to push images. There's no restriction that only the CI ServiceAccount can push. Manual pushes are technically possible — and frequently used.
  4. Build instructions document manual docker build/push: The README says: "To deploy: docker build -t ... ; docker push ..." Developers follow the documented process — which bypasses all CI security controls.
  5. CI pipeline too slow — developers push directly: The CI pipeline takes 15 minutes to build and push. Developers push directly from laptops in 30 seconds. The "faster" path becomes the default — and every security gate is lost.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CI pipeline down — developers push manually: CI is experiencing an outage. To meet a deployment deadline, developers push images manually. The manual push becomes a habit — even after CI is restored.
  2. Developer's laptop has malware that infects the image: The developer's machine has undetected malware that modifies the Docker build process. The image contains a backdoor that the developer didn't intentionally include — but pushed anyway.
  3. Uncommitted code changes baked into the image: The developer has local code changes that are not in Git. The image includes these uncommitted changes — production is running code that doesn't exist in any branch, making bug investigation impossible.
  4. Environment variables from developer's shell baked in: docker build --build-arg DATABASE_URL=$DATABASE_URL captures the developer's local environment variables — including potentially sensitive values — in the image build metadata.
  5. Image includes developer's SSH keys or credentials: COPY . /app in the Dockerfile copies everything in the build context — including ~/.ssh/id_rsa if present. The developer's SSH key is now in the production image.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CI/CD pipeline not set up yet: Early-stage startup, "we'll set up CI after the MVP." The MVP is in production — built and pushed from a laptop.
  2. Registry push credentials shared with all developers: The Docker Hub / ECR push credentials are in a shared 1Password vault. Every developer can push images — there's no restriction to the CI ServiceAccount.
  3. No registry policy restricting image sources: The registry doesn't differentiate between CI-built images and laptop-built images. Both are accepted and deployable.
  4. No admission policy requiring CI provenance: Kyverno could reject images without SLSA provenance (which only CI can generate). Without this policy, laptop-built images are admitted.
  5. Deployment process predates containerization: The team used to deploy tarballs from laptops. When they migrated to containers, they kept the same process — just with docker push instead of scp.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker inspect <image> | jq '.[0].ContainerConfig.Labels | keys' | grep -iE "build|ci|jenkins|github|gitlab" CI-built images typically have build metadata labels (build number, CI run ID, git commit). Absence of these suggests a manual laptop build.
cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance <image> 2>&1 Laptop builds CANNOT generate SLSA provenance (no builder ID, no trusted build environment). No provenance attestation = likely manual build.
kubectl get deployment -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[].spec.template.spec.containers[].image' | while read img; do cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance "$img" 2>&1 || echo "UNTRUSTED: $img"; done Find all running images without provenance. Each one is a supply chain blind spot that may have been built outside CI.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Container images are built and pushed directly from developer laptops instead of through a CI/CD pipeline. Manual builds bypass every supply chain security control: vulnerability scanning, SAST, image signing, SBOM generation, and provenance attestation.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set up CI/CD pipeline for ALL image builds Every image must be built by CI — never manually. The pipeline includes: lint → test → SAST → build → scan → sign → SBOM → provenance → push. No step is skippable.
2. Restrict registry push to CI ServiceAccount ONLY Registry IAM policy: only the CI ServiceAccount has push permission. All developers have pull only. Manual docker push is rejected at the registry level.
3. Require CI provenance attestation at admission Kyverno policy: reject pods where the image lacks a valid SLSA provenance attestation signed by the CI pipeline. Laptop-built images cannot pass this check.
4. Audit registry for images without CI metadata Query registry: find all images without org.opencontainers.image.source label or CI provenance. Flag these for review — rebuild them through CI or confirm they're legitimate.
5. Make CI fast enough that no one wants to bypass it If CI takes 15 minutes, developers WILL bypass it. Invest in CI speed: caching, parallel builds, incremental scans. A 2-minute CI pipeline with security checks removes the incentive to bypass.
💡 Personal Advice:
Every image pushed from a laptop is an unauditable black box. You can't prove what source code it contains, what tests were run, or whether it has vulnerabilities. If it's built outside CI, it's untrusted. Period. Block manual pushes at the registry level and enforce provenance at admission time.
Make CI the path of least resistance. If manual push takes 30 seconds and CI takes 15 minutes, developers will choose manual push every time. Make CI fast (2-3 minutes), reliable, and the ONLY way to get an image to production. Convenience drives compliance.
SC11
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC11
No Admission Control for Image Registries — Any Registry Allowed

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f - <<EOF; apiVersion: v1; kind: Deployment; spec: containers: [{name: evil, image: docker.io/attacker/backdoor:latest}] creates a pod pulling from an UNTRUSTED public registry. There's no OPA/Kyverno policy restricting which container registries pods can pull from. An attacker who gains deploy permissions (or compromises a CI token) can deploy a pod from docker.io/attacker/backdoor — an image they control — and run arbitrary code in the cluster. Only anihpj.azurecr.io images should be allowed, but ANY registry is accepted.

  kubectl run evil --image=docker.io/attacker/backdoor:latest -n anihpj
  pod/evil created   ← SHOULD HAVE BEEN REJECTED!

  kubectl get clusterpolicy -A | grep -i "allowed-registries\|image-registry"
  # No output — no registry allowlist policy
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No registry allowlist admission policy: No Kyverno ClusterPolicy or OPA ConstraintTemplate defining which registries are allowed. Any image from any registry — Docker Hub, quay.io, GHCR, attacker's private registry — can be deployed.
  2. Default-deny admission not configured: The approach is "allow everything unless blocked." The secure approach is "block everything, allow only approved registries." Without a default-deny posture, new registries are automatically trusted.
  3. Image tag omits registry (implicit docker.io): image: nginx:latest actually pulls from docker.io/library/nginx:latest. Without a registry prefix, Docker Hub is used implicitly — the largest public registry with millions of untrusted images.
  4. CI ServiceAccount can deploy arbitrary images: The CI pipeline has permissions to create pods and Deployments. If CI is compromised, the attacker can deploy images from their own registry — and no admission policy blocks it.
  5. Developers can deploy images from Docker Hub for testing: To test a third-party tool, a developer deployed docker.io/some-tool:latest in the cluster. The practice became normalized — anyone can deploy from any registry.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Registry allowlist configured but bypassed via mirror: Policy allows anihpj.azurecr.io/* but an attacker sets up a registry mirror that proxies anihpj.azurecr.io — but serves malicious images. The allowlist pattern matches the mirror.
  2. Allowlist uses tag patterns that don't cover digests: Policy allows anihpj.azurecr.io/*:* but images pinned by digest (anihpj.azurecr.io/anihpj-api@sha256:abc) don't match the :* pattern — and are BLOCKED. The fix was to remove the allowlist entirely instead of fixing the pattern.
  3. Internal Harbor registry not in allowlist: The team deployed Harbor for internal images but forgot to add harbor.internal.anihpj.com/* to the allowlist. Pods from Harbor are blocked — so the allowlist was removed to "fix" it.
  4. Allowlist enforced by mutating webhook instead of validating: A mutating webhook RE-WRITES the image registry to the approved one — but the original image's content is still pulled if the mutation fails silently. Use validating admission (reject), not mutating (rewrite).
  5. No image tag suffix restrictions: Policy allows anihpj.azurecr.io/* but doesn't block :latest tags. Developers deploy floating :latest images from the approved registry — still a supply chain risk, just from an approved source.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Kyverno/OPA not deployed: No policy engine installed. Admission control consists only of the built-in plugins — no custom policies for registry allowlisting.
  2. No image source policy defined: The organization hasn't decided which registries are "approved." Without a policy, there's nothing to enforce.
  3. All hands-on-deck during early development: Everyone deploys whatever they need to get started. Registry restrictions would "slow things down" — they're deferred indefinitely.
  4. Registry allowlist considered too restrictive for third-party tools: The cluster needs images from Docker Hub (nginx-ingress, cert-manager, Prometheus). The team blocks everything or nothing — no granular policy per namespace for system vs. user workloads.
  5. No image registry in the threat model: "Supply chain attacks via registry" is not in the team's threat model. The focus is on runtime attacks — the deployment path is unguarded.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get clusterpolicy -A -o yaml | grep -iE "image.*registr|allowed.*registr" Check if any Kyverno policy restricts image registries. If no results, any registry is allowed — including attacker-controlled ones.
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].image' | sed 's|/.*||' | sort -u List all unique registries used by running pods. Each registry outside your approved list is a supply chain risk.
kubectl run test --image=docker.io/busybox:latest --dry-run=server -n anihpj Test if you can deploy from an arbitrary public registry. If the dry-run succeeds (no rejection), there's no registry allowlist.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No admission policy restricts which container registries pods can pull from. Any image from any registry — including Docker Hub (millions of untrusted public images) or an attacker's private registry — can be deployed and run with the pod's ServiceAccount permissions.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Deploy Kyverno policy for registry allowlist apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1 kind: ClusterPolicy spec: rules: - name: allowed-registries validate: message: "Images must come from approved registries" pattern: spec: containers: - image: "anihpj.azurecr.io/* | harbor.internal.anihpj.com/*" Only images from your private registry and approved internal registries are allowed. Reject everything else.
2. Create per-namespace registry policies kube-system: allow registry.k8s.io/* and quay.io/jetstack/* (cert-manager). anihpj: allow ONLY anihpj.azurecr.io/*. System namespaces need broader access; user namespaces should be tightly restricted.
3. Block :latest and floating tags Kyverno policy: reject images with :latest tag or without a digest. Require explicit version tags or SHA256 digests for all images except in kube-system.
4. Mirror approved external images to your private registry Instead of allowing docker.io/*, mirror specific images (nginx-ingress, cert-manager, Prometheus) to your private registry. Pods only reference anihpj.azurecr.io/* — never external registries.
5. Monitor and alert on rejected registry violations Kyverno generates events on policy violations. Set up alerts: if someone attempts to deploy from an unapproved registry, notify the security team. This could indicate a compromised CI token or malicious insider.
💡 Personal Advice:
If you don't control which registries your pods pull from, attackers control what runs in your cluster. An attacker who gets deploy access just needs to push a malicious image to Docker Hub and reference it in a pod spec. A registry allowlist at admission time is the ONLY control that prevents this. Without it, your cluster trusts the entire internet.
Namespace-scoped registry policies are practical. kube-system needs images from Kubernetes, your CNI, and cert-manager. User namespaces should ONLY pull from your private registry. Separate policies per namespace make this possible without blocking essential infrastructure.
SC12
📦 CATEGORY 5: SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY — Issue SC12
Docker Build Cache Poisoned — Stale Layers Carry Old Vulns

🔍 Symptom: The CI pipeline uses Docker layer caching to speed up builds. docker build --cache-from anihpj/jobpost-api:latest reuses cached layers from previous builds. If the base image is updated (new security patches), the cached RUN apt-get update && apt-get install layer is NOT rebuilt — it uses the OLD layer with OLD packages and OLD vulnerabilities. The image appears up-to-date (new tag) but contains layers from 3 months ago with known CVEs. Cache poisoning also enables attackers: if a malicious layer is cached and the cache key matches, future builds use the poisoned layer without detection.

  docker build --cache-from anihpj/jobpost-api:latest -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.3 .
  Step 3/8 : RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
  ---> Using cache   ← REUSING 3-MONTH-OLD CACHED LAYER!
  # curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u7 (OLD) instead of curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u10 (PATCHED)

  docker history anihpj/jobpost-api:v1.3 | grep "apt-get"
  <missing>   /bin/sh -c apt-get update && apt-get install   3 months ago
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. --cache-from reuses stale layers: docker build --cache-from pulls cached layers from the registry. If the layer's cache key hasn't changed (same RUN command), Docker uses the cached version — even if it's months old. The layer is never rebuilt.
  2. apt-get update cached indefinitely: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl is cached. The apt-get update that fetches the latest package list happened 3 months ago. New packages with security patches are never seen because the update step is cached.
  3. No --no-cache flag on periodic rebuilds: The CI pipeline always uses cache. There's no scheduled weekly build with --no-cache to rebuild all layers from scratch with the latest packages. Images slowly drift out of date.
  4. apt list cache is inside the same RUN as install: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install combines update and install in ONE RUN. Docker caches the entire step. Separate into RUN apt-get update then RUN apt-get install — the install layer is rebuilt when packages change.
  5. Build cache shared across pipelines/developers: CI and developers share the same Docker layer cache. A developer's local build with compromised packages could poison the cache — and CI picks up the poisoned layer on the next build.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Dockerfile COPY/ADD cache invalidation failure: COPY requirements.txt /app/ should invalidate the cache when the file changes. If the file has the same content (pinned versions) but the packages have new CVEs, the cache is NOT invalidated. The old packages are used.
  2. BuildKit cache mounted across builds: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt shares the apt cache across builds. A compromised or stale cache persists — affecting all subsequent builds until the cache is manually cleared.
  3. Layer caching in CI runners (GitHub Actions, GitLab): CI runners cache Docker layers in /var/lib/docker. Across pipeline runs, stale layers persist on the runner. The image appears freshly built but uses layers from previous runs on the same runner.
  4. Cache poisoned by compromised base image: The base image layer is cached. If the base image was compromised and then fixed, the CI still has the compromised cached version. The fix is never picked up because the cache key hasn't changed.
  5. No cache validation or TTL: There's no maximum age for cached layers. A layer cached 6 months ago is used without question. Implement cache TTL: layers older than 7 days are rebuilt regardless of cache hit.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CI configured for speed over security: The pipeline was optimized for build speed. Caching was enabled globally without understanding the security implications of stale layers.
  2. No scheduled full rebuild (--no-cache): No cron job or scheduled pipeline that rebuilds all images with --no-cache weekly. Images accumulate stale layers indefinitely.
  3. Same Dockerfile RUN structure as tutorials: Tutorials use RUN apt-get update && apt-get install in one layer for efficiency. This collapses the update+install into one cached unit — preventing partial invalidation.
  4. No SBOM diffing that would detect stale packages: SBOMs are generated but not compared between builds. A diff would show: "curl version changed from X to Y — but our image still has X." Stale layers are detectable but undetected.
  5. No image layer age monitoring: No tool checking: "when was each layer in this image created?" Layers older than 30 days in a freshly-tagged image indicate cache poisoning or excessive caching.
🔍 What to Look At:
