🔐 Category 1: Cluster Setup Security Lab ScenariosS1–S15

🟢 anihpj/jobpost — Full-Stack Django + PostgreSQL Application

What is anihpj/jobpost? A Django-based job board application where employers post jobs and applicants apply. It consists of a Django web server, PostgreSQL database, and Redis cache. Each scenario deploys a part of this app with intentional security misconfigurations — your job is to find and fix them. Category 1 covers Cluster Setup Security (CKS Domain 1): NetworkPolicy enforcement, TLS/etcd security, RBAC, Node restrictions, CIS benchmarks, and API server hardening. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario before applying!

S1
🧪 SCENARIO S1 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security NetPol Debug

Deploy anihpj with Deny-All NetworkPolicy — Pods Still Communicate

The Problem: You deploy the anihpj/jobpost Django app + PostgreSQL in namespace anihpj, then apply a deny-all-ingress NetworkPolicy to isolate the namespace. But to your surprise, pods can still communicate — the NetworkPolicy has NO effect. The API server accepts the policy, kubectl get netpol shows it, but traffic flows freely. Your job: find why the NetworkPolicy is silently ignored and make it actually enforce isolation.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Single-node KinD cluster for Security labs
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Deny-All NetworkPolicy (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a Django job board app. Employers post jobs, applicants apply. Django serves the REST API at /api, admin at /admin. PostgreSQL stores: users, jobs, applications. The security team demands network isolation — but the deny-all policy you applied has zero effect. Pods can still reach each other. The app works fine, but the isolation requirement is FAILED.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S1): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL Deployment + Service (port 5432)
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django Deployment + Service (port 8000)
├── 03-deny-all-netpol.yaml        ← Deny-All Ingress NetworkPolicy (THE "FIX")
└── 04-test-pod.yaml               ← Busybox test pod to verify isolation
BASH — Deploy anihpj app + apply deny-all NetworkPolicy 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S1: Deny-All NetPol — CNI Doesn't Support It
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 2. DEPLOY POSTGRESQL DATABASE
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-db
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: anihpj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
EOF

# 3. DEPLOY DJANGO WEB APP
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: django:4.2-slim
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: "postgres://anihpj:secret123@anihpj-db:5432/jobpost"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
EOF

# 4. WAIT FOR PODS TO BE READY
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# 5. DEPLOY TEST POD (busybox with curl/nslookup)
kubectl run test-pod -n anihpj --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600

# 6. VERIFY CONNECTIVITY (before NetPol — should succeed)
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web:8000
# → Should return Django welcome page HTML

# 7. APPLY DENY-ALL INGRESS NETWORKPOLICY
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}        # Selects ALL pods in the namespace
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  # No ingress rules → denies ALL incoming traffic
EOF

# 8. TEST ISOLATION (should FAIL — but will SUCCEED due to no CNI)
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web:8000
# → STILL returns HTML! The deny-all had NO effect 🐛
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. The NetworkPolicy exists: kubectl get netpol -n anihpj → deny-all-ingress is present
✗2. Pod labels match: kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels → all pods have labels
✗3. Test pod can STILL reach web: kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- http://anihpj-web:8000 → returns HTML!
✗4. The deny-all NetworkPolicy is being silently ignored — no errors, no warnings
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check NetworkPolicy details: kubectl describe netpol deny-all-ingress -n anihpj
→ Policy looks correct: podSelector={}, no ingress rules, policyTypes=[Ingress]
2Check if ANY NetworkPolicy controller is running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -iE 'calico|weave|cilium|flannel|canal|network.policy'
→ NOTHING! No NetworkPolicy controller found
3Check the CNI in use: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -iE 'kindnet|calico|weave|cilium|flannel'
→ Only kindnet pods are running (kindnet does NOT support NetworkPolicy)
4Confirm CNI lacks NetPol support: kubectl get nodes -o wide then kubectl describe node kind-cl1-control-plane | grep -A5 'NetworkUnavailable\|CNI\|Conditions'
→ CNI: kindnet (default KinD CNI — NO NetworkPolicy support!)
5Root cause: The default KinD CNI (kindnet) does NOT implement the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy API. NetworkPolicy objects are accepted and stored by the API server but NEVER enforced. You MUST install a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, Weave Net).
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
NetPol applied but traffic flows → Check enforcement
②
kubectl get pods -n kube-system → Look for NP controller
③
Only kindnet found → kindnet does NOT support NetPol
④
CNI must support NetworkPolicy API → Install Calico
⑤
Re-test → wget times out → NetPol enforced ✅

Tenet: NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes API resource — the API server always accepts and stores it. But enforcement is done by the CNI plugin, NOT by Kubernetes itself. If your CNI doesn't implement the NetworkPolicy API (like kindnet, the default KinD CNI), your policies are silently ignored with zero errors. On the CKS exam, you must know which CNIs support NetworkPolicy: Calico, Cilium, Weave Net, Antrea (yes) vs Flannel, kindnet (no). Always verify: a working NetPol means traffic is actually blocked.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get netpol -n anihpj NAME POD-SELECTOR AGE deny-all-ingress <none> 5m
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web:8000 <!DOCTYPE html> <html>...Django welcome page...</html> ← STILL accessible! ❌
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -iE 'calico|weave|cilium|canal|kindnet' kindnet-abcde 1/1 Running 0 10m kindnet-fghij 1/1 Running 0 10m
$ kubectl describe netpol deny-all-ingress -n anihpj Name: deny-all-ingress Namespace: anihpj PodSelector: <none> (Allowing the specific traffic to all pods) Allowing ingress traffic: <none> (Selected pods are isolated for ingress connectivity) Policy Types: Ingress ⚠️ Policy looks correct but kindnet silently ignores it
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (Calico installed)
$ kubectl get pods -n calico-system NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE calico-kube-controllers-xxxxx 1/1 Running 0 2m calico-node-yyyyy 1/1 Running 0 2m calico-typha-zzzzz 1/1 Running 0 2m
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=5 http://anihpj-web:8000 wget: download timed out ✅ NetPol NOW ENFORCED!
🔧
BASH — Install Calico on KinD cluster (replaces kindnet) 
# Step 1: Install the Calico operator + custom resources on KinD
kubectl create -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/tigera-operator.yaml

# Step 2: Apply Calico custom resources (pod CIDR must match KinD: 10.244.0.0/16)
# For KinD, the default pod CIDR is 10.244.0.0/16
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: operator.tigera.io/v1
kind: Installation
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  calicoNetwork:
    ipPools:
    - name: default-ipv4-ippool
      blockSize: 26
      cidr: 10.244.0.0/16
      encapsulation: VXLANCrossSubnet
      natOutgoing: Enabled
      nodeSelector: all()
---
apiVersion: operator.tigera.io/v1
kind: APIServer
metadata:
  name: default
spec: {}
EOF

# Step 3: Wait for Calico pods to be ready (calico-system namespace)
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n calico-system --timeout=180s

# Step 4: Delete the old kindnet DaemonSet (Calico replaces it)
kubectl delete daemonset kindnet -n kube-system --ignore-not-found

# Step 5: Restart coredns (may need new IP after CNI switch)
kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system

# Step 6: Re-apply the NetworkPolicy (ensure it's picked up by Calico)
kubectl delete netpol deny-all-ingress -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
EOF

# Step 7: VERIFY — test pod can NO LONGER reach the web service
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=5 http://anihpj-web:8000
# Expected: "wget: download timed out" — NetPol is NOW enforced! ✅
✓

✅ Verify — NetworkPolicy Is Enforcing Isolation

After installing Calico and re-applying the deny-all NetworkPolicy, kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=5 http://anihpj-web:8000 returns "wget: download timed out". The deny-all policy is now actually enforced by Calico's felix agent. Pods in the anihpj namespace are fully isolated from ingress traffic.

💡 Key takeaway: NetworkPolicy objects are just declarative intent stored in etcd — the API server accepts them regardless. Enforcement requires a CNI plugin that implements the NetworkPolicy API. The default KinD CNI (kindnet) does NOT support NetworkPolicy. Always check kubectl get pods -n kube-system for a NetworkPolicy controller. Calico, Cilium, and Weave Net are the three most common CNIs that support NetworkPolicy on CKS.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside (pods, svc, netpol, test-pod)
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Remove Calico (if you want to revert to kindnet for other labs)
kubectl delete installation default
kubectl delete apiserver default
kubectl delete -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/tigera-operator.yaml --ignore-not-found

# Reinstall kindnet (optional — KinD auto-reinstalls it after Calico removal)
# kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aojea/kindnet/main/install-kindnet.yaml

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,netpol -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get pods -n calico-system 2>/dev/null
S2
🧪 SCENARIO S2 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security RBAC Debug

Deploy anihpj Pod with ServiceAccount — It Can Delete Any Pod Cluster-Wide

The Problem: You create a ServiceAccount anihpj-runner for the anihpj/jobpost app and bind it to a ClusterRole. But someone accidentally bound it to the built-in cluster-admin ClusterRole. Now any pod using this ServiceAccount has full administrative power over the ENTIRE cluster — it can delete pods in kube-system, read secrets in any namespace, even create new cluster roles. This is a critical privilege escalation vulnerability. Your job: detect the over-permission, create a properly scoped Role with minimal permissions, and rebind the ServiceAccount.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy anihpj ServiceAccount + Over-Permissive ClusterRoleBinding (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a Django job board. The Django app needs to list its own pods for health checks and read its own ConfigMaps. A ServiceAccount anihpj-runner was created. But the binding uses cluster-admin — giving the Django pod power to delete anything in the cluster, including kube-system pods. This is the #1 RBAC mistake on CKS: using cluster-admin for app ServiceAccounts.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S2): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml                     ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-serviceaccount.yaml                ← anihpj-runner ServiceAccount
├── 02-clusterrolebinding.yaml            ← BROKEN: binds anihpj-runner → cluster-admin
├── 03-test-pod.yaml                      ← Pod using anihpj-runner SA (runs kubectl)
├── 04-limited-clusterrole.yaml           ← ✅ FIX: Proper limited ClusterRole
└── 05-corrected-clusterrolebinding.yaml  ← ✅ FIX: Corrected binding
BASH — Deploy namespace, SA, over-permissive ClusterRoleBinding, test pod 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S2: SA Gets ClusterAdmin — RBAC Privilege Escalation
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 2. CREATE SERVICEACCOUNT for anihpj-runner
kubectl create serviceaccount anihpj-runner -n anihpj

# 3. CREATE THE OVER-PERMISSIVE ClusterRoleBinding (THE BUG!)
# ⚠️ This binds anihpj-runner to cluster-admin — giving it FULL CLUSTER POWER
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: anihpj-runner-binding
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: anihpj-runner
  namespace: anihpj
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-admin     # ❌ BUG! Should NOT be cluster-admin
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
EOF

# 4. DEPLOY TEST POD — runs as anihpj-runner SA, has kubectl inside
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-test
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-runner   # ← Uses the over-permissioned SA
  containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    # Note: In a real cluster, kubectl inside the pod needs to be installed
    # For CKS, you would use: kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner
EOF

# 5. TEST THE PRIVILEGE ESCALATION (run from your workstation, not the pod)
# Check what the SA can do — it should ONLY need pod list in its namespace
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner
# → yes ✅ (this is fine, the SA needs this)

kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner
# → yes ❌ BUG! The SA can delete kube-system pods!

kubectl auth can-i list secrets -A --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner
# → yes ❌ BUG! The SA can read ALL secrets in ALL namespaces!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check the ClusterRoleBinding: kubectl get clusterrolebinding anihpj-runner-binding -o yaml | grep 'name: cluster-admin' → cluster-admin!
✗2. SA can delete system pods: kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner → yes
✗3. SA can list all secrets: kubectl auth can-i list secrets -A --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner → yes
✗4. A compromised Django pod with this SA = full cluster takeover — attackers can delete everything
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1List all ClusterRoleBindings referencing the SA: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B10 'anihpj-runner'
→ Found: anihpj-runner-binding → roleRef: cluster-admin
2Check what cluster-admin can actually do: kubectl describe clusterrole cluster-admin
→ Verbs: ["*"], Resources: ["*.*"] — COMPLETE UNRESTRICTED ACCESS
3Audit what the Django app ACTUALLY needs: kubectl get pods,configmaps -n anihpj
→ App only needs: list/get pods and get configmaps in anihpj namespace
4Compare: SA needs 2 verbs on 2 resources in 1 namespace — cluster-admin grants ALL verbs on ALL resources in ALL namespaces
5Root cause: The ClusterRoleBinding references the built-in "cluster-admin" ClusterRole instead of a custom limited ClusterRole. This is a violation of least-privilege principle. Every ServiceAccount should get ONLY the exact permissions it needs — never cluster-admin.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
SA can delete kube-system pods → Check binding
②
ClusterRoleBinding → roleRef: cluster-admin → BUG!
③
Audit actual app needs → list pods, get configmaps only
④
Create limited ClusterRole → verbs: [get, list], single namespace
⑤
Rebind SA → verify can't delete system pods → Least privilege enforced ✅

Tenet: The built-in cluster-admin ClusterRole grants unrestricted access to every resource in every namespace — including secrets, pods, nodes, and RBAC objects. Binding ANY ServiceAccount to cluster-admin is a CRITICAL security violation. On the CKS exam, you must audit ClusterRoleBindings and identify any that grant excessive permissions. The fix is always: create a custom ClusterRole with ONLY the verbs and resources the app actually needs, using resourceNames to further scope access if possible.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get clusterrolebinding anihpj-runner-binding -o yaml apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRoleBinding metadata: name: anihpj-runner-binding roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: ClusterRole name: cluster-admin ← ❌ FULL CLUSTER ADMIN! subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount name: anihpj-runner namespace: anihpj
$ kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner Resources Non-Resource URLs Resource Names Verbs *.* [*] [*] [*] * [] [*] [*] ← ALL resources, ALL verbs!
$ kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner yes ❌ SA can delete coredns, kube-proxy, etc!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (Limited ClusterRole)
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner yes ✅ SA can list pods in its own namespace (needed)
$ kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner no ✅ SA can NO LONGER delete system pods!
$ kubectl auth can-i list secrets -A --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner no ✅ SA can NO LONGER access secrets cluster-wide!
🔧
BASH — Delete old binding, create limited ClusterRole, rebind correctly 
# Step 1: DELETE the dangerous ClusterRoleBinding
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding anihpj-runner-binding

# Step 2: Create a LIMITED ClusterRole — ONLY what the Django app actually needs
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: anihpj-limited-role
rules:
# Allow listing pods (needed for health checks) — scoped to anihpj namespace via RoleBinding
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
# Allow reading ConfigMaps (needed for app configuration)
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
# Allow reading Secrets (ONLY in anihpj namespace — scoped via RoleBinding)
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]
  verbs: ["get"]
EOF

# Step 3: Create a NAMESPACE-SCOPED RoleBinding (NOT ClusterRoleBinding)
# This limits the ClusterRole's power to ONLY the anihpj namespace
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: anihpj-runner-binding
  namespace: anihpj
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: anihpj-runner
  namespace: anihpj
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: anihpj-limited-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
EOF

# Step 4: VERIFY — SA should NO LONGER have cluster-wide power
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner
# Expected: "no" ✅

kubectl auth can-i list pods -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner
# Expected: "yes" ✅ (still works within its namespace)
✓

✅ Verify — Least Privilege Is Enforced

After deleting the old cluster-admin binding and creating a limited ClusterRole with a namespace-scoped RoleBinding, the SA anihpj-runner can only get/list pods, get configmaps, and get secrets — all scoped to the anihpj namespace only. kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-runner now returns no.

💡 Key takeaway: The cluster-admin ClusterRole is the Kubernetes equivalent of root. Never bind application ServiceAccounts to it. Always create a custom ClusterRole with only the verbs and resources the app needs. Use a RoleBinding (not ClusterRoleBinding) to scope the ClusterRole to a single namespace. This pattern — ClusterRole + RoleBinding — lets you reuse the same role definition across namespaces while keeping each binding scoped.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside (SA, pod, RoleBinding)
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete the ClusterRole and old ClusterRoleBinding (not namespaced)
kubectl delete clusterrole anihpj-limited-role
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding anihpj-runner-binding --ignore-not-found

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get sa,rolebinding -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get clusterrole,clusterrolebinding | grep anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S3
🧪 SCENARIO S3 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security CIS Debug

Deploy anihpj — Discover Kubelet Accepts Unauthenticated Requests

The Problem: You deploy the anihpj/jobpost app on worker nodes. While checking node security, you discover that the kubelet on each node accepts unauthenticated HTTPS requests on port 10250. Anyone with network access to the node can run curl -k https://node-ip:10250/pods and get a complete list of all pods running on that node — including their names, namespaces, container images, and labels. This violates CIS Benchmark rule 4.1.1: "Ensure that the kubelet --anonymous-auth argument is set to false." Your job: find the misconfiguration, fix it via the kubelet config file, and verify authentication is enforced.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster (cp, wk1, wk2)
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Probe Kubelet for Unauthenticated Access (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is deployed across 2 worker nodes. Django pods run on wk1 and wk2. PostgreSQL is on cp. During a routine security audit, you check if the kubelet API is properly secured. To your alarm, you can curl the kubelet's /pods endpoint with NO authentication token and get a full list of running pods — including pods from other tenants on the same node. This is a CIS Benchmark violation and a serious information disclosure risk.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S3): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL on cp node
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django on wk1 + wk2 (nodeSelector)
├── 03-django-service.yaml         ← ClusterIP Service
└── 04-probe-kubelet.sh            ← Script to test kubelet anonymous access
BASH — Deploy anihpj + Test kubelet anonymous access 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S3: Kubelet Anonymous-Auth Enabled — CIS 4.1.1 Violation
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 2. DEPLOY POSTGRESQL (cp node)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: ""
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: anihpj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
EOF

# 3. DEPLOY DJANGO (wk1 + wk2 workers)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

# 4. WAIT FOR PODS
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# 5. PROBE KUBELET — TEST FOR UNAUTHENTICATED ACCESS (THE BUG!)
# Get the IP of worker node wk1
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node wk1 -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
echo "Probing kubelet on wk1: $NODE_IP"

# Try to access kubelet /pods endpoint WITHOUT authentication
curl -k https://$NODE_IP:10250/pods 2>/dev/null | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}' | head -30
# → RETURNS POD LIST! ❌ No auth required — CIS 4.1.1 FAILED

# 6. CHECK KUBELET CONFIGURATION (on the node)
# SSH to wk1 or use docker exec for KinD nodes
docker exec -it kind-cka-lab-worker cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep -A2 anonymous
# → anonymous: enabled: true  ← BUG! Should be false
# → authentication: anonymous: enabled: true
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. curl kubelet WITHOUT token: curl -k https://NODE_IP:10250/pods → returns full pod list!
✗2. No Authorization header needed — anyone on the network can query kubelet
✗3. Check kubelet config: cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep anonymous → enabled: true
✗4. CIS Benchmark 4.1.1 explicitly requires --anonymous-auth=false — this cluster FAILS
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check kubelet config file on node: docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
→ authentication.anonymous.enabled: true ← CIS VIOLATION
2Check kubelet startup flags: ps aux | grep kubelet on the node
→ --anonymous-auth=true (or missing = defaults to true)
3Run CIS benchmark scan: kube-bench run --targets node --check 4.1.1
→ [FAIL] 4.1.1 Ensure that the kubelet --anonymous-auth argument is set to false
4Check what data is exposed: curl -k https://NODE_IP:10250/pods reveals all pod names, namespaces, images, labels
5Root cause: The kubelet configuration has authentication.anonymous.enabled set to true. This allows anyone with network access to the node to query the kubelet API on port 10250 without any authentication. CIS Benchmark rule 4.1.1 requires this to be false for all nodes. Combined with --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow (another CIS fail), unauthenticated users can read AND modify pod state.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
curl kubelet /pods → returns data without auth → anon enabled
②
Check kubelet config.yaml → authentication.anonymous.enabled: true
③
CIS 4.1.1 requires anonymous-auth=false → FAIL
④
Edit config.yaml → set enabled: false → restart kubelet
⑤
curl again → 401 Unauthorized → CIS 4.1.1 PASS ✅

Tenet: The kubelet API (port 10250) is the control interface for pods on a node. It can list, create, and delete pods, access container logs, and execute commands inside containers. Anonymous authentication means ANYONE with network access to the node has these powers. CIS Benchmark 4.1.1 is non-negotiable: --anonymous-auth=false must be set. On the CKS exam, you must know how to check kubelet configuration via /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml and verify with kube-bench or manual curl tests.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -k https://10.89.0.3:10250/pods 2>/dev/null | jq '.items[0].metadata.name' "anihpj-web-7d8f9c6b-abcde" ← Pod name exposed WITHOUT auth!
$ docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep -A3 anonymous authentication: anonymous: enabled: true ← ❌ CIS 4.1.1 FAIL webhook: enabled: true
$ kube-bench run --targets node --check 4.1.1 [FAIL] 4.1.1 Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false Remediation: Edit the kubelet config file /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml and set authentication.anonymous.enabled to false.
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -k https://10.89.0.3:10250/pods 2>&1 Unauthorized ✅ Authentication now REQUIRED!
$ kube-bench run --targets node --check 4.1.1 [PASS] 4.1.1 Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false ✅
🔧
BASH — Edit kubelet config.yaml on EACH node + restart kubelet 
# Step 1: For KinD, exec into each node container
# Repeat for every node: cp, wk1, wk2

# On worker node wk1:
docker exec -it kind-cka-lab-worker sh -c "
# Step 2: Edit the kubelet config file
# Change: authentication.anonymous.enabled: true → false
sed -i 's/enabled: true/enabled: false/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

# Also ensure authorization mode is NOT AlwaysAllow
# Change: authorization.mode: AlwaysAllow → Webhook
sed -i 's/mode: AlwaysAllow/mode: Webhook/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

# Step 3: Restart kubelet to apply changes
systemctl restart kubelet
# OR for KinD nodes without systemd: kill and let container runtime restart it
pkill kubelet
"

# Step 4: Wait for node to be Ready again
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready node/wk1 --timeout=60s

# Step 5: VERIFY — anonymous access is now BLOCKED
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node wk1 -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
curl -k https://$NODE_IP:10250/pods 2>&1
# Expected: "Unauthorized" ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Kubelet Requires Authentication

After editing /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml on each node and setting authentication.anonymous.enabled: false plus authorization.mode: Webhook, the kubelet now rejects all unauthenticated requests. curl -k https://NODE_IP:10250/pods returns 401 Unauthorized. Only authenticated requests with a valid bearer token or client certificate are now accepted. The node passes CIS Benchmark 4.1.1.

💡 Key takeaway: The kubelet config file is at /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (or /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf on kubeadm). CIS 4.1.1 requires authentication.anonymous.enabled: false. Combined with CIS 4.1.2 (authorization.mode: Webhook, not AlwaysAllow), this ensures only the API server can talk to kubelets. On the CKS exam, you must fix this on ALL nodes — worker nodes are often forgotten but are equally vulnerable.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Revert kubelet config (restore anonymous auth for lab purposes)
# docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker sed -i 's/enabled: false/enabled: true/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker pkill kubelet

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S4
🧪 SCENARIO S4 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security TLS Debug

Deploy anihpj with Ingress — Discover TLS Is Completely Missing

The Problem: You deploy anihpj/jobpost with an Nginx Ingress to expose the web app externally. The Ingress YAML has NO TLS section at all — it only serves plain HTTP on port 80. Anyone on the network can intercept traffic, steal session cookies, and read job applications in transit. The security team requires ALL external traffic to be HTTPS with TLS 1.2+. Your job: find the missing TLS configuration, create a TLS Secret from a certificate, and update the Ingress to enforce HTTPS while redirecting HTTP to HTTPS.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD, Ingress controller pre-installed
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Ingress Without TLS (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a public job board. Employers and applicants access it at jobs.anihpj.com. The Ingress was deployed quickly to get the app online — but no TLS was configured. All traffic between users and the job board is in plaintext. Login credentials, session tokens, and submitted job applications are visible to anyone on the network path. This fails compliance and exposes user data.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S4): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django Deployment (port 8000)
├── 02-django-service.yaml         ← ClusterIP Service
├── 03-ingress-http-only.yaml      ← BROKEN: Ingress WITHOUT TLS section
├── 04-tls-secret-openssl.sh       ← Script to generate TLS cert + Secret
└── 05-ingress-https-fixed.yaml    ← ✅ FIX: Ingress WITH TLS + HTTP→HTTPS redirect
BASH — Deploy anihpj web app with HTTP-only Ingress (NO TLS!) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S4: Ingress Without TLS — Plain HTTP Exposure
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 2. DEPLOY DJANGO WEB APP
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF

# 3. DEPLOY INGRESS — NO TLS SECTION! (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: jobs.anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-web
            port:
              number: 80
  # ❌ BUG: NO tls: section! All traffic is plain HTTP!
EOF

# 4. TEST — curl returns plain HTTP (no HTTPS redirect, no TLS)
INGRESS_IP=$(kubectl get ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')
curl -v http://$INGRESS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>&1 | grep -E "HTTP|Server|<"
# → HTTP/1.1 200 OK   ← Plain HTTP! No TLS! ❌

curl -v https://$INGRESS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>&1 | grep -E "HTTP|SSL|failed"
# → SSL connection failed or no HTTPS listener   ← HTTPS doesn't even work! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Ingress has NO tls section: kubectl get ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 'tls:' → NOTHING!
✗2. curl to HTTP works: curl -I http://JOBS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" → HTTP/1.1 200 OK
✗3. curl to HTTPS fails: curl -k https://JOBS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" → connection refused / no listener
✗4. All user credentials and job applications travel in plaintext — compliance FAILED
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Inspect the Ingress YAML: kubectl get ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -o yaml
→ spec only has "rules:" — NO "tls:" section exists at all
2Check for TLS Secrets: kubectl get secrets -n anihpj | grep tls
→ No TLS secrets found — no certificate has been created
3Verify nginx.conf inside Ingress controller: kubectl exec -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller -- cat /etc/nginx/nginx.conf | grep -A5 'jobs.anihpj.com'
→ Only "listen 80;" — NO "listen 443 ssl;" — HTTPS not configured
4Security impact: Session cookies, passwords, and PII in job applications are transmitted in plaintext
5Root cause: The Ingress resource was deployed WITHOUT a tls: section. An Ingress without tls: only listens on port 80 (HTTP). To enable HTTPS, you need: (1) a TLS certificate stored as a Kubernetes Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls, (2) a tls: section in the Ingress spec referencing that secret, and (3) an annotation to force HTTP→HTTPS redirect.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
curl HTTP works, HTTPS fails → No TLS configured on Ingress
②
kubectl get ingress -o yaml → spec.tls is MISSING
③
No TLS Secret exists → Generate cert + create Secret
④
Update Ingress → add tls: + force-ssl-redirect annotation
⑤
curl HTTPS → 200 OK → curl HTTP → 308 Redirect → TLS enforced ✅

Tenet: An Ingress resource without a tls: section is an HTTP-only endpoint. TLS termination happens at the Ingress controller — you need BOTH a TLS Secret (containing cert + key) AND the tls: block in the Ingress spec. Simply having a certificate doesn't enable HTTPS; the Ingress must reference it. On CKS, you must also enforce HTTP→HTTPS redirect via the nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true" annotation — otherwise users can still connect over plain HTTP.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 tls # No output — tls: section does NOT exist! ❌
$ curl -v http://10.96.1.5 -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>&1 | grep "< HTTP" < HTTP/1.1 200 OK ← Plain HTTP, no encryption ❌
$ curl -v https://10.96.1.5 -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>&1 | head -5 * connect to 10.96.1.5 port 443 failed: Connection refused ← No HTTPS listener at all ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (TLS enabled)
$ curl -kv https://10.96.1.5 -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>&1 | grep "< HTTP" < HTTP/2 200 OK ← HTTPS with TLS encryption ✅
$ curl -v http://10.96.1.5 -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>&1 | grep "< HTTP" < HTTP/1.1 308 Permanent Redirect ← HTTP auto-redirects to HTTPS ✅
🔧
BASH — Create TLS Secret + Patch Ingress for HTTPS enforcement 
# Step 1: GENERATE a self-signed TLS certificate for jobs.anihpj.com
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout anihpj-tls.key \
  -out anihpj-tls.crt \
  -subj "/CN=jobs.anihpj.com/O=anihpj"

# Step 2: CREATE a Kubernetes TLS Secret from the certificate
kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls \
  --cert=anihpj-tls.crt \
  --key=anihpj-tls.key \
  -n anihpj

# Step 3: PATCH the Ingress to ADD the tls: section
kubectl patch ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj --type='json' \
  -p='[{
    "op": "add",
    "path": "/spec/tls",
    "value": [{
      "hosts": ["jobs.anihpj.com"],
      "secretName": "anihpj-tls"
    }]
  }]'

# Step 4: ADD force-ssl-redirect annotation to redirect HTTP → HTTPS
kubectl annotate ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj \
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect="true" --overwrite

# Step 5: VERIFY — HTTPS works, HTTP redirects
INGRESS_IP=$(kubectl get ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')
curl -k https://$INGRESS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"
# Expected: 200 ✅

curl -I http://$INGRESS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>/dev/null | head -1
# Expected: HTTP/1.1 308 Permanent Redirect ✅
✓

✅ Verify — TLS Is Enforced on All Traffic

After generating a TLS certificate, creating a kubernetes.io/tls Secret, adding the tls: section to the Ingress, and applying the force-ssl-redirect annotation, the anihpj/jobpost job board now: (1) serves HTTPS on port 443 with TLS encryption, (2) automatically redirects all HTTP requests to HTTPS with a 308 Permanent Redirect, and (3) encrypts all user credentials and job application data in transit.

💡 Key takeaway: TLS for Ingress requires THREE things: (1) a kubernetes.io/tls Secret with tls.crt and tls.key, (2) a tls: block in the Ingress spec referencing the secret, and (3) the force-ssl-redirect annotation to prevent plain HTTP access. Without ALL three, your app is either unreachable via HTTPS or still serves plain HTTP alongside HTTPS. On CKS, use kubectl create secret tls — it automatically sets the correct type and data keys.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside (deploy, svc, ingress, secrets)
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Remove local cert files
rm -f anihpj-tls.key anihpj-tls.crt

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,ingress,secrets -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null

🧪 SCENARIO S5 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security NodeSec Debug

Deploy anihpj — Anyone Can Query kubelet readOnlyPort 10255

The Problem: After deploying anihpj/jobpost, you perform a node security audit and discover that the kubelet read-only port (10255) is open and accessible. A simple curl http://NODE_IP:10255/pods — with NO authentication, NO HTTPS — returns a complete list of all pods running on that node. This port exposes pod metadata, resource usage, and node configuration to anyone with network access. CIS Benchmark rule 4.1.3 requires this port to be disabled (--read-only-port=0). Your job: find the exposed port, disable it in the kubelet config, and verify the port is no longer accessible.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Probe kubelet Read-Only Port 10255 (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is deployed on the production kubeadm cluster. During a routine Nmap scan, the security team flags port 10255 as open on all nodes. This is the kubelet's unauthenticated read-only API — it requires zero authentication and serves pod lists, node stats, and container metrics over plain HTTP. An attacker on the same network can enumerate all pods, their images, and resource usage without leaving any auth log. CIS 4.1.3: "Ensure that the --read-only-port is set to 0."
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S5): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL Deployment
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django Deployment (port 8000)
└── 03-probe-readonly-port.sh      ← Script to probe port 10255
BASH — Deploy anihpj + Test kubelet read-only port exposure 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S5: Kubelet readOnlyPort 10255 Exposed — CIS 4.1.3 Violation
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE + DEPLOY ANIHPJ
kubectl create namespace anihpj

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# 2. PROBE READ-ONLY PORT 10255 (NO AUTH, PLAIN HTTP!)
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node anih -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
echo "Probing node anih at $NODE_IP"

# List ALL pods on this node — NO authentication needed!
curl -s http://$NODE_IP:10255/pods | python3 -m json.tool | head -30
# → RETURNS COMPLETE POD LIST with metadata! ❌ CIS 4.1.3 FAIL

# Get node stats — CPU, memory, network
curl -s http://$NODE_IP:10255/stats/summary | python3 -m json.tool | head -20
# → RETURNS resource usage data! ❌

# 3. SCAN FOR OPEN PORT
nmap -p 10255 $NODE_IP 2>/dev/null | grep 10255
# → 10255/tcp open   ← Port is EXPOSED
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Port 10255 is open: nmap -p 10255 NODE_IP → open
✗2. No auth, plain HTTP: curl http://NODE_IP:10255/pods → full pod list returned
✗3. Check kubelet flags: ps aux | grep kubelet | grep read-only-port → --read-only-port=10255 (or absent = default 10255)
✗4. CIS 4.1.3 requires --read-only-port=0 — this cluster is wide open
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if port 10255 is listening: ss -tlnp | grep 10255 (on the node)
→ LISTEN 0.0.0.0:10255 — kubelet process
2Check kubelet config: cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep readOnlyPort
→ readOnlyPort: 10255 (or absent = default 10255)
3What data is leaked: pod names, namespaces, images, labels, annotations, node CPU/memory stats
4Difference from port 10250: 10250 is the authenticated kubelet API (HTTPS), 10255 is the read-only unauthenticated port (HTTP) — even more dangerous because there are zero auth logs
5Root cause: The kubelet read-only port (10255) provides an UNauthenticated, plain-HTTP endpoint that exposes pod lists, node metrics, and container information. CIS Benchmark 4.1.3 mandates setting readOnlyPort: 0 (disabled). This legacy port was kept for backwards compatibility but has been deprecated since Kubernetes 1.10 and is a well-known reconnaissance vector for attackers.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
nmap shows port 10255 open → Check what it serves
②
curl /pods returns data without auth → read-only port active
③
Check config.yaml → readOnlyPort: 10255 → CIS 4.1.3 FAIL
④
Set readOnlyPort: 0 → restart kubelet → port closed
⑤
nmap again → port filtered/closed → CIS 4.1.3 PASS ✅

Tenet: Port 10255 is the kubelet's legacy read-only API — it requires zero authentication, uses plain HTTP (not HTTPS), and exposes pod lists, node stats, and container specs to anyone who can reach the node. This is a goldmine for attackers doing reconnaissance. CIS 4.1.3 requires readOnlyPort: 0. Unlike port 10250 (which you fix with anonymous-auth=false), port 10255 has NO authentication layer at all — it must be completely disabled.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ nmap -p 10255 192.168.1.10 2>/dev/null | grep 10255 10255/tcp open unknown ← Port exposed! ❌
$ curl -s http://192.168.1.10:10255/pods | python3 -c "import sys,json; [print(p['metadata']['name'],p['metadata']['namespace']) for p in json.load(sys.stdin)['items']]" anihpj-web-7d8f-abcde anihpj ← Pod names leaked! anihpj-web-7d8f-fghij anihpj ← No authentication at all ❌
$ cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep readOnlyPort readOnlyPort: 10255 ← Should be 0 per CIS 4.1.3 ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ nmap -p 10255 192.168.1.10 2>/dev/null | grep 10255 10255/tcp closed unknown ← Port DISABLED ✅
$ curl -s --connect-timeout 3 http://192.168.1.10:10255/pods curl: (7) Failed to connect — Connection refused ✅
🔧
BASH — Edit kubelet config + restart kubelet on each node 
# Step 1: Edit kubelet config on the node (kubeadm cluster)
# The kubelet config file is at /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
sudo sed -i 's/readOnlyPort: 10255/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

# If readOnlyPort line doesn't exist, add it under the top-level config:
# sudo sh -c 'echo "readOnlyPort: 0" >> /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml'

# Step 2: Also ensure the kubelet startup flags include --read-only-port=0
# On kubeadm, check: /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf
# Or the kubelet drop-in file. Add: --read-only-port=0

# Step 3: Restart kubelet to apply changes
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# Step 4: Wait for node to be Ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready node/anih --timeout=120s

# Step 5: VERIFY port is closed
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node anih -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
curl -s --connect-timeout 3 http://$NODE_IP:10255/pods 2>&1
# Expected: "Connection refused" ✅

nmap -p 10255 $NODE_IP 2>/dev/null | grep 10255
# Expected: "10255/tcp closed" ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Kubelet Read-Only Port Is Disabled

After setting readOnlyPort: 0 in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml and restarting the kubelet, port 10255 is now closed. nmap -p 10255 NODE_IP shows closed and curl returns Connection refused. The node now passes CIS Benchmark 4.1.3. The only kubelet API remaining is port 10250, which requires authentication.

💡 Key takeaway: Port 10255 is a legacy read-only kubelet API that was deprecated in Kubernetes 1.10. It has NO authentication and uses plain HTTP. CIS 4.1.3 requires readOnlyPort: 0. Unlike anonymous-auth (which you set to false), the read-only port must be completely disabled because it has no auth layer at all. On CKS, always check both 10250 (auth) and 10255 (read-only) when auditing node security.

🧹

kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Revert kubelet config (restore readOnlyPort for lab purposes)
# sudo sed -i 's/readOnlyPort: 0/readOnlyPort: 10255/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null

🧪 SCENARIO S6 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security API Debug

Deploy anihpj — Discover API Server Accepts Anonymous Requests

The Problem: You deploy anihpj/jobpost. While testing, you accidentally run kubectl get pods WITHOUT any kubeconfig and it succeeds. The API server's --anonymous-auth flag is set to true, allowing anyone with network access to the API server to make requests as user system:anonymous. Combined with an overly permissive RBAC binding to this anonymous user, unauthenticated users can list, read, and potentially modify cluster resources. CIS Benchmark rule 1.1.1 requires anonymous-auth=false. Your job: detect the anonymous access, identify what the anonymous user can do, and disable anonymous authentication on the API server.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Test Anonymous API Access (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is running on the production kubeadm cluster. A developer reports they accidentally ran kubectl without a kubeconfig file and to their shock, it worked — they could list pods! The API server's anonymous-auth is enabled, and system:anonymous user has been granted view permissions via a misconfigured ClusterRoleBinding. Anyone on the network can query the API server without credentials.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S6): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django Deployment
└── 02-test-anonymous-access.sh    ← Script testing anonymous API calls
BASH — Deploy + Test anonymous API server access 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S6: API Server Anonymous-Auth Enabled — CIS 1.1.1 Violation
# ============================================

# 1. DEPLOY ANIHPJ
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# 2. TEST ANONYMOUS ACCESS (THE BUG!)
# Query API server without ANY credentials — no kubeconfig, no token, no cert
API_SERVER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')
echo "API Server: $API_SERVER"

# Try listing pods as anonymous user
curl -k -s $API_SERVER/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj/pods \
  -H "Accept: application/json" 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | head -30
# → RETURNS POD LIST! ❌ Anonymous user has access!

# Check what the anonymous user can do
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n anihpj --as=system:anonymous
# → yes ❌ BUG! Anonymous shouldn't be able to do ANYTHING

# 3. CHECK API SERVER CONFIGURATION
# On the control plane node, check the API server manifest
sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep anonymous-auth
# → --anonymous-auth=true   ← CIS 1.1.1 FAIL! Should be false
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Anonymous can list pods: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:anonymous → yes
✗2. Anonymous can read nodes: kubectl auth can-i get nodes --as=system:anonymous → yes
✗3. curl without token returns data: curl -k $API_SERVER/api/v1/pods → pod list returned
✗4. API server manifest: --anonymous-auth=true — CIS 1.1.1 FAILED
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check API server flags: sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep '\-\-anonymous-auth'
→ --anonymous-auth=true ← CIS 1.1.1 requires false
2Check what anonymous can do: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:anonymous
→ Resources: pods, nodes, namespaces, configmaps — Verbs: get, list — WAY too much
3Check if system:anonymous has RBAC bindings: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B5 'system:anonymous'
→ Found binding: system:anonymous → view ClusterRole (read-only access to most resources)
4Without anonymous-auth=false, even without RBAC bindings, anonymous users can still hit discovery endpoints and leak API structure
5Root cause: The API server has --anonymous-auth=true (CIS 1.1.1 violation). While anonymous requests are supposed to be blocked by RBAC, a misconfigured ClusterRoleBinding grants system:anonymous the view ClusterRole, giving unauthenticated users read access to almost all resources cluster-wide. The fix requires BOTH: (1) set --anonymous-auth=false on the API server, AND (2) remove any RBAC bindings for system:anonymous.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Anonymous user lists pods → API server accepts unauthenticated
②
Check kube-apiserver manifest → --anonymous-auth=true
③
Check RBAC → system:anonymous bound to view ClusterRole
④
Edit manifest → --anonymous-auth=false → remove binding
⑤
Anonymous curl → 401 Unauthorized → CIS 1.1.1 PASS ✅

Tenet: The API server's --anonymous-auth flag controls whether requests without credentials are accepted as user system:anonymous. When true, RBAC still applies — but if someone accidentally binds system:anonymous to any ClusterRole, unauthenticated users gain those permissions. The defense-in-depth fix: set --anonymous-auth=false AND never bind system:anonymous to any role. On CKS, this is CIS Benchmark 1.1.1 — one of the first checks in any security audit.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:anonymous yes ❌ Anonymous user has pod list access!
$ sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep anonymous - --anonymous-auth=true ← CIS 1.1.1 FAIL ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:anonymous no ✅ Anonymous user BLOCKED!
$ curl -k $API_SERVER/api/v1/pods 2>&1 | head -1 {"kind":"Status","status":"Failure","reason":"Unauthorized"} ✅
🔧
BASH — Edit API server manifest + remove anonymous bindings 
# Step 1: Edit the kube-apiserver manifest ON THE CONTROL PLANE NODE
# Change --anonymous-auth=true to --anonymous-auth=false
sudo sed -i 's/--anonymous-auth=true/--anonymous-auth=false/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Step 2: Wait for API server to restart (kubelet auto-restarts it)
sleep 30
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-apiserver
# Wait until the new API server pod is Running

# Step 3: Remove ALL RBAC bindings for system:anonymous
# Find any ClusterRoleBindings referencing system:anonymous
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="system:anonymous") | .metadata.name' | \
  xargs -I {} kubectl delete clusterrolebinding {}

# Also check RoleBindings in all namespaces
kubectl get rolebinding -A -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="system:anonymous") | "\(.metadata.namespace) \(.metadata.name)"' | \
  while read ns name; do kubectl delete rolebinding $name -n $ns; done

# Step 4: VERIFY anonymous access is BLOCKED
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: "no" ✅
✓

This is a CRITICAL CIS Benchmark violation (rules 2.1-2.4). Your job: enable TLS on etcd client connections, require client certificates, and verify encryption.

📋 Deploy anihpj + Audit etcd for TLS (CONTAINS THE BUG)

During a security audit, you check etcd's configuration and find --client-cert-auth=false — meaning etcd accepts clients without verifying certificates. An attacker with network access to port 2379 can connect via etcdctl and read every Secret in the cluster, including database passwords and API tokens.

spec:

EOF

# 3. AUDIT ETCD — Check if TLS is enforced for client connections

sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep -E 'client-cert-auth|cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file'

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check etcd manifest: sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep client-cert-auth → false
✗2. etcd accepts unauthenticated gRPC: anyone on the network can connect to port 2379
✗3. The Secret anihpj-db-creds is stored in etcd — readable by anyone with network access
✗4. CIS 2.1-2.4 require TLS for ALL etcd connections — this cluster FAILS all 4 checks
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Inspect etcd manifest: sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
→ --client-cert-auth=false ← CIS 2.2: Must be true
2Check if cert files are specified: grep -E 'cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
→ All cert paths are set but --client-cert-auth=false means they're OPTIONAL
3Check if auto-tls is enabled: grep 'auto-tls' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
→ --auto-tls=true would generate self-signed certs automatically (also CIS fail)
4Data at risk: ALL Secrets, ConfigMaps, Deployments, Services, RBAC rules, ServiceAccount tokens — the entire cluster state
5Root cause: The etcd server has --client-cert-auth=false. This means client TLS certificates are OPTIONAL — etcd will accept connections without verifying a client certificate. An attacker with network access to port 2379 can read/write ALL cluster data. CIS rules 2.1 (cert-file+key-file), 2.2 (client-cert-auth=true), 2.3 (auto-tls=false), and 2.4 (peer-cert-file+peer-key-file) are all related to etcd TLS hardening.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
etcd stores ALL Secrets → Must be encrypted in transit
②
Check etcd manifest → --client-cert-auth=false → optional TLS
③
CIS 2.2 requires true → Attacker can bypass TLS entirely
④
Set --client-cert-auth=true → restart etcd
⑤
Test connection without cert → rejected → etcd secured ✅

Tenet: etcd is the brain of Kubernetes — it stores every object in the cluster. If etcd is compromised, the ENTIRE cluster is compromised. --client-cert-auth=true is non-negotiable: it forces all clients (API server, backups, operators) to present valid TLS certificates. Without it, anyone on the network can read Secrets, modify Deployments, or delete entire namespaces via direct etcd access. On CKS, etcd security is a CORE topic — you must know all 4 etcd CIS checks (2.1-2.4).

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep client-cert-auth - --client-cert-auth=false ← ❌ CIS 2.2 FAIL
$ kube-bench run --targets etcd --check 2.2 [FAIL] 2.2 Ensure that the --client-cert-auth argument is set to true Remediation: Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml Set --client-cert-auth=true
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kube-bench run --targets etcd --check 2.2 [PASS] 2.2 Ensure that the --client-cert-auth argument is set to true ✅
$ sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep client-cert-auth - --client-cert-auth=true ✅ All clients must present valid certs
🔧
BASH — Edit etcd manifest + verify TLS enforcement 
# Step 1: Edit etcd manifest on control plane node
# Change --client-cert-auth=false to --client-cert-auth=true
sudo sed -i 's/--client-cert-auth=false/--client-cert-auth=true/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# Step 2: Also ensure --auto-tls is false (CIS 2.3)
# If --auto-tls=true is present, change to false
sudo sed -i 's/--auto-tls=true/--auto-tls=false/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# If absent, add it: add the line before the 'volumes:' section

# Step 3: Wait for etcd pod to restart automatically
sudo crictl ps | grep etcd
# kubelet will detect manifest change and restart etcd
sleep 15

# Step 4: Verify API server can still connect (it has valid certs)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep etcd
# Should show: etcd-anih  1/1  Running

# Step 5: Verify etcd endpoint health
kubectl -n kube-system exec -it etcd-anih -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health
# Expected: "is healthy" ✅
✓

✅ Verify — etcd Requires Client Certificates

After setting --client-cert-auth=true and --auto-tls=false in the etcd manifest, the etcd server now requires valid TLS client certificates for all connections. The API server (which has valid certs mounted) can still connect and the cluster is operational. Any attempt to connect to etcd without a valid certificate is rejected. The anihpj-db-creds Secret is now protected by TLS encryption between the API server and etcd.

💡 Key takeaway: etcd TLS certs are stored at /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ on kubeadm clusters. The kubelet auto-restarts static pods when their manifests change — no manual restart needed. On CKS, you must know: --client-cert-auth=true (CIS 2.2), --auto-tls=false (CIS 2.3), --peer-client-cert-auth=true (CIS 2.4 for etcd-to-etcd peer communication). Recovery: if API server loses etcd connectivity after this change, check that --etcd-certfile and --etcd-keyfile in kube-apiserver.yaml match valid etcd client certs.

🧪 SCENARIO S8 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security NetPol Debug

Apply Deny-All Egress NetworkPolicy — anihpj Pods Can't Resolve DNS

The Problem: You apply a strict NetworkPolicy that denies ALL egress traffic from the anihpj namespace — intending to prevent data exfiltration. But immediately, all pods break — Django can't reach PostgreSQL by service name, health checks fail, and even nslookup times out. The deny-all egress policy also blocks DNS queries (UDP port 53) to CoreDNS. Without DNS, pods can't resolve ANY service names. Your job: find why pods can't communicate, identify the missing DNS egress rule, and fix the NetworkPolicy to allow DNS while still blocking other egress.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Single-node KinD with Calico installed
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Deny-All Egress NetPol (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is running. The security team mandates that pods must NOT make outbound calls to the internet (data exfiltration prevention). You deploy a deny-all-egress NetworkPolicy. Immediately, everything breaks — Django can't reach PostgreSQL, the health endpoint returns 500, and the monitoring dashboard shows all pods as unhealthy. The deny-all egress blocked DNS, so no service name can be resolved.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S8): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL Deployment + Service
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django Deployment + Service
├── 03-allow-dns-egress.yaml       ← ✅ FIX: Allow DNS to CoreDNS only
├── 04-allow-db-egress.yaml        ← ✅ FIX: Allow egress to PostgreSQL
└── 05-test-pod.yaml               ← Busybox test pod
BASH — Deploy app + broken deny-all-egress NetworkPolicy 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S8: Deny-All Egress Breaks DNS — NetworkPolicy Pitfall
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE + DEPLOY APP
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment anihpj-db -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-db -n anihpj --port=80
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --port=80

# 2. DEPLOY TEST POD
kubectl run test-pod -n anihpj --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600

# 3. VERIFY DNS WORKS (before NetPol)
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- nslookup anihpj-db
# → Server: 10.96.0.10 (kube-dns), Address: anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local ✅

# 4. APPLY DENY-ALL EGRESS (THE BUG!)
# This blocks ALL egress, including DNS — pods can't resolve anything
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-egress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  # No egress rules = DENY ALL outbound traffic, including DNS!
EOF

# 5. TEST DNS — NOW BROKEN!
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- nslookup anihpj-db 2>&1
# → ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached ❌

kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default 2>&1
# → TIMEOUT — even kubernetes.default can't resolve! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. DNS fails: nslookup anihpj-db → connection timed out
✗2. All service names unresolvable: nslookup kubernetes.default → timeout
✗3. Check NetPol: kubectl get netpol -n anihpj → deny-all-egress with no egress rules
✗4. Pods can't reach anything by name — the app is effectively offline
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check DNS directly by IP: kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns -o wide
→ CoreDNS ClusterIP: 10.96.0.10 — can we reach it by IP?
2Test UDP connectivity to DNS: kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- sh -c 'echo test | nc -u -w2 10.96.0.10 53'
→ UDP 53 blocked — deny-all-egress blocks ALL egress including DNS
3Check NetPol rules: kubectl describe netpol deny-all-egress -n anihpj
→ Egress: <none> — No DNS allow rule exists!
4DNS uses UDP port 53 — must be explicitly allowed in any egress-restricted NetworkPolicy
5Root cause: The deny-all-egress NetworkPolicy blocks ALL outbound traffic, including UDP port 53 to CoreDNS. Without DNS, pods cannot resolve ANY service names — they can only communicate by raw IP. The fix is to add an explicit egress rule allowing UDP/TCP port 53 to the kube-dns service in kube-system namespace, BEFORE any deny-all rule. DNS is the #1 forgotten egress rule in NetworkPolicy design.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
nslookup times out after NetPol applied → DNS blocked
②
Check NetPol → policyTypes: Egress with no rules = deny all
③
DNS runs on UDP 53 → Must whitelist kube-dns namespace
④
Add egress rule: allow UDP 53 to kube-system
⑤
nslookup works → service communication restored ✅

Tenet: A deny-all egress NetworkPolicy is powerful for preventing data exfiltration, but it will always break DNS unless you explicitly allow UDP port 53 to CoreDNS. This is the #1 NetworkPolicy mistake. DNS uses UDP (not TCP) on port 53, and CoreDNS runs in the kube-system namespace (not the pod's namespace). Every egress-restricted NetworkPolicy MUST include a DNS allow rule. On CKS, expect scenarios where pods can't resolve service names after a NetworkPolicy change — the fix is always the DNS egress allow rule.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- nslookup anihpj-db ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached ❌ DNS BLOCKED!
$ kubectl describe netpol deny-all-egress -n anihpj Policy Types: Egress Egress: <none> ← Blocks EVERYTHING including DNS!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (DNS allowed)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- nslookup anihpj-db Name: anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local Address: 10.96.1.5 ✅ DNS WORKS!
🔧
BASH — Replace deny-all-egress with DNS-aware NetworkPolicy 
# Step 1: DELETE the broken deny-all-egress policy
kubectl delete netpol deny-all-egress -n anihpj

# Step 2: APPLY a corrected NetworkPolicy that allows DNS first, then denies everything else
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-dns-only
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  # RULE 1: Allow DNS (UDP + TCP port 53) to CoreDNS in kube-system
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
  # RULE 2: Allow egress to PostgreSQL in same namespace (for the app)
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj-db
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
  # NOTE: All other egress is DENIED (data exfiltration blocked)
EOF

# Step 3: VERIFY DNS works
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- nslookup anihpj-db
# Expected: Resolves to ClusterIP ✅
✓

✅ Verify — DNS Works, Egress Is Restricted

After replacing the blanket deny-all-egress with a NetworkPolicy that explicitly allows DNS (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns) and PostgreSQL egress, pods can resolve service names and reach the database. All other egress (including internet access) remains blocked — satisfying the data exfiltration prevention requirement. nslookup anihpj-db now returns the ClusterIP address.

💡 Key takeaway: DNS is the #1 forgotten egress rule in NetworkPolicies. CoreDNS runs in kube-system with label k8s-app: kube-dns. Always use namespaceSelector to target kube-system and podSelector to target kube-dns. Allow BOTH UDP and TCP on port 53 — large DNS responses may use TCP. On CKS, remember: no DNS = no service communication = app is dead.

🧹

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,netpol -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null

# → Lists ALL secrets cluster-wide! ❌

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check API server flags: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep insecure
→ --insecure-port=8080 (or missing = defaults to 8080 in old versions)
2Check insecure-bind-address: grep insecure-bind-address /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
→ --insecure-bind-address=127.0.0.1 (localhost only, but still dangerous)
3Even bound to localhost, any process on the control plane node (or an attacker with SSH access) can query the API with zero auth
4Deprecated since Kubernetes 1.10, removed in 1.24 — but older clusters or custom builds may still have it
5Root cause: The API server's --insecure-port is set to 8080 (or not explicitly set to 0). This deprecated port accepts HTTP requests with NO authentication, NO TLS, and NO authorization. It completely bypasses all security controls. CIS 1.1.2 requires --insecure-port=0 (disabled). Even if bound to localhost, any compromised pod with hostNetwork or node access can exploit this.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Port 8080 open → Check what's listening → kube-apiserver
②
curl without token → returns pod list → insecure port active
③
Check manifest → --insecure-port=8080 → CIS 1.1.2 FAIL

⑤
curl localhost:8080 → connection refused → CIS PASS ✅

Tenet: The API server insecure port is a relic from early Kubernetes when TLS was optional. It provides completely unauthenticated, unencrypted HTTP access to the entire Kubernetes API — no token, no cert, no RBAC check. It was deprecated in v1.10 and removed in v1.24. Modern clusters should always have --insecure-port=0. On CKS, CIS 1.1.2 checks this — even if you're running a newer version where the flag doesn't exist, you should verify port 8080 is NOT listening on the API server.

# Alternatively, if the flag is present with 0, or you want to remove it entirely:
# Comment out or delete the --insecure-port line

# Step 2: If --insecure-bind-address is also set, it becomes irrelevant when port=0
# but it's safe to also remove it: delete or comment the line

# Step 3: Wait for API server to restart

kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-apiserver

# Step 4: VERIFY port 8080 is no longer listening
ss -tlnp | grep 8080
# Expected: No output ✅

curl --connect-timeout 3 http://localhost:8080/api 2>&1
# Expected: Connection refused ✅

✅ Verify — Insecure Port Is Completely Disabled

After setting --insecure-port=0 and letting the API server restart, port 8080 is no longer listening. curl http://localhost:8080/api returns Connection refused. The only API endpoint now is the secure port 6443, which requires TLS and authentication. The cluster passes CIS Benchmark 1.1.2.

💡 Key takeaway: The insecure port predates RBAC and TLS in Kubernetes. It was maintained for backwards compatibility but has been fully removed since v1.24. On CKS, you must verify --insecure-port=0 is either set or the flag is completely absent (modern versions). Always scan for port 8080 on control plane nodes — if it's open, it's a critical finding.
