🧪 SCENARIO S10 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security TLS Debug

Deploy anihpj with Ingress TLS — Browser Shows "Not Secure" Warning

The Problem: You deploy anihpj/jobpost with an Ingress that HAS a TLS section and an HTTPS listener — but when users visit https://jobs.anihpj.com, their browser shows a scary "Your connection is not private" warning (NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID). The TLS certificate is self-signed and not trusted by any Certificate Authority — meaning while traffic IS encrypted, there's no way to verify the server's identity, making the app vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. Your job: identify the untrusted cert, generate a proper CA-signed certificate (or use cert-manager), and replace it so browsers trust the connection.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD with Ingress controller
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Self-Signed TLS Certificate (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a public-facing job board at jobs.anihpj.com. TLS was set up with a quick openssl req -x509 self-signed certificate. The Ingress serves HTTPS, but every user sees a "Not Secure" warning. Self-signed certs work for encryption but FAIL authentication — the browser can't verify who owns the certificate. For a production job board handling PII, this is unacceptable.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S10): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django Deployment + Service
├── 02-ingress-tls.yaml            ← Ingress with TLS (self-signed cert)
├── 03-generate-selfsigned.sh      ← Script that created the BUGGY self-signed cert
└── 04-create-ca-signed.sh         ← ✅ FIX: Create proper CA + signed cert
BASH — Deploy anihpj with self-signed TLS (THE BUG) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S10: Self-Signed TLS — Browser Trust Failure
# ============================================

# 1. DEPLOY ANIHPJ
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --port=80

# 2. GENERATE SELF-SIGNED CERTIFICATE (THE BUG!)
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout anihpj.key -out anihpj.crt \
  -subj "/CN=jobs.anihpj.com/O=anihpj"

# 3. CREATE TLS SECRET FROM SELF-SIGNED CERT
kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls -n anihpj \
  --cert=anihpj.crt --key=anihpj.key

# 4. DEPLOY INGRESS WITH TLS (uses self-signed cert)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - jobs.anihpj.com
    secretName: anihpj-tls        # ← Self-signed cert — browser won't trust!
  rules:
  - host: jobs.anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

# 5. TEST — curl with -k (ignore cert validation) works, but without -k fails
INGRESS_IP=$(kubectl get ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')
curl -k https://$INGRESS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"
# → 200 (works with -k, ignoring cert validation)

curl https://$INGRESS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>&1 | head -5
# → SSL certificate problem: self signed certificate ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. curl without -k fails: curl https://JOBS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" → SSL cert problem
✗2. curl with -k works: curl -k https://JOBS_IP → 200 (encryption works)
✗3. Browser shows NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID — self-signed cert not trusted
✗4. openssl shows Issuer=Subject (self-signed signature — no CA chain)
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Inspect the certificate: openssl x509 -in anihpj.crt -text -noout | grep -E 'Issuer:|Subject:'
→ Issuer: CN=jobs.anihpj.com, Subject: CN=jobs.anihpj.com — SAME! Self-signed!
2Check cert chain: openssl s_client -connect JOBS_IP:443 -servername jobs.anihpj.com
→ Verify return code: 18 (self-signed certificate)
3Self-signed means: the certificate signs itself — no trusted third party vouches for it
4For production: need a CA-signed cert (Let's Encrypt, cert-manager, or corporate CA)
5Root cause: The TLS certificate was created with openssl req -x509 (self-signed), which means there is NO Certificate Authority chain. Browsers and TLS clients only trust certificates signed by a known CA. A self-signed cert provides encryption (HTTPS) but NO authentication — anyone can create a self-signed cert claiming to be "jobs.anihpj.com". The fix: create a CA, sign the server cert with it, and distribute the CA cert to clients (or use Let's Encrypt/cert-manager for auto-trusted certs).
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
HTTPS works with -k but not without → Self-signed cert
②
openssl x509 → Issuer == Subject → No CA chain
③
Create CA cert + key → Sign server cert with CA
④
Update TLS Secret with CA-signed cert → Trust chain exists
⑤
curl without -k → 200 → CA trust established ✅

Tenet: Self-signed certificates provide encryption but NOT authentication. They're fine for internal dev but unacceptable for production. The CKS exam tests your understanding of TLS trust chains: a certificate must be signed by a CA whose certificate is in the client's trust store. For Kubernetes Ingress, use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt for automated trusted certificates, or configure your corporate CA chain correctly.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ openssl x509 -in anihpj.crt -issuer -subject -noout issuer=CN=jobs.anihpj.com, O=anihpj subject=CN=jobs.anihpj.com, O=anihpj ← SAME! Self-signed ❌
$ curl https://10.96.1.5 -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" 2>&1 | head -3 curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: self signed certificate ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (CA-signed)
$ openssl verify -CAfile ca.crt anihpj-signed.crt anihpj-signed.crt: OK ✅ Signed by trusted CA!
$ curl --cacert ca.crt https://10.96.1.5 -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" 200 ✅ Trusted TLS connection!
🔧
BASH — Generate CA, sign server cert, update TLS Secret 
# Step 1: CREATE A CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY (CA)
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 2048
openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 -key ca.key -out ca.crt \
  -subj "/CN=anihpj-CA/O=anihpj"

# Step 2: CREATE SERVER KEY + CSR (Certificate Signing Request)
openssl genrsa -out anihpj-server.key 2048
openssl req -new -key anihpj-server.key -out anihpj-server.csr \
  -subj "/CN=jobs.anihpj.com/O=anihpj"

# Step 3: SIGN THE SERVER CERT WITH THE CA
openssl x509 -req -in anihpj-server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key \
  -CAcreateserial -out anihpj-server.crt -days 365

# Step 4: UPDATE THE TLS SECRET with CA-signed cert
kubectl delete secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj
kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls -n anihpj \
  --cert=anihpj-server.crt --key=anihpj-server.key

# Step 5: VERIFY — curl with CA cert succeeds without -k
INGRESS_IP=$(kubectl get ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')
curl --cacert ca.crt https://$INGRESS_IP -H "Host: jobs.anihpj.com" -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"
# Expected: 200 ✅ (no -k flag needed!)
✓

✅ Verify — Certificate Is Trusted by CA

After creating a CA, signing the server certificate with it, and updating the TLS Secret, the anihpj/jobpost Ingress now serves a certificate with a proper trust chain. Clients that trust the CA (e.g., by adding ca.crt to their trust store) can verify the server's identity. In production, you would use cert-manager + Let's Encrypt instead of a self-managed CA for publicly trusted certificates.

💡 Key takeaway: The difference between self-signed and CA-signed: a self-signed cert's Issuer == Subject (no trust chain). A CA-signed cert has Issuer=CA and Subject=Server — creating a trust chain. On CKS, you must know: use openssl x509 -text -noout to inspect certs, check Issuer vs Subject, and use cert-manager for automated certificate lifecycle. Self-signed = encryption only. CA-signed = encryption + authentication.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Remove local cert files
rm -f ca.key ca.crt ca.srl anihpj.key anihpj.crt anihpj-server.key anihpj-server.csr anihpj-server.crt

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,ingress,secrets -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S11
🧪 SCENARIO S11 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security RBAC Debug

Deploy anihpj — Custom ClusterRole Has verbs:["*"] and resources:["*"]

The Problem: A developer created a "limited" ClusterRole named anihpj-deployer for the CI/CD pipeline, intending to only allow creating Deployments. But the YAML has verbs: ["*"] and resources: ["*"] — wildcards that grant unrestricted access to every resource in the cluster. This ClusterRole is functionally equivalent to cluster-admin but was named to look innocuous. Your job: audit the ClusterRole, identify the wildcard permissions, and scope it down to ONLY the verbs and resources needed for CI/CD.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Wildcard ClusterRole (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The CI/CD pipeline for anihpj/jobpost needs to deploy new versions. A ClusterRole anihpj-deployer was created — the developer says it's "limited to deployment operations." But inspection reveals verbs: ["*"] and resources: ["*"] — giving the pipeline's ServiceAccount complete cluster control. A compromised pipeline token could delete everything.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S11): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml                    ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-serviceaccount.yaml               ← anihpj-cicd SA
├── 02-clusterrole-wildcard.yaml         ← BROKEN: verbs:["*"], resources:["*"]
├── 03-clusterrolebinding.yaml           ← Binds SA to wildcard ClusterRole
└── 04-clusterrole-scoped.yaml           ← ✅ FIX: Properly scoped ClusterRole
BASH — Deploy wildcard ClusterRole + test its power 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S11: ClusterRole with Wildcard Verbs/Resources
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create serviceaccount anihpj-cicd -n anihpj

# CREATE THE "LIMITED" CLUSTERROLE (ACTUALLY UNLIMITED!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: anihpj-deployer
rules:
- apiGroups: ["*"]      # ❌ Wildcard — ALL API groups!
  resources: ["*"]      # ❌ Wildcard — ALL resources!
  verbs: ["*"]          # ❌ Wildcard — create, delete, patch, escalate, everything!
EOF

kubectl create clusterrolebinding anihpj-cicd-binding \
  --clusterrole=anihpj-deployer \
  --serviceaccount=anihpj:anihpj-cicd

# TEST THE "LIMITED" SA — it can actually do EVERYTHING
kubectl auth can-i delete nodes --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd
# → yes ❌ Can delete NODES! Not "limited" at all!

kubectl auth can-i create clusterroles --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd
# → yes ❌ Can create ClusterRoles — privilege escalation!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. verbs:["*"] — allows create, delete, update, patch, escalate, bind, impersonate — EVERYTHING
✗2. resources:["*"] — includes pods, secrets, nodes, namespaces, RBAC objects
✗3. SA can escalate privileges: --as=SA kubectl auth can-i create clusterroles → yes
✗4. The ClusterRole name "anihpj-deployer" is misleading — it's actually cluster-admin-equivalent
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Inspect the ClusterRole: kubectl describe clusterrole anihpj-deployer
→ Resources: *.*, Verbs: [*] — COMPLETE ACCESS
2Check what CI/CD actually needs: only Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps in anihpj namespace
3Even if verbs were limited to ["get","list","create","update","patch","delete"], resources:["*"] includes secrets, RBAC, nodes
4Privilege escalation check: with verbs:["*"] the SA can create new ClusterRoles and bind itself to cluster-admin
5Root cause: The ClusterRole uses wildcards ("*") for apiGroups, resources, AND verbs. This grants unrestricted access equivalent to cluster-admin. The principle of least privilege requires specifying EXACTLY which apiGroups, resources, and verbs a role needs. Use kubectl auth can-i --list to audit what a ServiceAccount can actually do before deploying to production.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
ClusterRole has verbs:[*], resources:[*] → Unlimited power
②
Audit actual needs → Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps only
③
Never use wildcards → Specify exact resources + verbs
④
Delete wildcard ClusterRole → Create properly scoped one
⑤
SA can't delete nodes → Least privilege enforced ✅

Tenet: Wildcards in RBAC are a security anti-pattern. verbs: ["*"] includes dangerous verbs like escalate and bind — allowing privilege escalation. resources: ["*"] includes secrets, nodes, and RBAC objects. Always specify exact resource names. On CKS, use kubectl auth can-i --list --as=SA to audit what any ServiceAccount can do.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe clusterrole anihpj-deployer Name: anihpj-deployer Resources Verbs *.* [*] ← Complete unrestricted access ❌
$ kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd | head -5 Resources Verbs *.* [*] ← Everything! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i delete nodes --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd no ✅ SA is properly scoped!
🔧
BASH — Delete wildcard role + create properly scoped ClusterRole 
# Step 1: Delete the wildcard ClusterRoleBinding + ClusterRole
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding anihpj-cicd-binding
kubectl delete clusterrole anihpj-deployer

# Step 2: Create PROPERLY SCOPED ClusterRole — only what CI/CD needs
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: anihpj-deployer
rules:
# CI/CD needs: create/update/patch/get/list deployments, services, configmaps
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["services", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
# Read-only access to pods (for checking deployment status)
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
# NOTE: NO access to secrets, nodes, namespaces, or RBAC objects
EOF

# Step 3: Re-bind the SA using RoleBinding (namespace-scoped)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: anihpj-cicd-binding
  namespace: anihpj
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: anihpj-cicd
  namespace: anihpj
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: anihpj-deployer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
EOF

# Step 4: VERIFY — SA is now properly scoped
kubectl auth can-i delete nodes --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd
# Expected: no ✅
✓

✅ Verify — ClusterRole Uses Specific Resources and Verbs

The CI/CD ServiceAccount can now only get/list/create/update/patch on deployments, services, configmaps, and pods — all scoped to the anihpj namespace via a RoleBinding. kubectl auth can-i delete nodes returns no.

💡 Key takeaway: Never use verbs: ["*"] or resources: ["*"] in RBAC roles. The wildcard * includes dangerous escalation verbs (escalate, bind, impersonate). On CKS, audit all ClusterRoles with: kubectl get clusterrole -o yaml | grep -E 'verbs.*\*|resources.*\*'. Replace wildcards with explicit lists. Use a RoleBinding (not ClusterRoleBinding) to scope ClusterRoles to a single namespace.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete cluster-scoped resources
kubectl delete clusterrole anihpj-deployer --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding anihpj-cicd-binding --ignore-not-found

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get clusterrole,clusterrolebinding | grep anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S12
🧪 SCENARIO S12 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security PodSec Debug

Deploy anihpj — Pod Can Access Node's /proc Filesystem via hostPath

The Problem: An anihpj/jobpost pod manifest includes a hostPath volume mount of /proc — the node's process filesystem. This allows the container to see ALL processes running on the host node, including other tenants' pods, the kubelet, and system daemons. An attacker who compromises this pod can read process arguments (exposing secrets), enumerate all running containers, and potentially escape to the node. CIS Benchmark 5.1.1 requires restricting hostPath mounts. Your job: detect the dangerous hostPath, remove it, and add Pod Security Admission to block privileged pods.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj pod with hostPath /proc mount (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A developer added a hostPath mount of /proc to the Django pod "for debugging." This means the container can read /proc/1/environ on the host node, exposing ALL environment variables of ALL processes — including kubelet credentials, other pods' secrets passed as env vars, and system service configurations. This is effectively a container escape to the node level.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S12): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-dangerous-pod.yaml          ← BROKEN: Pod with hostPath /proc mount
├── 02-test-access.sh              ← Script demonstrating node process access
└── 03-fixed-pod.yaml              ← ✅ FIX: Pod without hostPath
BASH — Deploy pod with dangerous hostPath + test node access 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S12: hostPath Mount to /proc — Node Escape Risk
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# DEPLOY POD WITH DANGEROUS hostPath (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-debug
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: host-proc
      mountPath: /host-proc        # ← Mounts the NODE's /proc!
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: host-proc
    hostPath:
      path: /proc                  # ❌ BUG! Node's process filesystem exposed!
      type: Directory
EOF

# WAIT FOR POD
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/anihpj-debug -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# TEST NODE ACCESS — Read host process info!
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-debug -- ls /host-proc | head -10
# → Shows ALL PIDs from the NODE, not just this container!

# Read host environment variables (may leak secrets!)
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-debug -- cat /host-proc/1/environ 2>/dev/null | tr '\0' '\n' | head -10
# → Shows environment of PID 1 on the HOST! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Pod has hostPath: kubectl get pod anihpj-debug -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 hostPath → /proc
✗2. Container sees host processes: ls /host-proc → all node PIDs visible
✗3. Can read host env vars: cat /host-proc/1/environ → leaks host process secrets
✗4. CIS 5.1.1: hostPath mounts should be restricted — this pod violates the baseline policy
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod volumes: kubectl describe pod anihpj-debug -n anihpj | grep -A5 'host-proc'
→ Type: HostPath, Path: /proc — DIRECT node filesystem access
2Why /proc is dangerous: it exposes all running processes, their cmdline args, env vars, and file descriptors
3Even readOnly doesn't help: reading /proc exposes sensitive data — kubelet tokens, DB passwords in env, etc.
4Check for other dangerous hostPaths: /sys, /var/run/docker.sock, /etc/kubernetes
5Root cause: The pod spec contains hostPath: /proc, giving the container direct access to the node's process filesystem. This is a container escape risk — an attacker can read secrets from other processes' environment variables, discover other containers running on the node, and gather information for lateral movement. CIS 5.1.1 recommends restricting hostPath mounts and using Pod Security Admission (restricted profile) to block them entirely.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod has hostPath → check what's mounted → /proc
②
Container sees host PIDs → Node isolation broken
③
Remove hostPath from pod → apply Pod Security restricted
④
Recreate pod without hostPath → Pod Security blocks bad YAML
⑤
Container only sees its own /proc → Containment restored ✅

Tenet: hostPath mounts break container isolation by giving pods access to the node's filesystem. /proc is especially dangerous — it exposes ALL processes running on the node. On CKS, you must identify dangerous hostPath mounts (/proc, /sys, /var/run/docker.sock, /etc/kubernetes) and either remove them or restrict them via Pod Security Admission. The fix: label the namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted to block privileged pods including those with hostPath volumes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-debug -- ls /host-proc | wc -l 247 ← 247 host processes visible! ❌
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-debug -- cat /host-proc/1/cmdline 2>/dev/null /sbin/init ← Host init process visible from container! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec anihpj-secure -n anihpj -- ls /host-proc 2>&1 ls: /host-proc: No such file or directory ✅ Node isolation restored
🔧
BASH — Remove dangerous pod + apply Pod Security Admission 
# Step 1: DELETE the dangerous pod immediately
kubectl delete pod anihpj-debug -n anihpj

# Step 2: LABEL namespace for Pod Security restricted (blocks hostPath)
kubectl label namespace anihpj \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  --overwrite

# Step 3: CREATE SECURE pod WITHOUT hostPath
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-secure
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
    # NO hostPath, NO privileged, NO hostNetwork — fully restricted
EOF

# Step 4: VERIFY — pod has no access to host /proc
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-secure -- ls /proc 2>&1 | wc -l
# Shows only container's own /proc, not host's ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Container Isolation Is Restored

After deleting the dangerous pod and applying Pod Security Admission restricted profile, the new anihpj-secure pod has no hostPath mounts, runs as non-root, and has all capabilities dropped. /proc inside the container only shows the container's own processes — not the host node's processes. The namespace is now protected against future dangerous pod specs.

💡 Key takeaway: hostPath is one of the most dangerous volume types. It bypasses container isolation entirely. On CKS, know the dangerous paths: /proc (process info), /sys (kernel params), /var/run/docker.sock (container control), /etc/kubernetes (cluster certs). Pod Security Admission restricted profile blocks all hostPath mounts by default. Use kubectl label ns NAME pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted to protect namespaces.

kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S13
🧪 SCENARIO S13 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security Binary Debug

anihpj Cluster Audit — kube-apiserver Binary Checksum Doesn't Match

The Problem: During a CIS compliance audit, you verify the platform binaries on the control plane node. You compute the SHA256 checksum of /usr/bin/kube-apiserver and compare it against the official Kubernetes release checksum. They don't match. Either the binary has been tampered with (supply chain attack) or it was downloaded from an unofficial source. CIS Benchmark 1.1.13 requires verifying platform binaries before deployment. Your job: verify all Kubernetes binaries against official checksums, identify the mismatched one, and replace it with the verified version.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Verify Kubernetes Binaries Against Official Checksums (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost has been running for months. A security bulletin warns about compromised Kubernetes binaries circulating on unofficial mirrors. You're tasked with verifying all control plane binaries against the official Kubernetes release signatures. One binary — kube-apiserver — has a checksum that doesn't match the official release. This could indicate tampering or a corrupted download.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S13): 
Binary verification checklist:
/usr/bin/kube-apiserver       ← CHECK
/usr/bin/kube-controller-manager ← CHECK
/usr/bin/kube-scheduler       ← CHECK
/usr/bin/kubelet              ← CHECK
/usr/bin/kubectl              ← CHECK
/usr/local/bin/etcd           ← CHECK
BASH — Verify platform binary checksums against official releases 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S13: Platform Binary Verification — CIS 1.1.13
# ============================================

# 1. IDENTIFY THE KUBERNETES VERSION
kubectl version --short 2>/dev/null || kubectl version
# → Server Version: v1.32.13

# 2. DOWNLOAD OFFICIAL CHECKSUM FILE
K8S_VERSION=$(kubectl version -o json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['serverVersion']['gitVersion'].lstrip('v'))")
curl -sLO "https://dl.k8s.io/v${K8S_VERSION}/kubernetes-server-linux-amd64.tar.gz.sha256"

# 3. COMPUTE LOCAL BINARY CHECKSUMS
echo "=== Verifying Kubernetes Binaries ==="
for binary in kube-apiserver kube-controller-manager kube-scheduler kubelet kubectl; do
  BIN_PATH="/usr/bin/${binary}"
  if [ -f "$BIN_PATH" ]; then
    LOCAL_SHA=$(sha256sum $BIN_PATH | awk '{print $1}')
    echo "  $binary: $LOCAL_SHA"
  fi
done

# 4. COMPARE WITH OFFICIAL CHECKSUMS (THE BUG!)
# Extract the expected SHA for kube-apiserver from official file
EXPECTED_SHA=$(grep 'kube-apiserver' kubernetes-server-linux-amd64.tar.gz.sha256 | awk '{print $1}')
LOCAL_SHA=$(sha256sum /usr/bin/kube-apiserver | awk '{print $1}')
echo "Expected: $EXPECTED_SHA"
echo "Local:    $LOCAL_SHA"
# → MISMATCH! ❌ Binary may be tampered or from unofficial source
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. SHA256 of kube-apiserver: sha256sum /usr/bin/kube-apiserver → doesn't match official
✗2. Other binaries (kubelet, kubectl, etc.) match — only kube-apiserver is wrong
✗3. Binary size also differs: ls -la /usr/bin/kube-apiserver → different from expected
✗4. CIS 1.1.13 FAILED — running unverified binaries is a supply chain risk
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check binary modification time: stat /usr/bin/kube-apiserver | grep Modify
→ Modified 2 weeks ago — after the official release date
2Check file origin: dpkg -S /usr/bin/kube-apiserver or rpm -qf /usr/bin/kube-apiserver
→ Not from a package manager — manually installed
3Check running binary version: /usr/bin/kube-apiserver --version
→ Reports correct version but checksum mismatches — possible modified binary
4Compare with official: download fresh binary from dl.k8s.io, compare checksums
5Root cause: The kube-apiserver binary was downloaded from an unofficial mirror or manually replaced. Its SHA256 checksum does not match the official Kubernetes release. This could indicate a supply chain attack where a backdoored binary was substituted. CIS 1.1.13 requires ALL platform binaries to be verified against official checksums before deployment and periodically thereafter.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Compute local SHA256 → Download official checksum file
②
Compare → kube-apiserver mismatch → possible tampering
③
Download verified binary from dl.k8s.io → Verify checksum
④
Stop API server → Replace binary → Restart
⑤
Re-verify checksum → Match → CIS 1.1.13 PASS ✅

Tenet: Platform binary verification is a critical supply chain security control. Every Kubernetes binary (kube-apiserver, kubelet, etcd, etc.) should have its SHA256 checksum verified against the official Kubernetes release. On CKS, CIS 1.1.13-1.1.18 cover binary verification. Always download from dl.k8s.io (the official CDN) and verify checksums before deploying.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sha256sum /usr/bin/kube-apiserver a1b2c3d4... /usr/bin/kube-apiserver ← MISMATCH with official! ❌
$ grep kube-apiserver kubernetes-server-linux-amd64.tar.gz.sha256 e5f6a7b8... kubernetes/server/bin/kube-apiserver ← OFFICIAL checksum
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sha256sum /usr/bin/kube-apiserver e5f6a7b8... /usr/bin/kube-apiserver ✅ MATCHES official!
🔧
BASH — Download verified binary + replace + verify checksum 
# Step 1: Download OFFICIAL binary and checksum from dl.k8s.io
K8S_VERSION="v1.32.13"
curl -sLO "https://dl.k8s.io/${K8S_VERSION}/bin/linux/amd64/kube-apiserver"
curl -sLO "https://dl.k8s.io/${K8S_VERSION}/bin/linux/amd64/kube-apiserver.sha256"

# Step 2: VERIFY the downloaded binary checksum
echo "$(cat kube-apiserver.sha256)  kube-apiserver" | sha256sum -c
# Expected: kube-apiserver: OK ✅

# Step 3: BACKUP the old binary, replace with verified one
sudo cp /usr/bin/kube-apiserver /usr/bin/kube-apiserver.bak
sudo cp kube-apiserver /usr/bin/kube-apiserver
sudo chmod 755 /usr/bin/kube-apiserver

# Step 4: kubelet will detect the manifest change and restart the API server
# Verify the new API server pod is running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-apiserver

# Step 5: RE-VERIFY the replaced binary
sha256sum /usr/bin/kube-apiserver
# Should match kube-apiserver.sha256 ✅
✓

✅ Verify — All Binaries Match Official Checksums

After replacing the mismatched kube-apiserver binary with the verified version from dl.k8s.io, the SHA256 checksum now matches the official release. The API server restarted successfully and the cluster is operational. A verification script should be run regularly to detect any future tampering.

💡 Key takeaway: Always download Kubernetes binaries from dl.k8s.io — the official CNCF-managed CDN. Verify SHA256 checksums (not MD5 — it's cryptographically broken). On CKS, CIS 1.1.13-1.1.18 require verification of ALL platform binaries. Automate this with a cron job that compares hashes and alerts on mismatch. Record verification results for audit compliance.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Remove downloaded files
rm -f kube-apiserver kube-apiserver.sha256 kubernetes-server-linux-amd64.tar.gz.sha256

# Restore original binary from backup (if needed for lab)
# sudo cp /usr/bin/kube-apiserver.bak /usr/bin/kube-apiserver
S14
🧪 SCENARIO S14 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security etcd Debug

anihpj etcd Audit — auto-tls Generates Self-Signed Certs Automatically

The Problem: During an etcd security audit, you discover --auto-tls=true in the etcd configuration. This dangerous flag tells etcd to automatically generate self-signed TLS certificates if proper certificates aren't provided — meaning etcd falls back to weak, untrusted encryption without warning. CIS Benchmark 2.3 explicitly requires --auto-tls=false. With auto-tls enabled, an etcd node that loses its cert files will silently generate new self-signed certs and continue operating with no real security — no alerts, no errors, just silently degraded to zero trust.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Audit etcd auto-tls Setting (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost stores PII in Secrets. A routine CIS scan flags etcd check 2.3: auto-tls is enabled. This means if etcd's certificate files are accidentally deleted or corrupted, etcd will silently generate new self-signed certificates and continue running — but with no real TLS security. The anihpj DB credentials would be transmitted over a connection that looks encrypted but has zero trust verification.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S14): 
etcd security audit checklist:
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml   ← CHECK --auto-tls flag
/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/             ← Verify certs exist
CIS checks 2.1-2.4                    ← Run kube-bench
BASH — Audit etcd for auto-tls (CIS 2.3 Violation) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S14: etcd auto-tls=true — CIS 2.3 Violation
# ============================================

# 1. CHECK ETCD MANIFEST FOR auto-tls
sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep -E 'auto-tls|client-cert-auth'
# → --auto-tls=true   ← BUG! CIS 2.3 FAILED
# → --client-cert-auth=true

# 2. WHAT auto-tls=true MEANS
# If etcd can't find its cert files, it GENERATES self-signed certs automatically
# No error, no alert — just silently downgrades to untrusted TLS
# This defeats the entire purpose of TLS: you can't verify who you're connecting to

# 3. RUN CIS BENCHMARK CHECK
kube-bench run --targets etcd --check 2.3
# → [FAIL] 2.3 Ensure that the --auto-tls argument is not set to true

# 4. TEST: Simulate cert loss (DON'T do this in production!)
# If certs were missing, etcd would auto-generate new ones and keep running
# The API server would connect but with NO trust verification
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. etcd manifest: grep auto-tls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml → --auto-tls=true
✗2. kube-bench reports: [FAIL] 2.3 — auto-tls must be false
✗3. Silent security degradation: cert loss = auto-generated self-signed = no trust
✗4. CIS 2.3: auto-tls must be false to prevent automatic generation of self-signed certs
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1auto-tls=true bypasses proper certificate management: certs should be manually provisioned and rotated
2Self-signed certs provide encryption only, NOT authentication: anyone can generate a self-signed cert claiming to be etcd
3Combined with client-cert-auth=false, auto-tls creates a completely untrusted environment
4Production impact: Secret data (like anihpj DB passwords) transmitted without verifiable trust
5Root cause: --auto-tls=true allows etcd to silently generate self-signed certificates when proper certs are unavailable. This creates a false sense of security — TLS appears enabled (port 2379 shows HTTPS) but the certificates are self-generated and untrusted. CIS 2.3 mandates auto-tls=false to ensure etcd ONLY uses explicitly provisioned, CA-signed certificates.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kube-bench scan etcd → CIS 2.3 FAIL
②
Check etcd manifest → --auto-tls=true
③
auto-tls silently downgrades security → Set to false
④
Restart etcd → Verify certs still work (they do — they're proper certs)
⑤
kube-bench re-run → 2.3 PASS → Proper TLS enforced ✅

Tenet: --auto-tls=true is a dangerous convenience feature. It means "if you forget to provide certs, I'll make some up." The result is TLS that looks enabled but provides zero trust. CIS 2.3 requires --auto-tls=false. Always provision etcd certificates explicitly and verify them. On CKS, etcd CIS checks 2.1-2.4 are must-know: cert-file+key-file set (2.1), client-cert-auth=true (2.2), auto-tls=false (2.3), peer-cert-file+peer-key-file set (2.4).

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kube-bench run --targets etcd --check 2.3 [FAIL] 2.3 Ensure that the --auto-tls argument is not set to true ❌
$ sudo grep auto-tls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml - --auto-tls=true ← CIS 2.3 FAIL ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kube-bench run --targets etcd --check 2.3 [PASS] 2.3 Ensure that the --auto-tls argument is not set to true ✅
🔧
BASH — Edit etcd manifest + restart 
# Step 1: Change --auto-tls=true to --auto-tls=false
sudo sed -i 's/--auto-tls=true/--auto-tls=false/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# Step 2: Wait for etcd to restart automatically
sleep 15
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep etcd

# Step 3: Verify etcd health
kubectl -n kube-system exec -it etcd-anih -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health

# Step 4: Re-run CIS check
kube-bench run --targets etcd --check 2.3
# Expected: [PASS] ✅
✓

✅ Verify — etcd Uses Only Explicitly Provisioned Certificates

With --auto-tls=false, etcd will refuse to start if its certificate files are missing or invalid — rather than silently generating untrusted self-signed certs. The anihpj DB credentials stored in etcd Secrets are now protected by proper, CA-signed TLS with verifiable trust.

💡 Key takeaway: --auto-tls=true is the "fail-open" setting — it keeps etcd running at the cost of security. --auto-tls=false is "fail-closed" — etcd refuses to start without proper certs, alerting you to the problem. Always prefer fail-closed for security-critical components. On CKS, remember: auto-tls + client-cert-auth=false = zero trust TLS.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Revert for lab purposes
# sudo sed -i 's/--auto-tls=false/--auto-tls=true/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
S15
🧪 SCENARIO S15 — Category 1: Cluster Setup Security NetPol Debug

Deploy anihpj — NetworkPolicy namespaceSelector Allows Cross-Namespace Access

The Problem: You deploy a NetworkPolicy for anihpj that is supposed to only allow ingress from pods in the same namespace. But the policy uses namespaceSelector: {} (empty — matches ALL namespaces) instead of a specific label selector. This means pods from any namespace can reach anihpj pods — including pods in default, kube-system, or any tenant namespace. The empty {} selector is a subtle but critical bug — it silently opens the namespace to the entire cluster.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Single-node KinD with Calico
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + NetworkPolicy with Empty namespaceSelector (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost should only accept traffic from its own namespace. A NetworkPolicy was created with namespaceSelector: {} — the developer thought this meant "only same namespace." It actually means ALL namespaces. Now a pod in the default namespace (or any other) can freely connect to anihpj-web, bypassing the intended isolation.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S15): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace-anihpj.yaml       ← kubectl create ns anihpj + label it
├── 01-namespace-attacker.yaml     ← kubectl create ns attacker (cross-ns test)
├── 02-anihpj-web.yaml             ← Django Deployment + Service
├── 03-netpol-broken.yaml          ← BROKEN: namespaceSelector: {}
├── 04-test-pod-anihpj.yaml        ← Test pod in anihpj namespace
├── 05-test-pod-attacker.yaml      ← Test pod in attacker namespace
└── 06-netpol-fixed.yaml           ← ✅ FIX: Specific namespaceSelector
BASH — Deploy with broken namespaceSelector={} NetworkPolicy 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S15: namespaceSelector: {} Opens ALL Namespaces
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACES + LABEL anihpj
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj team=jobpost
kubectl create namespace attacker

# 2. DEPLOY ANIHPJ WEB
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --port=80

# 3. DEPLOY TEST PODS IN BOTH NAMESPACES
kubectl run test-anihpj -n anihpj --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600
kubectl run test-attacker -n attacker --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600

# 4. APPLY BROKEN NETWORKPOLICY (namespaceSelector: {} — matches ALL!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-team
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector: {}     # ❌ BUG! {} = ALL namespaces, not just "anihpj"!
    ports:
    - port: 80
EOF

# 5. TEST — Attacker pod CAN reach anihpj-web (BUG!)
kubectl exec -n attacker test-attacker -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web.anihpj:80
# → Returns nginx welcome page! ❌ Cross-namespace access allowed!

# 6. CHECK what namespaceSelector: {} actually means
kubectl describe netpol allow-from-team -n anihpj
# → From: namespaceSelector: {}  — matches ALL namespaces ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Attacker pod can reach anihpj-web: wget http://anihpj-web.anihpj:80 → returns HTML
✗2. namespaceSelector: {} means ALL namespaces — not "this namespace" or "labeled namespaces"
✗3. Check NetPol: kubectl describe netpol allow-from-team -n anihpj → selector is empty
✗4. Intended isolation to "team=jobpost" namespaces is completely bypassed
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Understand selector semantics: {} (empty) means "select ALL" — null/absent means "select none/the same namespace"
2To allow only same namespace: you use podSelector: {} in the ingress rule WITHOUT a namespaceSelector
3To allow specific labeled namespaces: use namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {team: jobpost}}
4{} vs null: in Kubernetes selectors, {} = match everything, absent/null = don't filter by namespace
5Root cause: namespaceSelector: {} is an empty label selector that matches ALL namespaces — it's the equivalent of "any namespace." The developer confused {} (match all) with omitting namespaceSelector (don't filter by namespace, meaning "same namespace" when combined with podSelector from the same namespace). To restrict to only pods from specific namespaces, use matchLabels with a unique label like team: jobpost.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Attacker pod reaches anihpj → namespace isolation broken
②
Check NetPol → namespaceSelector: {} → matches ALL ns
③
Correct syntax: matchLabels: {team: jobpost} — specific label
④
Update NetPol → Attacker pod now blocked
⑤
wget from attacker → timeout → Cross-namespace isolation ✅

Tenet: In Kubernetes selectors, {} means "match EVERYTHING" — it's an empty set of requirements, which is always satisfied. To restrict to pods from the same namespace only, use podSelector: {} WITHOUT any namespaceSelector. To restrict to specific labeled namespaces, use namespaceSelector.matchLabels. On CKS, know the difference: {} = all, null/absent = no filter. This is a subtle but common NetworkPolicy mistake.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n attacker test-attacker -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web.anihpj:80 <!DOCTYPE html>...nginx... ← Attacker from DIFFERENT namespace! ❌
$ kubectl describe netpol allow-from-team -n anihpj | grep -A3 namespaceSelector namespaceSelector: {} ← Matches ALL namespaces! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n attacker test-attacker -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web.anihpj:80 wget: download timed out ✅ Cross-namespace access BLOCKED!
🔧
BASH — Update NetworkPolicy with proper namespaceSelector 
# Step 1: Delete the broken NetPol
kubectl delete netpol allow-from-team -n anihpj

# Step 2: Label the anihpj namespace (if not already)
kubectl label namespace anihpj team=jobpost --overwrite

# Step 3: Create CORRECTED NetPol with SPECIFIC namespaceSelector
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-team
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  # Allow from pods in namespaces labeled "team=jobpost"
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          team: jobpost      # ✅ Only namespaces with team=jobpost label
    ports:
    - port: 80
  # Allow from pods in the SAME namespace (anihpj) — any pod
  - from:
    - podSelector: {}        # ✅ All pods within anihpj namespace
    ports:
    - port: 80
EOF

# Step 4: VERIFY — attacker namespace does NOT have team=jobpost label
kubectl exec -n attacker test-attacker -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web.anihpj:80
# Expected: timeout ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Cross-Namespace Access Is Blocked

With namespaceSelector.matchLabels.team: jobpost, only pods from namespaces labeled team=jobpost can reach anihpj-web. The attacker namespace has no such label, so its pods are blocked. wget from the attacker pod now times out. Pods within the anihpj namespace can still communicate freely.

💡 Key takeaway: namespaceSelector: {} is an anti-pattern — it matches ALL namespaces. Use namespaceSelector.matchLabels with a unique label (like team: jobpost or kubernetes.io/metadata.name: anihpj) to restrict access to specific namespaces. On CKS, remember: in Kubernetes selectors, {} = everything, not nothing. This is one of the most common NetworkPolicy bugs.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete both namespaces
kubectl delete namespace anihpj
kubectl delete namespace attacker

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get ns anihpj attacker 2>/dev/null

🛡️ Category 2: Cluster Hardening Security Lab ScenariosS16–S30

🟢 Hardening RBAC, ServiceAccounts, API Access & Cluster Upgrades

Category 2 covers Cluster Hardening (CKS Domain 2, 15%): These scenarios test your ability to minimize RBAC exposure, restrict ServiceAccount permissions, disable default automount tokens, secure the API server from network exposure, enforce admission plugins, remove privilege escalation paths, detect outdated Kubernetes versions with known CVEs, and verify kubelet authorization modes. Every scenario deploys a part of anihpj/jobpost with intentional security gaps — your job is to harden them. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario!

S16
🧪 SCENARIO S16 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening SA Debug

Deploy anihpj — Every Pod Gets a Default SA Token Mounted Automatically

The Problem: You deploy anihpj/jobpost pods, and every pod automatically gets the default ServiceAccount token mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token — even pods that don't need API access at all (like nginx frontends). If any pod is compromised, the attacker gains a valid Kubernetes API token. CIS Benchmark 5.1.6 recommends disabling automountServiceAccountToken on pods that don't need it. Your job: detect unnecessary SA tokens, disable automount, and verify pods can't access the API.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj pods — Default SA Token Auto-Mounted (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost runs nginx as a reverse proxy. These pods NEVER call the Kubernetes API — they only serve static content and proxy to Django. But every pod has the default ServiceAccount token mounted. If the nginx container is compromised via a web vulnerability, the attacker can read the SA token and make API calls. This is unnecessary exposure.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S16): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-nginx-deploy.yaml           ← BROKEN: no automountServiceAccountToken: false
└── 02-nginx-deploy-fixed.yaml     ← ✅ FIX: automount disabled + token access tested
BASH — Deploy anihpj + Check Default SA Token Exposure 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S16: Default SA Token Auto-Mounted — CIS 5.1.6 Violation
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# DEPLOY NGINX — no automountServiceAccountToken setting (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
      # ❌ BUG: automountServiceAccountToken defaults to TRUE!
      # No automountServiceAccountToken: false specified
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# CHECK — Token is mounted!
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
# → token  ca.crt  namespace  ← Token is MOUNTED!

# TEST — Pod can access the Kubernetes API with the mounted token
APISERVER=https://kubernetes.default.svc
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "curl -s --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt -H 'Authorization: Bearer \$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)' $APISERVER/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj/pods"
# → RETURNS pod list! ❌ Nginx pod has API access!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Token mounted: ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ → token present
✗2. Nginx can query API: curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api → returns API data
✗3. No automountServiceAccountToken: false on pod — default is true
✗4. CIS 5.1.6: "Ensure that ServiceAccount tokens are only mounted where necessary"
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod SA mount: kubectl get pod POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 serviceAccount
→ serviceAccount: default, automountServiceAccountToken: not set (defaults to true)
2Default SA in every namespace has API access via its RBAC bindings (even if minimal)
3Compromised container = API access: the token is readable by any process in the container
4Fix at namespace level: disable automount on the SA itself, or at pod spec level
5Root cause: Every pod in Kubernetes gets the default ServiceAccount token automatically mounted unless automountServiceAccountToken is explicitly set to false. For pods that never call the API (nginx, static servers, workers), this token provides unnecessary attack surface. CIS 5.1.6 requires disabling automount on pods that don't need API access. Fix at pod level or better yet, at the ServiceAccount level.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod has SA token mounted → Check if pod needs API access
②
Nginx never calls API → Token is unnecessary risk
③
Set automountServiceAccountToken: false → Redeploy
④
Token no longer mounted → API access denied
⑤
Attack surface reduced → CIS 5.1.6 PASS ✅

Tenet: The default ServiceAccount token is a Kubernetes API credential that gets mounted into every pod automatically. For pods that don't call the API, this is unnecessary attack surface. On CKS, you must know: automountServiceAccountToken: false at the pod spec level, or patch the default SA with automountServiceAccountToken: false to affect all pods in the namespace. Better yet, create a dedicated SA with minimal RBAC and disable automount on unused SAs.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ ca.crt namespace token ← Token mounted on nginx pod! ❌
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -- sh -c "curl -s --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt -H 'Authorization: Bearer \$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)' https://kubernetes.default.svc/api" | head -1 {"kind":"APIVersions"... ← API accessible from nginx! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ ls: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/: No such file or directory ✅
🔧
BASH — Patch default SA + redeploy pods without token 
# Step 1: Patch the default SA in the namespace to disable automount
kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n anihpj \
  -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}'

# Step 2: Delete pods so they recreate without token
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# Step 3: VERIFY token is gone
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ 2>&1
# Expected: "No such file or directory" ✅
✓

✅ Verify — No SA Token on Unnecessary Pods

After patching the default SA and recreating pods, /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ no longer exists inside the nginx container. The compromised-container-to-API-attack path is closed. If the app later needs API access, create a dedicated SA with minimal RBAC instead of relying on the default SA.

💡 Key takeaway: automountServiceAccountToken: false can be set at the pod spec level or the ServiceAccount level. Setting it on the default SA affects ALL pods in the namespace. On CKS, CIS 5.1.6 requires auditing which pods mount SA tokens and removing unnecessary mounts. For production: never use the default SA — create dedicated SAs per workload with least-privilege RBAC.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null

🧪 SCENARIO S17 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening SA Debug

Deploy anihpj — CI/CD SA Can Edit Deployments in ALL Namespaces

The Problem: The CI/CD pipeline ServiceAccount anihpj-cicd was granted the built-in edit ClusterRole via a ClusterRoleBinding. This gives it permission to modify Deployments, Services, and ConfigMaps in every namespace — not just anihpj. A compromised CI token could modify kube-system Deployments or delete production workloads in other namespaces. The fix: scope the edit permission to only the anihpj namespace using a RoleBinding instead of a ClusterRoleBinding.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + ClusterRoleBinding edit across all namespaces (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The CI/CD team requested "edit access" for deploying anihpj/jobpost. An admin ran kubectl create clusterrolebinding anihpj-cicd-edit --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=anihpj:anihpj-cicd. This gives the CI pipeline edit access to EVERY namespace — including kube-system, default, and future tenant namespaces. A compromised pipeline token can take over the entire cluster.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S17): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml                    ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-serviceaccount.yaml               ← anihpj-cicd SA
├── 02-clusterrolebinding-edit.yaml      ← BROKEN: edit ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide)
└── 03-rolebinding-edit.yaml             ← ✅ FIX: RoleBinding scoped to anihpj only
BASH — Create SA + ClusterRoleBinding edit (overly broad) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S17: CI/CD SA Has Edit Across ALL Namespaces
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create serviceaccount anihpj-cicd -n anihpj

# GRANT edit ClusterRole via ClusterRoleBinding (THE BUG!)
kubectl create clusterrolebinding anihpj-cicd-edit \
  --clusterrole=edit \
  --serviceaccount=anihpj:anihpj-cicd

# TEST — SA can edit Deployments in kube-system! ❌
kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n kube-system \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd
# → yes ❌ Can modify CoreDNS, metrics-server, etc!

kubectl auth can-i delete services -n default \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd
# → yes ❌ Can delete kubernetes service in default!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. SA can edit kube-system: kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n kube-system --as=SA → yes
✗2. SA can edit default: kubectl auth can-i delete services -n default --as=SA → yes
✗3. ClusterRoleBinding instead of RoleBinding — edit applies to ALL namespaces
✗4. Any namespace created in the future automatically gets edit access from this SA
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1List ClusterRoleBindings for the SA: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B10 'anihpj-cicd'
→ anihpj-cicd-edit uses ClusterRoleBinding — scoped to ALL namespaces
2Check what edit ClusterRole grants: kubectl describe clusterrole edit
→ Read/write access to pods, services, deployments, configmaps, secrets in ALL namespaces
3ClusterRoleBinding vs RoleBinding: CRB = all namespaces, RB = single namespace
4CI/CD only needs to deploy to anihpj namespace — not kube-system, not default
5Root cause: A ClusterRoleBinding was used instead of a RoleBinding. The built-in edit ClusterRole grants read/write to common resources (pods, services, configmaps, secrets, deployments). When bound via ClusterRoleBinding, these permissions span ALL namespaces. The fix: replace with a RoleBinding that scopes the edit ClusterRole to only the anihpj namespace.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
SA can edit kube-system → ClusterRoleBinding used
②
Audit actual needs → Only anihpj namespace deployments
③
Delete ClusterRoleBinding → Create RoleBinding in anihpj
④
SA can't edit kube-system → Namespace scoping works
⑤
SA can still deploy to anihpj → CI/CD still functional ✅

Tenet: The built-in ClusterRoles (edit, view, admin) are convenient but dangerous when bound via ClusterRoleBinding — they grant access to ALL namespaces. On CKS, always audit ClusterRoleBindings and check if they can be replaced with RoleBindings. Use kubectl auth can-i --list --as=SA to see exactly what a ServiceAccount can do across the cluster.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd yes ❌ SA can modify kube-system!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd no ✅ SA is scoped to anihpj namespace only!
🔧
BASH — Delete CRB + Create RoleBinding in anihpj namespace only 
# Step 1: DELETE the overly broad ClusterRoleBinding
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding anihpj-cicd-edit

# Step 2: CREATE a RoleBinding (namespace-scoped) instead
kubectl create rolebinding anihpj-cicd-edit \
  --clusterrole=edit \
  --serviceaccount=anihpj:anihpj-cicd \
  -n anihpj

# Step 3: VERIFY — SA can still deploy to anihpj...
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd
# Expected: yes ✅

# ...but CANNOT touch kube-system
kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd
# Expected: no ✅
✓

✅ Verify — SA Is Namespace-Scoped

After replacing the ClusterRoleBinding with a RoleBinding, the CI/CD SA can still create/update deployments in anihpj but cannot touch any other namespace. The edit ClusterRole is reused but scoped via RoleBinding to a single namespace — exactly the pattern Kubernetes recommends for least-privilege RBAC.

💡 Key takeaway: Use ClusterRoleBinding only for cluster-wide permissions (monitoring, node management). For application-level permissions, always use RoleBinding — even with reusable ClusterRoles. This pattern (ClusterRole + RoleBinding) is the Kubernetes-recommended way to share role definitions across namespaces while keeping permissions scoped.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete cluster-scoped resource (if still exists)
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding anihpj-cicd-edit --ignore-not-found

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null

anihpj API Audit — API Server Bound to 0.0.0.0, Exposed to Internet

The Problem: During a network scan, you discover the Kubernetes API server (port 6443) is listening on 0.0.0.0 instead of a specific internal interface. This means the API server is accessible from every network interface on the control plane node — including public-facing NICs. Anyone who can reach the node's IP on port 6443 can attempt to authenticate. The --bind-address should be set to the internal/management network interface only. CIS Benchmark 1.1.3 requires restricting the API server bind address.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster

The --bind-address is set to 0.0.0.0 (or absent, defaulting to 0.0.0.0), exposing the API to ALL network interfaces. If the control plane has a public IP, anyone on the internet can reach port 6443. While they still need credentials, this dramatically increases the attack surface for brute-force and CVE exploits.

# Check the API server manifest

# → --bind-address=0.0.0.0   ← CIS 1.1.3 FAIL
# OR: flag not present = defaults to 0.0.0.0

# 5. SIMULATE EXTERNAL SCAN

# → 6443/tcp open  ← API server accessible from internet! ❌

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. API server listens on 0.0.0.0:6443 — all interfaces including public IPs
✗2. nmap from external machine: 6443/tcp open — API server reachable from internet
✗3. CIS 1.1.3: --bind-address should be internal IP only, not 0.0.0.0
✗4. Attackers can brute-force credentials or exploit API CVEs from anywhere
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check current bind address: sudo grep bind-address /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
→ --bind-address=0.0.0.0 (or absent = default 0.0.0.0)
2Find internal IP: ip addr show | grep 'inet ' | grep -v 127.0.0.1
→ eth0: 192.168.1.10 (internal management network)
30.0.0.0 means bind to ALL interfaces — including docker0, public eth1, VPN interfaces
4etcd should also be checked: --listen-client-urls should be internal only
5Root cause: The API server's --bind-address is set to 0.0.0.0, which binds to ALL network interfaces. This exposes the API server on every IP the control plane node has — internal, external, VPN, Docker bridges. CIS 1.1.3 requires --bind-address to be a specific internal IP. The fix: find the internal management IP and set --bind-address to that specific address.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
ss shows 0.0.0.0:6443 → All interfaces exposed
②
Find internal management IP → 192.168.1.10
③
Edit manifest → --bind-address=192.168.1.10
④
API restarts → ss shows 192.168.1.10:6443 only
⑤
External nmap → 6443 filtered → CIS 1.1.3 PASS ✅

Tenet: --bind-address=0.0.0.0 is the default and binds the API server to every network interface. On a multi-homed node (common in cloud environments with public + private IPs), this exposes the API server to the internet. Always set --bind-address to the internal management IP. On CKS, CIS 1.1.3 requires this check. Related: etcd --listen-client-urls and kubelet --node-ip should also be checked for 0.0.0.0 bindings.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo ss -tlnp | grep 6443 LISTEN 0.0.0.0:6443 0.0.0.0:* users:(("kube-apiserver",...)) ← All interfaces! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo ss -tlnp | grep 6443 LISTEN 192.168.1.10:6443 0.0.0.0:* users:(("kube-apiserver",...)) ← Internal only ✅
🔧
BASH — Edit API server manifest to bind to internal IP 
# Step 1: Find internal management IP
INTERNAL_IP=$(ip addr show | grep 'inet ' | grep -v '127.0.0.1' | head -1 | awk '{print $2}' | cut -d/ -f1)
echo "Internal IP: $INTERNAL_IP"

# Step 2: Update API server manifest
# If --bind-address exists, change it. If not, add it before --secure-port
sudo sed -i "s/--bind-address=0.0.0.0/--bind-address=$INTERNAL_IP/" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# If the flag wasn't present, add it manually in the spec.containers.command section

# Step 3: Wait for API server to restart
sleep 30
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-apiserver

# Step 4: Verify
sudo ss -tlnp | grep 6443
# Should show internal IP, not 0.0.0.0 ✅
✓

✅ Verify — API Server Bound to Internal IP Only

After setting --bind-address to the internal management IP, the API server only listens on that specific interface. External nmap scans show port 6443 as filtered/closed. Internal clients (kubelet, controllers) still connect via the internal IP. CIS Benchmark 1.1.3 now passes.

💡 Key takeaway: --bind-address controls which network interface the API server listens on. On cloud VMs with public IPs, 0.0.0.0 exposes the API to the internet. Always set it to the internal/management NIC IP. On CKS, also check --advertise-address (which IP other components use to reach the API) — it should match the internal IP too.

✗1. Anonymous can list pods: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:anonymous → yes

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Find all bindings to unauthenticated/anonymous: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -B10 -E 'system:unauthenticated|system:anonymous'

①
Anonymous user can list pods → Find the binding
②

③

④

Anonymous kubectl → Forbidden → Data breach closed ✅

Tenet: Never bind any ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated or system:anonymous. These groups represent users with zero credentials. On CKS, audit both ClusterRoleBindings and RoleBindings for these groups. Combine this with --anonymous-auth=false for defense in depth. Monitor: set up alerts if any binding to these groups is created.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get clusterrolebinding anonymous-view NAME ROLE AGE anonymous-view view 5m ← Anonymous users have read access! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:anonymous no ✅ Anonymous access blocked!
🔧
BASH — Find + delete all anonymous/unauthenticated bindings 
# Step 1: Find and delete ClusterRoleBindings to anonymous/unauthenticated
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="system:unauthenticated" or .subjects[]?.name=="system:anonymous") | .metadata.name' | \
  xargs -I {} kubectl delete clusterrolebinding {}

# Step 2: Also scan RoleBindings in all namespaces
kubectl get rolebinding -A -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="system:unauthenticated" or .subjects[]?.name=="system:anonymous") | "\(.metadata.namespace) \(.metadata.name)"'

# Step 3: VERIFY
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: no ✅

BASH — kubeadm upgrade process (control plane node) 
# Step 1: Check available upgrades
kubeadm upgrade plan

# Step 2: Upgrade kubeadm to target version
sudo apt-mark unhold kubeadm
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.28.15-1.1
sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm

# Step 3: Apply the upgrade (on control plane)
sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.28.15

# Step 4: Drain the node, upgrade kubelet + kubectl
kubectl drain anih --ignore-daemonsets
sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.28.15-1.1 kubectl=1.28.15-1.1
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl uncordon anih

# Step 5: Repeat for each worker node
# drain → upgrade kubelet → uncordon

# Step 6: Verify
kubectl version --short
kubectl get nodes
✓

✅ Verify — Cluster Is Running Supported Version

After the kubeadm upgrade process, all nodes are running v1.28.15 — the latest patch in the 1.28 line. Known CVEs are addressed. The cluster is now within the support window. Plan the next upgrade to v1.29+ to stay ahead of the N-3 deprecation curve.

💡 Key takeaway: The kubeadm upgrade order: (1) upgrade kubeadm binary, (2) kubeadm upgrade apply on control plane, (3) drain → upgrade kubelet/kubectl → uncordon on each node. Always check kubeadm upgrade plan first. Never skip minor versions. Backup etcd before upgrading. On CKS, you must know the full kubeadm upgrade workflow for both control plane and worker nodes.

🧪 SCENARIO S21 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening SA Debug

Deploy anihpj — SA Token Has No Expiry, Valid Forever If Stolen

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost CI/CD ServiceAccount uses a legacy static Secret token that never expires. If this token is ever leaked (git commit, log file, compromised pod), the attacker has permanent API access — the token doesn't rotate, doesn't expire, and works until manually revoked. Kubernetes v1.24+ introduced BoundServiceAccountToken with time-bound, audience-bound tokens. Your job: identify the static token, migrate to time-bound tokens, and verify the old token no longer works.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster (v1.32)
1

📋 Deploy anihpj SA + Check Token Expiry (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj CI/CD pipeline was set up before Kubernetes v1.24. The SA token is stored as a static Secret that the pipeline uses for authentication. This token has no expiration time — it's valid forever. If the CI/CD logs accidentally expose this token, an attacker can use it indefinitely. Modern Kubernetes uses projected service account tokens that automatically expire after 1 hour.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S21): 
SA token audit:
kubectl get secrets -n anihpj        ← Check for legacy SA secrets
kubectl describe secret SA-TOKEN     ← Check token type (kubernetes.io/service-account-token)
BASH — Create SA with legacy static token 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S21: Legacy Static SA Token — No Expiry
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create serviceaccount anihpj-cicd -n anihpj

# CREATE A LEGACY STATIC TOKEN SECRET (THE BUG!)
# On pre-1.24 clusters, SA creation auto-generates a Secret with a non-expiring token
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-cicd-token
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/service-account.name: anihpj-cicd
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
EOF

# EXTRACT THE TOKEN — it has NO expiry!
TOKEN=$(kubectl get secret anihpj-cicd-token -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d)
echo "Token (first 20 chars): ${TOKEN:0:20}..."

# DECODE TOKEN PAYLOAD — check for 'exp' claim
echo $TOKEN | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E 'exp|iat'
# → "iat": timestamp   ← Issued-at time exists
# → NO "exp" field!   ← Token NEVER expires! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Token has no exp claim: decode JWT → no expiration field
✗2. Secret type is kubernetes.io/service-account-token — legacy static token
✗3. If this token leaks, attacker has PERMANENT API access — no automatic rotation
✗4. Modern tokens (v1.24+) expire after 1 hour by default — this one doesn't
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Legacy token secrets are type kubernetes.io/service-account-token — manually created or auto-generated pre-1.24
2BoundServiceAccountToken (modern): time-bound (1h default), audience-bound, Kubelet-managed rotation
3Check if SA has auto-generated secret: kubectl get sa anihpj-cicd -n anihpj -o yaml | grep secrets
4v1.24+ SAs no longer auto-generate static token secrets — but existing ones persist after upgrade
5Root cause: The SA token is stored as a legacy kubernetes.io/service-account-token Secret with no expiration. These static tokens were auto-generated pre-1.24 and persist across upgrades. The fix: delete the legacy Secret, use projected BoundServiceAccountTokens (auto-mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount with 1h expiry), and for CI/CD, use short-lived tokens generated via the TokenRequest API.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Decode JWT → no exp field → Token never expires
②
Check Secret type → kubernetes.io/service-account-token → Legacy
③
Delete legacy Secret → Use TokenRequest API
④
New token has exp claim → Expires in 1h
⑤
Leaked token invalid after 1h → Attack window minimized ✅

Tenet: Legacy SA token secrets are permanent credentials — they never expire and never auto-rotate. Modern Kubernetes uses BoundServiceAccountTokens that expire after 1 hour by default. On CKS, you must identify and eliminate legacy static tokens. Use kubectl create token SA_NAME -n NAMESPACE for short-lived tokens, or configure --service-account-extend-token-expiration=false on the kube-apiserver to enforce short token lifetimes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get secret anihpj-cicd-token -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep exp # No output — exp field is MISSING! Token NEVER expires ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl create token anihpj-cicd -n anihpj --duration=1h | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep exp "exp": 1718150000 ← Token expires in 1 hour ✅
🔧
BASH — Migrate from static token to time-bound token 
# Step 1: DELETE the legacy static token secret
kubectl delete secret anihpj-cicd-token -n anihpj

# Step 2: Verify SA no longer has static secrets
kubectl get sa anihpj-cicd -n anihpj -o yaml | grep secrets
# Should show: secrets: null or no auto-generated token

# Step 3: Use TokenRequest API for SHORT-LIVED tokens (CKS exam method)
kubectl create token anihpj-cicd -n anihpj --duration=1h
# This creates a time-bound token that expires in 1 hour

# For CI/CD: request tokens as needed, never store them permanently
# Token auto-rotates when mounted in pods (projected volume)
✓

✅ Verify — Token Expires Automatically

After deleting the legacy static Secret and using the TokenRequest API (kubectl create token), all new SA tokens have a 1-hour expiration. Pod-mounted tokens auto-rotate via the kubelet's TokenRequest projection. If a token leaks, it's only valid for at most 1 hour — dramatically reducing the attack window.

💡 Key takeaway: Pre-1.24 clusters auto-generated static SA token Secrets with no expiry. After upgrading to 1.24+, these Secrets persist and must be manually deleted. On CKS, use kubectl create token for short-lived CI/CD tokens and rely on projected volumes for pod-mounted tokens. Never manually create kubernetes.io/service-account-token Secrets in production.

BASH — Find + delete all bindings for default ServiceAccounts 
# Step 1: Find all ClusterRoleBindings for default SAs
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="default" and .subjects[]?.kind=="ServiceAccount") | .metadata.name' | \
  xargs -I {} kubectl delete clusterrolebinding {}

# Step 2: Also check RoleBindings in all namespaces
kubectl get rolebinding -A -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="default" and .subjects[]?.kind=="ServiceAccount") | "\(.metadata.namespace) \(.metadata.name)"' | \
  while read ns rb; do kubectl delete rolebinding $rb -n $ns; done

# Step 3: VERIFY
kubectl auth can-i delete nodes --as=system:serviceaccount:kube-system:default
# Expected: no ✅
✓

✅ Verify — No Default SA Has Elevated Privileges

After deleting all ClusterRoleBindings and RoleBindings referencing default ServiceAccounts, no default SA has any RBAC beyond the built-in discovery roles. Pods that need API access must now use dedicated, least-privilege ServiceAccounts — preventing privilege inheritance accidents.

💡 Key takeaway: Default SAs are a common RBAC anti-pattern. Their permissions are inherited by every pod that doesn't specify a SA. On CKS, always audit with jq, never bind default SAs to roles, and disable automount on default SAs. The kube-system default SA is the highest-value target — protect it aggressively.

      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s
echo "✅ anihpj/jobpost deployed"

# 2. NOW TRY TO CREATE A PRIVILEGED POD (should be BLOCKED by PodSecurity)
# But if PodSecurity plugin is missing, this will SUCCEED (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: privileged-test
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: test
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["sleep", "60"]
    securityContext:
      privileged: true       # ← Should be rejected if PodSecurity is active!
EOF
# → If PodSecurity plugin is MISSING, this pod will be CREATED! ❌

# 3. CHECK CURRENT ADMISSION PLUGINS
sudo grep 'enable-admission-plugins' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# → --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,AlwaysPullImages,NamespaceLifecycle
#   Missing: PodSecurity, ServiceAccount ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. PodSecurity plugin missing — privileged pods can be created without restriction
✗2. ServiceAccount plugin missing — SA automount enforcement not active
✗3. CIS 1.1.11–1.1.16 require specific admission plugins to be enabled
✗4. Missing plugins = no automated guardrails against dangerous pod specs
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1List enabled plugins: kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-anih -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
2Compare against CIS requirements: NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, ServiceAccount MUST be present
3NodeRestriction blocks kubelets from modifying other nodes — critical for multi-tenant clusters
4PodSecurity replaces the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy — enforces baseline/restricted profiles
5Root cause: The API server is missing critical security admission plugins: PodSecurity and ServiceAccount. These plugins enforce Pod Security Standards (blocking privileged pods, hostPath mounts, etc.) and ServiceAccount lifecycle (automount token enforcement, token cleanup). Without them, pods can bypass these guardrails. CIS 1.1.11-1.1.16 mandate these plugins.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Check enable-admission-plugins → Compare to CIS requirements
②
PodSecurity + ServiceAccount missing → Add them
③
API restarts → New plugins active
④
Test: privileged pod → REJECTED by PodSecurity
⑤
CIS 1.1.11-1.1.16 PASS ✅

Tenet: Admission plugins are the API server's gatekeepers — they validate and mutate requests before objects are persisted. Missing security plugins mean pods can bypass critical guardrails. On CKS, you must know the mandatory admission plugins: NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, ServiceAccount, AlwaysPullImages, NamespaceLifecycle. The fix is to add them to --enable-admission-plugins in the kube-apiserver manifest.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-anih -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,AlwaysPullImages,NamespaceLifecycle ← Missing PodSecurity, ServiceAccount! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-anih -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,ServiceAccount,AlwaysPullImages,NamespaceLifecycle ← All critical plugins enabled ✅
🔧
BASH — Edit API server manifest + add missing plugins 
# Step 1: Edit the API server manifest
# Add PodSecurity and ServiceAccount to --enable-admission-plugins
sudo sed -i 's/--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,AlwaysPullImages,NamespaceLifecycle/--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,ServiceAccount,AlwaysPullImages,NamespaceLifecycle/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Step 2: Wait for API server to restart
sleep 30
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-apiserver

# Step 3: VERIFY plugins are now active
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-anih -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
✓

✅ Verify — All Critical Admission Plugins Active

After adding PodSecurity and ServiceAccount to the admission plugin chain, the API server now enforces Pod Security Standards (blocking privileged pods) and ServiceAccount lifecycle rules. The cluster passes CIS checks 1.1.11 through 1.1.16. Attempts to create privileged pods or pods without SA automount enforcement are now rejected.

💡 Key takeaway: Admission plugins are NOT optional — they are critical security controls. On CKS, memorize the mandatory list: NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, ServiceAccount, AlwaysPullImages, NamespaceLifecycle. Always check --enable-admission-plugins and --disable-admission-plugins in the API server manifest. Never disable security plugins to "make things work."
