S24
🧪 SCENARIO S24 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening SA Debug

Deploy anihpj — SA Has Explicit Secret Token + Unnecessary automount

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost deployment uses a manually created kubernetes.io/service-account-token Secret that is mounted as a volume into pods. This is a double vulnerability: (1) the static token never expires, (2) the Secret is mounted even though the pod spec already gets an auto-mounted SA token via the default SA. The result is two valid API tokens inside the container, doubling the attack surface. Your job: identify the unnecessary static token, remove it, and rely only on the projected BoundServiceAccountToken.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj with static Secret token mounted (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A developer followed an old tutorial and manually created a SA token Secret, then mounted it as a volume in the Django pod. Meanwhile, Kubernetes also auto-mounts the default SA's projected token. The pod now has two API tokens: one that auto-rotates (good) and one static token that never expires (dangerous). If the pod is compromised, the attacker gets a permanent token.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S24): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-sa-token-secret.yaml        ← BROKEN: Static SA token Secret
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: Mounts the static Secret as volume
└── 03-django-deploy-fixed.yaml    ← ✅ FIX: No static token, projected token only
BASH — Deploy pod with both static + projected token (THE BUG) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S24: Dual Tokens — Static + Projected
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# CREATE STATIC TOKEN SECRET (THE BUG!)
kubectl create serviceaccount anihpj-app -n anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-legacy-token
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/service-account.name: anihpj-app
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
EOF

# DEPLOY POD — mounts static Secret + gets projected SA token
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-app
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    volumeMounts:
    - name: legacy-token
      mountPath: /var/run/secrets/legacy    # Static token
  volumes:
  - name: legacy-token
    secret:
      secretName: anihpj-legacy-token       # ❌ Permanent token!
EOF

# CHECK — Pod has TWO token locations!
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
# → token (projected, auto-rotates) + ca.crt + namespace
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /var/run/secrets/legacy/
# → token (static, NEVER expires) + ca.crt + namespace ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Two token files: ls /var/run/secrets/ → legacy + kubernetes.io (doubled attack surface)
✗2. Static Secret type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token — legacy, non-expiring
✗3. Volume mount of SA token Secret is unnecessary — the projected token already works
✗4. If either token leaks, attacker has API access — the static one provides permanent access
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check all mounted volumes: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep -A5 volumes
2Identify which Secrets are SA tokens: kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.type=="kubernetes.io/service-account-token") | .metadata.name'
3Modern pods (v1.24+) get a projected SA token automatically — no Secret needed at all
4Static tokens are never rotated — if leaked, they remain valid until the Secret is deleted
5Root cause: The pod mounts a legacy kubernetes.io/service-account-token Secret alongside the auto-projected BoundServiceAccountToken. The legacy token never expires and was created manually. Modern Kubernetes uses projected tokens that auto-rotate — the static Secret is unnecessary and dangerous. Remove the static Secret volume mount and rely only on the projected token.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod has two token sources → Check why
②
Static Secret is manual kubernetes.io/service-account-token → Legacy
③
Remove volume mount → Delete static Secret
④
Pod uses only projected token → Auto-rotates safely
⑤
Single token source → Attack surface halved ✅

Tenet: Pods automatically get a projected BoundServiceAccountToken since Kubernetes v1.24. Manually creating and mounting SA token Secrets is a legacy anti-pattern that creates permanent credentials. On CKS, audit all Secrets of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token and eliminate them in favor of projected tokens. Use kubectl create token for CI/CD.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.type=="kubernetes.io/service-account-token") | .metadata.name' "anihpj-legacy-token" ← Static, non-expiring token! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /var/run/secrets/ kubernetes.io ← Only projected token, auto-rotates ✅
🔧
BASH — Remove legacy token, rely on projected token only 
# Step 1: Delete the pod (can't edit volumes on running pod)
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 2: Delete the static token Secret
kubectl delete secret anihpj-legacy-token -n anihpj

# Step 3: Recreate pod WITHOUT static token volume mount
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-app
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
  # NO volume mount — uses projected SA token only
EOF

# Step 4: VERIFY only one token source
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /var/run/secrets/
# Should show only "kubernetes.io" ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Single Token Source, Auto-Rotating

After removing the static Secret and its volume mount, the pod relies only on the projected BoundServiceAccountToken. This token auto-rotates every hour by default (kubelet-managed). No permanent credentials exist inside the container. If the pod is compromised, the attacker's token becomes invalid within at most 1 hour.

💡 Key takeaway: Never manually create kubernetes.io/service-account-token Secrets. Since v1.24, Kubernetes automatically provides projected SA tokens via the kubelet's TokenRequest API. On CKS, scan for legacy token Secrets with kubectl get secrets -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.type=="kubernetes.io/service-account-token")' and delete them.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace
kubectl delete namespace anihpj
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S25
🧪 SCENARIO S25 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening RBAC Debug

Deploy anihpj — Developer SA Can Exec Into Pods in ALL Namespaces

The Problem: A ClusterRole named developer-access grants pods/exec on resources ["pods"] with apiGroups: [""] — and it's bound via ClusterRoleBinding to a developer group. This means developers can exec into pods in ANY namespace, including kube-system (CoreDNS, etcd, API server proxy pods). A compromised developer account = full command execution across the entire cluster. The fix: scope exec permissions to only the anihpj namespace via RoleBinding.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + ClusterRoleBinding for pod/exec (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj development team requested "kubectl exec access for debugging." An admin created a ClusterRole with pods/exec and bound it via ClusterRoleBinding to the entire dev team. Now any dev can exec into CoreDNS pods, view etcd proxy logs, or run commands inside kube-system — effectively giving them node-level access via privileged DaemonSet pods.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S25): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml                       ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-clusterrole-exec.yaml                ← BROKEN: pods/exec on ALL namespaces
├── 02-clusterrolebinding-exec.yaml         ← BROKEN: ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide)
└── 03-rolebinding-exec.yaml                ← ✅ FIX: RoleBinding scoped to anihpj only
BASH — Grant developer pods/exec across all namespaces (THE BUG) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S25: pods/exec on ALL Namespaces
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine

# CREATE CLUSTERROLE WITH pods/exec (THE BUG!)
kubectl create clusterrole developer-exec --verb=create --resource=pods/exec
kubectl create clusterrolebinding developer-exec-binding \
  --clusterrole=developer-exec \
  --group=developers

# TEST — Developer can exec into kube-system pods! ❌
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default
# → yes ❌ (if the SA is in the developers group)
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. pods/exec across all namespaces: kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n kube-system --as=DEV → yes
✗2. ClusterRoleBinding instead of RoleBinding — exec works cluster-wide
✗3. Exec into a privileged DaemonSet pod = node root access possible
✗4. pods/exec combined with ClusterRoleBinding is one of the most dangerous RBAC patterns
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Find all ClusterRoles with pods/exec: kubectl get clusterrole -o yaml | grep -B5 'pods/exec'
2pods/exec is NOT a namespace-scoped resource — it gives command execution inside any pod
3Scope to development namespaces only: devs should only exec into their own app pods
4pods/exec + kube-system = potential node root access via privileged controller pods
5Root cause: The developer-exec ClusterRole grants pods/exec and is bound via ClusterRoleBinding — meaning developers can exec into ANY pod in ANY namespace. pods/exec is a highly privileged verb that allows command execution inside containers. When scoped cluster-wide, it's almost equivalent to node SSH access. Fix: replace ClusterRoleBinding with RoleBinding to limit exec to only the anihpj namespace.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Developer can exec into kube-system → Binding too broad
②
Delete ClusterRoleBinding → Create RoleBinding in anihpj
③
Dev can exec into anihpj pods → Dev can't exec into kube-system
④
Least privilege: devs can only debug their own apps
⑤
pods/exec is now namespace-scoped ✅

Tenet: pods/exec and pods/log are high-risk verbs — they allow command execution and data access inside containers. Never grant them via ClusterRoleBinding. Always scope them to specific namespaces via RoleBinding. On CKS, audit all ClusterRoles with pods/exec and verify their bindings are namespace-scoped.

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default no ✅ Exec is now scoped to anihpj namespace only!
🔧
BASH — Replace ClusterRoleBinding with RoleBinding 
# Step 1: Delete the cluster-wide binding
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding developer-exec-binding

# Step 2: Create namespace-scoped RoleBinding
kubectl create rolebinding developer-exec-binding \
  --clusterrole=developer-exec \
  --group=developers \
  -n anihpj

# Step 3: VERIFY — can exec in anihpj, but NOT kube-system
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default
# → yes ✅ (only in their namespace)
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default
# → no ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Exec Is Namespace-Scoped

Developers can now exec into pods only within the anihpj namespace. They cannot exec into kube-system or any other namespace. The ClusterRole definition is preserved (reusable pattern) but scoped via RoleBinding.

💡 Key takeaway: pods/exec is one of the most dangerous RBAC verbs — it grants shell access inside containers. Always scope it with RoleBinding, never ClusterRoleBinding. On CKS, remember that pods/exec + privileged container = node root access. Audit with: kubectl get clusterrole -o yaml | grep -B10 'pods/exec'.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace + cluster-scoped resources
kubectl delete namespace anihpj
kubectl delete clusterrole developer-exec --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding developer-exec-binding --ignore-not-found

🧪 SCENARIO S26 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening API Debug

anihpj Cluster — API Server Profiling Endpoint Exposes Internals

The Problem: The API server has --profiling=true enabled, which exposes /debug/pprof/ endpoints. These endpoints reveal detailed runtime information: heap dumps, goroutine stacks, CPU profiles, and memory allocation patterns. An attacker who accesses these endpoints can learn API server internals, discover request patterns, and potentially extract sensitive data from memory dumps. CIS Benchmark 1.1.10 requires --profiling=false. Your job: detect the profiling endpoint, disable it, and verify it's no longer accessible.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Check API Server Profiling (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj platform team notices unusual CPU usage patterns. Investigating, they discover the API server's profiling endpoint is publicly accessible to anyone who can reach the API server. The /debug/pprof/heap endpoint reveals memory allocation data that could leak Secret contents, request paths, and internal token patterns. This debugging feature should never be enabled in production.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S26): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL Deployment + Service
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django Deployment + Service
└── 03-audit-profiling.sh          ← Audit script for API server profiling

API server audit:
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml   ← Check --profiling flag
curl -k https://API_IP:6443/debug/pprof/        ← Test profiling access

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s
echo "✅ anihpj/jobpost deployed"

# 2. CHECK PROFILING FLAG (THE BUG!)
sudo grep 'profiling' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# → --profiling=true   ← CIS 1.1.10 FAIL ❌

# 3. TEST PROFILING ENDPOINT
API_IP=$(kubectl get endpoints kubernetes -o jsonpath='{.subsets[0].addresses[0].ip}')
curl -k https://$API_IP:6443/debug/pprof/ 2>/dev/null | head -5
# → Returns profiling index page with heap, goroutine, etc. ❌

# 4. WHAT PROFILING EXPOSES
# /debug/pprof/heap      — Memory dump (may contain Secrets, tokens)
# /debug/pprof/goroutine — All goroutine stacks
# /debug/pprof/profile   — CPU profile
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. --profiling=true in API server manifest — CIS 1.1.10 FAIL
✗2. /debug/pprof/ accessible — heap dumps, goroutine stacks exposed
✗3. Memory dumps could leak Secrets, tokens, request payloads
✗4. Also check controller-manager + scheduler for same flag
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Profiling exposes: /debug/pprof/heap (memory dump), /debug/pprof/goroutine (all goroutine stacks), /debug/pprof/profile (CPU profile)
2Memory dumps can contain Secret data, token values, and request payloads being processed
3CIS 1.1.10 requires false — profiling should only be enabled temporarily for debugging
4Also check: kube-controller-manager (CIS 1.3.2) and kube-scheduler (CIS 1.4.1) for the same flag
5Root cause: --profiling=true exposes the Go pprof debugging endpoints on the API server. These endpoints reveal detailed runtime internals including memory dumps that may contain sensitive data. CIS 1.1.10 requires --profiling=false. The same applies to kube-controller-manager (1.3.2) and kube-scheduler (1.4.1).
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
--profiling=true detected → Check all control plane components
②
Change to false in API server + controller-manager + scheduler
③
Restart components → /debug/pprof/ returns 403
④
CIS 1.1.10, 1.3.2, 1.4.1 all PASS
⑤
No runtime internals exposed ✅

Tenet: Go's pprof endpoints expose detailed runtime information — heap dumps, goroutine stacks, CPU profiles. In production, these must be disabled. On CKS, CIS 1.1.10 (API server), 1.3.2 (controller-manager), and 1.4.1 (scheduler) all require --profiling=false. Enable only temporarily via a debug build, never in production manifests.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo grep profiling /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml - --profiling=true ← CIS 1.1.10 FAIL ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -k https://API_IP:6443/debug/pprof/ 2>&1 forbidden ✅ Profiling endpoint disabled!
🔧
BASH — Set --profiling=false on API server + controller-manager + scheduler 
# Step 1: Disable profiling on API server
sudo sed -i 's/--profiling=true/--profiling=false/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Step 2: Disable profiling on controller-manager (CIS 1.3.2)
sudo sed -i 's/--profiling=true/--profiling=false/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml

# Step 3: Disable profiling on scheduler (CIS 1.4.1)
sudo sed -i 's/--profiling=true/--profiling=false/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml

# Step 4: Wait for pods to restart, then verify
sleep 20
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'apiserver|controller|scheduler'
✓

✅ Verify — Profiling Disabled on All Control Plane Components

After setting --profiling=false on the API server, controller-manager, and scheduler, the /debug/pprof/ endpoints return 403 Forbidden. No runtime internals are exposed. CIS checks 1.1.10, 1.3.2, and 1.4.1 all pass.

💡 Key takeaway: Profiling is for debugging only — never in production. On CKS, check ALL three control plane manifests for --profiling. Use grep profiling /etc/kubernetes/manifests/*.yaml to audit at once. If profiling is needed for a production incident, enable temporarily and disable immediately after.

S27
🧪 SCENARIO S27 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening Kubelet Debug

Deploy anihpj — Kubelet Authorization Mode Is "AlwaysAllow"

The Problem: The kubelet on worker nodes has --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow — meaning ANY authenticated request to the kubelet API is automatically authorized. Combined with anonymous-auth enabled, this means anyone can access the kubelet API and perform destructive operations like running commands in containers, reading logs, or even deleting pods directly. CIS Benchmark 4.1.2 requires --authorization-mode=Webhook so the API server's RBAC controls kubelet access.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Check Kubelet Authorization Mode (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: During a node security scan of the anihpj cluster, you check the kubelet configuration on worker nodes. The authorization mode is set to AlwaysAllow — a legacy setting that authorizes every authenticated request to the kubelet API. Combined with anonymous-auth issues, this gives attackers unrestricted node-level access. CIS 4.1.2 requires Webhook mode, which delegates authorization to the API server's RBAC.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S27): 
Kubelet audit:
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   ← Check authorization.mode
ps aux | grep kubelet          ← Check --authorization-mode flag
BASH — Deploy + Audit kubelet authorization mode 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S27: Kubelet AlwaysAllow Authorization — CIS 4.1.2
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine

# CHECK KUBELET AUTHORIZATION MODE
docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep -A3 authorization
# → authorization:
#     mode: AlwaysAllow   ← CIS 4.1.2 FAIL! ❌

# WHAT AlwaysAllow MEANS:
# Any request that passes authentication (or anonymous if enabled)
# is AUTOMATICALLY authorized — no RBAC checks at all.
# An attacker can: exec into pods, read logs, delete pods, access /run
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. authorization.mode: AlwaysAllow — all authenticated requests are authorized
✗2. CIS 4.1.2 requires mode: Webhook — delegates to API server RBAC
✗3. Combined with anonymous-auth, attackers get unrestricted kubelet access
✗4. Kubelet API can run commands, read logs, delete pods — node-level control
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check config.yaml: authorization.mode: AlwaysAllow is the legacy default
2Webhook mode: sends SubjectAccessReview to the API server for every kubelet request
3AlwaysAllow bypasses all RBAC, Pod Security, and node restrictions at the kubelet level
4Fix applies to ALL worker nodes — each node's kubelet config must be updated
5Root cause: The kubelet's authorization mode is AlwaysAllow, which authorizes every request without checking RBAC. CIS 4.1.2 requires Webhook mode, where the kubelet sends a SubjectAccessReview to the API server to verify the requester has the appropriate RBAC permissions. AlwaysAllow is a legacy setting — modern clusters must use Webhook.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kubelet config → AlwaysAllow → No RBAC enforcement
②
Change to Webhook → Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
③
Restart kubelet on ALL nodes
④
Kubelet now checks RBAC for every request
⑤
CIS 4.1.2 PASS + anonymous blocked → Node secured ✅

Tenet: Kubelet authorization mode must be Webhook, not AlwaysAllow. In Webhook mode, the kubelet calls the API server's SubjectAccessReview API for every request — meaning your existing RBAC policies apply to kubelet API access too. On CKS, CIS 4.1.2 is a must-know check. Fix on all nodes: edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, set authorization.mode to Webhook, and restart kubelet.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep -A2 authorization authorization: mode: AlwaysAllow ← CIS 4.1.2 FAIL ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep -A2 authorization authorization: mode: Webhook ← RBAC enforced ✅
🔧
BASH — Edit kubelet config on EACH node + restart 
# Step 1: Edit kubelet config on worker node
# Change authorization.mode from AlwaysAllow to Webhook
docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker sed -i 's/mode: AlwaysAllow/mode: Webhook/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

# Step 2: Also ensure anonymous-auth is disabled
docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker sed -i 's/enabled: true/enabled: false/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

# Step 3: Restart kubelet (kill process, container runtime restarts it)
docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker pkill kubelet

# Step 4: Wait for node to be Ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready node/wk1 --timeout=60s

# Step 5: REPEAT for ALL worker nodes
✓

✅ Verify — Kubelet Uses Webhook Authorization

After changing authorization to Webhook and restarting kubelet on all nodes, every kubelet API request is now validated against the API server's RBAC. Attackers who reach the kubelet API are subject to the same RBAC policies that protect the cluster API. CIS 4.1.2 passes on all nodes.

💡 Key takeaway: Kubelet authorization mode should always be Webhook. This delegates authorization decisions to the API server, ensuring consistent RBAC enforcement. On CKS, combine CIS 4.1.1 (anonymous-auth=false) with CIS 4.1.2 (authorization=Webhook) for complete kubelet API hardening. The kubelet config is at /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml on standard installations.

🧪 SCENARIO S28 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening RBAC Debug

Deploy anihpj — Custom ClusterRole Grants "escalate" Verb

The Problem: A custom ClusterRole named anihpj-operator was created for the platform team. It includes the escalate verb on roles and clusterroles — a dangerous permission that allows users to create or modify ClusterRoles with permissions exceeding their own. This is a direct privilege escalation path: a user with this ClusterRole can grant themselves cluster-admin. Your job: detect the escalate verb, remove it, and verify the SA can no longer escalate.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + ClusterRole with escalate verb (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team managing anihpj/jobpost has a ClusterRole that includes the escalate verb. This verb allows users to create or update ClusterRoles even if the new role has permissions the user doesn't currently have. A team member could accidentally grant themselves cluster-admin by creating a new ClusterRole with full permissions. The escalate verb should NEVER be included in custom roles.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S28): 
RBAC audit:
kubectl get clusterrole -o yaml | grep -B5 '"escalate"'
→ Find any ClusterRole with the escalate verb
BASH — Create ClusterRole with escalate + test privilege escalation 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S28: RBAC escalate Verb — Privilege Escalation
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create serviceaccount anihpj-ops -n anihpj

# CREATE CLUSTERROLE WITH escalate (THE BUG!)
kubectl create clusterrole anihpj-operator \
  --verb=get,list,create,update,escalate \
  --resource=roles,clusterroles

kubectl create clusterrolebinding anihpj-ops-binding \
  --clusterrole=anihpj-operator \
  --serviceaccount=anihpj:anihpj-ops

# TEST — SA can escalate to cluster-admin!
kubectl auth can-i create clusterroles --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-ops
# → yes ❌ This SA can create new ClusterRoles beyond its own permissions!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. escalate verb on roles/clusterroles: kubectl describe clusterrole anihpj-operator → escalate
✗2. SA can create ClusterRoles: kubectl auth can-i create clusterroles --as=SA → yes
✗3. With escalate, the SA can create roles that exceed its own permissions
✗4. escalate + create clusterroles = path to cluster-admin in one step
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1The escalate verb bypasses the RBAC restriction that prevents granting permissions you don't have
2Find all roles with escalate: kubectl get clusterrole -o yaml | grep -B10 'escalate'
3Also check for bind verb — allows binding any role to any subject, equally dangerous
4Escalate should only exist in the built-in cluster-admin role — never in custom roles
5Root cause: The anihpj-operator ClusterRole includes the escalate verb on roles/clusterroles. This allows the SA to create or modify ClusterRoles with permissions exceeding what the SA itself possesses. The escalate and bind verbs must NEVER be included in custom ClusterRoles. They should only exist in the built-in cluster-admin role.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
ClusterRole has escalate → Privilege escalation path found
②
Remove escalate from the role → SA can no longer escalate
③
SA can still manage roles → But must stay within its own permissions
④
Audit all other roles for escalate + bind
⑤
No privilege escalation paths → Cluster hardened ✅

Tenet: The escalate and bind verbs are the most dangerous RBAC permissions after wildcards. escalate allows creating roles with more permissions than the creator has. bind allows binding any role to any subject. Both enable privilege escalation to cluster-admin. On CKS, never include these in custom ClusterRoles. Audit with: kubectl get clusterrole -o yaml | grep -E 'escalate|bind'.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe clusterrole anihpj-operator Resources Verbs roles.rbac [get list create update escalate] ← escalate! ❌ clusterroles.rbac [get list create update escalate] ← escalate! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe clusterrole anihpj-operator Resources Verbs roles.rbac [get list create update] ← No escalate ✅
🔧
BASH — Patch ClusterRole to remove escalate verb 
# Step 1: Delete and recreate the ClusterRole without escalate
kubectl delete clusterrole anihpj-operator

kubectl create clusterrole anihpj-operator \
  --verb=get,list,create,update \
  --resource=roles,clusterroles

# Step 2: VERIFY — SA can still manage roles but CANNOT escalate
kubectl auth can-i create clusterroles --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-ops
# → yes (still can create roles, but WITHOUT escalate, RBAC prevents
#          creating roles with permissions beyond what the SA already has)
✓

✅ Verify — No Escalate Verb in Custom Roles

After removing the escalate verb from the ClusterRole, the SA can still manage roles, but RBAC's built-in escalation prevention ensures it cannot create roles with permissions exceeding its own. The privilege escalation path to cluster-admin is closed.

💡 Key takeaway: escalate and bind are the two most dangerous RBAC verbs. They must ONLY exist in cluster-admin. Audit with: kubectl get clusterrole -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.rules[]?.verbs[]?=="escalate" or .rules[]?.verbs[]?=="bind") | .metadata.name'. On CKS, this is a critical finding — escalate + create clusterroles = instant cluster-admin.

🧹

kubectl delete namespace anihpj
kubectl delete clusterrole anihpj-operator --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding anihpj-ops-binding --ignore-not-found

🧪 SCENARIO S30 — Category 2: Cluster Hardening Upgrade Debug

anihpj Cluster — Kubelet Versions Mismatched Across Worker Nodes

The Problem: After upgrading the control plane (S20), you discover the worker nodes are running different kubelet versions — wk1 has v1.28.15, wk2 is still on v1.28.0 with known CVEs. Nodes with outdated kubelets are vulnerable to the same CVEs the control plane upgrade fixed. CIS 1.1.20 requires all nodes to run the same supported version. Your job: identify mismatched node versions, drain the outdated nodes, upgrade their kubelet, and verify version consistency across the cluster.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster (multi-node)
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Check Node Version Consistency (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: After completing the control plane upgrade, the anihpj platform team verifies all nodes. They discover worker node wk2 is still on v1.28.0 — 15 patch versions behind. This node has all the original CVEs and is the weak link in the cluster. Any pod scheduled on wk2 is exposed to kubelet-level vulnerabilities that the control plane upgrade was supposed to fix.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S30): 
Node version audit:
kubectl get nodes -o wide                    ← Check all node versions
kubectl drain NODE                           ← Safely evict pods before upgrade
sudo apt-get install kubelet=VERSION         ← Upgrade kubelet
BASH — Check node versions + upgrade outdated workers 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S30: Mismatched Kubelet Versions — CIS 1.1.20
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2

# CHECK ALL NODE VERSIONS
kubectl get nodes -o wide
# → anih   v1.28.15   Ready   control-plane   ← UPGRADED
# → wk1    v1.28.15   Ready   <none>          ← UPGRADED
# → wk2    v1.28.0    Ready   <none>          ← OUTDATED! ❌

# CHECK KUBELET VERSION ON OUTDATED NODE
kubectl get node wk2 -o jsonpath='{.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion}'
# → v1.28.0   ← 15 patches behind, CVEs unpatched ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Node versions differ: kubectl get nodes → wk2 is v1.28.0 vs others at v1.28.15
✗2. CIS 1.1.20 requires all nodes to run the same supported version
✗3. Outdated kubelet = vulnerable to CVE exploits even if control plane is patched
✗4. Pods scheduled on wk2 are exposed to unpatched kubelet vulnerabilities
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Worker node upgrade was skipped during the control plane upgrade process
2Kubelet version must match across all nodes — mixed versions = inconsistent security posture
3Upgrade process for workers: drain → upgrade kubelet + kubectl → uncordon
4Maximum version skew: kubelet can be up to N-2 minor versions behind API server. Patch versions should always match.
5Root cause: Worker node wk2 was not upgraded after the control plane upgrade. Its kubelet is running v1.28.0 while the rest of the cluster is on v1.28.15. This means wk2 has 15 unpatched CVEs. CIS 1.1.20 requires all nodes to run a supported version. The fix: drain wk2, upgrade its kubelet, and uncordon.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kubectl get nodes → wk2 version mismatch
②
Drain wk2 → Upgrade kubelet → Uncordon
③
All nodes now v1.28.15 → Consistent security posture
④
CIS 1.1.20 PASS on all nodes
⑤
Full cluster on same patched version ✅

Tenet: A Kubernetes upgrade is not complete until ALL nodes — control plane AND workers — are on the same version. Worker nodes are often forgotten after a control plane upgrade. On CKS, always verify with kubectl get nodes -o wide and check the VERSION column. The kubeadm upgrade process for workers: drain → apt-get install kubelet → systemctl restart kubelet → uncordon.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS VERSION anih Ready v1.28.15 wk1 Ready v1.28.15 wk2 Ready v1.28.0 ← OUTDATED! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS VERSION anih Ready v1.28.15 wk1 Ready v1.28.15 wk2 Ready v1.28.15 ← All nodes matched ✅
🔧
BASH — Drain + upgrade kubelet on outdated worker node 
# Step 1: Drain the outdated node (pods move to other nodes)
kubectl drain wk2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# Step 2: Upgrade kubelet on the worker node
# (Run these commands ON THE WORKER NODE, not the control plane)
sudo apt-mark unhold kubelet
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.28.15-1.1
sudo apt-mark hold kubelet
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# Step 3: Uncordon the node (allow pods to schedule again)
kubectl uncordon wk2

# Step 4: VERIFY version matches
kubectl get nodes
# All nodes should now show v1.28.15 ✅
✓

✅ Verify — All Nodes on Same Supported Version

After draining wk2, upgrading its kubelet, and uncordoning, all nodes in the cluster are now running v1.28.15. The cluster has a consistent security posture — no node is running vulnerable, unpatched software. CIS 1.1.20 passes on all nodes.

💡 Key takeaway: A Kubernetes upgrade is a two-phase process: (1) control plane (kubeadm upgrade apply), (2) workers (drain → upgrade kubelet → uncordon). Always verify with kubectl get nodes after each phase. Workers are easy to forget but equally important — a single outdated node compromises the entire cluster's security posture. On CKS, you must know both phases of the kubeadm upgrade workflow.

🖥️ Category 3: System Hardening Security Lab ScenariosS31–S40

🟢 Kernel Hardening, AppArmor, Seccomp, Capabilities & Pod Security Contexts

Category 3 covers System Hardening (CKS Domain 3, 10%): These scenarios test your ability to minimize the host OS attack surface using AppArmor profiles, Seccomp profiles, dropping Linux capabilities, enforcing non-root users, setting read-only filesystems, and restricting dangerous pod spec fields like hostNetwork and hostPID. Every scenario deploys a part of anihpj/jobpost with intentional system-level security gaps — your job is to harden them. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario!

S31
🧪 SCENARIO S31 — Category 3: System Hardening AppArmor Debug

Deploy anihpj — Pod Runs Without AppArmor Profile (Unconfined)

The Problem: You deploy anihpj/jobpost pods, but no AppArmor profile is applied. The container runs in unconfined mode, meaning it has full access to all Linux capabilities and system calls that AppArmor would normally restrict. An attacker who compromises the Django pod can read /etc/shadow, write to /proc/sys, and access files outside the container — kernel-level protections are completely absent. Your job: load an AppArmor profile, annotate the pod to use it, and verify the profile is enforced.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster (AppArmor supported on worker nodes)
1

📋 Deploy anihpj pod WITHOUT AppArmor — Runs Unconfined (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost Django pods are deployed without any AppArmor profile. This means the container has unrestricted kernel access — it can read sensitive host files (like /etc/shadow), write to /proc/sys, and make syscalls that should be blocked. AppArmor is a Mandatory Access Control (MAC) system that restricts what a container can do at the kernel level. Without it, a compromised Django pod is one kernel exploit away from full node compromise.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S31): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL Deployment + Service
├── 02-django-unconfined.yaml      ← BROKEN: Django pod without AppArmor annotation

# SCENARIO S31: No AppArmor — Container Runs Unconfined

EOF

# 2. DEPLOY DJANGO — NO AppArmor annotation (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# 3. PROVE THE BUG — Container can access files AppArmor should block
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/attr/current
# → unconfined   ← NO AppArmor profile applied! ❌

# Try to write to /etc inside container
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "echo 'test' >> /etc/hostname" 2>&1
# → SUCCEEDS! Writable /etc — AppArmor not protecting the filesystem ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. AppArmor status: cat /proc/1/attr/current → unconfined — no profile loaded
✗2. Container can write to /etc: echo test >> /etc/hostname → succeeds
✗3. No container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io annotation on pod
✗4. Any kernel exploit in nginx/Django = full node compromise possible
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod annotations: kubectl describe deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj | grep -i apparmor
→ No AppArmor annotation found — pod was deployed without any profile
2Check available AppArmor profiles on node: cat /sys/kernel/security/apparmor/profiles
→ Shows loaded profiles: docker-default, cri-containerd.apparmor.d, etc.
3AppArmor is a Mandatory Access Control (MAC) — without a profile, the container is unconfined
4Docker's default profile blocks writes to /etc, /proc/sys, and restricts mounts — but only if applied
5Root cause: The pod was deployed without the AppArmor annotation container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/NGINX: localhost/deny-write. Kubernetes does NOT apply AppArmor profiles automatically — you must explicitly annotate each pod or container. Without it, the container runs unconfined with full kernel access.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cat /proc/1/attr/current → unconfined → No AA profile
②
Check node for available profiles → docker-default exists
③
Add AA annotation to pod → Recreate pod
④
cat /proc/1/attr/current → deny-write (enforcing)
⑤
echo test >> /etc/hostname → Permission denied ✅

Tenet: AppArmor is a Linux kernel security module that restricts what containers can do at the syscall level. On CKS, you must know how to load profiles and annotate pods. The annotation format is container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<CONTAINER_NAME>: localhost/<PROFILE_NAME>. Without it, containers run unconfined. Always apply at least the docker-default or runtime/default profile.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/attr/current unconfined ← No AppArmor profile! ❌
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "echo test >> /etc/hostname" # Command succeeds — writable /etc! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/attr/current deny-write (enforce) ← AppArmor profile ACTIVE! ✅
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "echo test >> /etc/hostname" sh: /etc/hostname: Permission denied ✅ AppArmor enforcing!
🔧
BASH — Load AppArmor profile on worker nodes + recreate pod with annotation 
# Step 1: Load the deny-write AppArmor profile on ALL worker nodes
# KinD: docker exec into worker containers
docker exec kind-cka-lab-worker bash -c "
cat > /etc/apparmor.d/deny-write << 'EOF'
#include <tunables/global>
profile deny-write flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  file,
  deny /etc/** w,
  deny /proc/sys/** w,
}
EOF
apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/deny-write
echo 'Profile loaded'
"

# Step 2: Delete unconfined deployment
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 3: Recreate WITH AppArmor annotation (THE FIX!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
      annotations:
        container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/nginx: localhost/deny-write
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# Step 4: VERIFY profile is enforced
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/attr/current
# Expected: deny-write (enforce) ✅
✓

✅ Verify — AppArmor Is Enforcing File Restrictions

After loading the deny-write profile on the worker node and annotating the pod with container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/nginx: localhost/deny-write, the container now runs under AppArmor enforcement. Writes to /etc and /proc/sys are blocked at the kernel level. Even if nginx is compromised, the attacker cannot modify system files.

💡 Key takeaway: AppArmor must be loaded on EACH worker node AND annotated on EACH pod. The annotation format is critical: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<CONTAINER_NAME> must match the container name exactly. On CKS, know the difference between complain mode (logs violations, doesn't block) and enforce mode (blocks violations). Always test with cat /proc/1/attr/current inside the container.

🧹

🧪 SCENARIO S32 — Category 3: System Hardening Seccomp Debug

Deploy anihpj — Pod Can Make Dangerous Syscalls (Seccomp Unconfined)

The Problem: You deploy anihpj/jobpost pods, but no Seccomp profile is set. The container runs with the default Unconfined seccomp profile, which allows ALL 300+ Linux system calls. An attacker who compromises the pod can make dangerous syscalls like ptrace (attach to other processes), mount (mount filesystems), and reboot (reboot the node). Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) restricts which syscalls a container can use. RuntimeDefault blocks ~60 dangerous syscalls. Your job: apply a Seccomp profile and verify dangerous syscalls are blocked.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj pod WITHOUT Seccomp profile (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost Django pods are deployed to production. During a security review, you discover no Seccomp profile is applied — the containers can make all 300+ Linux syscalls including dangerous ones like ptrace, mount, and reboot. Seccomp is the last line of defense: even if an attacker escapes the container namespace, Seccomp can block the kernel calls they need for privilege escalation. Without Seccomp, a container escape is a node compromise.

├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL Deployment + Service
├── 02-django-unconfined.yaml      ← BROKEN: No seccompProfile set

BASH — Deploy anihpj without Seccomp + test dangerous syscalls 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S32: No Seccomp — All 300+ Syscalls Allowed
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create deployment anihpj-db -n anihpj --image=postgres:15-alpine

# DEPLOY DJANGO POD — NO seccompProfile (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
  # ❌ BUG: No securityContext.seccompProfile — defaults to Unconfined!
  # This allows ALL syscalls including ptrace, mount, reboot
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# CHECK SECCOMP STATUS — it's Unconfined (all syscalls allowed)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp
# → Seccomp: 0   ← 0 = disabled/unconfined! ❌ (2 = enforcing)

# PROVE — container can call dangerous syscalls (strace to see)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "apk add strace 2>/dev/null; strace -e mount ls / 2>&1 | head -5"
# → mount() succeeds — should be blocked by RuntimeDefault! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Seccomp status: cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp → 0 (disabled)
✗2. Container can call mount(), ptrace(), reboot() — all dangerous syscalls allowed
✗3. No securityContext.seccompProfile in pod spec — defaults to Unconfined
✗4. RuntimeDefault would block ~60 dangerous syscalls — but it's not applied
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod securityContext: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep -A5 securityContext
→ No seccompProfile section — defaults to Unconfined (all syscalls)
2RuntimeDefault profile blocks: mount, ptrace, reboot, clock_settime, delete_module, and ~55 more
3Unconfined = Seccomp disabled — every syscall the container makes passes through unfiltered
4Seccomp is per-container: must be set in securityContext of each container
5Root cause: The pod has no securityContext.seccompProfile set. Kubernetes defaults to Unconfined when no profile is specified, meaning all 300+ Linux syscalls are allowed. RuntimeDefault (the container runtime's default seccomp profile) would block ~60 dangerous syscalls but must be explicitly set per container.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Seccomp: 0 → Unconfined → All syscalls allowed
②
Add seccompProfile RuntimeDefault to securityContext
③
Recreate pod → Seccomp: 2 (enforcing)
④
mount() → Operation not permitted → Blocked ✅
⑤
~60 dangerous syscalls now blocked ✅

Tenet: Seccomp is the kernel's syscall firewall. RuntimeDefault blocks dangerous syscalls without breaking normal application functionality. On CKS, you must set seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault on every container. Check with cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp — 0=disabled, 1=strict, 2=filter. Always aim for 2 (filter/enforcing).

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp Seccomp: 0 ← Unconfined — all syscalls allowed! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp Seccomp: 2 ← Filter mode — ~60 dangerous syscalls blocked ✅
🔧
BASH — Delete pod + recreate with seccompProfile RuntimeDefault 
# Step 1: Delete unconfined pod
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 2: Recreate WITH seccompProfile (THE FIX!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault    # ✅ Blocks ~60 dangerous syscalls!
EOF

# Step 3: VERIFY
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp
# Expected: Seccomp: 2 ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Seccomp Is Filtering Dangerous Syscalls

After adding seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault, the container now runs with Seccomp in filter mode (Seccomp: 2). Approximately 60 dangerous syscalls including mount, ptrace, and reboot are blocked at the kernel level. Even if an attacker escapes the container namespace, Seccomp prevents the kernel calls needed for privilege escalation.

💡 Key takeaway: seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault should be on EVERY production container. It's the container runtime's default seccomp profile. On CKS, this is a must-know: Seccomp: 0=disabled, 1=strict, 2=filter. RuntimeDefault uses filter mode (2). Set it in securityContext at the container level — never leave it as default Unconfined.

🧪 SCENARIO S33 — Category 3: System Hardening Priv Debug

Deploy anihpj — Pod Runs in Privileged Mode with Full Host Access

The Problem: A developer added securityContext.privileged: true to the anihpj/jobpost Django pod "to fix a permission issue." This gives the container complete host access — it can see all host devices (/dev), load kernel modules, modify sysctls, and access host namespaces. A privileged container is essentially a root shell on the node. CIS Benchmark 5.2.1 requires that privileged containers are NOT used. Your job: detect the privileged flag, remove it, and add proper securityContext instead.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj pod with privileged: true (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The Django pod was marked as privileged because of a volume mount issue. Now this container has unrestricted access to the host — it sees all host devices in /dev, can modify kernel parameters, and can even load kernel modules. If this pod is compromised, the attacker owns the node. Privileged containers bypass almost all container isolation.

anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-privileged.yaml      ← BROKEN: securityContext.privileged: true
└── 02-django-secure.yaml          ← ✅ FIX: No privileged + proper securityContext

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S33: Privileged Container — CIS 5.2.1 Violation
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# DEPLOY PRIVILEGED POD (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      privileged: true    # ❌ BUG! Full host root access!
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# PROVE HOST ACCESS — privileged container sees host devices!
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /dev | wc -l
# → 200+ devices (host's /dev!) ❌ Non-privileged would show ~15

# Can modify kernel parameters (requires host access)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward" 2>&1
# → SUCCEEDS! Container modified host kernel parameter! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. privileged: true in pod spec — CIS 5.2.1 FAIL
✗2. Container sees ALL host devices: ls /dev → 200+ devices
✗3. Can modify kernel params: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward → succeeds
✗4. Container has ALL Linux capabilities — essentially root on the node
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod securityContext: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep privileged
→ privileged: true ← CIS 5.2.1 FAIL
2Privileged containers get all Linux capabilities + access to all host devices + no Seccomp/AppArmor
3Common excuse: "needed for Docker-in-Docker, volume mounts, or networking" — all achievable without privileged
4Fix: remove privileged: true, add specific capabilities if needed, use seccomp + AppArmor
5Root cause: securityContext.privileged: true was set on the container, granting it full host access. This is almost never needed — specific Linux capabilities (like NET_ADMIN for networking) can be added individually without the nuclear option of privileged mode. CIS 5.2.1 requires privileged containers to be forbidden cluster-wide.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
privileged: true → Remove it immediately
②
Add specific capabilities if actually needed
③
Add seccomp + AppArmor + runAsNonRoot
④
ls /dev → only ~15 devices (container, not host)
⑤
CIS 5.2.1 PASS — no privileged containers ✅

Tenet: Privileged containers bypass ALL container isolation — they have root on the node, not just in the container. On CKS, CIS 5.2.1 is a non-negotiable. Use PodSecurity admission restricted profile to block privileged pods cluster-wide. If a specific capability is needed (e.g., NET_ADMIN for VPN pods), add it individually with capabilities.add — never use privileged: true.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep privileged privileged: true ← CIS 5.2.1 FAIL ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- ls /dev | wc -l 16 ← Only container devices, not host ✅

BASH — Delete privileged pod + recreate with secure config 
# Step 1: Delete the privileged pod
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 2: Recreate WITHOUT privileged (THE FIX!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      privileged: false
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 101
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
EOF

# Step 3: VERIFY
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /dev | wc -l
# Expected: ~16 (not 200+) ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Container Is Properly Isolated

After removing privileged: true and adding allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, runAsNonRoot: true, dropped capabilities, and RuntimeDefault seccomp, the container is properly isolated. ls /dev shows only ~16 container devices, not the host's devices. Kernel parameter modification is blocked.

💡 Key takeaway: Never use privileged: true. If you need specific capabilities (NET_ADMIN, SYS_TIME), add them with capabilities.add. But first ask: does the app actually need it? 99% of apps run fine with capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]. On CKS, CIS 5.2.1 requires privileged containers to be blocked by PodSecurity admission (restricted profile).

This bypasses ALL NetworkPolicies (they don't apply to hostNetwork pods), exposes the pod on the node's IP directly, and allows the pod to bind to any port on the node — potentially hijacking kubelet (10250) or other critical services. CIS Benchmark 5.2.4 requires hostNetwork to be restricted.

NetworkPolicies are silently ignored (they only apply to pod network traffic). The pod can bind to any port on the node — potentially conflicting with kubelet, CRI, or other system services. This is a critical isolation bypass.

1hostNetwork: true makes the pod share the node's network namespace — bypassing CNI, NetworkPolicies, and pod IPAM

Application pods should never use hostNetwork — only system daemons that genuinely need node-level network access.

④
Apply PodSecurity restricted to block future hostNetwork pods
⑤
CIS 5.2.4 PASS ✅

On CKS, CIS 5.2.4 requires restricting hostNetwork. Use PodSecurity admission restricted profile to block it. Only system daemons (kube-proxy, CNI agents, node_exporter) legitimately need hostNetwork — never application pods.

Deploy anihpj — Container Has Dangerous Linux Capabilities (CAP_SYS_ADMIN)

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Django container was deployed without capabilities.drop, leaving it with the default set of Linux capabilities including CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW, and CAP_SYS_PTRACE. Your job: drop ALL capabilities and verify the container still functions.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj with default capabilities (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The Django container runs with the default Linux capabilities — CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW, and several others. CAP_SYS_ADMIN alone is almost equivalent to root — it allows mounting filesystems, setting domain names, and performing admin operations. For a web app that only needs to bind to port 80 and read files, this is massive over-privilege. An attacker who exploits nginx can mount a malicious filesystem over /etc and hijack the container.

anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-default-caps.yaml    ← BROKEN: No capabilities.drop
└── 02-django-drop-all.yaml        ← ✅ FIX: capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]

# SCENARIO S36: Dangerous Linux Capabilities — CIS 5.2.6
# ============================================

# DEPLOY WITH DEFAULT CAPABILITIES (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -

kind: Deployment

  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:

  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    # ❌ BUG: No capabilities.drop — inherits ALL default capabilities!
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# CHECK CURRENT CAPABILITIES
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep -i cap
# → CapInh/ CapPrm/ CapEff show non-zero values — MANY capabilities active ❌

# PROVE DANGEROUS CAP — mount a tmpfs (requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "mkdir -p /tmp/test && mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /tmp/test && echo 'MOUNT SUCCEEDED!'" 2>&1
# → MOUNT SUCCEEDED! ❌ CAP_SYS_ADMIN is present!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Capabilities not dropped: cat /proc/1/status | grep Cap → non-zero values
✗2. Container can mount filesystems: mount -t tmpfs → succeeds (needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN)
✗3. Web app only needs NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind to port 80) — everything else is unnecessary
✗4. CIS 5.2.6: capabilities should be minimized to what the app actually needs
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Default capabilities include CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, and others
2CAP_SYS_ADMIN is the "new root" — allows mounts, swapon, sethostname, and dozens of admin operations
3Nginx only needs: CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind port 80), CAP_CHOWN (change file ownership) — maybe not even those
4Drop all + add back specific is better than starting with default and trying to remove
5Root cause: The container has no capabilities.drop in securityContext, so it inherits the full default capability set. This includes CAP_SYS_ADMIN (mount, swapon), CAP_NET_RAW (raw sockets), and CAP_SYS_PTRACE (process tracing). CIS 5.2.6 requires dropping ALL capabilities and only adding back those explicitly needed.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
mount succeeds → CAP_SYS_ADMIN present → Overprivileged
②
Drop ALL capabilities → Add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE
③
mount fails → CAP_SYS_ADMIN gone ✅
④
Nginx still binds port 80 → App still works
⑤
CIS 5.2.6 PASS — minimal capabilities ✅

Tenet: Linux capabilities break root's power into fine-grained permissions. Default containers get ~15 capabilities — most are unnecessary. On CKS, always drop: ["ALL"] and add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] for web apps. CAP_SYS_ADMIN is especially dangerous — it's the closest thing to root without actually being UID 0. Use cat /proc/1/status | grep Cap to audit.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- sh -c "mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /tmp/test 2>&1 && echo 'MOUNTED'" MOUNTED ← CAP_SYS_ADMIN present! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- sh -c "mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /tmp/test 2>&1" mount: permission denied ✅ CAP_SYS_ADMIN dropped!
🔧
BASH — Recreate pod with minimal capabilities 
# Step 1: Delete overprivileged pod
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 2: Recreate with ALL capabilities dropped (THE FIX!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]                  # ✅ Drop everything
        # Nginx needs NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind port 80 on some configs:
        # add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]      # Uncomment if needed
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 101
EOF

# Step 3: VERIFY
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff
# Expected: 0000000000000000 ✅ (all caps dropped)
✓

✅ Verify — Container Runs with Zero Capabilities

After dropping ALL capabilities, CapEff: 0000000000000000 shows the container has no Linux capabilities. mount() fails, raw sockets are blocked, and the attack surface is dramatically reduced. Nginx still serves traffic because it doesn't actually need capabilities for normal operation.

💡 Key takeaway: drop: ["ALL"] is the single most impactful securityContext setting after runAsNonRoot. On CKS, CIS 5.2.6 requires minimizing capabilities. If the app breaks after dropping ALL, add back ONLY what's needed — typically NET_BIND_SERVICE for web servers. Never start with defaults and selectively remove.

  name: anihpj-web

spec:

    matchLabels:

💡 Key takeaway: runAsNonRoot: true is the single most important securityContext setting. It must be on every production pod. On CKS, CIS 5.2.5 requires it. Know common non-root UIDs: nginx=101, postgres=999, node=1000. If the image only supports root, find a different image — running as root is not acceptable for production.

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Can write files: echo test > /tmp/test → succeeds
✗2. Can modify /bin: touch /bin/new-binary → succeeds
✗3. No readOnlyRootFilesystem in securityContext — defaults to false
✗4. CIS 5.2.7: root filesystem should be read-only — prevents malware persistence
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1readOnlyRootFilesystem: true mounts the root filesystem as read-only — prevents any writes
2If app needs to write (logs, temp files), mount an emptyDir volume at /tmp or /var/log
3Immutable containers can't be modified post-deployment — prevents malware persistence
4Combined with runAsNonRoot, even root-in-container can't write to the FS if it's read-only
5Root cause: The container has no readOnlyRootFilesystem set. The default is false, allowing writes anywhere the container user has permissions. CIS 5.2.7 requires readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. If the app needs writable directories, mount specific emptyDir volumes — don't make the entire root FS writable.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Can write to /bin → Root FS writable → Immutability broken
②
Set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true → Add emptyDir for /tmp
③
touch /bin/test → Read-only filesystem error
④
CIS 5.2.7 PASS ✅
⑤
Malware persistence blocked — container is immutable

Tenet: An immutable container filesystem is a key defense against malware persistence. On CKS, CIS 5.2.7 requires readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. Use emptyDir volumes for directories that need writes (/tmp, /var/log, /var/run). Combined with runAsNonRoot and dropped capabilities, even a compromised container can't persist malware.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- touch /bin/evil && echo "WRITABLE" WRITABLE ← Root filesystem is writable! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- touch /bin/evil 2>&1 touch: /bin/evil: Read-only file system ✅ Immutable!
🔧
BASH — Recreate pod with read-only root FS 
# Step 1: Delete writable pod
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 2: Recreate with readOnlyRootFilesystem (THE FIX!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true    # ✅ Root FS is read-only!
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 101
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp                 # Writable emptyDir for temp files
    - name: nginx-cache
      mountPath: /var/cache/nginx     # Nginx needs this writable
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: nginx-cache
    emptyDir: {}
EOF

# Step 3: VERIFY — can write to /tmp but NOT /bin
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /tmp/test && echo "/tmp writable ✅"
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /bin/test 2>&1
# Expected: Read-only file system ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Root Filesystem Is Read-Only

After setting readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and mounting emptyDir volumes for directories that need writes (/tmp, /var/cache/nginx), the container's root filesystem is immutable. Writes to /bin, /etc, /usr are blocked. The app can still write to /tmp and /var/cache via the emptyDir mounts.

💡 Key takeaway: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is a powerful immutability control. On CKS, CIS 5.2.7 requires it. Common writable directories to mount as emptyDir: /tmp, /var/log, /var/cache, /var/run. Never leave the root FS writable in production — it's the first thing an attacker uses to establish persistence.

kubectl delete namespace anihpj
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S39
🧪 SCENARIO S39 — Category 3: System Hardening AppArmor Debug

Deploy anihpj — AppArmor Profile Exists But Pod Not Annotated

The Problem: The security team loaded an AppArmor profile on all worker nodes, but the anihpj/jobpost Django pod was deployed without the required annotation. The profile is loaded and ready on the node — but the pod doesn't use it because the annotation is missing. This creates a false sense of security: the team thinks AppArmor is protecting the pod, but it's actually running unconfined. Your job: verify the profile exists on the node, add the missing annotation, and confirm enforcement.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj without AppArmor annotation (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team spent hours creating and loading AppArmor profiles on all worker nodes. But the Django pod YAML is missing the annotation that tells Kubernetes to apply the profile. The profile sits unused on the node while the pod runs unconfined. This is the most common AppArmor mistake: loading the profile but forgetting the annotation.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S39): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-load-profile.sh             ← Script to load AppArmor profile on node
├── 02-django-no-annotation.yaml   ← BROKEN: Pod without AppArmor annotation
└── 03-django-with-annotation.yaml ← ✅ FIX: Pod WITH annotation
BASH — Load AppArmor profile + deploy pod WITHOUT annotation 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S39: AppArmor Profile Loaded, Pod Not Annotated
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 1. PROFILE IS LOADED ON THE NODE (correctly installed)
# On the worker node:
# sudo cat /sys/kernel/security/apparmor/profiles | grep anihpj
# → anihpj-deny-write (enforce)   ← Profile IS loaded ✅

# 2. DEPLOY POD WITHOUT ANNOTATION (THE BUG!)
# The profile exists but Kubernetes doesn't know to apply it
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
  # ❌ BUG: Missing annotation! Profile loaded but NOT applied!
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# 3. PROVE THE BUG — container is unconfined despite profile being loaded
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/attr/current
# → unconfined   ← PROFILE NOT APPLIED! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Profile loaded on node: cat /sys/kernel/security/apparmor/profiles → anihpj-deny-write exists
✗2. Container status: cat /proc/1/attr/current → unconfined — profile NOT applied
✗3. Pod has no container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io annotation
✗4. False sense of security — team thinks AppArmor is working, it's not
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1AppArmor requires TWO steps: (1) load profile on node, (2) annotate pod to use it
2Annotation format: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<CONTAINER>: localhost/<PROFILE>
3Without the annotation, Kubernetes doesn't know which profile to apply — even if it's loaded
4This is the #1 AppArmor mistake — loading profiles but forgetting pod annotations
5Root cause: The AppArmor profile is correctly loaded on the worker node, but the pod is missing the required annotation to apply it. Kubernetes only applies AppArmor when the pod metadata includes container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io annotation. Without it, the container runs unconfined regardless of what profiles are loaded on the node.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Profile exists on node → Pod unconfined → Missing annotation
②
Add annotation to pod metadata → Recreate pod
③
cat /proc/1/attr/current → anihpj-deny-write (enforce)
④
AppArmor enforcing — writes to /etc blocked ✅
⑤
Automate with admission webhook to enforce annotation

Tenet: AppArmor is a two-step process: load profile on node, annotate pod. Both are required. On CKS, know the annotation format exactly: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/CONTAINER_NAME: localhost/PROFILE_NAME. The container name must match the name in the pod spec. Automate annotation enforcement with an admission controller like OPA/Gatekeeper.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo cat /sys/kernel/security/apparmor/profiles | grep anihpj anihpj-deny-write (enforce) ← Profile loaded ✅
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- cat /proc/1/attr/current unconfined ← But NOT applied! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web -n anihpj -- cat /proc/1/attr/current anihpj-deny-write (enforce) ← Profile NOW applied! ✅
🔧
BASH — Delete pod + recreate WITH annotation 
# Step 1: Delete unannotated pod
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 2: Recreate WITH AppArmor annotation (THE FIX!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/nginx: localhost/anihpj-deny-write
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
EOF

# Step 3: VERIFY profile is NOW applied
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/attr/current
# Expected: anihpj-deny-write (enforce) ✅
✓

✅ Verify — AppArmor Is Applied and Enforcing

After adding the annotation container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/nginx: localhost/anihpj-deny-write to the pod metadata, the container now runs under the AppArmor profile. /proc/1/attr/current shows enforcing mode. The profile blocks writes to /etc and other protected paths — even though the profile was loaded before, it only takes effect after the annotation links the pod to the profile.

💡 Key takeaway: AppArmor = profile on node + annotation on pod. Both must be present. On CKS, this is a common trick question: the profile is loaded but the pod is unconfined. Always verify with cat /proc/1/attr/current. Automate with OPA/Gatekeeper to ensure every pod has the required annotation.
