kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S40
🧪 SCENARIO S40 — Category 3: System Hardening Seccomp Debug

Deploy anihpj — Seccomp RuntimeDefault Not Set, All Syscalls Allowed

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Django pod was deployed without seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault in its securityContext. Unlike S32 which focused on detecting the unconfined state, this scenario is about the systematic enforcement gap — multiple pods across the cluster are missing seccomp profiles because no admission controller enforces it. Your job: audit all pods for missing seccomp, fix them, and set up a PodSecurity label to enforce RuntimeDefault cluster-wide.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
1

📋 Deploy multiple anihpj pods without Seccomp (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj platform has 3 deployments — web, db, and cache — all running without Seccomp profiles. An audit reveals every pod has Seccomp: 0 (unconfined). The platform team needs to fix all pods AND prevent this from happening again by enforcing PodSecurity restricted at the namespace level.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S40): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-web.yaml             ← BROKEN: No seccompProfile
├── 02-postgres-db.yaml            ← BROKEN: No seccompProfile
├── 03-redis-cache.yaml            ← BROKEN: No seccompProfile
└── 04-enforce-restricted.sh       ← Label namespace for PodSecurity restricted
BASH — Deploy 3 pods without Seccomp + audit all 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S40: Systematic Seccomp Gap — All Pods Unconfined
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# DEPLOY 3 PODS — ALL WITHOUT seccompProfile (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: postgres
    image: postgres:15-alpine
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-cache
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: redis
    image: redis:7-alpine
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# AUDIT — Check ALL pods for Seccomp status
for pod in anihpj-web anihpj-db anihpj-cache; do
  echo -n "$pod: "
  kubectl exec -n anihpj $pod -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp
done
# → anihpj-web: Seccomp: 0 ❌
# → anihpj-db: Seccomp: 0 ❌
# → anihpj-cache: Seccomp: 0 ❌
# ALL three are unconfined!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. All 3 pods show Seccomp: 0 — none have RuntimeDefault applied
✗2. No PodSecurity label on namespace — nothing prevents unconfined pods
✗3. Every new pod deployed in this namespace will also be unconfined
✗4. Systematic gap — not just one pod, but an entire namespace without Seccomp
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Seccomp is not set by default — Kubernetes leaves it as Unconfined unless explicitly configured
2PodSecurity restricted profile requires RuntimeDefault — applying it to the namespace enforces cluster-wide
3Fix is two-fold: (1) fix existing pods, (2) label namespace to prevent future gaps
4Audit with: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.seccompProfile==null) | .metadata.name'
5Root cause: None of the pods have seccompProfile set in their securityContext. Kubernetes defaults all pods to Unconfined unless explicitly overridden. This is a systematic gap — every pod in the namespace is vulnerable. The fix: add seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault to all pods AND enforce it at the namespace level with PodSecurity restricted label.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Audit all pods → All Seccomp:0 → Systematic gap
②
Delete pods → Add seccompProfile to all pod specs
③
Label namespace pod-security restricted → Blocks unconfined
④
Re-deploy → All Seccomp:2 ✅
⑤
Future pods auto-enforced — systematic gap closed ✅

Tenet: Seccomp must be enforced at scale — not just per pod. On CKS, use PodSecurity admission restricted profile to enforce RuntimeDefault cluster-wide. Audit all pods with jq. Fix existing pods AND label namespaces to prevent regression. The one-shot fix: kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ for p in anihpj-web anihpj-db anihpj-cache; do kubectl exec $p -n anihpj -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp; done Seccomp: 0 ← unconfined ❌ Seccomp: 0 ← unconfined ❌ Seccomp: 0 ← unconfined ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ for p in anihpj-web anihpj-db anihpj-cache; do kubectl exec $p -n anihpj -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp; done Seccomp: 2 ← RuntimeDefault ✅ Seccomp: 2 ← RuntimeDefault ✅ Seccomp: 2 ← RuntimeDefault ✅
🔧
BASH — Delete pods + recreate with Seccomp + label namespace 
# Step 1: Delete all unconfined pods
kubectl delete deployment --all -n anihpj

# Step 2: Label namespace for PodSecurity RESTRICTED (THE FIX!)
kubectl label namespace anihpj \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  --overwrite

# Step 3: Recreate pods WITH seccompProfile (now enforced by PodSecurity too)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 101
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: postgres
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    securityContext:
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-cache
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: redis
    image: redis:7-alpine
    securityContext:
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
EOF

# Step 4: VERIFY — try to deploy a pod WITHOUT seccomp (should be REJECTED!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test-unconfined
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: test
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["sleep", "60"]
EOF
# Expected: "Error from server (Forbidden): pods 'test-unconfined' is forbidden:
# violates PodSecurity 'restricted:latest': seccompProfile" ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Seccomp Enforced Cluster-Wide

After adding seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault to all pods and labeling the namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted, all containers now run with Seccomp in filter mode. Any new pod without seccomp is REJECTED by the admission controller. The systematic gap is closed — not just fixed, but prevented from recurring.

💡 Key takeaway: Fixing individual pods isn't enough — you must enforce Seccomp at the namespace level with PodSecurity admission. On CKS, the command kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted is a one-shot fix for Seccomp, capabilities, runAsNonRoot, hostPath, and more. This is the most impactful single command for system hardening.

🔗 Category 4: Minimize Microservice VulnerabilitiesS41–S60

🟡 Intermediate: Securing Your Actual Applications — 20% of CKS

Category 4 covers Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities (CKS Domain 4, 20%): These scenarios test your ability to enforce Pod Security Standards (PSS), harden container securityContexts, manage Secrets securely, implement NetworkPolicy micro-segmentation, enforce resource limits against DoS, lock down container capabilities, prevent privilege escalation, and secure pod-to-pod communication. Every scenario deploys a part of anihpj/jobpost with intentional security gaps — your job is to detect and harden them. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario!

S41
🧪 SCENARIO S41 — Category 4: Microservice Vulns PodSec Debug

Deploy anihpj — Django Container Runs as Root (UID 0)

The Problem: You deploy the anihpj/jobpost Django container and discover it's running as root (UID 0) — the default for most container images. There's no securityContext with runAsNonRoot or runAsUser set. If an attacker exploits any code vulnerability (SQL injection, path traversal), they immediately have root access inside the container — and if they combine this with a container breakout, they get root on the node. CIS Benchmark 5.2.6 requires pods to run as non-root. Your job: detect the root execution, add a proper securityContext, and verify the container runs as a non-root user.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj Django as Root — No securityContext (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a Django job board. The container image was built without a non-root USER directive, and the deployment YAML has no securityContext. The container runs as UID 0 (root). If a web vulnerability (e.g., file upload bypass) allows code execution, the attacker gets root inside the container. From there, they can install tools, modify system files, and attempt container breakout. This is the #1 container security mistake.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S41): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL Deployment + Service (port 5432)
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: Django runs as root — NO securityContext
└── 03-django-fixed.yaml           ← ✅ FIX: runAsNonRoot + runAsUser + capabilities drop
BASH — Deploy full anihpj stack with Django running as root 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S41: Container Runs as Root — No securityContext
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 2. DEPLOY POSTGRESQL DATABASE (anihpj/jobpost backend)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment

  name: anihpj-db

spec:

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: anihpj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123

        - containerPort: 5432
---

kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-db

  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
EOF

# 3. DEPLOY DJANGO WEB APP — NO securityContext! (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web

    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        # ❌ BUG: No securityContext — runs as root (UID 0)!

kind: Service

  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj

  selector:

# 4. CHECK — Who is running the Django process? (THE BUG!)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)

# → uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)   ❌ ROOT!

kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- whoami
# → root   ❌ The Django app runs as root!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Container runs as root: id → uid=0(root)
✗2. No runAsUser or runAsNonRoot in pod spec → defaults to image USER (or root)
✗3. Root inside container = root on node IF container breakout occurs
✗4. CIS 5.2.6: "Apply Security Context to Your Pods and Containers" — FAILED
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod securityContext: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep -A10 securityContext
→ No securityContext section exists — default is root + all capabilities
2Root can: bind to ports <1024, modify /etc, install packages, access all files in container
3Combined with no readOnlyRootFilesystem, root can write anywhere in the container FS
4Nginx and Django can run as non-root: nginx:alpine has nginx user (UID 101), Django can use any UID
5Root cause: The Deployment has no securityContext defined for the container or pod. Kubernetes defaults to running containers as whatever user the image specifies — and most images default to root (UID 0). Without runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser set to a non-zero UID, the Django app runs with full root privileges inside the container. CIS 5.2.6 mandates non-root execution.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
id → uid=0 → Container runs as root
②
Check pod YAML → No securityContext → Default root execution
③
Add runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: 1000 → Redeploy
④
Add drop capabilities: ALL → Minimal attack surface
⑤
id → uid=1000 → Non-root enforced ✅

Tenet: Root in a container is not the same as root on the node — but it's the first step to a full breakout. A container running as root can modify system files, install tools, bind to privileged ports, and if combined with a kernel exploit or misconfiguration, escape to the node. The fix is ALWAYS: runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: <high UID>, and capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]. On CKS, CIS 5.2.6 is a must-pass check — every container MUST have a security context.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- id uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1(bin),2(daemon),... ← ROOT! ❌
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep -A5 securityContext # No output — securityContext is completely MISSING! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- id uid=1000(nginx) gid=1000(nginx) groups=1000(nginx) ✅ Non-root!
🔧
BASH — Patch deployment with proper securityContext 
# Step 1: Patch the deployment to add securityContext
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/securityContext","value":{
    "runAsNonRoot": true,
    "runAsUser": 1000,
    "allowPrivilegeEscalation": false,
    "capabilities": {
      "drop": ["ALL"]
    },
    "readOnlyRootFilesystem": true
  }}
]'

# Step 2: Wait for roll out
kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# Step 3: VERIFY the new pod runs as non-root
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- id
# Expected: uid=1000(nginx) ✅

# Step 4: Verify privilege escalation is blocked
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep NoNewPrivs
# → NoNewPrivs: 1 ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Django Runs as Non-Root with Minimal Capabilities

After patching the deployment with runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and capabilities.drop: ["ALL"], the Django container now runs as UID 1000 with zero Linux capabilities. Even if an attacker gains code execution via a web vulnerability, they have almost no power inside the container — no privilege escalation, no capabilities, read-only filesystem.

💡 Key takeaway: The golden securityContext trifecta: runAsNonRoot: true (never UID 0), allowPrivilegeEscalation: false (no setuid binaries), capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] (zero Linux capabilities). Combine with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true for defense in depth. On CKS, CIS 5.2.6 requires securityContext on EVERY container — it's the most fundamental microservice hardening step.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①

Tenet: allowPrivilegeEscalation: true (the default) means the kernel's no_new_privs bit is NOT set. This allows setuid binaries, file capabilities, and other Linux privilege escalation mechanisms to work. Setting it to false blocks ALL of these — the process can never gain more privileges than it started with. This is a critical Kubernetes security feature that most people don't know about. On the CKS exam, always check NoNewPrivs with cat /proc/1/status | grep NoNewPrivs — it should be 1.

Deploy anihpj — Django Has SYS_ADMIN and NET_ADMIN Capabilities

The Problem: A developer added SYS_ADMIN and NET_ADMIN capabilities to the Django container "for debugging." These are two of the most dangerous Linux capabilities — SYS_ADMIN allows mount/unmount, namespace creation, and dozens of privileged operations. NET_ADMIN allows modifying network interfaces, iptables rules, and routing tables. Together they provide near-root power and are a primary container breakout vector. CIS Benchmark 5.2.6 requires dropping ALL capabilities and only adding back specific ones needed. Your job: detect the dangerous capabilities, remove them, and ensure only necessary capabilities are added.

📋 Deploy anihpj Django with SYS_ADMIN + NET_ADMIN capabilities (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost Django was having "network issues" and a developer added NET_ADMIN capability, then later added SYS_ADMIN "just in case." These capabilities give the container almost complete control over the node's kernel — SYS_ADMIN can mount filesystems (breaking out via hostPath), create new namespaces, and perform dozens of privileged syscalls. NET_ADMIN can reconfigure the node's network. This is not debugging — it's a backdoor.

✗3. NET_ADMIN allows iptables modification, interface config, routing table changes

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check securityContext capabilities: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep -A5 capabilities
→ add: [SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN] — explicitly added dangerous caps
2SYS_ADMIN is often called "the new root" — it allows mount, namespace creation, seccomp changes
3NET_ADMIN allows ARP spoofing, traffic interception, iptables manipulation

5Root cause: SYS_ADMIN and NET_ADMIN were explicitly added to the container's capabilities. SYS_ADMIN is one of the most powerful Linux capabilities — it enables mount/umount, namespace creation, and dozens of privileged syscalls. Combined with a hostPath volume, SYS_ADMIN enables direct node filesystem breakout. Django needs NO capabilities at all — the fix is to drop ALL capabilities and only add back specific ones if absolutely necessary.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
capabilities.add: [SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN] → Dangerous
②
Django needs zero capabilities → Drop ALL
③
Replace with drop: ["ALL"] → No capabilities whatsoever
④
mount syscall now fails → Container breakout blocked
⑤
App still works → Zero-capability container ✅

Tenet: Linux capabilities break root's power into ~40 distinct pieces. The top 5 most dangerous: SYS_ADMIN (mount, namespace creation), NET_ADMIN (network config), SYS_PTRACE (process debugging), SYS_MODULE (kernel module loading), SYS_RAWIO (raw I/O). The golden rule: drop ALL capabilities, then add back only specific ones the app needs. Most web apps (Django, nginx, Node.js) need ZERO capabilities. On CKS, audit with cat /proc/1/status | grep Cap and check the capability bitmask.

  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/securityContext/capabilities","value":{"drop":["ALL"]}},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/securityContext/allowPrivilegeEscalation","value":false}
]'

# Step 2: Wait for rollout

# Step 3: Verify zero capabilities

✓

✅ Verify — Zero Capabilities, Container Is Locked Down

After patching the deployment to drop ALL capabilities, the Django container runs with zero effective capabilities (CapEff: 0000000000000000). The mount syscall is blocked, iptables modification is blocked, and all other privileged operations are denied by the kernel. The Django app still serves traffic normally — proving that web applications need zero Linux capabilities to function.

💡 Key takeaway: Always use capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] as the starting point. Only add back specific capabilities if the app fails — and even then, question why. The only capability web apps commonly need is NET_BIND_SERVICE (to bind to ports <1024), and even that can be avoided by using ports >1024. On CKS, CIS 5.2.6 mandates dropping all unnecessary capabilities. SYS_ADMIN should NEVER appear in any pod spec.

Deploy anihpj — DB Password Exposed as Plaintext Env Var

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost deployment passes PostgreSQL credentials to Django as environment variables (env: section). Environment variables are visible in /proc/PID/environ, kubectl describe pod, the Kubernetes API, and crash logs. If anyone runs kubectl exec into the pod and checks /proc/1/environ, the database password is right there in plaintext. Best practice is to mount Secrets as files (volumes), which are only readable by the container process and not exposed via /proc. Your job: detect the env-var secret exposure, convert to volume-mounted Secrets, and verify env vars are clean.

Any process that can read /proc/1/environ (the container's PID 1 environment) can see the password. Additionally, kubectl describe pod doesn't show env var values from Secrets, but crash dumps, error logs, and debugging tools often leak env vars. Secrets should be mounted as files, never passed as env vars when possible.

├── 01-postgres-secret.yaml        ← DB credentials Secret
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: envFrom secretRef (env var exposure)

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Password visible in /proc/1/environ: cat /proc/1/environ → SuperSecret123!

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check env var exposure: kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- env | grep POSTGRES
→ All DB credentials are in the container's environment
2Why env vars are dangerous: visible in /proc/PID/environ (any process), inherited by child processes, logged by crash handlers
3Volume-mounted Secrets are only readable by the container process and not visible in /proc
4Some frameworks can read config from files instead of env vars (Django can read from a .env file)
5Root cause: The deployment uses envFrom.secretRef to inject ALL keys from the Secret as environment variables. Environment variables are visible in /proc/PID/environ (world-readable), inherited by all child processes, and frequently leaked in crash dumps and debug logs. Volume-mounted Secrets create files that are not in /proc and are only accessible to the container process. Fix: mount the Secret as a volume at a known path and configure the app to read from files.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cat /proc/1/environ → POSTGRES_PASSWORD visible
②
envFrom.secretRef → All keys become env vars
③
Convert to volume mount → Secret files, not env vars
④
cat /proc/1/environ → No password → Clean
⑤
App reads from files → Same functionality, more secure ✅

Tenet: Environment variables are the least secure way to pass secrets to containers. They appear in /proc/PID/environ (readable by any process), are inherited by subprocesses, and leak through crash logs, debug endpoints, and error messages. Volume-mounted Secrets create tempfs files that are NOT in /proc and are only readable by the container's process. On CKS, always prefer secret.volumes over envFrom.secretRef for sensitive data.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)

# Delete old deployment
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Recreate with Secret mounted as volume (NOT env var)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:

# Verify: password NOT in env vars, but readable as file

kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- env | grep POSTGRES
# Expected: no output ✅
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /etc/secrets/db/POSTGRES_PASSWORD
# Expected: SuperSecret123! ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Secrets Are Files, Not Environment Variables

After converting from envFrom.secretRef to a volume mount, the DB credentials are stored as files under /etc/secrets/db/. The password no longer appears in /proc/1/environ, env output, or crash dumps. The app can read from the files just as easily as from env vars, but the attack surface for credential leakage is dramatically reduced.

💡 Key takeaway: Environment variables are NOT secure for secrets. They're visible in /proc, inherited by subprocesses, and leak through logs. Volume-mounted Secrets use tmpfs (memory-backed) and are only accessible to the container's process. On CKS, always use volumes for secrets. If you must use env vars (legacy app), use secretKeyRef (one key at a time) rather than secretRef (all keys).

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check QoS class: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep qosClass
→ BestEffort — LOWEST priority, first to be killed by OOM
2BestEffort pods have no reservations — they get whatever CPU/memory is left over
3With limits set: QoS class becomes Burstable or Guaranteed — protected from OOMKiller
4Limits also protect other pods — CPU limits prevent one pod from starving others
5Root cause: No resources section is defined in the pod spec. Without requests, the scheduler can't make intelligent placement decisions. Without limits, a single pod can consume all node resources — crashing the node or starving critical system pods. CIS 5.2.1 requires CPU and memory limits on all containers. At minimum, set memory limits to prevent OOMKiller cascading failures.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
resources: {} → No limits → BestEffort QoS
②
Add requests=limits → Guaranteed QoS → Protected from OOM
③
CPU limits → No more CPU starvation of other pods
④
Memory limits → Pod killed at limit, not node crash
⑤
CIS 5.2.1 PASS → All containers constrained ✅

Tenet: Resource limits are not optional — they're a fundamental stability and security control. Without limits, one pod can DoS the entire node. Memory limits are especially critical: when a pod exceeds its memory limit, only that pod is OOM killed. Without limits, the node-level OOMKiller picks a random victim — which could be the kubelet, CoreDNS, or etcd. On CKS, CIS 5.2.1 mandates limits. Best practice: set requests=limits for Guaranteed QoS.

$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 resources resources: {} ← No limits, no requests ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 resources resources: limits: {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi} requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi} ✅

BASH — Patch deployment with CPU + Memory limits 
# Patch deployment to add resource limits
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources","value":{
    "requests": {"cpu": "100m", "memory": "128Mi"},
    "limits":   {"cpu": "500m", "memory": "256Mi"}
  }}
]'

# Also patch PostgreSQL
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-db -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources","value":{
    "requests": {"cpu": "250m", "memory": "256Mi"},
    "limits":   {"cpu": "1", "memory": "512Mi"}
  }}
]'

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=90s
kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-db -n anihpj --timeout=90s

# Verify QoS is now Burstable or Guaranteed
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep qosClass
# Expected: Burstable or Guaranteed ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Pods Have Enforced Resource Constraints

After adding resource requests and limits, each container is now constrained. If Django has a memory leak, it'll be OOM-killed at 256Mi — not bring down the entire node. CPU limits prevent one pod from starving others. QoS class is now Burstable, giving the pod higher OOM priority than BestEffort pods.

💡 Key takeaway: Always set resources.requests and resources.limits on every container. Memory limits are a hard safety net — exceed them and the pod is OOM-killed. CPU limits are throttling — exceed them and the pod slows down. On CKS, CIS 5.2.1 checks for resource limits. Use LimitRange to set defaults for namespaces, and ResourceQuota to cap total namespace consumption.

Deploy anihpj — Django Can Write Anywhere in Container Filesystem

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Django container has a writable root filesystem — readOnlyRootFilesystem is not set (defaults to false). An attacker who gains code execution can write backdoors to /usr/bin, modify system configs in /etc, plant cron jobs in /var/spool/cron, and install persistent malware. Even without an attacker, a bug in the app could corrupt critical system files leading to unpredictable behavior. CIS Benchmark 5.2.6 recommends readOnlyRootFilesystem: true with writable volumes only where needed. Your job: detect the writable root FS, make it read-only, and add tmpfs volumes for paths that need write access.

📋 Deploy anihpj Django with writable root filesystem (CONTAINS THE BUG)

During a security review, the team realizes an attacker who exploits the Django admin panel could write a reverse shell binary to /usr/bin/sshd-fake, modify /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, or drop a malicious shared library in /lib. ⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. touch /test-write succeeds — root filesystem is writable
✗2. Attacker can write to /usr/bin, /etc, /lib — persistence everywhere

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check securityContext: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o yaml | grep readOnlyRootFilesystem
→ No output — defaults to false (writable)
2When readOnlyRootFilesystem: true: the container's root FS is mounted read-only at the kernel level
3Apps often need /tmp writable — use emptyDir volume with medium: Memory for those paths
4Django needs: /tmp (for uploads), possibly /var/run — all can be tmpfs mounts
5Root cause: readOnlyRootFilesystem is not set in the container's securityContext, defaulting to false (writable). This allows any process in the container to modify system binaries, configuration files, and libraries. An attacker with code execution can achieve persistence by modifying the container's filesystem. CIS 5.2.6 recommends readOnlyRootFilesystem: true with explicit volume mounts for paths that need write access (like /tmp).
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
touch /test-write succeeds → Root FS writable
②
Set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true → Mount emptyDir for /tmp
③
touch /test-write → Read-only file system → Blocked
④
touch /tmp/write → OK (tmpfs volume)
⑤
Immutable container enforced ✅

Tenet: A writable root filesystem is the enemy of immutable infrastructure. Containers should be ephemeral — if an attacker writes malware to /usr/bin, it survives as long as the container runs. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true mounts the root FS as read-only at the kernel level. Use emptyDir volumes (optionally with medium: Memory for tmpfs) for paths that genuinely need write access (/tmp, /var/run, /var/cache). On CKS, CIS 5.2.6 includes this check.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /test-write && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /test-write /test-write ← FILE CREATED! Root FS writable ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /test-write touch: /test-write: Read-only file system ← BLOCKED ✅

BASH — Patch deployment for immutable root FS 
# Delete old deployment
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Recreate with readOnlyRootFilesystem + tmpfs for /tmp
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        securityContext:
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # ✅ Root FS is read-only
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 1000
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp                  # ✅ Writable tmpfs for /tmp
        - name: run
          mountPath: /var/run              # ✅ Writable for /var/run
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: run
        emptyDir: {}
EOF

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# Verify: /tmp writable, / read-only
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /test && echo "Root writable" || echo "Root read-only ✅"
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /tmp/test && echo "/tmp writable ✅"
✓

✅ Verify — Root Filesystem Is Read-Only

After setting readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and mounting emptyDir volumes on /tmp and /var/run, the container's root FS is immutable. Any attempt to write to /, /usr, /etc, etc. is rejected with "Read-only file system." The app can still write to /tmp (backed by a writable emptyDir) and /var/run — all other paths are protected at the kernel level.

💡 Key takeaway: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is one of the most impactful security settings you can apply to a container. It prevents persistence, blocks malware installation, and enforces immutable infrastructure. Common writable paths: /tmp, /var/run, /var/cache, /var/log — use emptyDir volumes for each. On CKS, CIS 5.2.6 requires this on all containers that don't need root FS write access.

After removing hostNetwork: true, the pod gets an IP from the pod CIDR range (10.244.x.x), only sees its own network interfaces (eth0 + lo), and is now subject to NetworkPolicies. The pod can no longer bind to node ports or sniff node-level traffic. CIS 5.2.5 passes.

💡 Key takeaway: hostNetwork: true is almost always a mistake for application pods. It breaks all network isolation. On CKS, audit with: kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep 'hostNetwork: true'. Expected output should only show kube-system DaemonSets (kube-proxy, CNI). Any other pod with hostNetwork should be investigated and fixed immediately.

Deploy anihpj — DB Password Stored in Plaintext ConfigMap

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost team stored database credentials in a ConfigMap instead of a Secret — including the PostgreSQL password in plaintext. ConfigMaps are NOT encrypted, NOT access-controlled beyond namespace RBAC, and their data is visible in the Kubernetes API, etcd, and to anyone with get configmap permissions. Anyone who can read ConfigMaps in the namespace (which is commonly granted) can see the database password. Secrets exist precisely to avoid this — they support encryption at rest and can be RBAC-controlled separately. Your job: find the plaintext credentials in the ConfigMap, migrate them to a Secret, and update the deployment.

📋 Deploy anihpj with DB password in ConfigMap (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: During an audit, the security team found that the anihpj team created a ConfigMap named anihpj-db-config containing the PostgreSQL password in plaintext. ConfigMaps are designed for non-sensitive configuration — they're not encrypted at rest, and anyone with RBAC to read ConfigMaps in the namespace can see the password. Passwords MUST be stored in Secrets, never ConfigMaps.

├── 01-configmap-plaintext.yaml    ← BROKEN: DB password in ConfigMap (plaintext!)

# → Shows ALL keys including password! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Password in ConfigMap: kubectl get cm anihpj-db-config -o yaml → SuperSecret123!
✗2. ConfigMaps are NOT encrypted at rest — password visible in etcd
✗3. Anyone with get configmap RBAC can read the password (commonly granted)
✗4. Secrets should be used for ALL sensitive data — never ConfigMaps
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Scan for sensitive data in ConfigMaps: kubectl get configmap -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -iE 'pass|secret|key|token'
→ DB_PASSWORD found in anihpj-db-config
2ConfigMaps vs Secrets: ConfigMaps are plaintext in etcd. Secrets can be encrypted at rest if EncryptionConfiguration is set.
3ConfigMaps have no size limit (Secrets have 1MB limit), but that doesn't justify using them for passwords
4RBAC separation: you can grant ConfigMap read access without granting Secret read access
5Root cause: Database credentials are stored in a ConfigMap (anihpj-db-config) instead of a Secret. ConfigMaps are designed for non-sensitive configuration data and store all values as plaintext in etcd. Secrets provide the same functionality but with encryption-at-rest support, separate RBAC controls, and stricter access patterns. All passwords, tokens, and keys MUST be stored in Secrets.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kubectl get cm -o yaml → DB_PASSWORD visible → ConfigMap misuse
②
Create Secret → kubectl create secret generic
③
Delete ConfigMap → Update deployment to use Secret
④
Password not visible in ConfigMap list → Migrated
⑤
All sensitive data in Secrets → Audit clean ✅

Tenet: ConfigMaps and Secrets are almost identical in how they work — the critical difference is intent and security: Secrets signal "this is sensitive" and support encryption at rest (when EncryptionConfiguration is enabled). ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive config like feature flags and app settings. On CKS, always audit ConfigMaps for passwords/tokens/keys with: kubectl get cm -A -o yaml | grep -iE 'pass|secret|token|key|pwd'. Migrate all sensitive data to Secrets.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get configmap anihpj-db-config -n anihpj -o yaml | grep PASSWORD DB_PASSWORD: SuperSecret123! ← PLAINTEXT password in ConfigMap! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get secret anihpj-db-creds -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d SuperSecret123! ← Now properly stored as Secret ✅
🔧
BASH — Create Secret + Update deployment 
# Step 1: Create Secret (NOT ConfigMap) for sensitive data
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-db-creds -n anihpj \
  --from-literal=DB_HOST=anihpj-db \
  --from-literal=DB_PORT=5432 \
  --from-literal=DB_NAME=jobpost \
  --from-literal=DB_USER=anihpj \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=SuperSecret123!

# Step 2: Delete the dangerous ConfigMap
kubectl delete configmap anihpj-db-config -n anihpj

# Step 3: Patch deployment to use Secret instead of ConfigMap
kubectl set env deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj --from=secret/anihpj-db-creds

# Step 4: Verify ConfigMap password is gone
kubectl get configmap -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
# → No more DB config ConfigMap ✅
✓

✅ Verify — All Sensitive Data in Secrets

The database credentials are now stored in a Kubernetes Secret (anihpj-db-creds). The ConfigMap has been deleted. The Secret values are base64-encoded in etcd and can be encrypted at rest when EncryptionConfiguration is enabled. The deployment reads from the Secret, and the application functions identically — but with proper security boundaries.

💡 Key takeaway: The rule is absolute: if it's sensitive (password, token, key, cert, API key), it goes in a Secret — NEVER a ConfigMap. On CKS, audit with the grep command above. Also: enable Secret encryption at rest with EncryptionConfiguration to protect Secrets in etcd. ConfigMaps = non-sensitive config only. Secrets = all sensitive data.

🧪 SCENARIO S50 — Category 4: Microservice Vulns PSS Debug

Deploy anihpj — Namespace Has No Pod Security Standard Label

The Problem: The anihpj namespace has no Pod Security Standard (PSS) labels — meaning pods can use ANY security context: root users, privileged mode, hostPath volumes, all capabilities. Without pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted, there are NO guardrails preventing dangerous pod specs. A developer could accidentally (or an attacker could deliberately) deploy a privileged pod that compromises the node. PSS labels replaced PodSecurityPolicy in Kubernetes 1.25 and are now the standard enforcement mechanism. Your job: check the namespace labels, apply the restricted PSS profile, and verify privileged pods are blocked.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster (v1.32)
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Test That Privileged Pods Are Allowed (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj/jobpost namespace was created without Pod Security Standard labels. A new team member deployed a test pod with privileged: true and it was accepted without any warning. Without PSS enforcement, the namespace is completely open to dangerous pod specs. PSS labels are the primary guardrail against privileged pods in Kubernetes 1.25+.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S50): 
Namespace security audit:
kubectl describe ns anihpj              ← Check for PSS labels
kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security... ← Apply restricted enforcement
BASH — Deploy anihpj + Test PSS enforcement gap 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S50: No Pod Security Standard — Privileged Pods Allowed
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 1. CHECK CURRENT PSS LABELS (THE BUG!)
kubectl get namespace anihpj -o yaml | grep pod-security
# → No output — NO Pod Security Standard labels! ❌

# 2. TRY TO CREATE A PRIVILEGED POD (should be BLOCKED by restricted PSS)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: privileged-test
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
  - name: test
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    securityContext:
      privileged: true               # ← Should be BLOCKED by PSS restricted!
EOF
# → POD CREATED! ❌ No PSS enforcement — privileged pod accepted!

kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web
# → privileged-test-xxx  Running   ← Privileged pod is RUNNING! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. No PSS labels: kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep pod-security → empty
✗2. Privileged pod created and running — zero enforcement
✗3. Without PSS, any pod can use hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged, SYS_ADMIN
✗4. PSS restricted is the standard baseline for multi-tenant clusters
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1PSS labels are: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce, warn, and audit — set to privileged/baseline/restricted
2No labels = no enforcement — the namespace defaults to "privileged" mode (allow everything)
3Restricted profile blocks: privileged pods, hostPath, hostNetwork, hostPID, non-root, capability adds, and more
4warn mode: shows warnings but doesn't block — useful for testing before enforcing
5Root cause: The anihpj namespace has no Pod Security Standard labels. Kubernetes 1.25+ uses PSS (not PodSecurityPolicy) to enforce security at the namespace level. Without labels, the namespace operates in "privileged" mode — allowing any pod spec, including privileged containers, host namespaces, and all capabilities. Fix: label the namespace with enforce=restricted to block dangerous pod specs.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Privileged pod accepted → No PSS enforcement
②
Label namespace: enforce=restricted + warn=restricted
③
Try privileged pod → REJECTED by admission controller
④
Safe pod (non-root, drop ALL caps) → Accepted
⑤
Namespace hardened → PSS restricted enforced ✅

Tenet: Pod Security Standards are the replacement for the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy. They work via namespace labels and are enforced by the built-in PodSecurity admission plugin. Three levels: privileged (anything goes), baseline (blocks known dangerous settings), restricted (hardened — enforces non-root, drops ALL caps, blocks hostPath, etc.). On CKS, always label namespaces with at least enforce=baseline, preferably restricted.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep pod-security # No output — No PSS labels! ❌
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj privileged-test-xxx Running ← Privileged pod ACCEPTED! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl apply -f privileged-pod.yaml Error from server (Forbidden): pods "privileged-test" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest" ← BLOCKED ✅
🔧
BASH — Label namespace + delete privileged pod 
# Step 1: Delete the privileged pod (it was allowed only because PSS was missing)
kubectl delete deployment privileged-test -n anihpj

# Step 2: Apply Pod Security Standard RESTRICTED to the namespace
kubectl label namespace anihpj \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  --overwrite

# Step 3: TEST — try the privileged pod again (should be REJECTED)
kubectl apply -f privileged-test.yaml 2>&1
# Expected: Error — PodSecurity violation ✅

# Step 4: Deploy a COMPLIANT pod (non-root, no caps, read-only FS)
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"nginx","securityContext":{"runAsNonRoot":true,"runAsUser":1000,"capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]}}}]}}}}'
# This pod should be ACCEPTED by PSS restricted ✅
✓

✅ Verify — PSS Restricted Enforces Security Guardrails

After labeling the namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted, any attempt to create a privileged pod, a pod running as root, or a pod with added capabilities is REJECTED by the PodSecurity admission controller. The anihpj namespace is now hardened — only compliant pods can be deployed.

💡 Key takeaway: PSS labels are the first line of defense against dangerous pod specs. Always apply them to every namespace: enforce (block violations), warn (show warnings), audit (log violations). Use restricted for application namespaces, baseline for system namespaces. On CKS, check every namespace: kubectl get ns -o yaml | grep pod-security. No labels = critical finding.

S51
🧪 SCENARIO S51 — Category 4: Microservice Vulns Image Debug

Deploy anihpj — Django Uses Floating :latest Tag with No Digest

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Django deployment uses image: nginx:latest — a floating tag. The :latest tag moves every time a new image is pushed, meaning today's deployment runs a different image than yesterday's — even though the tag looks the same. If an attacker compromises the image registry and replaces :latest with a malicious image, all new pods will run the attacker's code. Best practice is to pin images by digest (SHA256), ensuring immutable, verifiable image references. Your job: find the floating tag, replace it with a pinned digest, and verify image immutability.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj with floating :latest image tag (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost was deployed with image: nginx:latest. The team assumed :latest was "the latest stable version." But :latest is just a tag that moves — it could point to a new major version, a nightly build, or a compromised image tomorrow. Floating tags break build reproducibility and create a supply chain attack vector. Pinning by digest ensures the exact same image is always used.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S51): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: image: nginx:latest (floating tag)
└── 02-django-fixed.yaml           ← ✅ FIX: image: nginx@sha256:abc123 (digest pinned)
BASH — Deploy Django with floating :latest tag 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S51: Floating :latest Tag — Supply Chain Risk
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# DEPLOY WITH FLOATING :latest TAG (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:latest        # ❌ BUG! Floating tag — could change anytime!
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# CHECK — What image is actually running?
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}'
# → docker.io/library/nginx@sha256:abc123...   ← The tag resolved to THIS sha
# But tomorrow :latest could resolve to a DIFFERENT sha! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. image: nginx:latest — floating tag, no digest pinning
✗2. Running imageID differs from the tag — tag resolves to a mutable reference
✗3. Tomorrow's pod restart could pull a DIFFERENT image with the same tag
✗4. Supply chain risk: compromised registry = attacker replaces :latest → all new pods infected
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check imagePullPolicy: if Always (default for :latest), every restart re-pulls — getting potentially different image
2Digest format: image: nginx@sha256:e784b0...digest... — immutable, always resolves to the SAME image
3:latest is not a version — it's a moving pointer. Use semantic versions or digests
4Get current digest: kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}' — then use this in the deployment
5Root cause: The deployment uses a floating image tag (:latest) without a SHA256 digest. Tags are mutable — the same tag can point to different images over time. If the registry is compromised or an unintended image push occurs, all pods with imagePullPolicy: Always will silently pull and run the new (potentially malicious) image. Pinning by digest (image@sha256:...) guarantees immutability.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
image: nginx:latest → Floating tag detected
②
Get current digest → kubectl get pod -o jsonpath
③
Update deployment → nginx@sha256:abc123...
④
imagePullPolicy=IfNotPresent → Use cached image
⑤
Immutable image reference → Supply chain hardened ✅

Tenet: Image tags are mutable pointers — only digests are immutable. On CKS, you must know the difference: nginx:1.25 (tag — can be overwritten), nginx@sha256:abc... (digest — forever unique). Pinning by digest prevents supply chain attacks and ensures build reproducibility. Use imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent or Never to avoid unnecessary registry pulls.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}' nginx:latest ← Floating tag! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}' nginx@sha256:abc123def456... ← Digest-pinned! ✅
🔧
BASH — Get digest + patch deployment with pinned image 
# Step 1: Get the current image digest
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
DIGEST=$(kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}')
echo "Current digest: $DIGEST"
# → docker.io/library/nginx@sha256:abc123...

# Step 2: Extract just the sha256: part for the container image field
SHA_ONLY=$(echo $DIGEST | sed 's|docker.io/library/||')
echo "Pinned image: $SHA_ONLY"

# Step 3: Patch deployment with digest-pinned image + IfNotPresent policy
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -p "{\"spec\":{\"template\":{\"spec\":{\"containers\":[{\"name\":\"django\",\"image\":\"$SHA_ONLY\"}]}}}}"

# Step 4: Set imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent (avoid unnecessary pulls)
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"django","imagePullPolicy":"IfNotPresent"}]}}}}'

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# Step 5: Verify
kubectl get deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'
# → nginx@sha256:abc123... ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Image Is Pinned by Digest

The deployment now uses a SHA256 digest-pinned image reference. The same exact image will always be used — even if the :latest tag moves, even if the registry is compromised and a new image is pushed. With imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent, the kubelet uses the cached image and doesn't pull from the registry at all unless the image is missing.

💡 Key takeaway: Always pin images by digest in production: image: registry/name@sha256:abc.... Tags are for humans, digests are for machines. On CKS, audit with: kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' | sort -u. Flag any :latest tags and any tags without @sha256 — these are supply chain risks.

kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null

Deploy anihpj — Django Has NET_RAW Capability for Packet Sniffing

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Django container has NET_RAW capability — which allows creating raw sockets. With raw sockets, a process can sniff all network traffic on the pod network, craft spoofed packets, and perform ARP poisoning. This is a default capability in many container runtimes but is almost never needed by applications. An attacker who compromises the Django pod can run tcpdump and capture all traffic — including database queries, auth tokens, and other pods' data. Your job: detect NET_RAW capability, drop it, and verify raw sockets are blocked.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy Django with default capabilities (includes NET_RAW) (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The Django container was deployed without explicitly dropping capabilities. The container runtime's default capability set includes NET_RAW (allows raw sockets). An attacker who gains code execution can install tcpdump and sniff pod-to-pod traffic — potentially capturing database credentials, session tokens, and API keys transmitted between services. NET_RAW should always be explicitly dropped.

anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: default capabilities (includes NET_RAW)
└── 02-django-fixed.yaml           ← ✅ FIX: drop ALL, including NET_RAW

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -

kind: Deployment

spec:

---

kind: Service
metadata:

spec:
  selector:

  - port: 80
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# CHECK — Can the container create raw sockets?

kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff
# → CapEff: 00000000a80425fb   ← NET_RAW bit IS set! ❌

# Raw sockets = packet sniffing with tcpdump, arpspoof, etc.

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. NET_RAW in default capability set — allows raw socket creation
✗2. Raw sockets = tcpdump, packet crafting, ARP spoofing possible
✗3. Most applications (Django, nginx, Node.js) NEVER need raw sockets
✗4. CIS 5.2.6: drop ALL capabilities — NET_RAW should always be dropped
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Container runtime default caps include: CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FSETID, FOWNER, SETGID, SETUID, SETPCAP, NET_BIND_SERVICE, NET_RAW, SYS_CHROOT, KILL, AUDIT_WRITE, MKNOD, SETFCAP
2NET_RAW (capability bit 13) allows: raw socket creation (AF_PACKET), packet sniffing, ARP manipulation
3Should be explicitly dropped: NET_RAW is almost never needed by application containers
4Even with runAsNonRoot, NET_RAW allows network-level attacks that don't require root
5Root cause: The container does not explicitly drop capabilities. The container runtime's default capability set includes NET_RAW (bit 13), which allows creating raw sockets. With raw sockets, an attacker can sniff all pod network traffic (tcpdump), craft spoofed packets, and perform ARP attacks. The fix: explicitly drop ALL capabilities, which removes NET_RAW along with all other unnecessary caps.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Check CapEff → NET_RAW bit set → Raw sockets possible
②
Add drop: ["ALL"] → All caps removed including NET_RAW
③
Check CapEff → NET_RAW bit gone → Raw sockets blocked
④
No tcpdump/arpspoof possible → Network isolation restored
⑤
Only explicitly needed caps re-added (if any) → Least privilege ✅

Tenet: NET_RAW is one of the default Linux capabilities granted to containers. It enables raw sockets (AF_PACKET), which are the foundation for packet sniffing, ARP spoofing, and network-based attacks. Almost no web application needs raw sockets. On CKS, always drop ALL capabilities and only selectively add back what's needed. Use cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff to verify the effective capability set.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff CapEff: 00000000a80425fb ← NET_RAW bit set (visible in hex mask) ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff CapEff: 0000000000000000 ← ALL caps dropped, including NET_RAW ✅
🔧
BASH — Patch deployment to drop all capabilities 
# Drop ALL capabilities — including NET_RAW
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/securityContext","value":{
    "capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]},
    "allowPrivilegeEscalation": false,
    "runAsNonRoot": true,
    "runAsUser": 1000
  }}
]'

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# Verify: NET_RAW is gone from CapEff
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff
# Expected: 0000000000000000 ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Zero Capabilities, NET_RAW Blocked

After explicitly dropping ALL capabilities, the container's effective capability set is 0000000000000000 — zero capabilities. NET_RAW is no longer available, meaning raw sockets, packet sniffing, and ARP manipulation are blocked at the kernel level. The Django app continues to serve traffic normally — proving that web applications need zero Linux capabilities.

💡 Key takeaway: The container runtime's default capability set includes many caps that applications don't need. NET_RAW is the most dangerous "default" capability — it enables raw sockets for packet sniffing. On CKS, always explicitly drop ALL capabilities and verify with cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff. The only commonly needed capability is NET_BIND_SERVICE (for ports <1024), which can be avoided by using ports >1024.

Deploy anihpj — Django Can Fill Node Disk with Logs/Uploads

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Django container has no ephemeral storage limit. The container's writable layer, emptyDir volumes, and container logs share the node's disk. If Django generates excessive logs, processes a large file upload, or the /tmp directory fills up, it can exhaust the entire node's disk space — crashing not just the Django pod but the kubelet, container runtime, and ALL pods on that node. Ephemeral storage limits prevent a single pod from DoS-ing the entire node. Your job: add ephemeral storage requests/limits and verify the pod is constrained.

1

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost Django handles job applications with file uploads (resumes). The uploads are stored in /tmp (an emptyDir backed by node disk). Without ephemeral storage limits, a malicious user uploading a 50GB file could fill the node's disk. The kubelet would then be unable to write logs, pull images, or operate — taking down the entire node. Ephemeral storage limits protect the node from disk exhaustion.

├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: No ephemeral-storage limit
└── 02-django-fixed.yaml           ← ✅ FIX: ephemeral-storage limit + request set

  - port: 80

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 resources
# → resources: {}   ← No CPU, memory, OR ephemeral-storage limits! ❌

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. No ephemeral-storage limit — pod can consume all node disk space
✗2. emptyDir backed by node disk — unlimited size, can fill the partition
✗3. Disk exhaustion kills kubelet + container runtime — node becomes NotReady
✗4. Use emptyDir.sizeLimit or ephemeral-storage resource limits to protect the node
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Ephemeral storage includes: container writable layer, emptyDir volumes, container logs, image layers
2Two ways to limit: resources.limits.ephemeral-storage (pod-level) and emptyDir.sizeLimit (volume-level)
3When limit exceeded: pod is Evicted (like memory OOM), preventing node disk full
4Also request: resources.requests.ephemeral-storage for scheduling — kubelet checks disk free before placing pod
5Root cause: The deployment has no ephemeral-storage resource limits or requests. Without limits, a single pod can exhaust the node's disk by writing to its container layer, emptyDir volumes, or generating excessive logs. When the node disk fills, the kubelet and container runtime fail — taking down ALL pods on the node. Fix: add resources.limits.ephemeral-storage and/or set emptyDir.sizeLimit on all volumes.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
No ephemeral-storage in resources → Unlimited disk use
②
Add limits.ephemeral-storage + emptyDir.sizeLimit
③
Pod evicted when limit exceeded → Node disk protected
④
Schduler uses request for placement → Prevents overcommit
⑤
Node disk exhaustion prevented ✅

Tenet: Ephemeral storage is the "forgotten resource" — everyone sets CPU and memory limits but forgets disk. A single pod can fill the node's disk via logs, /tmp, or emptyDir volumes. On CKS, always set resources.limits.ephemeral-storage and emptyDir.sizeLimit. Use medium: Memory for emptyDir to use tmpfs (RAM-backed, not disk-backed) where appropriate.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 resources resources: {} ← No ephemeral-storage limit! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 resources resources: limits: {ephemeral-storage: "512Mi"} requests: {ephemeral-storage: "128Mi"} ✅
🔧
BASH — Patch deployment with storage limits 
# Add ephemeral-storage limits + emptyDir sizeLimit
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources","value":{
    "requests":{"ephemeral-storage":"128Mi","cpu":"100m","memory":"128Mi"},
    "limits":{"ephemeral-storage":"512Mi","cpu":"500m","memory":"256Mi"}
  }},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/volumes/0/emptyDir","value":{"sizeLimit":"256Mi"}}
]'

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# Verify
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep ephemeral-storage
# Expected: ephemeral-storage limit + request set ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Has Enforced Storage Limits

After adding ephemeral-storage limits (512Mi) and requests (128Mi), plus emptyDir.sizeLimit (256Mi), the pod is now constrained. If uploads or logs exceed the limit, the pod is evicted — protecting the node from disk exhaustion. The scheduler also uses the request value to avoid placing pods on nodes without sufficient free disk space.

💡 Key takeaway: Ephemeral storage is one of three resource types (CPU, memory, ephemeral-storage). Always set limits on all three. Use emptyDir.medium: Memory for small, high-performance writable directories (backed by RAM, not disk). On CKS, audit with: kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -B2 ephemeral-storage — flag any pod without limits.

①
nc to port 5432 → plaintext response → No TLS
②
Generate TLS cert → Create Secret → Mount to PostgreSQL
③
Configure PostgreSQL ssl=on → Update Django sslmode=require
④
nc → connection rejected → TLS required
⑤
Django connects with TLS → Traffic encrypted ✅

Tenet: Pod-to-pod traffic inside Kubernetes is NOT encrypted by default — the CNI provides connectivity, not encryption. On CKS, you must know how to enable TLS at the application layer (PostgreSQL TLS, HTTPS between services) or deploy a service mesh for transparent mTLS. 📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "echo '' | nc -w1 anihpj-db 5432 2>&1" Connected — database accepts plain TCP! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "echo '' | nc -w1 anihpj-db 5432 2>&1" Ncat: Connection refused — TLS required, plaintext blocked ✅

BASH — Generate TLS cert + Enable PostgreSQL SSL + Update Django 
# Step 1: Generate self-signed TLS cert for PostgreSQL
openssl req -new -x509 -days 365 -nodes -text -out server.crt \
  -keyout server.key -subj "/CN=anihpj-db.anihpj.svc"

# Step 2: Create Secret with cert + key
kubectl create secret tls postgres-tls -n anihpj \
  --cert=server.crt --key=server.key

# Step 3: Mount TLS cert + enable PostgreSQL SSL
# (In production, use a custom PostgreSQL image with ssl=on in postgresql.conf)
# For CKS: demonstrate the concept — configure postgres with ssl=on pointing to mounted cert

# Step 4: Update Django DATABASE_URL to use sslmode=require
kubectl set env deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj \
  DATABASE_URL="postgresql://anihpj:secret123@anihpj-db:5432/jobpost?sslmode=require"

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s
✓

✅ Verify — Database Traffic Is Encrypted

With PostgreSQL TLS enabled and Django using sslmode=require, all database traffic between Django and PostgreSQL is now encrypted. Plaintext connections are rejected by PostgreSQL. An attacker sniffing the pod network sees only encrypted TLS traffic — protecting PII, credentials, and query data.

💡 Key takeaway: Kubernetes does NOT encrypt pod-to-pod traffic by default. You must implement encryption at the application layer (TLS for each service) or use a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd for transparent mTLS). On CKS, know how to enable TLS for common services (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis) and configure client connections accordingly. Always check connection strings for sslmode/sslmode=tls.

📖 APP STORY: A developer configured the liveness probe to hit Django's /debug/health endpoint. This endpoint was designed for development only — it returns Django settings (including SECRET_KEY), database config, middleware stack, and installed packages. The probe itself works fine, but the debug endpoint is accessible to anyone who can reach the pod.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S55): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: livenessProbe hits debug endpoint
└── 02-django-fixed.yaml           ← ✅ FIX: probe uses /healthz (safe endpoint)
BASH — Deploy Django with debug endpoint probe 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S55: Debug Endpoint as Liveness Probe
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /debug/health       # ❌ BUG! Debug endpoint as probe!
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /debug/status       # ❌ Another debug endpoint!
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# CHECK — Probe is hitting debug endpoint
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl describe pod $POD -n anihpj | grep -A3 Liveness
# → Liveness: http-get http://:80/debug/health ❌

# Anyone can curl the debug endpoint!
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- curl -s localhost/debug/health 2>/dev/null | head -5
# → Returns debug info — settings, packages, env! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Liveness probe path: /debug/health — debug endpoint in production
✗2. Readiness probe path: /debug/status — also debug endpoint
✗3. Debug endpoint exposes Django settings, SECRET_KEY, DB config
✗4. Probes should use dedicated, minimal health check endpoints
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Debug endpoints typically expose: app version, config, env vars, package list, DB status — too much info
2Proper health endpoint: returns 200 OK with minimal body (e.g., "ok"), no config details
3Kubelet hits probes every periodSeconds — so the debug endpoint is constantly being accessed anyway
4Probes should be: /healthz, /ready, /live — never /debug/*
5Root cause: The liveness and readiness probes are configured to hit debug endpoints (/debug/health, /debug/status). These endpoints expose internal application details — settings, environment variables, and configuration — that should never be accessible in production. Probes should use minimal health check endpoints that return only HTTP status without sensitive data.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Probe path: /debug/* → Debug endpoint exposed
②
Replace with /healthz → Simple health check
③
Add nginx location block for /healthz → Returns 200 only
④
Disable /debug/* endpoints in production
⑤
Probes safe, debug hidden → Information leak closed ✅

Tenet: Debug endpoints are the #1 source of information leaks in web applications. They expose configuration, environment, and internal state. Probes should hit dedicated endpoints that return only HTTP status codes. On CKS, audit all probes: kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -E 'path:.*debug|path:.*admin'. Also check: never expose Django DEBUG mode, Spring Boot actuator without auth, or Express debug routes in production.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe pod $POD -n anihpj | grep -A3 Liveness Liveness: http-get http://:80/debug/health delay=5s ← Debug exposed ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe pod $POD -n anihpj | grep -A3 Liveness Liveness: http-get http://:80/healthz delay=5s ← Safe endpoint ✅
🔧
BASH — Patch probes to use safe /healthz endpoint

kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/httpGet/path","value":"/healthz"},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/path","value":"/ready"}
]'

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# Verify
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl describe pod $POD -n anihpj | grep -A3 Liveness
# Expected: /healthz ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Probes Use Safe Health Endpoints

After changing probes from /debug/health and /debug/status to /healthz and /ready, the debug endpoints are no longer exposed. Probes hit minimal endpoints that return only HTTP 200 — no configuration details, no environment variables, no debug data.

💡 Key takeaway: Probe paths are visible to anyone with kubectl describe pod access. Debug endpoints leak internal details. On CKS, audit probes and ensure they use dedicated minimal health check paths. Disable all debug/admin endpoints in production via environment variable (DEBUG=False for Django, management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=none for Spring Boot).

Deploy anihpj — Django Has NO Security Hardening Whatsoever

This is what you get if you deploy a container with zero security hardening — and it's unfortunately common. The pod is effectively a privileged process with full container access. Your job: apply the complete security hardening checklist to transform this pod from completely vulnerable to fully hardened.

1

📋 Deploy Django with ZERO security hardening (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: This is the "default Kubernetes experience" — a pod deployed with no securityContext. It runs as root, has writable filesystem, all capabilities, privilege escalation allowed. Everything S41-S55 warned about individually is combined here. Your task: apply ALL fixes learned so far to harden this pod completely.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S56): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: Completely unhardened pod (root + writable + all caps)

BASH — Deploy completely unhardened Django pod (ALL THE BUGS!) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S56: Zero Hardening — Everything Wrong
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# DEPLOY COMPLETELY UNHARDENED POD (ALL THE BUGS!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:latest              # ❌ :latest tag (floating)
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        # ❌ No securityContext at ALL:
        #    - Runs as root (UID 0)
        #    - Writable root filesystem
        #    - Privilege escalation allowed
        #    - All default capabilities (NET_RAW, SETUID, SYS_CHROOT, etc.)
        # ❌ No resources section (CPU/memory/storage limits)
        # ❌ No Pod Security Standard labels on namespace
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# VERIFY — Check all the things that are wrong
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
echo "=== Security Audit of $POD ==="
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- id                               # → root ❌
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep NoNewPrivs  # → 0 ❌
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff      # → full caps ❌
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /test-write                     # → succeeds ❌

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Root user: UID 0, GID 0 — no runAsNonRoot
✗2. Privilege escalation: NoNewPrivs=0 — setuid binaries work
✗3. All capabilities: NET_RAW, SETUID, SYS_CHROOT — full default set
✗4. Writable root FS, no resource limits, floating :latest tag — everything wrong
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check user: id → uid=0(root) ❌ — should be runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: 1000
2Check privilege escalation: cat /proc/1/status | grep NoNewPrivs → 0 ❌ — should be 1
3Check capabilities: cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff → full set ❌ — should be 0000000000000000
4Check root FS: touch /test → succeeds ❌ — should fail (readOnlyRootFilesystem: true)
5Root cause: The pod has zero security hardening — no securityContext at all. This means: root user, writable root FS, all capabilities, privilege escalation allowed, no resource limits, floating image tag. This is the default Kubernetes behavior and must be explicitly hardened for every production pod.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Full audit: root + writable + all caps + esc allowed
②
Checklist: non-root, no escalation, drop caps, read-only FS, limits, digest
③
Apply ALL fixes at once → Recreate pod
④
Re-audit: non-root + NoNewPrivs=1 + zero caps + RO FS
⑤
Fully hardened pod → CIS 5.2.6 PASS ✅

Tenet: Kubernetes does NOT harden pods by default — you must do it explicitly. The complete securityContext hardening checklist: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser>0, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, capabilities.drop=["ALL"], readOnlyRootFilesystem=true, resources limits set, image pinned by digest. On CKS, this is the core of microservice security — every pod must have ALL of these.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "id; cat /proc/1/status|grep NoNewPrivs; cat /proc/1/status|grep CapEff"; kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /test && echo "Root FS writable" || echo "Root FS read-only" uid=0(root) ← ❌ NoNewPrivs: 0 ← ❌ CapEff: a80425fb ← ❌ Root FS writable ← ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- sh -c "id; cat /proc/1/status|grep NoNewPrivs; cat /proc/1/status|grep CapEff"; kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- touch /test 2>&1 uid=1000 ✅ NoNewPrivs: 1 ✅ CapEff: 0000000000000000 ✅ Read-only file system ✅
