BASH — Delete + recreate with full hardening 
# Delete unhardened deployment
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Recreate with FULL hardening applied
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx@sha256:abc123...    # Digest-pinned ✅
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true              # ✅ No root
          runAsUser: 1000                 # ✅ Specific non-root UID
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false # ✅ No setuid
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]                 # ✅ Zero capabilities
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true    # ✅ Immutable FS
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
        - name: run
          mountPath: /var/run
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
            ephemeral-storage: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
            ephemeral-storage: "512Mi"
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {sizeLimit: "128Mi"}
      - name: run
        emptyDir: {}
EOF

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- id           # Expected: uid=1000 ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Is Fully Hardened

After applying all hardening measures: non-root user (UID 1000), privilege escalation blocked (NoNewPrivs=1), all capabilities dropped (CapEff: 0), read-only root filesystem, resource limits set, and image pinned by digest. This pod now passes CIS 5.2.6 and follows Kubernetes security best practices.

💡 Key takeaway: This is the target state for every application pod. The complete hardening checklist: (1) runAsNonRoot + runAsUser, (2) allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, (3) capabilities.drop: [ALL], (4) readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, (5) resources limits/requests set, (6) image pinned by digest, (7) namespace PSS label: enforce=restricted. On CKS, you must apply ALL of these to every pod.

🧪 SCENARIO S57 — Category 4: Microservice Vulns NetPol Debug

Deploy anihpj — All Pods Can Talk to Each Other Freely

The Problem: The anihpj namespace has no NetworkPolicies — the default Kubernetes behavior allows ALL traffic between all pods. Django can talk to PostgreSQL, yes — but a compromised nginx container can also reach etcd, the API server, kubelet endpoints, and other tenants' pods. NetworkPolicy micro-segmentation is the principle of "default deny, explicit allow" — only permit the specific traffic flows the app needs. Your job: audit current traffic flows, create a deny-all default policy, and add explicit allow rules for only the necessary connections (web→DB, DNS).

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Single-node KinD with Calico
1

📋 Deploy anihpj stack with NO NetworkPolicies (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost has Django, PostgreSQL, and Redis all in the same namespace with no NetworkPolicies. The application works — but every pod can reach every other pod (and external services) with no restrictions. A compromised Django pod can scan the entire pod network, access kube-system APIs, and exfiltrate data. Zero Trust networking: default deny, explicit allow.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S57): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← PostgreSQL Deployment + Service
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django Deployment + Service
├── 03-netpol-deny-all.yaml        ← ✅ Default deny all ingress+egress
├── 04-netpol-allow-dns.yaml       ← ✅ Allow DNS (UDP 53 to kube-dns)
├── 05-netpol-allow-db.yaml        ← ✅ Allow Django → PostgreSQL
└── 06-test-pod.yaml               ← Test pod for verification
BASH — Deploy anihpj with no NetworkPolicies (default allow-all) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S57: No Micro-Segmentation — All Pods Talk Freely
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 1. DEPLOY FULL STACK (Django + PostgreSQL + Redis)
kubectl create deployment anihpj-db -n anihpj --image=postgres:15-alpine
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-db -n anihpj --port=5432
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --port=80
kubectl run test-pod -n anihpj --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# 2. TEST — Test pod can reach everything (THE BUG!)
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web:80 2>&1 | head -1
# → HTML returned — test pod can reach web! ❌
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- nc -zv anihpj-db 5432 2>&1
# → Connection succeeded — test pod can reach DB! ❌

# 3. CHECK — No NetworkPolicies exist!
kubectl get netpol -n anihpj
# → No resources found in anihpj namespace ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. No NetworkPolicies: all pods can reach all other pods freely
✗2. Test pod can reach web + DB — even though it shouldn't
✗3. Zero-trust principle violated: no explicit traffic whitelisting
✗4. Kubernetes default is allow-all — you must explicitly deny
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Kubernetes default: all pods can communicate with all other pods — no restrictions
2NetworkPolicies are namespace-scoped: they control traffic within and across namespaces
3Policy types: Ingress (incoming traffic to pods), Egress (outgoing from pods)
4Default deny policy: empty podSelector {} with no ingress/egress rules = deny all
5Root cause: No NetworkPolicies exist in the anihpj namespace. Kubernetes defaults to allow-all traffic between pods. Without NetworkPolicies, any pod can reach any other pod (cross-namespace too if no policies exist). Fix: create a default-deny policy, then add explicit allow rules for only the required flows (web→DB, DNS, etc.).
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
No NetPol → all pods talk freely → Zero-trust violated
②
Apply default deny ingress + egress → All traffic blocked
③
Add DNS allow (UDP 53 to kube-dns)
④
Add web→DB allow (TCP 5432) + ingress to web (TCP 80)
⑤
Test pod blocked → Only needed flows permitted ✅

Tenet: NetworkPolicies implement zero-trust networking in Kubernetes. The default posture must be "deny all" with explicit allows for necessary traffic. Remember: DNS (UDP 53 to kube-dns) is the #1 forgotten rule. On CKS, always create a complete NetPol ruleset: default-deny ingress, default-deny egress, DNS allow, and app-specific allows. Verify with test pods that should be blocked.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get netpol -n anihpj No resources found in anihpj namespace. ← Zero micro-segmentation ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web:80 2>&1 wget: download timed out ← Test pod BLOCKED from web! ✅
🔧
BASH — Create complete NetworkPolicy ruleset 
# Step 1: Default deny ALL ingress
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
EOF

# Step 2: Allow web pods to receive traffic on port 80
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-web-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - ports:
    - port: 80
EOF

# Step 3: Allow Django→PostgreSQL traffic on port 5432
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj-web
    ports:
    - port: 5432
EOF

# Step 4: Allow DNS egress (UDP 53 + TCP 53 to kube-dns)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
EOF

# Step 5: Verify — test pod should NOW be blocked from web + DB
kubectl exec -n anihpj test-pod -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web:80
# Expected: timeout ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Micro-Segmentation Enforced

After applying default-deny ingress, web ingress allow, DB allow (only from web), and DNS egress allow, the anihpj namespace is now micro-segmented. The test pod (which has no allow rules) cannot reach the web service or database. Only explicitly permitted traffic flows between labeled pods.

💡 Key takeaway: NetworkPolicy micro-segmentation is a fundamental CKS topic. The pattern is always: (1) default deny ingress + egress, (2) DNS allow (ALWAYS!), (3) app-specific allows using podSelector and namespaceSelector. On CKS, be prepared to create a complete NetworkPolicy ruleset from scratch. Remember that a CNI supporting NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium) must be installed — the default KinD CNI (kindnet) does NOT enforce NetworkPolicies.

🧪 SCENARIO S58 — Category 4: Microservice Vulns Encrypt Debug

anihpj Audit — Secrets Stored as Plaintext in etcd

The Problem: By default, Kubernetes stores all Secret data as base64-encoded plaintext in etcd — NOT encrypted. Anyone who gains access to etcd data (backup files, disk access, etcd API) can decode every Secret in the cluster. CIS Benchmark 1.2.33 requires enabling EncryptionConfiguration with a strong encryption provider (aescbc or secretbox) to encrypt Secrets at rest in etcd. Your job: check if encryption at rest is enabled, create an EncryptionConfiguration, and verify Secrets are encrypted in etcd.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster (v1.32)
1

📋 Deploy anihpj + Check if Secret Encryption at Rest Is Enabled (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost stores DB credentials, API keys, and TLS certificates in Kubernetes Secrets. A security audit reveals that EncryptionConfiguration is NOT enabled — all Secret data is stored as base64-encoded plaintext in etcd. If an attacker gets access to etcd (backup leak, compromised node, etcd API access), every Secret in the cluster is instantly readable. Encryption at rest is the last line of defense for Secret data.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S58): 
Encryption audit:
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml       ← Check --encryption-provider-config
/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml               ← Check if this file exists
kubectl get secret -n anihpj anihpj-db-creds -o yaml ← Shows base64 (not encrypted)
BASH — Deploy anihpj + Check Secret encryption status 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S58: Secrets Not Encrypted at Rest — CIS 1.2.33
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-db-creds -n anihpj \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=SuperSecret123!

# 1. CHECK IF ENCRYPTION AT REST IS CONFIGURED (THE BUG!)
sudo grep 'encryption-provider-config' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# → No output! EncryptionProviderConfig NOT set! ❌

# 2. CHECK THE SECRET — it's only base64, NOT encrypted!
kubectl get secret anihpj-db-creds -n anihpj -o yaml | grep DB_PASSWORD
# → DB_PASSWORD: U3VwZXJTZWNyZXQxMjMh   ← Just base64, NOT encrypted!

# 3. IF someone accesses etcd directly, they can decode ALL secrets
# etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj/anihpj-db-creds | decode → plaintext password!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. --encryption-provider-config NOT set in API server manifest
✗2. Secrets are base64-encoded only — NOT encrypted — readable by anyone with etcd access
✗3. CIS 1.2.33: "Ensure that encryption providers are appropriately configured" — FAILED
✗4. etcd backups contain ALL secrets in plaintext — backup leak = total cluster compromise
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1EncryptionConfiguration is a YAML file specifying encryption providers (aescbc, secretbox, kms) and resources to encrypt (secrets, configmaps)
2First provider in the list is used for encryption. Subsequent providers are used for decryption of old data during key rotation.
3Recommended: aescbc (AES-CBC with PKCS7 padding, requires 32-byte key) or secretbox (XSalsa20+Poly1305 from NaCl)
4After enabling, all NEW Secrets are encrypted. Existing Secrets need to be re-written (kubectl get secret -A -o yaml | kubectl replace -f -)
5Root cause: EncryptionConfiguration is not enabled on the API server. By default, Kubernetes stores Secrets as base64-encoded plaintext in etcd. CIS 1.2.33 requires configuring an encryption provider (aescbc or secretbox) to encrypt Secrets at rest. Without this, anyone with etcd access (backup, compromise, API) can read all Secrets in the cluster.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Check API server manifest → No encryption-provider-config
②
Create EncryptionConfiguration with aescbc → Mount to API server
③
Add --encryption-provider-config flag → Restart API server
④
Re-write all existing Secrets → Encrypted in etcd
⑤
CIS 1.2.33 PASS → Secrets encrypted at rest ✅

Tenet: Base64 is NOT encryption — it's encoding. Anyone can decode base64 to plaintext with one command. Encryption at rest is a CIS requirement and should be enabled on EVERY production cluster. On CKS, you must know how to create an EncryptionConfiguration, mount it to the API server, and re-write existing Secrets. Use aescbc (32-byte key) or secretbox as the encryption provider.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo grep encryption-provider-config /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml # No output — Encryption NOT configured! ❌
$ kubectl get secret anihpj-db-creds -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d SuperSecret123! ← Plaintext accessible from etcd! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo grep encryption-provider-config /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml ✅
🔧
BASH — Create EncryptionConfiguration + Configure API server 
# Step 1: Generate a 32-byte encryption key
ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)
echo "Save this key securely: $ENCRYPTION_KEY"

# Step 2: Create EncryptionConfiguration file
sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
    - secrets
    providers:
    - aescbc:
        keys:
        - name: key1
          secret: BASE64_32BYTE_KEY_HERE      # Replace with actual key
    - identity: {}                              # Fallback for reading unencrypted data
EOF

# Step 3: Add --encryption-provider-config flag to API server manifest
# AND mount the config file as a volume
# (Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml)

# Step 4: Wait for API server restart, then re-write all Secrets
kubectl get secrets -A -o yaml | kubectl replace -f -

# Step 5: New Secrets are now encrypted in etcd ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Secrets Are Encrypted at Rest

After configuring EncryptionConfiguration with aescbc provider and re-writing all Secrets, all Secret data is now encrypted in etcd. Anyone accessing etcd directly sees encrypted data, not base64-encoded plaintext. The cluster passes CIS 1.2.33. The encryption key must be stored securely (KMS, HSM, or vault) and rotated periodically.

💡 Key takeaway: Base64 is encoding, NOT encryption. Without EncryptionConfiguration, all Secrets are plaintext in etcd. On CKS, CIS 1.2.33 requires encryption at rest. The configuration file is at /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml (custom path), referenced by --encryption-provider-config in the API server manifest. Always use aescbc or secretbox, never identity as the primary provider. Re-write all Secrets after enabling encryption.

🧹

# Delete namespace
kubectl delete namespace anihpj
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S59
🧪 SCENARIO S59 — Category 4: Microservice Vulns Immutable Debug

Deploy anihpj — ConfigMaps and Secrets Can Be Modified at Runtime

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost ConfigMaps and Secrets are mutable (the default). Any process with RBAC to update them can change configuration at runtime — modifying database connection strings, injecting malicious values, or replacing TLS certificates. Even worse, a compromised controller or CI pipeline could silently modify a ConfigMap, and the pod won't know until it restarts. Setting immutable: true on ConfigMaps and Secrets makes them read-only after creation — preventing runtime tampering. Your job: identify mutable configs, set immutable: true, and verify modification is blocked.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj with mutable ConfigMaps and Secrets (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost stores app settings in a ConfigMap and credentials in a Secret — both mutable. During a security review, the team discovers that a CI pipeline bug could overwrite the database connection string in the ConfigMap. Combined with a rolling restart, the app would silently pick up the malicious config. Immutable configs are a key defense-in-depth measure against configuration tampering.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S59): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-configmap-mutable.yaml      ← BROKEN: ConfigMap without immutable: true
├── 02-secret-mutable.yaml         ← BROKEN: Secret without immutable: true
├── 03-configmap-immutable.yaml    ← ✅ FIX: immutable: true (cannot be changed)
└── 04-secret-immutable.yaml       ← ✅ FIX: immutable: true
BASH — Deploy mutable ConfigMaps + Secrets 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S59: Mutable ConfigMaps & Secrets — Runtime Tampering
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 1. CREATE MUTABLE CONFIGMAP (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: anihpj-config
  namespace: anihpj
  # ❌ BUG: No immutable: true — can be modified at any time!
data:
  DB_HOST: "anihpj-db"
  DEBUG: "false"
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
EOF

# 2. CREATE MUTABLE SECRET
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-creds
  namespace: anihpj
  # ❌ BUG: No immutable: true — can be modified at any time!
stringData:
  DB_PASSWORD: "SuperSecret123!"
  API_KEY: "sk-abc123xyz"
EOF

# 3. MODIFY THE CONFIGMAP — it works! (THE BUG!)
kubectl patch configmap anihpj-config -n anihpj -p '{"data":{"DB_HOST":"malicious-db.evil.com"}}'
kubectl get configmap anihpj-config -n anihpj -o yaml | grep DB_HOST
# → DB_HOST: malicious-db.evil.com   ← MODIFIED! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. ConfigMap modified successfully: DB_HOST changed to malicious value
✗2. Secret can also be modified — API keys can be replaced at runtime
✗3. No immutable: true on either — default is mutable
✗4. RBAC with update permission can silently change config data
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1immutable: true makes a ConfigMap/Secret read-only after creation — any update/patch is rejected
2Once set, immutable cannot be changed — you must delete and recreate the resource
3Benefits: prevents accidental/malicious config changes, improves kubelet performance (no watching for changes), ensures config consistency
4Version management: use naming conventions like anihpj-config-v1, v2 — create new, update deployment ref, delete old
5Root cause: Neither the ConfigMap nor Secret has immutable: true set (the default). This allows runtime modification of configuration data. A compromised RBAC principal or a CI pipeline bug can change database hosts, credentials, or API keys — and the app will pick up the changes on the next config reload or pod restart. Immutable configs prevent runtime tampering.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Patch ConfigMap → succeeds → Mutable config
②
Delete + recreate with immutable: true
③
Try to patch → REJECTED → Immutable enforced
④
New version = new resource name → Safe rollout
⑤
Config tampering prevented ✅

Tenet: immutable: true is a simple but powerful Kubernetes feature (GA since v1.21). It prevents any modification after creation — updates must go through a proper change management process (create new, test, migrate, delete old). On CKS, always set immutable: true on production ConfigMaps and Secrets. Use versioned naming (config-v1, config-v2) to manage changes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl patch configmap anihpj-config -n anihpj -p '{"data":{"DB_HOST":"evil.com"}}' configmap/anihpj-config patched ← Modified! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch configmap anihpj-config-v1 -n anihpj -p '{"data":{"DB_HOST":"evil.com"}}' Error: configmap "anihpj-config-v1" is immutable and cannot be patched ← BLOCKED ✅
🔧
BASH — Delete + recreate with immutable: true 
# Step 1: Delete mutable ConfigMap + Secret
kubectl delete configmap anihpj-config -n anihpj
kubectl delete secret anihpj-creds -n anihpj

# Step 2: Recreate with immutable: true
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: anihpj-config-v1
  namespace: anihpj
immutable: true       # ✅ Cannot be modified after creation
data:
  DB_HOST: "anihpj-db"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-creds-v1
  namespace: anihpj
immutable: true       # ✅ Cannot be modified after creation
stringData:
  DB_PASSWORD: "SuperSecret123!"
EOF

# Step 3: VERIFY — attempt to modify should FAIL
kubectl patch configmap anihpj-config-v1 -n anihpj -p '{"data":{"DB_HOST":"evil.com"}}' 2>&1
# Expected: "is immutable and cannot be patched" ✅
✓

✅ Verify — ConfigMaps and Secrets Are Immutable

After recreating the ConfigMap and Secret with immutable: true, any attempt to patch or modify them is rejected by the API server. Configuration changes now require a deliberate process: create a new versioned resource, update deployments to reference it, and delete the old version.

💡 Key takeaway: immutable: true is available on ConfigMaps and Secrets since Kubernetes v1.21 (GA). It's a one-line change with significant security benefits: prevents runtime tampering, improves API server performance (reduced watch overhead), and enforces proper change management. On CKS, always audit: kubectl get cm,secret -A -o yaml | grep -B5 'immutable: false\|^ data:' | grep -v 'immutable: true' to find mutable resources.

kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S60
🧪 SCENARIO S60 — Category 4: Microservice Vulns Priv Debug

Deploy anihpj — Privileged Container Has Full Root on Node

The Problem: An anihpj/jobpost "debug" pod was deployed with privileged: true, hostPID: true, hostNetwork: true, and hostPath mount of / (the entire node root filesystem). This is the worst possible container configuration — the container has root on the node. It can see ALL processes, access ALL files (including /etc/kubernetes certs, container runtime sockets, other pods' data), modify kernel parameters, and load kernel modules. This is essentially a root shell on the node — NOT a container. Your job: find this dangerous pod, understand the scope of the exposure, delete it immediately, and ensure Pod Security Standards block such pods in the future.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Single-node KinD with Calico
1

📋 Deploy DANGEROUS privileged pod (CONTAINS ALL THE BUGS)

📖 APP STORY: A developer deployed a "debug helper" pod for the anihpj team. The YAML has privileged: true (all capabilities, no restrictions), hostPID: true (all node processes), hostNetwork: true (node network), and hostPath mount of / (entire node filesystem). This pod is NOT a container — it's a root shell on the Kubernetes node. If an attacker compromises this pod, they OWN the node. This is the ultimate CKS "spot the problem" scenario.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S60): 
⚠️ IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED:
1. Identify and DELETE the privileged pod
2. Label namespace with PSS enforce=restricted
3. Audit ALL namespaces for similar pods
BASH — Deploy the ULTIMATE dangerous pod (DO NOT RUN IN PRODUCTION!) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S60: Privileged Container = Root on Node (CRITICAL!)
# This is the WORST possible pod configuration
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# DEPLOY THE DANGEROUS POD (ALL THE BUGS IN ONE!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-debug
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      hostPID: true               # ❌ Sees ALL node processes!
      hostNetwork: true           # ❌ Uses node network stack!
      containers:
  - name: debug
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    securityContext:
      privileged: true            # ❌ ALL capabilities + disabled protections!
    volumeMounts:
    - name: host-root
      mountPath: /host            # ❌ ENTIRE node filesystem mounted!
  volumes:
  - name: host-root
    hostPath:
      path: /                     # ❌ Mounts the ENTIRE node root!
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# DEMONSTRATE THE EXPOSURE
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)

# 1. Read Kubernetes certificates (node root!)
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /host/etc/kubernetes/pki/
# → ca.crt, apiserver.crt, etcd/* — ALL cluster certs exposed! ❌

# 2. See all node processes
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ps aux | wc -l
# → 150+ processes — entire node process tree! ❌

# 3. Access container runtime socket
kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /host/var/run/docker.sock 2>/dev/null || echo "containerd socket at /host/run/containerd/containerd.sock"
# → Socket is accessible! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. privileged: true — disables ALL container isolation, grants all capabilities
✗2. hostPID: true — can see and kill ANY node process (kubelet, etcd, containerd)
✗3. hostNetwork: true — can intercept all node traffic, bypass all NetworkPolicies
✗4. hostPath: / — can read/write ANY file on the node including /etc/kubernetes, container runtimes
✗5. Combined: This is NOT a container — it's a ROOT SHELL ON THE NODE
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1privileged: true is the nuclear option — it grants ALL capabilities + disables AppArmor/SELinux/seccomp + makes all devices available
2hostPID + hostNetwork + hostPath / combine to give the pod unfettered node access
3From this pod, an attacker can: steal etcd certs (→ cluster takeover), kill kubelet (→ node crash), modify system binaries, extract all Secrets
4NO legitimate application should ever have this configuration — only system DaemonSets (CNI plugins, kube-proxy) need partial host access
5Root cause: The pod has privileged: true + hostPID + hostNetwork + hostPath:/ — the most dangerous possible combination. This effectively grants the container unrestricted root access to the Kubernetes node. The fix is NOT to harden this pod — it must be DELETED immediately. Then label the namespace with PSS enforce=restricted to prevent any future privileged pods. Audit ALL namespaces for similar configurations.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Privileged + hostPID + hostNetwork + hostPath:/ → ROOT ON NODE
②
IMMEDIATELY DELETE the pod → kubectl delete deploy
③
Label namespace: PSS enforce=restricted → Blocks future privileged pods
④
Audit cluster: kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep 'privileged: true'
⑤
Zero privileged pods in app namespaces → Cluster secured ✅

Tenet: A privileged pod is NOT a container — it's a root shell on the Kubernetes node with ALL protections disabled. privileged: true alone grants all capabilities, disables AppArmor/SELinux/seccomp/lsm, and makes all host devices available. Combined with host namespace access, the pod bypasses ALL container isolation. On CKS, the audit command: kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -B5 'privileged: true' — any match in a non-kube-system namespace is a CRITICAL finding.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -B5 'privileged: true' containers: - image: alpine:3.19 securityContext: privileged: true ← CRITICAL FINDING! ❌
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- ls /host/etc/kubernetes/pki/ ca.crt apiserver.crt etcd/ ← NODE CERTS ACCESSIBLE! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj No resources found in anihpj namespace. ← Privileged pod DELETED ✅
$ kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep pod-security pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted ← PSS blocks future privileged pods ✅
🔧
BASH — Emergency fix + prevention 
# Step 1: DELETE THE DANGEROUS POD IMMEDIATELY
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-debug -n anihpj

# Step 2: Apply Pod Security Standard RESTRICTED (blocks all privileged pods)
kubectl label namespace anihpj \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  --overwrite

# Step 3: AUDIT entire cluster for privileged pods
kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -B10 'privileged: true' | grep -E 'name:|namespace:|privileged:'
# Expected output should ONLY show kube-system DaemonSets (Calico, kube-proxy)
# Any other namespace = investigate and remove

# Step 4: Deploy a PROPERLY hardened replacement (see S56 for full hardening)
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"nginx","securityContext":{"runAsNonRoot":true,"runAsUser":1000,"allowPrivilegeEscalation":false,"capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]},"readOnlyRootFilesystem":true}}]}}}}'
# This pod will be ACCEPTED by PSS restricted ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Privileged Pod Removed, Future Pods Blocked

The dangerous privileged pod has been deleted. The namespace is labeled with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted, which blocks any future attempt to create a privileged pod, a pod with host namespaces, or a pod with hostPath volumes. Only properly hardened pods (non-root, zero capabilities, read-only FS) can be deployed in this namespace.

💡 Key takeaway: privileged: true is the single most dangerous setting in Kubernetes. It disables ALL container isolation. Combined with host namespace access, it grants root on the node. On CKS, this is a CRITICAL finding. The audit command: kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -B5 'privileged: true'. Prevention: PSS restricted label + admission webhooks (Kyverno/OPA). There is NEVER a valid use case for a privileged pod in an application namespace.

📦 Category 5: Supply Chain SecurityS61–S80

🟡 Advanced: Securing Your Build Pipeline — 20% of CKS

Category 5 covers Supply Chain Security (CKS Domain 5, 20%): These scenarios test your ability to secure the container image lifecycle — from Dockerfile best practices and base image selection to image scanning, signing (Cosign), SBOM generation, trusted registries, image pull policies, and CI/CD pipeline hardening. Every scenario deploys part of anihpj/jobpost with intentional supply chain gaps — your job is to detect and fix them. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario!

S61
🧪 SCENARIO S61 — Category 5: Supply Chain Registry Debug

Deploy anihpj — Using Public Docker Hub Image Without Verification

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Django deployment pulls its container image directly from Docker Hub (public registry) with no image verification, no digest pinning, and no private registry mirror. Anyone who compromises the upstream image on Docker Hub (or performs a man-in-the-middle attack) can inject malicious code that runs in your production pods. Supply chain security starts with knowing where your images come from. Your job: detect images from untrusted public registries, configure a private registry mirror, verify image signatures, and pin images by digest.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj with untrusted public Docker Hub images (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a Django job board. The team uses public Docker Hub images directly — nginx:alpine and postgres:15-alpine. But there's no verification of who published these images, no digest pinning, and no image signing. A malicious actor who pushes a similarly-named image or compromises the upstream can replace your production containers. Always use a private registry or verify public images by digest + signature.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S61): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-postgres-deploy.yaml        ← BROKEN: image: postgres:15-alpine (untrusted public)
├── 02-django-deploy.yaml          ← BROKEN: image: nginx:alpine (untrusted public)
└── 03-private-registry-fix.yaml   ← ✅ FIX: image: registry.anihpj.com/nginx@sha256:abc...
BASH — Deploy anihpj with untrusted public images 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S61: Untrusted Public Registry Images
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 2. DEPLOY POSTGRESQL — from public Docker Hub (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-db
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine    # ❌ BUG: Public image, no digest, no private registry!
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: anihpj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
EOF

# 3. DEPLOY DJANGO — also from public Docker Hub
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine           # ❌ BUG: Public image, no digest!
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s

# 4. CHECK — Where did the images come from? (THE BUG!)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}'
# → nginx:alpine   ← No registry domain = defaults to docker.io! ❌

# 5. CHECK — What exact digest is running? Can we verify it?
kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}'
# → docker.io/library/nginx@sha256:abc... ← This digest is NOT pinned in the spec!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Images from docker.io (public Hub): kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep image: → nginx:alpine, postgres:15-alpine
✗2. No digest pinning: image tag can silently change — tomorrow could be a different image
✗3. No imagePullSecrets configured — can't pull from private registries at all
✗4. No image verification: no signing (Cosign), no vulnerability scan results checked
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check image sources: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}'
→ nginx:alpine, postgres:15-alpine — both default to docker.io
2No registry prefix = docker.io: nginx:alpine resolves to docker.io/library/nginx:alpine
3Anyone can push to Docker Hub — image names are not verified or owned
4Mitigation: private registry mirror + image digest pinning + Cosign signature verification
5Root cause: Container images are pulled from the public Docker Hub without any verification. No private registry is configured, no image digests are pinned in the deployment spec, and no image signing verification (Cosign) is performed. This means the images running in production could be tampered with at any time without detection. Supply chain security requires: (1) trusted private registry, (2) digest-pinned images, (3) signed images with Cosign verification.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Image: nginx:alpine → Defaults to docker.io → Public, untrusted
②
No digest pinned → Tag can move → Image changes silently
③
No private registry → No control over image source
④
Setup private registry → Push signed images → Pin by digest
⑤
Verify image source → Supply chain secured ✅

Tenet: Images without a registry prefix default to docker.io — a public registry where anyone can push. Container supply chain security requires three things: (1) a private, trusted registry that you control, (2) digest-pinned images (image@sha256:...) that are immutable, and (3) signed images verified with Cosign or Notary. On CKS, always check image sources in pod specs and flag any image without a private registry prefix or digest.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' postgres:15-alpine nginx:alpine ← docker.io (public Hub) — no digest, no private registry! ❌
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o yaml | grep imagePullPolicy imagePullPolicy: Always ← Repulls from public Hub every time! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' registry.anihpj.com/nginx@sha256:abc123def456... registry.anihpj.com/postgres@sha256:789... ← Private registry + digest! ✅

BASH — Setup private registry + update deployments with digest-pinned images 
# Step 1: Create a private registry (using Docker registry container)
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry registry:2

# Step 2: Tag and push images to private registry with digest
docker pull nginx:alpine
docker tag nginx:alpine localhost:5000/nginx-alpine:v1
docker push localhost:5000/nginx-alpine:v1
DIGEST=$(docker inspect localhost:5000/nginx-alpine:v1 --format='{{.RepoDigests}}' | grep -oP 'sha256:[a-f0-9]+')
echo "Digest: $DIGEST"

# Step 3: Create imagePullSecret for private registry
kubectl create secret docker-registry anihpj-regcred -n anihpj \
  --docker-server=localhost:5000 \
  --docker-username=admin \
  --docker-password=admin123

# Step 4: Update deployment with private registry + digest + pull secret
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image","value":"localhost:5000/nginx-alpine@'$DIGEST'"},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/imagePullSecrets","value":[{"name":"anihpj-regcred"}]}
]'

kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=90s
✓

✅ Verify — Images Come from Trusted Private Registry

After configuring a private registry, pushing signed images, and updating deployments to use digest-pinned image references, all anihpj containers now pull from a trusted source with immutable image references. The imagePullSecret authenticates with the private registry. If someone pushes a malicious image to Docker Hub with the same tag, it will NOT affect your pods — they pull from your private registry with pinned digests.

💡 Key takeaway: Never use public images without verification. Always: (1) push to a private registry, (2) pin by digest (@sha256:...), (3) use imagePullSecrets for private registry auth, (4) sign images with Cosign/Notary and verify before deployment. On CKS, image source verification is a core supply chain security topic — audit ALL pods for image sources.

①

BASH — Rebuild with patched base + integrate scanning

  django=nginx:1.27-alpine

# Step 2: Wait for rollout

# Step 3: Scan the NEW image BEFORE it enters production

IMAGE=$(kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}')
trivy image $IMAGE --severity CRITICAL,HIGH
# Expected: No CRITICAL or HIGH vulnerabilities ✅

# Step 4: CI/CD integration (add to pipeline)
# trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL $IMAGE || exit 1
✓

✅ Verify — Image Is Free of Critical CVEs

After upgrading to nginx:1.27-alpine (based on alpine:3.20+), the image scan shows zero CRITICAL or HIGH vulnerabilities. The trivy scan should be integrated into CI/CD with --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL to block any image with critical CVEs from reaching production.

💡 Key takeaway: Image scanning is NOT optional — it's a CKS requirement. Use trivy, grype, or snyk in your CI/CD pipeline. Key flags: --severity CRITICAL,HIGH to set the threshold, --exit-code 1 to fail the build on vulnerabilities. Rebuild images monthly (or weekly) to pick up base image patches. On CKS, know trivy well — it's the most commonly tested scanner.

🧪 SCENARIO S64 — Category 5: Supply Chain Sign Debug

Deploy anihpj — Container Image Is Not Signed with Cosign

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost team builds and pushes images to a registry — but never signs them. Without image signing (Cosign/Notary), there's no way to verify that the image in the registry is the same one that was built by the CI/CD pipeline. A compromised registry or man-in-the-middle attack could swap the image with a malicious one, and Kubernetes would deploy it without any verification. Cosign allows signing images with a private key and verifying the signature before deployment. Your job: check that images are unsigned, sign them with Cosign, and verify the signature before deployment.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj with unsigned images (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj CI/CD pipeline builds container images and pushes them to the registry. But the pipeline doesn't sign images. A security audit flags this: anyone with registry write access (or a compromised registry) can replace the image, and Kubernetes will deploy it blindly. Image signing provides cryptographic proof that the image was built by your trusted pipeline.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S64): 
Supply chain signing workflow:
├── cosign.key                     ← Private key for signing (NEVER commit)
├── cosign.pub                     ← Public key for verification
├── Dockerfile                     ← Dockerfile used to build the image
└── pipeline.yaml                  ← CI/CD pipeline with cosign sign step
BASH — Deploy anihpj + Check for image signatures 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S64: Unsigned Container Images — No Cosign
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

kubectl create deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# 1. CHECK IF IMAGE IS SIGNED (THE BUG!)
IMAGE=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}')
echo "Checking signatures for: $IMAGE"

# Verify with Cosign — no signature found!
cosign verify --key cosign.pub $IMAGE 2>&1
# → Error: no matching signatures found   ← UNSIGNED! ❌

# 2. WHAT THIS MEANS
# Anyone with registry access can replace this image
# Kubernetes will deploy the replacement without any verification
# This is a CRITICAL supply chain vulnerability
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. cosign verify returns: no matching signatures found — image is unsigned
✗2. No Cosign public key configured for verification in admission control
✗3. Kubernetes deploys ANY image from the registry — signed or unsigned
✗4. Registry compromise = total cluster compromise with no detection
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Cosign verify attempts: cosign verify --key cosign.pub IMAGE
→ "no matching signatures" — image was never signed
2Signing should happen in CI/CD: after docker build && docker push, run cosign sign
3Verification should happen at admission: Kyverno or OPA can enforce signature verification before pod creation
4Cosign supports: key-based signing (private/public key pair) and keyless signing (OIDC/Fulcio)
5Root cause: Container images are built and pushed without being signed. Cosign is the CNCF standard for container image signing — it creates a cryptographic signature stored in the registry alongside the image. Without signing, there's no way to verify the image's provenance. The fix: generate a Cosign key pair, sign images in CI/CD after pushing, and verify signatures at deployment time.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cosign verify → no signatures → Image unsigned
②
Generate Cosign key pair → cosign generate-key-pair
③
Sign image in CI/CD → cosign sign --key cosign.key IMAGE
④
Verify before deploy → cosign verify --key cosign.pub IMAGE
⑤
Signature verified → Image provenance confirmed ✅

Tenet: Image signing is a critical supply chain security control. Cosign (part of Sigstore) is the CNCF standard for signing and verifying container images. Key concepts: (1) generate key pair, (2) sign images after build/push, (3) verify signatures at deployment via admission controller (Kyverno/OPA). On CKS, know the basic Cosign commands: cosign generate-key-pair, cosign sign, cosign verify, cosign verify-attestation.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ cosign verify --key cosign.pub nginx:alpine Error: no matching signatures found ← UNSIGNED! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ cosign verify --key cosign.pub nginx:alpine Verification for nginx:alpine -- The following checks were performed... ✅ Signature verified!
🔧
BASH — Generate keys + Sign image + Verify signature 
# Step 1: Generate Cosign key pair (store private key securely!)
cosign generate-key-pair
# → Creates: cosign.key (private) + cosign.pub (public)

# Step 2: Sign the container image (in CI/CD pipeline)
cosign sign --key cosign.key nginx:alpine

# Step 3: Verify the signature before deployment
cosign verify --key cosign.pub nginx:alpine
# Expected: Verification successful ✅

# Step 4: Integrate into admission control (Kyverno/OPA policy)
# This ensures ONLY signed images can be deployed to the cluster
✓

✅ Verify — Images Are Signed and Verified

After generating Cosign keys, signing images in CI/CD, and verifying signatures before deployment, every container image now has a cryptographic proof of provenance. The private key is stored securely (not in git), and the public key is used by admission controllers to enforce signature verification for all pods.

💡 Key takeaway: Cosign supports two modes: key-based (private/public key pair) and keyless (OIDC/Fulcio). For CKS, know the key-based flow: generate-key-pair → sign → verify. Always store the private key in a secrets manager (not git). Use Kyverno or OPA with Cosign to enforce signature verification cluster-wide. On CKS, cosign verify-attestation also verifies SBOM attestations.

Deploy anihpj — Dockerfile Has No USER Directive (Runs as Root)

The Problem: The Dockerfile used to build the anihpj/jobpost Django image has no USER directive — meaning the container runs as root (UID 0) by default. Even if the Kubernetes securityContext sets runAsNonRoot, the Dockerfile itself should establish a non-root user as the best practice. The absence of USER in Dockerfile means every process in every container built from this image starts as root — a supply chain issue at the build level. Your job: audit the Dockerfile, add a non-root USER directive, rebuild the image, and verify it runs as non-root.

1

📋 Deploy anihpj built from Dockerfile without USER (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj team's Dockerfile was written quickly without a USER directive. Every container built from it runs as root. Even though Kubernetes sets runAsNonRoot: true in some deployments, the Dockerfile-level fix is more fundamental — it ensures the image itself doesn't rely on Kubernetes to enforce non-root. Dockerfile USER is the first line of defense, Kubernetes securityContext is the second.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S65): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj
├── 01-dockerfile-broken.txt       ← BROKEN: No USER directive → runs as root
├── 02-dockerfile-fixed.txt        ← ✅ FIX: USER 1001 + proper permissions
└── 03-django-deploy.yaml          ← Deployment using the image
BASH — Deploy anihpj + Audit Dockerfile for USER directive

# SCENARIO S65: Dockerfile Missing USER Directive
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 1. DEPLOY ANIHPJ (built from Dockerfile without USER)

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# 2. CHECK — Container runs as root because Dockerfile has no USER

# → uid=0(root)   ❌ Dockerfile didn't set USER!

# 3. INSPECT THE DOCKERFILE (THE BUG!)

RUN apk add --no-cache nginx
COPY . /app
# ❌ BUG: No USER directive! Container runs as root!
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
EOF

# Check if USER is set in the image metadata

# → "" (empty)   ← No USER set in Dockerfile! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Container UID: id → uid=0(root) — Dockerfile has no USER
✗2. docker inspect shows: Config.User: "" — no user specified at build time
✗3. Root at Dockerfile level means every process starts as root before Kubernetes intervenes
✗4. Defense in depth: Dockerfile USER + Kubernetes runAsNonRoot = both layers
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check image user: docker inspect IMAGE --format='{{.Config.User}}'
→ Empty string — no USER directive in Dockerfile
2Dockerfile best practice: USER should be one of the LAST directives (after COPY, before CMD)
3Create a dedicated user in the Dockerfile: RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
4Set permissions: RUN chown -R app:app /app before USER
5Root cause: The Dockerfile does not contain a USER directive. By default, Docker runs containers as root. The USER directive should be added to switch to a non-root user after setting up the application files and permissions. This is a supply chain issue — it should be fixed at the Dockerfile level, not just mitigated at the Kubernetes level.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
docker inspect → Config.User="" → No USER directive
②
Add USER 1001 + chown → Rebuild image
③
Container runs as UID 1001 → Non-root by default
④
Kubernetes securityContext = second layer → Defense in depth
⑤
Dockerfile-level security hardened ✅

Tenet: The USER directive in Dockerfile is the first line of defense against root containers. It should be combined with Kubernetes securityContext for defense in depth. On CKS, you must know Dockerfile best practices: use non-root USER, COPY files before USER, chown files to the non-root user, and never run as root in CMD/ENTRYPOINT.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ docker inspect nginx:alpine --format='{{.Config.User}}' ← EMPTY! No USER in Dockerfile! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ docker inspect anihpj-web:v2 --format='{{.Config.User}}' 1001 ← Non-root USER set in Dockerfile! ✅

DOCKERFILE — Fixed with non-root USER 
# Fixed Dockerfile with non-root USER
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache nginx
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup    # ✅ Create non-root user
COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup . /app                            # ✅ Set ownership
USER appuser                                                     # ✅ Switch to non-root user
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
✓

✅ Verify — Image Runs as Non-Root by Default

After adding USER appuser to the Dockerfile and rebuilding, the container runs as UID 1001 by default — no Kubernetes securityContext needed (though it should still be applied for defense in depth). The image metadata now shows Config.User=1001.

💡 Key takeaway: Dockerfile best practices for security: (1) use a minimal base image (alpine, distroless), (2) create a dedicated non-root user (adduser/addgroup), (3) COPY files with --chown, (4) USER before CMD, (5) never COPY sensitive files (use Secrets at runtime). On CKS, you must know these Dockerfile hardening patterns.

Deploy anihpj — Dockerfile Has Hardcoded Credentials and API Keys

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Dockerfile contains COPY .env.production /app/.env — copying a file with production database credentials, API keys, and secrets into the container image. Any image layer with secrets is permanent — even if you delete the file in a later layer, the secret remains in the image history. Anyone with access to the image (registry, image pull) can extract the credentials. Secrets must be injected at runtime via Kubernetes Secrets, never baked into images. Your job: detect the secrets baked into the image, remove them from the Dockerfile, and configure runtime Secret injection.

These secrets are now permanently embedded in the container image layers. Anyone who pulls the image (even unauthorized users if the registry is misconfigured) can extract them with docker history or by inspecting the image layers. Never COPY secrets into images — inject at runtime.

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Dockerfile has COPY .env.production — secrets in image layers permanently
✗2. docker history reveals the COPY command — secrets file path visible

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Inspect image layers: docker history IMAGE --no-trunc
→ Shows COPY .env.production — secrets baked into layer
2Even if deleted later: RUN rm /app/.env doesn't remove it from layer history
3Use .dockerignore: add .env* to prevent accidental COPY of sensitive files
4Runtime injection: Kubernetes Secrets mounted as volumes or env vars — never in the image
5Root cause: The Dockerfile copies a .env file containing production secrets into the container image. Docker image layers are immutable and permanent — once a secret is in a layer, it can never be fully removed. Anyone with access to the image registry or the running container can extract these secrets. Fix: remove the COPY of sensitive files, use .dockerignore, and inject all secrets at runtime via Kubernetes Secrets.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
docker history → COPY .env → Secrets in image
②
Remove COPY from Dockerfile → Add .dockerignore
③
Create K8s Secret → Mount as volume at runtime
④
Rebuild image without secrets → docker history clean
⑤
Secrets only at runtime → Image safe to share ✅

Tenet: Docker image layers are forever — any secret copied into an image is permanently accessible. Use .dockerignore to prevent accidental COPY of .env, credentials, or key files. All secrets must be injected at runtime via Kubernetes Secrets. On CKS, know how to audit images for secrets: docker history, docker save IMAGE | tar xO, and scanning tools like trivy/trufflehog.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ docker history IMAGE --no-trunc | grep COPY COPY .env.production /app/.env ← Secrets in image layer! ❌

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ docker history IMAGE --no-trunc | grep '.env' # No output — No secrets in image ✅
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- env | grep DB_PASSWORD DB_PASSWORD=SuperSecret123! ← From K8s Secret, NOT the image ✅
🔧
BASH — Fix Dockerfile + Create K8s Secret + Update deployment 
# Step 1: Create .dockerignore to prevent accidental COPY
echo ".env*" >> .dockerignore
echo "*.key" >> .dockerignore

# Step 2: Remove COPY .env from Dockerfile — rebuild image CLEAN

# Step 3: Create Kubernetes Secret for runtime injection
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-env -n anihpj \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=SuperSecret123! \
  --from-literal=SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123

# Step 4: Mount Secret as env vars at runtime
kubectl set env deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj --from=secret/anihpj-env
kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s
✓

✅ Verify — No Secrets in Image, Only at Runtime

After removing the COPY of sensitive files from the Dockerfile, adding .dockerignore, and injecting secrets via Kubernetes Secrets at runtime, the container image is clean — no secrets in layers. Secrets are only accessible to the running container process, not baked into the image.

💡 Key takeaway: Docker image layers are immutable — once a secret is in a layer, it can be extracted by anyone with image access. Always use .dockerignore, never COPY secrets, and inject all sensitive data at runtime via Kubernetes Secrets (mounted as volumes or env vars). Scan images for secrets with trufflehog or gitleaks in CI/CD. On CKS, this is a core supply chain security principle.

Your job: audit the pipeline, add a vulnerability scanning stage, and ensure images with CRITICAL CVEs are blocked.

The --exit-code flag makes trivy fail the pipeline if vulnerabilities are found. Also scan dependencies (pip-audit, npm audit) and base images. Archive scan results for compliance.

YAML — FIXED pipeline with security scan 
# ✅ FIXED: Added vulnerability scanning stage
  security-scan:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Scan image for vulnerabilities
        run: |
          trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH anihpj-web || exit 1
      - name: Scan dependencies
        run: pip-audit --ignore-vuln PYSEC-2024-123 || exit 1
  deploy:
    needs: security-scan      # ✅ Only deploys if scan passes!
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        run: kubectl apply -f deploy/

✅ Verify — Pipeline Blocks Vulnerable Images

After adding a security-scan stage between build and deploy, any image with CRITICAL or HIGH CVEs causes the pipeline to fail. Only clean images reach the deploy stage. Scan results are archived for compliance audit.

💡 Key takeaway: CI/CD pipeline stages should follow: Build → Test → Scan → Push → Deploy. The scan stage must use --exit-code 1 to fail the pipeline on vulnerabilities. On CKS, know the trivy command: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH IMAGE. Also scan app dependencies with language-specific tools (pip-audit, npm audit, bundler-audit).

$ kubectl apply -f untrusted-pod.yaml Error: admission webhook "validate-registry" denied: image must be from registry.anihpj.com ✅
🔧
BASH — Delete untrusted pod + Create Kyverno registry policy 
# Step 1: DELETE the untrusted pod immediately
kubectl delete deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 2: Create Kyverno ClusterPolicy — only allow approved registries
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-image-registries
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: validate-registries
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: [Pod]
    validate:
      message: "Images must come from registry.anihpj.com"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - image: "registry.anihpj.com/*"
EOF

# Step 3: Redeploy from TRUSTED registry
kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj \
  django=registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:v1.2
kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s
✓

✅ Verify — Only Trusted Registries Allowed

After deleting the untrusted image and deploying a Kyverno ClusterPolicy that restricts images to registry.anihpj.com/*, any attempt to deploy pods from Docker Hub or other untrusted registries is rejected by the admission controller. The cluster is now protected against third-party image injection.

💡 Key takeaway: Kubernetes has no built-in registry restrictions. Use Kyverno/OPA to enforce approved registries. On CKS, know the basic Kyverno ClusterPolicy structure: validate, match, pattern. Also consider the built-in ImagePolicyWebhook admission plugin for registry allowlisting without external tools.

kubectl delete namespace anihpj
kubectl delete clusterpolicy restrict-image-registries --ignore-not-found
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null

Without SBOMs, the anihpj team must manually scan every running image — a slow, error-prone process. SBOMs generated at build time (using syft or trivy) provide a machine-readable inventory of all dependencies — enabling instant CVE impact analysis. SBOMs are your dependency inventory — without them, you're blind.

📋 Deploy anihpj — CI/CD with hardcoded secrets (CONTAINS THE BUG)

The pipeline YAML is committed to git — meaning anyone with repo access (including former employees with cloned repos) has production credentials. Never hardcode credentials in pipeline YAML.

1Scan repo for secrets: gitleaks detect --source . or trufflehog filesystem .
→ Found: DOCKER_PASSWORD, KUBECONFIG_DATA, DB_MIGRATION_PASS
2GitHub Actions/GitLab CI provide encrypted secrets: Settings → Secrets → Add

gitleaks scan → Hardcoded credentials found

Deploy anihpj — CI/CD Uses Floating :latest Tags for Deployments

The Problem: The anihpj CI/CD pipeline tags every image as :latest and deploys using that floating tag. This means: (1) you can't roll back — :latest overwrites the previous image, (2) different environments may run different images with the same tag, (3) debugging is impossible because you can't identify which version is running. CI/CD should use immutable tags (git SHA, semantic version, or timestamp). Your job: detect the :latest tag pattern in CI/CD, switch to immutable versioned tags, and verify deployments are reproducible.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj — CI/CD pushes :latest tag (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj CI/CD pipeline builds and pushes images with the :latest tag — every build overwrites the previous one. When a production incident occurs, the team tries to roll back to "the previous version" but can't — :latest now points to the broken build. Floating tags destroy audit trails and prevent rollbacks.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S72): 
CI/CD tagging audit:
├── pipeline-broken.yaml    ← BROKEN: docker push anihpj-web:latest
└── pipeline-fixed.yaml     ← ✅ FIX: docker push anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA + anihpj-web:$VERSION
YAML — BROKEN pipeline with :latest tag 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# BROKEN: :latest tag — non-reproducible!
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
- name: Build and push
  run: |
    docker build -t anihpj-web .
    docker tag anihpj-web registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:latest  # ❌ BUG!
    docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:latest            # ❌ Overwrites previous!

# Cannot roll back — :latest now points to this build!
# Cannot identify which version caused the bug!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Image tagged :latest — overwritten every build, no rollback possible
✗2. No version history — can't identify which commit produced which image
✗3. Different envs may have different images with same :latest tag
✗4. Use git SHA, semantic version, or build timestamp for immutable tags
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check image tags: docker images registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web → only :latest exists, no history
2Immutable tagging: docker tag IMAGE registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA
3Also tag with semver: v1.2.3 for human-readable version tracking
4Combine with digest pinning in Kubernetes deployments for complete immutability
5Root cause: CI/CD pipeline tags images with :latest — a mutable tag that gets overwritten every build. This destroys the audit trail and prevents rollbacks. Fix: use immutable tags: (1) git SHA (always unique), (2) semantic version (v1.2.3), (3) build timestamp. Push multiple tags: $GIT_SHA for deployment, v1.2.3 for humans.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
:latest overwritten → No rollback possible
②
Tag with $GIT_SHA → Every build has unique tag
③
Deploy $GIT_SHA → Audit trail preserved
④
Rollback = deploy previous GIT_SHA → Instant recovery
⑤
Reproducible deployments ✅

Tenet: Mutable tags (:latest, :dev) destroy audit trails and prevent rollbacks. On CKS, always use immutable tags in CI/CD: git SHA (${{ github.sha }}), semantic version, or timestamp. Push at least two tags: one immutable (git SHA) for deployment, one human-readable (v1.2.3) for reference. Combine with Kubernetes digest pinning for defense in depth.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ docker images registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web --format "{{.Tag}}" latest ← Only one tag — all history lost! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ docker images registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web --format "{{.Tag}}" a1b2c3d v1.2.3 ← Immutable git SHA + version tag ✅
🔧
YAML — FIXED pipeline with immutable tags 
# ✅ FIXED: Immutable tags for reproducibility
- name: Build and push
  run: |
    GIT_SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
    docker build -t anihpj-web .
    docker tag anihpj-web registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA        # ✅ Immutable!
    docker tag anihpj-web registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:v1.2.3          # ✅ Semver!
    docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA
    docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:v1.2.3
✓

✅ Verify — Every Build Has Unique Immutable Tag

After switching to git SHA + semantic version tags, every build produces a unique, immutable image tag. Rollback is instant: deploy the previous git SHA tag. Audit trail is complete: every running image can be traced to its exact git commit. Combined with Kubernetes digest pinning, the deployment is fully reproducible.

💡 Key takeaway: Never use :latest in CI/CD pipelines. Use: ${{ github.sha }} (GitHub Actions), $CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA (GitLab CI), or $(git rev-parse --short HEAD) (generic). On CKS, know that immutable tags + digest pinning = complete supply chain traceability.

Deploy anihpj — Docker Image Includes gcc/git/build Tools in Runtime

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost Dockerfile uses a single-stage build — meaning compilers (gcc, g++), git, pip, and development headers are all present in the final runtime image. These build tools increase the attack surface: an attacker who compromises the container can use gcc to compile malware, git to clone attack tools, and pip to install backdoors. Multi-stage builds separate build dependencies from the runtime — only the compiled app and necessary runtime libraries go into the final image. Your job: check for build tools in the runtime image and convert to a multi-stage build.

1

📋 Deploy anihpj with build tools in runtime image (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj Docker image was built in a single stage — all build dependencies (gcc, git, pip, make) are still in the final image. An attacker who compromises the container can use these tools to compile malware, download attack scripts, and install additional backdoors. Runtime images should contain ONLY the app and the runtime — never build tools.

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. gcc, g++, git, make present in runtime — attacker can compile malware
✗2. pip available — attacker can install additional packages/backdoors

✗4. Multi-stage builds: separate builder stage from runtime stage

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check for build tools: kubectl exec $POD -- which gcc git make pip
→ All build tools are present in the runtime container
2Multi-stage pattern: FROM image AS builder → build → FROM minimal → COPY --from=builder
3Final image should be: only the compiled app + runtime libraries (no compilers, no git, no pip)
4Also use: pip install --no-cache-dir, remove apt cache (rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*)

These tools dramatically increase the attack surface — an attacker can use them to compile malware, download tools, or install backdoors. ①
gcc/git/pip in runtime → Build tools = attacker toolkit
②
Convert to multi-stage: builder + runtime
③
COPY --from=builder only app code + venv
④
Final image: 80MB, no compilers → Attack surface reduced
⑤
Minimal runtime image ✅

Tenet: Multi-stage builds are essential for supply chain security. The final runtime image should contain ONLY the application and its runtime dependencies — never compilers, build tools, or package managers. On CKS, know the pattern: FROM image AS builder → build → FROM alpine → COPY --from=builder. This is tested directly in the exam.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- which gcc git pip /usr/bin/gcc /usr/bin/git /usr/bin/pip ← Build tools in runtime! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) && kubectl exec -n anihpj $POD -- which gcc git pip which: no gcc/git/pip in PATH ← Clean runtime! ✅
🔧
DOCKERFILE — FIXED multi-stage build 
# ✅ FIXED: Multi-stage — build tools only in builder stage
# Stage 1: Build
FROM python:3.12-alpine AS builder
RUN apk add --no-cache gcc musl-dev
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Runtime (minimal!) — NO build tools!
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache python3 libpq
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local   # ✅ Only compiled deps
COPY . /app
USER 1001
CMD ["python3", "/app/manage.py", "runserver"]
# → Final image: 80MB, no gcc, no git, no pip ✅
✓

✅ Verify — No Build Tools in Runtime Image

After converting to a multi-stage build, the runtime image contains only the compiled Python packages and runtime libraries — no gcc, no git, no pip, no make. Image size reduced from 900MB to 80MB. Attack surface dramatically reduced: an attacker who compromises the container cannot compile malware or install additional packages.

💡 Key takeaway: Multi-stage builds are a CKS must-know pattern. Syntax: FROM x AS builder → FROM alpine → COPY --from=builder. Also: use pip install --no-cache-dir, apk add --no-cache, and clean apt/yum caches. The final image should NEVER contain compilers or package managers.

BASH — Deploy with Always pull policy 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S74: imagePullPolicy Always — Uncontrolled Updates
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine          # ❌ BUG: Floating tag!
        imagePullPolicy: Always     # ❌ BUG: Re-pulls every restart!
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s

# CHECK — Pull policy is Always (THE BUG!)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o yaml | grep imagePullPolicy
# → imagePullPolicy: Always   ❌ Re-pulls every time!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. imagePullPolicy: Always — re-pulls from registry on every pod start
✗2. Combined with floating tag — image can change without Git change
✗3. Registry compromise = immediate production impact with no detection
✗4. Use IfNotPresent + digest-pinned images for immutable deployments
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1imagePullPolicy values: Always (re-pull every start), IfNotPresent (use cached if exists), Never (only local)
2Always + :latest tag means the image is pulled fresh every time — no caching
3IfNotPresent + digest means the image is pulled once and verified — no registry trust needed after first pull
4Never pull policy requires pre-pulled images — most secure but harder to manage
5Root cause: imagePullPolicy: Always with a floating tag means every pod restart can pull a different image from the registry. This creates uncontrolled production changes. Fix: use IfNotPresent with digest-pinned images (image@sha256:...). This ensures the exact same image is always used, regardless of registry state.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Always + floating tag → Uncontrolled updates
②
Switch to IfNotPresent + digest pinning
③
Image cached locally → No registry trust needed
④
Pod restart uses same image → Immutable deployments
⑤
Registry compromise has no impact ✅

Tenet: imagePullPolicy: Always with floating tags creates a silent deployment channel. On CKS, use IfNotPresent with digest-pinned images to ensure immutability. The hierarchy: Never (most secure, pre-pulled) > IfNotPresent + digest > IfNotPresent > Always (least secure). Combined with private registry + Cosign signing for defense in depth.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E 'image:|imagePullPolicy' image: nginx:alpine ← Floating tag ❌ imagePullPolicy: Always ← Re-pulls every time ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E 'image:|imagePullPolicy' image: nginx@sha256:abc123... ← Digest-pinned ✅ imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent ← Cached, no re-pull ✅
🔧
BASH — Patch deployment 
# Step 1: Get the current image digest
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
DIGEST=$(kubectl get $POD -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}' | sed 's|docker.io/library/||')
echo "Digest: $DIGEST"

# Step 2: Patch to digest-pinned image + IfNotPresent
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image","value":"'$DIGEST'"},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"IfNotPresent"}
]'
kubectl rollout status deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=60s
✓

✅ Verify — Immutable Image Reference

After switching to IfNotPresent with a digest-pinned image, pod restarts will always use the exact same image — regardless of registry state. Even if the registry is compromised and the tag is replaced, your pods continue running the verified, cached image.

💡 Key takeaway: On CKS, know the three pull policies: Always (re-pull every time), IfNotPresent (use cache), Never (pre-pulled only). For production: IfNotPresent + digest-pinned images from private registry. Never use Always with floating tags in production.

🧪 SCENARIO S75 — Category 5: Supply Chain Sign Debug

Deploy anihpj — CI/CD Pipeline Builds But Never Signs Images

The Problem: The anihpj CI/CD pipeline builds and pushes images but never signs them with Cosign. Without signing, there's no cryptographic proof linking the image back to the CI/CD pipeline. An attacker who compromises the registry can replace images, and Kubernetes will deploy them without any verification. Image signing must be a mandatory step in every CI/CD pipeline — after docker push, run cosign sign. Your job: audit the pipeline for missing signing, add Cosign signing after push, and verify signatures before deployment.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node KinD cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj — CI builds but doesn't sign (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj CI/CD pipeline includes build → push → deploy, but there's no signing step. The security team can't verify that running images were actually built by the trusted CI pipeline. Cosign signing provides cryptographic proof of provenance — without it, any image in the registry is assumed trusted.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S75): 
CI/CD signing audit:
├── pipeline-broken.yaml    ← BROKEN: build → push → deploy (no sign!)
└── pipeline-fixed.yaml     ← ✅ FIX: build → push → cosign sign → deploy
YAML — BROKEN pipeline (no signing step) 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# BROKEN: No image signing in CI/CD!
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
- name: Build and push
  run: |
    docker build -t registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA .
    docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA
    # ❌ BUG: No cosign sign step! Image is unsigned!
- name: Deploy
  run: kubectl apply -f deploy/
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. No cosign sign step in pipeline — images pushed unsigned
✗2. Cannot verify that running images came from the CI/CD pipeline
✗3. Registry compromise = malicious images deployed with no detection
✗4. Add cosign sign --key cosign.key after docker push
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check if images are signed: cosign verify --key cosign.pub IMAGE
→ "no matching signatures" — pipeline doesn't sign images
2Cosign signing should happen after docker push in the CI pipeline
3Key management: cosign.key stored as GitHub Secret, cosign.pub distributed for verification
4Also sign SBOM attestations: cosign attest --predicate sbom.json IMAGE
5Root cause: The CI/CD pipeline does not include a Cosign signing step after docker push. Images are deployed without any cryptographic provenance. Fix: add cosign sign --key cosign.key IMAGE after docker push in the pipeline. Store cosign.key as an encrypted secret in the CI/CD system.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
cosign verify → no signatures → Pipeline doesn't sign
②
Add cosign sign after docker push → Signed in CI
③
cosign verify succeeds → Provenance confirmed
④
Admission controller enforces signing → Unsigned blocked
⑤
Complete supply chain trust ✅

Tenet: CI/CD signing is a mandatory supply chain control. Every pipeline should: Build → Test → Scan → Push → Sign → Deploy. The sign step (cosign sign --key cosign.key) creates a cryptographic signature stored in the registry. Verification (cosign verify --key cosign.pub) should happen at deployment time via admission controller. On CKS, know the complete CI/CD pipeline with security gates.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:v1 Error: no matching signatures found ← Pipeline doesn't sign! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:v1 Verification successful — Image signed by CI pipeline ✅
🔧
YAML — FIXED pipeline with Cosign signing 
# ✅ FIXED: Added Cosign signing step
- name: Build, push and sign
  run: |
    docker build -t registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA .
    docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA
    cosign sign --key ${{ secrets.COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY }} registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA     # ✅ SIGN!
- name: Verify signature before deploy
  run: cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-web:$GIT_SHA || exit 1
- name: Deploy
  run: kubectl apply -f deploy/
✓

✅ Verify — Every CI Build Produces Signed Images

After adding Cosign signing to the pipeline, every image pushed by CI/CD is cryptographically signed. The signature is verified before deployment. Any unsigned image (or image signed with a different key) is rejected by the admission controller.

💡 Key takeaway: The complete CI/CD pipeline for supply chain security: Build → Test → Scan (trivy) → Push → Sign (cosign) → Attest (SBOM) → Verify → Deploy. On CKS, know all these steps and the corresponding tools (trivy, cosign, syft, grype). The signing key must be stored as an encrypted CI/CD secret.

The anihpj Django image is affected because its base layer includes this vulnerable libcurl version. The image must be rebuilt with an updated base that includes the patched libcurl 8.5.0+. This is the standard CVE remediation workflow tested on CKS.
