B.8 Secrets Management & Encryption Commands 71–80
71kubectl create secret generic
kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
  --from-literal=POSTGRES_PASSWORD=SuperSecret123 \
  --from-literal=POSTGRES_USER=anihpj -n anihpj-prod
Create Secret from literal values. Never hardcode credentials in pod specs or env vars.
CKS: Secret creation
72kubectl create secret docker-registry
kubectl create secret docker-registry ecr-creds \
  --docker-server=12345.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com \
  --docker-username=AWS --docker-password=$(aws ecr get-login-password) -n ns
Create imagePullSecret for private registries (ECR, GCR, ACR). Required for private images.
CKS: Registry auth
73kubectl get secret -o jsonpath
kubectl get secret db-creds -n ns -o jsonpath='{.data.POSTGRES_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d
kubectl get secret db-creds -n ns -o json | jq '.data | map_values(@base64d)'
Decode Secret values. base64 is encoding NOT encryption. Anyone with kubectl access can decode.
CKS: Secret inspection
74Mount Secret as Volume (Best Practice)
# In Deployment spec:
volumes:
- name: db-creds
  secret:
    secretName: db-creds
    items:
    - key: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
      path: db-password.txt
Mount Secret as a file instead of env var. Prevents secrets from appearing in /proc/self/environ.
CKS: Secure mount
75Enable etcd Encryption at Rest
# Create /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources: [secrets]
  providers:
  - aescbc: {keys: [{name: key1, secret: $(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)}]}
  - identity: {}
# Mount in kube-apiserver.yaml: --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
Encrypt Secrets in etcd. Without this, all Secrets stored as plaintext base64.
CKS: Encryption at rest
76Verify etcd Encryption Works
kubectl create secret generic test-encrypt --from-literal=key=testvalue -n default
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  get /registry/secrets/default/test-encrypt | hexdump -C
Direct etcd query to verify Secret is encrypted (not plaintext). Should see k8s:enc:aescbc prefix.
CKS: Verify encryption
77Encrypt Existing Secrets
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
# This rewrites ALL secrets through the new encryption provider
Re-encrypt existing Secrets after enabling encryption. Only newly written secrets are encrypted.
CKS: Migrate secrets
78kubectl create secret tls
kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls \
  --cert=server.crt --key=server.key -n anihpj-prod
Create TLS Secret from certificate files. Used by Ingress for HTTPS termination.
CKS: TLS secret
79Verify TLS Secret Content
kubectl get secret anihpj-tls -n ns -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -E 'Subject:|DNS:|Not After'
Inspect certificate inside TLS Secret. Check CN, SANs, expiration. Common CKS exam task.
CKS: Cert inspection
80ExternalSecret (External Secrets Operator)
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata: {name: vault-db-creds, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef: {name: vault-backend, kind: SecretStore}
  target: {name: db-creds}
  data: [{secretKey: POSTGRES_PASSWORD, remoteRef: {key: secret/db, property: password}}]
EOF
Sync secrets from external vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) into Kubernetes.
CKS: External secrets
B.9 System Hardening & Kernel Security Commands 81–90
🛡️ DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH — Container Security Context Layers
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    POD SECURITY CONTEXT — ALL AVAILABLE FIELDS                   │
│                                                                                 │
│  spec:                                          # Pod-level (applies to ALL)    │
│    securityContext:                             ────────────────────────────    │
│      runAsUser: 1000              ← UID         Non-root user                  │
│      runAsGroup: 3000             ← GID         Non-root group                 │
│      runAsNonRoot: true           ← bool        Reject if UID=0                │
│      fsGroup: 2000                ← GID         Volume filesystem ownership    │
│      fsGroupChangePolicy: "OnRootMismatch"      Only change if root-owned      │
│      seccompProfile:                            Syscall whitelist/blacklist    │
│        type: Localhost                           ───────────────────────        │
│        localhostProfile: custom-profile.json                                    │
│    containers:                                  # Per-container (overrides pod) │
│    - name: anihpj-api                          ────────────────────────────     │
│      securityContext:                                                           │
│        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false          ← bool    No suid → root       │
│        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true             ← bool    Writeable root = ❌   │
│        privileged: false                        ← bool    Host device access    │
│        capabilities:                            ← []      Linux capabilities   │
│          drop: ["ALL"]                                                   │
│          add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]     # Only what's needed              │
│        procMount: "Default"             # /proc masking                   │
│                                                                                 │
│  EVERY PRODUCTION POD MUST HAVE: runAsNonRoot + drop ALL + readonlyRootFS +     │
│  allowPrivilegeEscalation:false + seccompProfile.                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
81kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items[].spec.securityContext'
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot!=true) | .metadata.name'
Find ALL pods running as root. Run this audit before the exam — every root pod is a finding.
CKS: Root audit
82Check Linux Capabilities
kubectl exec pod -- capsh --print
# Inside container: cat /proc/1/status | grep Cap
# Show capabilities in human-readable: capsh --decode=00000000a80425fb
List effective capabilities inside a container. Verify drop ALL + only needed caps.
CKS: Capability audit
83Create seccomp Profile
cat > /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/custom-profile.json <<EOF
{"defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
 "architectures": ["SCMP_ARCH_X86_64"],
 "syscalls": [{"names": ["set_mempolicy","mbind"], "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"}]}
EOF
Create custom seccomp profile. Default = deny all syscalls, whitelist only what the app needs.
CKS: Syscall restriction
84aa-status — AppArmor Status
aa-status
aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-anihpj
apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-anihpj
Check AppArmor profile status. Load/reload profiles. Verify profiles are in enforce mode.
CKS: AppArmor mgmt
85Check Kernel Modules
lsmod | grep -E 'dccp|sctp|rds|tipc'
cat /etc/modprobe.d/cis-blacklist.conf
# blacklist dccp / blacklist sctp / blacklist rds / blacklist tipc
Check and blacklist unnecessary kernel modules. CIS benchmark requires DCCP, SCTP, RDS, TIPC disabled.
CKS: Kernel hardening
86Check sysctl Kernel Parameters
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
sysctl kernel.randomize_va_space
sysctl -a | grep -E 'net\.ipv4\.(tcp_syncookies|conf\.all\.accept_redirects)'
Verify kernel security parameters. CIS benchmark checks: ASLR, TCP syncookies, ICMP redirects.
CKS: Kernel params
87Check open Ports
ss -tlnp
netstat -tlnp
ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(6443|2379|2380|10250|10255|10256)'
Audit listening ports. K8s control plane ports should be on loopback or internal IPs.
CKS: Port audit
88Check File Permissions
stat -c '%a %n' /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.key
stat -c '%a %n' /etc/kubernetes/*.conf
find /etc/kubernetes -name "*.key" -exec stat -c '%a %n' {} \;
Audit file permissions on PKI keys, kubeconfigs, etcd data. Keys should be 600, dirs 700.
CKS: Permission audit
89Disable kubelet Anonymous Auth
# Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml:
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false
  webhook:
    enabled: true
authorization:
  mode: Webhook
# Restart: systemctl restart kubelet
Disable anonymous kubelet access. Without this, curl node:10250/pods works without authentication.
CKS: Kubelet hardening
90checksec / Verify Binary Hashes
sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet
curl -sL https://dl.k8s.io/v1.32.13/bin/linux/amd64/kubelet.sha256
diff <(sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet | cut -d' ' -f1) <(curl -sL URL | cut -d' ' -f1)
Verify platform binary integrity. Compare local hash with official Kubernetes release checksums.
CKS: Binary integrity

⚡ Appendix C: CKS Exam Day — 20 Command Patterns You MUST KnowCRAM SHEET

🏆 Master Summary — How to Use These 20 Patterns

This appendix is your last-30-minutes-before-exam cram sheet. Every pattern here maps to a CKS exam task. They are organized by domain weight — start with Monitoring & Runtime Security (20%) and Supply Chain Security (20%) patterns first, as they make up 40% of your score.

📖
Step 1: Read all 20 patterns once (15 min)
✍️
Step 2: Type C.3, C.5, C.7, C.11, C.15 from memory (10 min)
✅
Step 3: Verify each command & take the exam (5 min buffer)
🎯 Implementation Strategy — How Each Pattern Maps to Exam Tasks
  • C.1–C.2 (Falco + Audit Policy): Guaranteed 2 tasks. Falco install + rule verification and audit policy configuration appear on every CKS exam. Type these from memory 5 times before exam.
  • C.3–C.5 (Trivy + Cosign + SBOM): Supply chain security is 20% of your score. Image scanning, signing, and SBOM generation are high-point-value tasks.
  • C.6, C.11, C.16 (RBAC + Encryption + NetworkPolicy): Cluster hardening tasks. RBAC audit, etcd encryption, and NetworkPolicy creation are core CKS competencies.
  • C.7, C.8, C.9 (securityContext + seccomp + PSA): System hardening and microservice vulnerability minimization. Know the complete securityContext pattern cold.
  • C.10, C.18 (kube-bench + AppArmor): CIS benchmark scanning and remediation. kube-bench is your starting point for every cluster setup security task.
  • C.12, C.13, C.14 (OPA/Kyverno + Capabilities + Binary Verify): Policy engine debugging and kernel-level security. OPA Rego errors and capability audits are common exam traps.
  • C.15, C.17, C.19 (Dockerfile + IR + IMDS): Multi-stage Dockerfile security, incident response isolation flow, and cloud metadata endpoint blocking.
  • C.20 (Full Assessment): The final aggregation pattern. Run all security tools and generate a combined report — increasingly common on modern CKS exams.

These are the 20 command patterns that appear on EVERY CKS exam. Memorize them cold. Practice typing them from memory — the exam has no autocomplete beyond kubectl built-in completion. Read this appendix in the 30 minutes before your exam.

C.1 — Falco Install & Shell Detection Testksw→120% weight
1

Install Falco via Helm (eBPF driver):

helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace \
  --set falco.driver.kind=ebpf \
  --set falco.driver.loader.initContainer.image.tag=0.39.0
kubectl get pods -n falco

Test shell detection — verify alerts fire:

# Terminal 1: Stream Falco logs
kubectl logs -l app=falco -n falco -f | grep -E 'Notice|Warning|Critical'

# Terminal 2: Trigger a shell in a pod
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj-sXX -- sh -c "cat /etc/shadow"

# Expected output: "A shell was spawned in a container..."

⚠️ If alerts don't fire: Check kubectl logs -l app=falco -n falco | grep -i error. Common issues: wrong driver type, kernel incompatibility, missing CAP_BPF.

C.2 — Audit Policy: RequestResponse for Secretsksw→120% weight
2

Create audit policy with full Secret logging:

cat > /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets"]
- level: Metadata
  omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
EOF

# Mount in kube-apiserver.yaml:
# --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
# --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
# --audit-log-maxage=30
# --audit-log-maxbackup=10
# --audit-log-maxsize=100

Verify audit logging works:

# Trigger a secret access
kubectl get secret db-creds -n anihpj-sXX -o yaml

# Check audit log contains RequestResponse (body + response)
tail -20 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets") | {user:.user.username, verb:.verb, stage:.stage, responseStatus:.responseStatus.code}'

⚠️ Key exam points: Log rotation params (maxage/maxsize/maxbackup). RequestResponse for Secrets. Metadata is NOT enough — exam wants full body capture.

C.3 — Trivy Image Scan: Fail on CRITICALksw→220% weight
3
# Scan local image for CVEs
trivy image python:3.12-slim

# Filter to CRITICAL+HIGH only (CI/CD gate)
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 python:3.12-slim
# exit code 1 = scan failed (CRITICAL/HIGH found) — blocks deployment

# Scan and output JSON for CI pipeline
trivy image --format json --severity CRITICAL,HIGH -o trivy-report.json python:3.12-slim

# Scan image in remote registry
trivy image anihpj/anihpj-api:v2.1

# Ignore unfixed vulnerabilities
trivy image --ignore-unfixed python:3.12-slim

⚠️ Exam tip: If the exam says "scan the image and ensure no CRITICAL CVEs exist," you need to fix the Dockerfile (update base image or packages) and re-scan. The scan is the diagnostic, not the fix.

C.4 — Cosign Keyless Sign & Verify (OIDC)ksw→220% weight
4
# Keyless sign (OIDC — no key management)
cosign sign --oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  anihpj/anihpj-api:v2.1

# Verify keyless signature
cosign verify \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost/.github/workflows/build.yml@refs/heads/main" \
  anihpj/anihpj-api:v2.1

# Key-based sign (when OIDC unavailable)
cosign generate-key-pair
cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj/anihpj-api:v2.1
cosign verify --key cosign.pub anihpj/anihpj-api:v2.1

# Attach SBOM attestation
cosign attest --type spdx --predicate sbom.spdx.json anihpj/anihpj-api:v2.1

⚠️ Key rotation: If private key leaked — generate new keypair, re-sign ALL images, revoke old key. Old signatures become invalid.

C.5 — SBOM Generation & CVE Impact Analysisksw→220% weight
5
# Generate SBOM with syft
syft python:3.12-slim -o spdx-json > anihpj-api-sbom.json
syft anihpj/anihpj-api:v2.1 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json

# Scan SBOM for vulnerabilities (offline-capable)
grype sbom:anihpj-api-sbom.json
grype sbom:sbom.json --only-fixed --fail-on high

# Search SBOM for a specific package (CVE impact check)
cat anihpj-api-sbom.json | jq '.packages[] | select(.name | test("openssl|libssl"))'

# Generate SLSA provenance (build attestation)
slsa-verifier verify-image anihpj/anihpj-api:v2.1 \
  --source-uri github.com/anihpj/jobpost \
  --builder-id https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator

⚠️ Exam scenario: "CVE-2024-XXXX announced in OpenSSL. Is anihpj-api affected?" → Generate SBOM → search for OpenSSL → check version → report impact.

C.6 — RBAC Security Audit: Find Overprivileged Usersksw→115% weight

# Find ALL cluster-admin bindings (non-system)
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .subjects[]? | select(.kind=="User" and (.name | startswith("system:") | not)) | "\(.kind) \(.name)"'

# Audit a specific ServiceAccount's permissions
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-api -n anihpj-prod

# Test specific action (dry-run — no side effects)
kubectl auth can-i delete secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-api -n anihpj-prod

# Find ServiceAccounts that auto-mount tokens
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.automountServiceAccountToken!=false) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'

# Create proper least-privilege RBAC
kubectl create role api-role --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods,services -n anihpj-prod
kubectl create rolebinding api-rb --role=api-role --serviceaccount=anihpj-prod:anihpj-api -n anihpj-prod

⚠️ Exam red flags: cluster-admin for non-admin users, "*" verbs, ServiceAccounts with secret access, unmounted token audit failed.

C.10 — kube-bench: Run CIS Scan & Remediateksw→115% weight

# Full CIS scan on master node

# JSON output — filter for FAIL items only

C.11 — etcd Encryption at Rest: Enable + Verifyksw→115% weight
11
# Step 1: Create encryption config
ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)
cat > /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources: ["secrets"]
  providers:
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: ${ENCRYPTION_KEY}
  - identity: {}
EOF

# Step 2: Mount in kube-apiserver.yaml
# --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml

# Step 3: Re-encrypt ALL existing secrets
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -

# Step 4: Verify — direct etcd query should show encrypted data
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  get /registry/secrets/default/test-secret | hexdump -C | head -5
# Expected: Should see "k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:key1:" prefix (encrypted)

⚠️ Critical: identity provider must be last in providers list. If it's first, new secrets are NOT encrypted. Existing secrets must be rewritten.

C.12 — OPA Gatekeeper: Debug Rego Policyksw→220% weight
12
# Check ConstraintTemplate sync status
kubectl get constrainttemplates
kubectl describe constrainttemplate k8srequiredlabels | grep -A5 Status

# Check constraint violations
kubectl get constraints
kubectl describe k8srequiredlabels require-ns-labels

# Common Rego fix: Add nil-check guard
# WRONG: input.review.object.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
# RIGHT:
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
  container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
  not container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg := "runAsNonRoot must be true"
}

# Test Rego with opa test
opa test policy.rego test_policy.rego -v

# Force audit re-sync
kubectl delete pod -l app=gatekeeper -n gatekeeper-system

⚠️ Common traps: nil-check missing (undefined → rule never matches), wrong field path (spec.containers.imageTag vs spec.containers[].image), stale Template cache after update.

C.13 — Capability Audit: Drop ALL, Add Minimalksw→110% weight
13
# Check current capabilities inside container
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj-sXX -- capsh --print
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj-sXX -- cat /proc/1/status | grep -i cap

# Decode capability mask to human-readable
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj-sXX -- capsh --decode=00000000a80425fb

# Apply minimal capabilities in securityContext
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj-api
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]  # Only what's needed for port <1024

# Audit ALL pods for excessive capabilities
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities.add != null and (.spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities.add | length > 2)) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'

⚠️ Most common needed caps: NET_BIND_SERVICE (port < 1024), CHOWN (file ownership), SETUID/SETGID (legacy apps). Everything else = suspicious.

C.14 — Verify Platform Binary Integrity (sha256)ksw→115% weight
14
# Get current kubelet version
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Download official sha256 checksum
VERSION=v1.32.13
curl -sL https://dl.k8s.io/${VERSION}/bin/linux/amd64/kubelet.sha256

# Compare local binary hash with official
sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet
diff <(sha256sum /usr/bin/kubelet | awk '{print $1}') <(curl -sL https://dl.k8s.io/${VERSION}/bin/linux/amd64/kubelet.sha256 | awk '{print $1}')

# If mismatch — replace tampered binary
curl -sL https://dl.k8s.io/${VERSION}/bin/linux/amd64/kubelet -o /usr/bin/kubelet
chmod 755 /usr/bin/kubelet
systemctl restart kubelet

⚠️ Exam scenario: "Verify kubelet binary has not been tampered with" → compare local sha256 with official → if mismatch, download + replace + restart.

C.15 — Multi-Stage Dockerfile: Non-Root + Distrolessksw→220% weight
15
# Multi-stage build — builder + distroless final
FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc123... AS builder
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --user -r requirements.txt

FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=builder /root/.local/lib/python3.12/site-packages /usr/lib/python3.12/
COPY --from=builder /root/.local/bin /usr/local/bin/
COPY anihpj/ /app/
USER 65532  # distroless nonroot user
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "anihpj.wsgi:application"]

# Build with pinned base image + no cache
docker build --no-cache -t anihpj-api:v2.1 .

# Verify: no root, no shell, minimal image
docker run --rm anihpj-api:v2.1 whoami  # Should return non-root
docker history anihpj-api:v2.1 | head -10  # Check layers

⚠️ Key exam elements: Multi-stage (builder → distroless), non-root USER, pinned base digest, no build tools in final stage, COPY --from pattern.

C.16 — NetworkPolicy: Default-Deny + Allow DNS + Allow Appksw→115% weight
16
# Step 1: Default-deny all ingress
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-all-ingress, namespace: anihpj-sXX}
spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: ["Ingress"]}
EOF

# Step 2: Allow DNS egress (UDP 53 to CoreDNS)
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: anihpj-sXX}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports:
    - {protocol: UDP, port: 53}
    - {protocol: TCP, port: 53}
EOF

# Step 3: Verify with test pod
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes.default

⚠️ Verify: Test ingress block (curl should fail), test DNS works, test app-specific allow rules. Always test from inside a pod.

C.17 — Incident Response: Isolate Compromised Podksw→120% weight
17
# Step 1: Detected — Falco alert on cryptominer / shell in pod

# Step 2: Immediately isolate (network quarantine)
kubectl label pod compromised-pod quarantine=true -n anihpj-sXX
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: quarantine, namespace: anihpj-sXX}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {quarantine: "true"}}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress","Egress"]
EOF

# Step 3: Snapshot for forensics
kubectl get pod compromised-pod -n anihpj-sXX -o yaml > forensic-snapshot.yaml
kubectl logs compromised-pod -n anihpj-sXX --timestamps > forensic-logs.txt

# Step 4: Cordon node (prevent spread)
NODE=$(kubectl get pod compromised-pod -n anihpj-sXX -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}')
kubectl cordon $NODE

# Step 5: Kill compromised pod
kubectl delete pod compromised-pod -n anihpj-sXX --force --grace-period=0

⚠️ IR order matters: Isolate (network) → Snapshot (evidence) → Cordon (node) → Kill (pod). Never delete first — lose forensic evidence.

C.18 — AppArmor Profile: Create + Apply to Podksw→110% weight

# Step 1: Create AppArmor profile on node
cat > /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-anihpj-api <<EOF
#include <tunables/global>
profile k8s-anihpj-api flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  #include <abstractions/python>
  file,
  network,
  capability,
  deny /etc/shadow r,
  deny /etc/kubernetes/** r,
  deny /proc/*/environ r,
  /tmp/media/uploads/** rw,
  /var/log/anihpj/** rw,
}
EOF

# Step 2: Load profile
apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-anihpj-api
aa-enforce k8s-anihpj-api

# Step 3: Apply in pod annotation
metadata:
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj-api: localhost/k8s-anihpj-api

# Verify: Check dmesg for AppArmor DENIED events
dmesg | grep -i apparmor

⚠️ Debugging: If app breaks → dmesg for audit: DENIED messages → add allow rules → reload profile → retry.

C.19 — Block Cloud Metadata Endpoint (IMDS)ksw→115% weight
19
# Block IMDS v1 (169.254.169.254) for all pods
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: block-imds, namespace: anihpj-sXX}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
        except:
        - 169.254.169.254/32
  - to:  # Allow DNS (needed for other traffic)
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports:
    - {protocol: UDP, port: 53}
EOF

# Verify block (should time out or connection refused)
kubectl run imds-test --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  curl -m 5 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/

# AWS: Also block IMDSv2 token endpoint
# curl -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token

⚠️ Cloud-agnostic: Works on AWS, GCP (metadata.google.internal), Azure (169.254.169.254). Block the IP, not the DNS name.

# 1. CIS Benchmark — kube-bench

# 2. Vulnerability Scan — Trivy

# 3. Runtime Security — Falco rules audit

# 6. Aggregate into single report
echo "=== CKS SECURITY POSTURE ASSESSMENT ===" > posture-report.txt
echo "Generated: $(date)" >> posture-report.txt
echo "" >> posture-report.txt
echo "=== CIS BENCHMARKS ===" >> posture-report.txt
jq -r '.Controls[].groups[].checks[] | select(.state=="FAIL") | "FAIL: \(.description)"' posture-cis.json >> posture-report.txt
echo "" >> posture-report.txt
echo "=== VULNERABILITIES (CRITICAL/HIGH) ===" >> posture-report.txt
jq -r '.Results[].Vulnerabilities[] | "\(.Severity): \(.VulnerabilityID) — \(.PkgName)@\(.InstalledVersion)"' posture-trivy.json >> posture-report.txt

⚠️ Exam final task: "Generate a comprehensive security report" means aggregate kube-bench + Trivy + Falco + RBAC + signing verification into one file.

🏆 CKS EXAM DAY SPEED TIPS
  • Alias kubectl: alias k=kubectl; complete -F __start_kubectl k — saves 30+ keystrokes per command
  • Verify context FIRST: Every task starts with kubectl config use-context <given-context>. Running on wrong cluster = zero points.
  • Use kubectl explain: Forget a securityContext field? kubectl explain pod.spec.securityContext --recursive
  • Generate YAML with --dry-run: kubectl create secret generic test --from-literal=key=val --dry-run=client -o yaml
  • Namespaces are your friend: Build each task in its own namespace. kubectl create ns cks-task1 && kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=cks-task1
  • Check cert expiration: kubeadm certs check-expiration — run this at the very start. If certs are expired, fix them FIRST.
  • Weighted scoring: Supply Chain (20%) + Monitoring/Runtime (20%) + Microservice Vulns (20%) = 60% of your score. Prioritize these patterns!
  • Leave no task blank: Partial security configurations earn partial credit. Even creating the namespace and YAML file with securityContext earns points.

D.1 — Complete Hardened Pod Spec (All securityContext Fields)System Hardening
1

Every field you can set in securityContext — copy the full block, delete what you don't need.

# COMPLETE HARDENED POD — Pod-level + Container-level securityContext
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-hardened
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    app: anihpj-api
    security-tier: restricted
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj-api: localhost/k8s-anihpj-api
spec:
  # ═══ POD-LEVEL SECURITY ═══
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 3000
    runAsNonRoot: true
    fsGroup: 2000
    fsGroupChangePolicy: "OnRootMismatch"
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault  # Or: Localhost with custom profile
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-api-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: true  # Only if API access needed
  # ═══ INIT CONTAINERS (also need securityContext!) ═══
  initContainers:
  - name: init-check
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z anihpj-db 5432; do sleep 2; done"]
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
  # ═══ MAIN CONTAINERS ═══
  containers:
  - name: anihpj-api
    image: anihpj-api:v2.1@sha256:abc123...
    imagePullPolicy: Always
    # ═══ CONTAINER-LEVEL SECURITY ═══
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      privileged: false
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
      protocol: TCP
    resources:
      requests: {memory: "128Mi", cpu: "100m"}
      limits:   {memory: "256Mi", cpu: "500m"}
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
    - name: db-creds
      mountPath: /etc/secrets/db
      readOnly: true
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}
      initialDelaySeconds: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
  # ═══ VOLUMES ═══
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir:
      sizeLimit: 1Gi  # Prevent disk exhaustion
  - name: db-creds
    secret:
      secretName: db-creds
D.2 — NetworkPolicy Templates (Deny-All, DNS, App-to-App)Cluster Setup
2
# ═══════ 2a: DEFAULT-DENY ALL INGRESS ═══════
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}       # ALL pods in namespace
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]

# ═══════ 2b: ALLOW DNS EGRESS (UDP 53 → CoreDNS) ═══════
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53

# ═══════ 2c: ALLOW anihpj-web → anihpj-api (port 8000) ═══════
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-web-to-api
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj-web
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8000

# ═══════ 2d: BLOCK IMDS (169.254.169.254) ═══════
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-imds
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
        except: ["169.254.169.254/32"]
  - to:  # Must also allow DNS
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]
D.3 — RBAC Templates (Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding)Cluster Hardening
3
# ═══════ 3a: NAMESPACED ROLE — Least Privilege ═══════
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-role
  namespace: anihpj-prod
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods/portforward"]
  verbs: ["create"]

# ═══════ 3b: ROLEBINDING — SA to Role ═══════
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-rb
  namespace: anihpj-prod
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: anihpj-api-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: anihpj-api-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

# ═══════ 3c: CLUSTERROLE — Read-Only Across Namespaces ═══════
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: readonly-pods
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "nodes"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

# ═══════ 3d: CLUSTERROLEBINDING ═══════
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: readonly-pods-binding
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: auditor
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: readonly-pods
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
D.4 — ServiceAccount with Bound Token (TokenRequest)Cluster Hardening
4
# ═══════ 4a: SERVICEACCOUNT (disable auto-mount) ═══════
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
automountServiceAccountToken: false

# ═══════ 4b: POD WITH BOUND TOKEN (projected volume) ═══════
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-api-sa
  containers:
  - name: anihpj-api
    image: anihpj-api:v2.1
    volumeMounts:
    - name: bound-token
      mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: bound-token
    projected:
      sources:
      - serviceAccountToken:
          path: token
          audience: api  # Bound to specific audience
          expirationSeconds: 3600  # 1-hour TTL

⚠️ Why: Legacy SA tokens have no audience, no expiry, no binding. Bound tokens (TokenRequest API) are audience-scoped, time-limited, and pod-bound.

D.6 — EncryptionConfiguration (etcd Encryption at Rest)Cluster Hardening
6
# File: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets
  providers:
  # Provider 1: AES-CBC (strong encryption)
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: <BASE64-ENCODED-32-BYTE-KEY>
  # Provider 2: identity (fallback — MUST be last!)
  - identity: {}

# Then mount in kube-apiserver.yaml static pod:
# spec:
#   containers:
#   - command:
#     - kube-apiserver
#     - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#     volumeMounts:
#     - name: enc-config
#       mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#       readOnly: true
#   volumes:
#   - name: enc-config
#     hostPath:
#       path: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#       type: File

⚠️ CRITICAL: identity must be LAST provider. If first, new secrets are NOT encrypted. After enabling, run kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f - to encrypt existing secrets.

D.7 — Audit Policy (Full Policy with All Stages)Runtime
7
# File: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]  # Reduce noise — only log completed requests
rules:
# Level 0: Don't log health checks or metrics
- level: None
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["events"]
  userGroups: ["system:serviceaccounts:kube-system"]

# Level 1: RequestResponse for SECRETS (full body capture)
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets"]
  namespaces: ["anihpj-prod","anihpj-staging"]

# Level 2: RequestResponse for RBAC changes
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
    resources: ["clusterroles","clusterrolebindings","roles","rolebindings"]

# Level 3: Metadata for all other resources
- level: Metadata
  omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]

# API server flags:
# --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
# --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
# --audit-log-maxage=30    (days to retain)
# --audit-log-maxbackup=10 (max rotated files)
# --audit-log-maxsize=100  (MB per file before rotation)
D.8 — OPA Gatekeeper: ConstraintTemplate + ConstraintMicroservice
8
# ═══════ 8a: CONSTRAINTTEMPLATE (the rule definition) ═══════
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8srequiredsecuritycontext
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sRequiredSecurityContext
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8srequiredsecuritycontext
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        # Check runAsNonRoot is explicitly set to true
        not container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot == true
        msg := sprintf("container <%v> must set runAsNonRoot: true", [container.name])
      }
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        # Check allowPrivilegeEscalation is explicitly set to false
        not container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == false
        msg := sprintf("container <%v> must set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false", [container.name])
      }

# ═══════ 8b: CONSTRAINT (enforce the template) ═══════
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredSecurityContext
metadata:
  name: require-security-context
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: ["Pod"]
    excludedNamespaces: ["kube-system","gatekeeper-system"]
D.9 — Kyverno Policy Templates (Validate + Mutate)Microservice
9
# ═══════ 9a: VALIDATE — Require non-root + drop ALL caps ═══════
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-non-root
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: true
  rules:
  - name: check-runAsNonRoot
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "runAsNonRoot must be set to true"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - securityContext:
              runAsNonRoot: true

# ═══════ 9b: MUTATE — Auto-add securityContext defaults ═══════
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: add-security-context
spec:
  rules:
  - name: add-default-securitycontext
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    mutate:
      patchStrategicMerge:
        spec:
          containers:
          - (name): "*"
            securityContext:
              +(allowPrivilegeEscalation): false
              +(readOnlyRootFilesystem): true
              +(runAsNonRoot): true
              +(capabilities):
                drop: ["ALL"]
D.10 — Falco Custom RulesRuntime
10
# File: /etc/falco/custom-rules.yaml

# Rule 1: Detect shell spawned in container
- rule: Shell in Container
  desc: A shell was spawned inside a running container
  condition: >
    spawned_process and container
    and shell_procs
    and proc.tty != 0
  output: >
    Shell spawned in container (user=%user.name container=%container.name
    shell=%proc.name parent=%proc.pname cmdline=%proc.cmdline)
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, shell, mitre_execution]

# Rule 2: Detect reading sensitive files
- rule: Read Sensitive File in Container
  desc: Attempt to read sensitive file (shadow, environ, kubeconfig)
  condition: >
    open_read and container
    and (fd.name contains "/etc/shadow"
         or fd.name contains "/proc/self/environ"
         or fd.name contains ".kube/config")
    and not proc.name in (known_system_procs)
  output: >
    Sensitive file read (file=%fd.name user=%user.name
    container=%container.name proc=%proc.name)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [filesystem, mitre_credential_access]

# Rule 3: Detect C2 beaconing (outbound to non-standard ports)
- rule: Outbound C2 Beaconing
  desc: Outbound connection to high port — possible C2
  condition: >
    evt.type=connect and container
    and fd.sport > 50000
    and not fd.snet in (rfc1918_addresses)
  output: >
    C2 beacon detected (ip=%fd.sip port=%fd.sport
    container=%container.name)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [network, c2, beacon]

# Macro: Define internal RFC1918 networks
- macro: rfc1918_addresses
  condition: >
    fd.snet = "10.0.0.0/8" or
    fd.snet = "172.16.0.0/8" or
    fd.snet = "192.168.0.0/16"

# Macro: Known system processes to exclude
- macro: known_system_procs
  condition: proc.name in (systemd, kubelet, containerd, dockerd)
D.11 — Pod Security Admission: Namespace LabelsCluster Setup
11
# Apply PSA labels to namespace (imperative — fastest on exam)
kubectl label ns anihpj-dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version=latest

kubectl label ns anihpj-staging \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version=latest

kubectl label ns anihpj-prod \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

# Verify labels applied
kubectl get ns anihpj-prod --show-labels | grep pod-security

PSA Levels: privileged (unrestricted) → baseline (minimal restrictions) → restricted (full pod hardening). Modes: audit (log only) → warn (warn user) → enforce (block).

# ═══════ 12a: RUNTIMECLASS DEFINITION ═══════
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass

  name: kata-containers
handler: kata  # Must match CRI handler name

  nodeSelector:
    runtime: kata-enabled  # Only schedule on nodes with Kata

# ═══════ 12b: POD USING RUNTIMECLASS ═══════
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: tenant-isolated
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  runtimeClassName: kata-containers  # VM-level isolation
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: tenant-app:latest

⚠️ Use case: Tenant isolation, untrusted workloads, compliance (PCI-DSS). Kata = lightweight VM per pod. gVisor = user-space kernel. Both provide stronger isolation than runc.

D.15 — Secure Multi-Stage Dockerfile (Distroless + Non-Root)Supply Chain
15
# ═══════ MULTI-STAGE SECURE DOCKERFILE ═══════
# Stage 1: Builder (includes compilers, headers — discarded)
FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc123def456... AS builder
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --user -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Final (distroless — no shell, no package manager, minimal)
FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12:nonroot@sha256:def789...
# Copy only what's needed from builder
COPY --from=builder /root/.local/lib/python3.12/site-packages /usr/lib/python3.12/
COPY --from=builder /root/.local/bin /usr/local/bin/
COPY anihpj/ /app/
WORKDIR /app
USER 65532  # distroless nonroot user (NOT 0)
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "4", "anihpj.wsgi:application"]

# Build with no cache (prevents cache poisoning):
# docker build --no-cache -t anihpj-api:v2.1 .
# docker push anihpj-api:v2.1
# cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj-api:v2.1

Security wins: Distroless = no shell, no package manager, 80% fewer CVEs. Non-root USER. Pinned base digests. Multi-stage drops build tools.

# ═══════ 16a: SECRETSTORE (connection to Vault/AWS) ═══════

kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: vault-backend
  namespace: anihpj-prod

kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: vault-db-creds
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h  # Auto-refresh every hour
  secretStoreRef:
    name: vault-backend
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: db-creds  # Creates/updates this K8s Secret
  data:
  - secretKey: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
    remoteRef:
      key: secret/db
      property: password
  - secretKey: POSTGRES_USER
    remoteRef:
      key: secret/db
      property: username

        "getdents64","getpid","getppid","getrandom","gettid",
        "ioctl","listen","lseek","madvise","mbind",
        "mkdir","mmap","mprotect","munmap","nanosleep",
        "newfstatat","openat","pipe2","pread64","prlimit64",
        "pwrite64","read","readlink","recvfrom","rename",
        "rt_sigaction","rt_sigprocmask","rt_sigreturn",
        "sched_getaffinity","sched_yield","sendto",
        "set_mempolicy","set_robust_list","set_tid_address",
        "setgid","setgroups","setuid","sigaltstack",

D.18 — AppArmor Profile TemplateSystem Hardening
18
# File: /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-anihpj-api
#include <tunables/global>

profile k8s-anihpj-api flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  # Inherit base filesystem + network access
  #include <abstractions/base>
  #include <abstractions/python>
  #include <abstractions/nameservice>

  # Allow application directories
  /app/** r,
  /app/**/__pycache__/** rw,
  /tmp/media/uploads/** rw,

  # Allow Python runtime
  /usr/lib/python3.12/** mr,
  /usr/local/lib/python3.12/** mr,

  # Allow logging
  /var/log/anihpj/** rw,
  /dev/log w,

  # Network (NECESSARY for web app)
  network inet stream,
  network inet dgram,

  # DENY sensitive paths
  deny /etc/shadow r,
  deny /etc/kubernetes/** r,
  deny /proc/*/environ r,
  deny /root/** rwx,
  deny /**/*.pem r,
  deny /**/*.key r,
}

# Load: apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-anihpj-api
# Enforce: aa-enforce k8s-anihpj-api
# Pod annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>: localhost/k8s-anihpj-api
D.19 — ImagePolicyWebhook (Admission Control for Signed Images)Supply Chain
19
# ═══════ 19a: IMAGEPOLICY CONFIG (kube-apiserver) ═══════
# File: /etc/kubernetes/imagepolicyconfig.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AdmissionConfiguration
plugins:
- name: ImagePolicyWebhook
  configuration:
    imagePolicy:
      kubeConfigFile: /etc/kubernetes/imagepolicy-kubeconfig.yaml
      allowTTL: 50
      denyTTL: 50
      retryBackoff: 500
      defaultAllow: false  # DENY if webhook unreachable

# ═══════ 19b: KUBECONFIG FOR WEBHOOK ═══════
# File: /etc/kubernetes/imagepolicy-kubeconfig.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- cluster:
    certificate-authority: /etc/kubernetes/pki/webhook-ca.crt
    server: https://image-policy-webhook.ns.svc:443/check-image
  name: image-policy
users:
- name: api-server
  user:
    client-certificate: /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt
    client-key: /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.key
contexts:
- context:
    cluster: image-policy
    user: api-server
  name: image-policy-ctx
current-context: image-policy-ctx

⚠️ Key setting: defaultAllow: false means if the webhook is down, ALL pod creations are denied. Set to true for less strict enforcement.

D.20 — Full Production Deployment (ALL Security Controls Applied)ALL
20
# ═══════ COMPLETE SECURE DEPLOYMENT — COPY-PASTE READY ═══════
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    app: anihpj-api
    security-tier: restricted
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
      annotations:
        container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj-api: localhost/k8s-anihpj-api
    spec:
      # ═══ POD SECURITY ═══
      securityContext:
        runAsUser: 1000
        runAsGroup: 3000
        runAsNonRoot: true
        fsGroup: 2000
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      serviceAccountName: anihpj-api-sa
      automountServiceAccountToken: true
      # ═══ IMAGE PULL SECRETS ═══
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: ecr-creds
      # ═══ INIT CONTAINERS ═══
      initContainers:
      - name: db-check
        image: busybox:1.36@sha256:...
        command: ["sh","-c","until nc -z anihpj-db 5432; do sleep 2; done"]
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          runAsNonRoot: true
          capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
      # ═══ MAIN CONTAINER ═══
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-api
        image: anihpj-api:v2.1@sha256:abc123...
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          privileged: false
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 1000
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
            add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          protocol: TCP
        resources:
          requests: {memory: "128Mi", cpu: "100m"}
          limits:   {memory: "256Mi", cpu: "500m"}
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
        - name: db-creds
          mountPath: /etc/secrets/db
          readOnly: true
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8000}
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {sizeLimit: "1Gi"}
      - name: db-creds
        secret: {secretName: db-creds}
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - weight: 100
            podAffinityTerm:
              labelSelector:
                matchLabels: {app: anihpj-api}
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

This template covers: Pod SC + Container SC + Init SC + ImagePullSecrets + Resource Limits + Probes + Anti-Affinity + emptyDir sizeLimit + Secret volume mounts. Apply this and you've solved 90% of CKS pod-hardening tasks.

kube-bench
CIS Benchmark Scanner

Runs CIS Kubernetes Benchmark checks against your cluster. The FIRST tool you run on every CKS cluster setup task. Identifies misconfigurations in API server, etcd, kubelet, controller-manager, scheduler.

# Install
curl -L https://github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/releases/download/v0.9.0/kube-bench_0.9.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
sudo mv kube-bench /usr/local/bin/

# Run full scan
kube-bench run --targets master
kube-bench run --targets node

# Check specific CIS section (e.g., kubelet)
kube-bench run --targets master --check 1.2.1

# JSON output + filter FAIL items
kube-bench run --json | jq '.Controls[].groups[].checks[] | select(.state=="FAIL")'
ksw→1 (kubeadm) 15% Cluster Setup binary (~50MB)

kube-hunter
Penetration Testing Tool

Active vulnerability scanner for Kubernetes. Hunts for exposed endpoints, weak authentication, and known CVEs. Runs as a pod inside the cluster OR remotely against external IPs.

kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/kube-hunter/main/job.yaml
kubectl logs kube-hunter-xxxxx

# Remote scan (external perspective)
pip install kube-hunter
kube-hunter --remote 192.168.1.100 --active

# Common findings on CKS:
# • Kubelet API exposed on 10250 without auth
# • etcd port 2379 reachable from any pod
# • Dashboard exposed without authentication

The #1 CKS image scanning tool. Scans container images, filesystems, and Git repos for CVEs, misconfigurations, and secrets. Every CKS supply chain task involves Trivy.

Cosign
Image Signing & Verification (Sigstore)

Sign and verify container images using Sigstore. Supports keyless (OIDC) and key-based signing. The standard for CKS image integrity verification tasks.

# Install
curl -LO https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/latest/download/cosign-linux-amd64
sudo mv cosign-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cosign && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/cosign

# Key-based sign + verify
cosign generate-key-pair
cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj-api:v2.1
cosign verify --key cosign.pub anihpj-api:v2.1

# Keyless sign (OIDC — GitHub Actions identity)
cosign sign --oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com anihpj-api:v2.1

# Attestation (SLSA provenance)
cosign attest --type slsaprovenance --predicate provenance.json anihpj-api:v2.1
cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance anihpj-api:v2.1
ksw→2 (kind-cka-lab) 20% Supply Chain curl binary

Syft

Generates Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) from container images and filesystems. Know every package, version, and dependency in your image. Essential for CVE impact analysis.

🔧 Tool Troubleshooting — Common Errors & Quick Fixes

Falco: "driver not found"

falco.driver.kind=ebpf not set → Helm install fails. Fix: --set falco.driver.kind=ebpf. If kernel < 5.8, use kmod driver instead.

Trivy: "unable to scan image"

Image not pulled locally. Fix: docker pull image:tag first, or use trivy image --skip-db-update for offline scan.

kube-bench: "command not found"

Not installed. Fix: curl -L https://github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/releases/download/v0.9.0/kube-bench_0.9.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz && sudo mv kube-bench /usr/local/bin/

Cosign: "no matching signatures"

Image not signed or signed with different key. Fix: verify with cosign verify --key cosign.pub. Re-sign if needed: cosign sign --key cosign.key image:tag.

OPA: "constraint not enforced"

ConstraintTemplate not synced or Rego has nil-check missing. Fix: kubectl describe constrainttemplate → check Status. Add not container.securityContext guard before checking fields.

etcdctl: "context deadline exceeded"

Wrong endpoint or TLS flags missing. Fix: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert/--cert/--key with correct paths.

🏗️ Appendix F: Architecture & Attack SurfaceTHREAT MODEL

Understand WHAT you're protecting before you protect it. This appendix maps the complete anihpj/jobpost architecture, identifies every attack surface, and shows how each CKS security control maps to real threats. You cannot defend what you cannot see.

☁️Cloud (Provider)

What it covers: Physical infrastructure, hypervisor, network fabric, region/availability zones. AWS/GCP/Azure shared responsibility. CKS relevance: IMDS blocking (169.254.169.254), IAM role least privilege, VPC/security group design.

⚙️Cluster (Kubernetes)

What it covers: API server, etcd, kubelet, scheduler, controller-manager, CoreDNS. CKS relevance: CIS benchmarks, RBAC, audit logging, etcd encryption, NetworkPolicy, PSA, cert rotation, kubelet hardening.

📦Container (Runtime)

What it covers: Container images, runtime (containerd/CRI-O), kernel syscalls, filesystem. CKS relevance: securityContext, seccomp, AppArmor, capabilities, readOnlyRootFS, non-root user, image scanning.

💻Code (Application)

What it covers: Application logic, dependencies, secrets handling, input validation. CKS relevance: Dockerfile hardening, SBOM, SAST/DAST, dependency scanning, Secret management, supply chain integrity.

👑 The "Crown Jewels" — What We're Protecting in anihpj/jobpost

1. PostgreSQL Data (PII): Job applicant names, emails, phone numbers, resumes. GDPR/CCPA regulated. Controls: Secret volume mount (never env), etcd encryption, NetworkPolicy db isolation.
2. Django SECRET_KEY: Session signing, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens. If leaked → full session hijacking. Controls: ExternalSecret from Vault, never in image layers.
3. API Tokens & ServiceAccount Credentials: JWT tokens, SA tokens, cloud IAM credentials. Controls: Bound tokens (audience+expiry), automountSA=false on DB, IMDS block.
4. Container Image Integrity: Tampered image = full compromise. Controls: Cosign keyless signing, ImagePolicyWebhook, digest pinning, Trivy CI gate.

🔴 Path 1: Compromised Web Pod → DB Exfiltration

Entry: XSS in anihpj-web → RCE in container
Step 1: curl anihpj-db.anihpj-prod:5432 → PostgreSQL accessible (no NetworkPolicy)
Step 2: cat /etc/secrets/db/POSTGRES_PASSWORD → Secret mounted as volume
Step 3: psql -h anihpj-db → Full database dump
Exfil: Base64 encode + DNS tunneling to attacker C2
🔴 CRITICAL — PII breach

Blocks: NetworkPolicy default-deny + allow only web→api, not web→db. ReadOnly secret volume.

🔴 Path 2: Privileged Pod → Node Escape

Entry: DevOps deploys test pod with privileged:true
Step 1: nsenter --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid --target 1 → host namespace
Step 2: Access /etc/kubernetes/pki/ → steal etcd certs
Step 3: etcdctl get /registry/secrets/ → all cluster secrets
Result: Full cluster compromise via single privileged pod
🔴 CRITICAL — Cluster admin

Blocks: PSA enforce=restricted, OPA/Kyverno deny privileged, Falco alert on nsenter.

🟠 Path 3: SA Token → API Server Pivot

Entry: Compromised anihpj-api pod
Step 1: cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
Step 2: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://kubernetes/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/secrets
Step 3: Discover SA has "list secrets" permission (overprivileged RBAC)
Step 4: Dump all secrets, find DB credentials, access DB
🟠 HIGH — Secret enumeration

Blocks: Least-privilege RBAC (no secret access), bound token (audience+expiry 1h), Falco alert on /proc/self/environ read.

🟠 Path 4: Malicious Image → Crypto Mining

Entry: Attacker publishes anihpj-api:v2.1 on docker.io (typosquat)
Step 1: Developer mistypes image: docker.io/anihp/anihpj-api:v2.1 (missing 'j')
Step 2: Image pulled from untrusted registry — contains xmrig miner
Step 3: Container starts, miner runs on /tmp/xmrig, CPU → 100%
Result: Resource exhaustion, node pressure, possible lateral movement
🟠 HIGH — Resource hijack

Blocks: Trusted registry policy (OPA), ImagePolicyWebhook + Cosign verification, ImagePullPolicy:Always+digest.

🟡 Path 5: IMDS → Cloud Credential Theft

Entry: SSRF vulnerability in anihpj-api (URL fetch without validation)
Step 1: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
Step 2: Retrieve AWS AccessKeyId + SecretAccessKey + Token
Step 3: Use credentials to access S3 buckets, RDS snapshots, other AWS services
Result: Cloud account compromise beyond Kubernetes
🟡 MEDIUM — Cloud pivot

Blocks: NetworkPolicy block-IMDS (169.254.169.254/32), IMDSv2 enforced (PUT token required), hop limit=1.

🟡 Path 6: etcd Backup Leak → All Secrets Exposed

Entry: etcd snapshot accidentally committed to public GitHub repo
Step 1: Attacker downloads /opt/etcd-backup.db
Step 2: etcdctl snapshot restore → /var/lib/etcd-restore
Step 3: Browse all cluster state — Secrets visible in plaintext (no encryption)
Result: Every Secret, every config, every token — all exposed
🟡 MEDIUM — Data leak

Blocks: EncryptionConfiguration (aescbc), .gitignore for backup files, restricted etcd directory permissions (700).

The CKS exam tests your ability to think in defense-in-depth layers. A single control (e.g., NetworkPolicy) is not enough — you need overlapping controls: if NetworkPolicy fails, Falco detects. If Falco misses it, audit logs capture it. Assume breach. Layer your defenses.

🔑
IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
AWS IAM + EKS

Assign AWS IAM roles to Kubernetes ServiceAccounts — no static credentials, no IAM user keys in pods. Uses OIDC federation between EKS cluster and IAM.

# 1. Create OIDC provider for EKS cluster
eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider --cluster=anihpj-cluster --approve

# 2. Create IAM role with trust policy (only SA can assume)
cat > trust-policy.json <<EOF
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow",
 "Principal":{"Federated":"arn:aws:iam::123456789:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.xxx"},
 "Action":"sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
 "Condition":{"StringEquals":{"oidc.eks.xxx:sub":"system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-api-sa"}}}]}
EOF

# 3. Annotate ServiceAccount with IAM role ARN
kubectl annotate sa anihpj-api-sa -n anihpj-prod \
  eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/anihpj-api-role
Cluster Hardening IRSA replaces static IAM keys
🐳
ECR — Private Registry + ScanOnPush
Amazon Elastic Container Registry

Private container registry with built-in vulnerability scanning (ScanOnPush), image tag immutability, and lifecycle policies. Integrates with AWS Inspector for deeper CVE analysis.

# Create ECR repository with scan-on-push + tag immutability
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name anihpj-api \
  --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE \
  --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true

# Authenticate Docker to ECR (keyless via IRSA in CI/CD)
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | \
  docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

# Check scan findings after push
aws ecr describe-image-scan-findings --repository-name anihpj-api \
  --image-id imageTag=v2.1 | jq '.imageScanFindings.findings[] | select(.severity=="CRITICAL")'

# Lifecycle policy: keep last 10 images, expire untagged after 7 days
aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy --repository-name anihpj-api \
  --lifecycle-policy-text '{"rules":[{"rulePriority":1,"selection":{"tagStatus":"untagged","countType":"sinceImagePushed","countUnit":"days","countNumber":7},"action":{"type":"expire"}},{"rulePriority":2,"selection":{"tagStatus":"any","countType":"imageCountMoreThan","countNumber":10},"action":{"type":"expire"}}]}'
Supply Chain Security ECR + Inspector = CVE scanning
🔒
AWS Secrets Manager + External Secrets
Secrets rotation + sync

Store database passwords, API keys in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation. Sync to Kubernetes via External Secrets Operator — no manual secret updates.

# Create secret in AWS Secrets Manager
aws secretsmanager create-secret --name anihpj/db/prod \
  --secret-string '{"POSTGRES_USER":"anihpj","POSTGRES_PASSWORD":"SuperSecret!","POSTGRES_DB":"anihpjdb"}'

# Enable automatic rotation (Lambda rotates every 30 days)
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id anihpj/db/prod \
  --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789:function:rotate-postgres \
  --rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30

# SecretStore for AWS Secrets Manager (uses IRSA!)
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: SecretStore
metadata: {name: aws-sm, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef: {name: anihpj-api-sa}
Cluster Hardening Secrets Manager + IRSA + ESO
🗝️
AWS KMS — Envelope Encryption for etcd
Key Management Service

Use AWS KMS as the root of trust for Kubernetes encryption-at-rest. KMS-managed keys provide envelope encryption: KMS encrypts the DEK, DEK encrypts the Secrets.

# Create KMS key for Kubernetes encryption
aws kms create-key --description "Kubernetes etcd encryption key" \
  --key-usage ENCRYPT_DECRYPT --customer-master-key-spec SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT

# EncryptionConfiguration using KMS plugin
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources: ["secrets"]
  providers:
  - kms:
      apiVersion: v2
      name: aws-kms-provider
      endpoint: unix:///var/run/kmsplugin/socket.sock
      cachesize: 1000
      timeout: 3s
  - identity: {}  # Fallback (MUST be last)

# Audit KMS key usage via CloudTrail
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes \
  AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=arn:aws:kms:...:key/xxx
Cluster Hardening KMS envelope encryption
🌐
VPC + Security Groups + NACLs
AWS Network Security

Network segmentation at the AWS layer. Security Groups = pod-level firewalls. NACLs = subnet-level firewalls. Combined with K8s NetworkPolicy for defense-in-depth.

# Security Group: Allow only from ALB to worker nodes (NodePort range)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-xxx \
  --protocol tcp --port 30000-32767 \
  --source-security-group sg-alb-xxx  # ONLY from ALB SG

# NACL: Block outbound to 169.254.169.254 (defense-in-depth for IMDS)
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id acl-xxx \
  --rule-number 100 --protocol -1 --egress \
  --cidr-block 169.254.169.254/32 --rule-action DENY

# VPC Flow Logs → CloudWatch for network forensics
aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type VPC --resource-id vpc-xxx \
  --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type cloud-watch-logs \
  --log-group-name /aws/vpc/anihpj-flow-logs
Cluster Setup VPC + SG + NACL + Flow Logs
🕵️
CloudTrail + GuardDuty for EKS
Audit + Threat Detection

CloudTrail records every AWS API call (including EKS, ECR, KMS). GuardDuty detects threats: EKS audit log monitoring, crypto mining detection, anomalous API calls.

# Enable GuardDuty EKS protection
aws guardduty create-detector --enable --finding-publishing-frequency FIFTEEN_MINUTES
aws guardduty update-detector --detector-id xxx \
  --features '[{"Name":"EKS_AUDIT_LOGS","Status":"ENABLED"},{"Name":"EKS_RUNTIME_MONITORING","Status":"ENABLED"}]'

# Query CloudTrail for K8s-related API calls
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes \
  AttributeKey=EventSource,AttributeValue=eks.amazonaws.com --max-results 50

# GuardDuty K8s findings: PrivilegedContainer, CryptoMining, AnonymousAccess
Runtime Security CloudTrail + GuardDuty EKS
🛡️
AWS WAF + Shield — L7 Firewall + DDoS
Application Layer Security

WAF protects your Ingress from web attacks (SQLi, XSS, rate-based blocking). Shield provides DDoS protection at Layers 3/4. WAF is your first line of defense before traffic reaches the cluster.

# Create WAF web ACL with rate-limit rule (1000 req/5min per IP)
aws wafv2 create-web-acl --name anihpj-api-waf --scope REGIONAL \
  --default-action '{"Allow":{}}' \
  --rules '[{"Name":"RateLimit","Priority":1,
    "Statement":{"RateBasedStatement":{"Limit":1000,"AggregateKeyType":"IP"}},
    "Action":{"Block":{}}}]'

# Associate WAF with ALB (which fronts nginx-ingress)
aws wafv2 associate-web-acl --web-acl-arn arn:aws:wafv2:...:regional/webacl/anihpj-api-waf/xxx \
  --resource-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:loadbalancer/app/anihpj-alb/xxx

# Managed rules: SQL injection, XSS, IP reputation, common threats
Cluster Setup WAF + Shield + ALB
📜
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
TLS Certificate Management

ACM provisions, manages, and auto-renews TLS certificates for ALB/CloudFront. Free public certificates with automatic renewal. Can also issue private certificates via ACM PCA for internal mTLS.

# Request public certificate (DNS validation — automatic renewal)
aws acm request-certificate --domain-name api.jobpost.com \
  --validation-method DNS --subject-alternative-names "*.jobpost.com"

# After DNS validation, attach to ALB listener
aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn arn:...:loadbalancer/app/anihpj-alb/xxx \
  --protocol HTTPS --port 443 \
  --certificates CertificateArn=arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123456789:certificate/xxx \
  --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=arn:...:targetgroup/anihpj-tg/xxx

# ACM PCA: issue private certs for internal pod-to-pod mTLS
aws acm-pca issue-certificate --certificate-authority-arn arn:...:certificate-authority/xxx \
  --csr file://internal-api.csr --signing-algorithm SHA256WITHRSA \
  --validity Value=365,Type=DAYS
Cluster Setup ACM + ALB TLS termination
🚫
IMDSv2 — Metadata Endpoint Hardening
Instance Metadata Service v2

IMDSv2 requires a session-oriented PUT request to get a token before accessing metadata. Prevents SSRF-based credential theft. Enforce via instance metadata options + K8s NetworkPolicy.

# Enforce IMDSv2 at EC2 launch (hop limit = 1)
aws ec2 run-instances --metadata-options \
  HttpTokens=required,HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1,HttpEndpoint=enabled

# Verify IMDSv2 is enforced (IMDSv1 should fail with 401)
curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/  # Should return 401 Unauthorized

# IMDSv2: Get session token first, then use it
TOKEN=$(curl -X PUT "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token" \
  -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600")
curl -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/

# Defense-in-depth: ALSO block IMDS via K8s NetworkPolicy
System Hardening IMDSv2 + NetworkPolicy block
📋
AWS Config — CIS Compliance Auditing
Continuous Compliance

AWS Config continuously evaluates your EKS cluster against CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. Detects drift: unencrypted ECR repos, public S3 buckets, unrestricted security groups.

# Enable AWS Config with managed CIS rules for EKS
aws configservice put-config-rule --config-rule '{
  "ConfigRuleName":"eks-endpoint-no-public-access",
  "Source":{"Owner":"AWS","SourceIdentifier":"EKS_ENDPOINT_NO_PUBLIC_ACCESS"}}'

# Query non-compliant resources
aws configservice describe-compliance-by-config-rules \
  --compliance-types NON_COMPLIANT

# Key EKS CIS rules:
# • EKS_ENDPOINT_NO_PUBLIC_ACCESS
# • EKS_SECRETS_ENCRYPTED
# • EC2_IMDSV2_CHECK
# • ECR_PRIVATE_IMAGE_TAG_IMMUTABILITY
ALL (Compliance) AWS Config + CIS Rules

🏆 AWS Security Integration Strategy for CKS

1
ELIMINATE
Static IAM keys, long-lived creds, passwords in YAML
2
FEDERATE
IRSA for pod→AWS, OIDC for CI/CD, IAM Identity Center for humans

The CKS exam doesn't test AWS-specific services, but understanding AWS security patterns makes you a better K8s security engineer. Every CKS control (RBAC, encryption, NetworkPolicy, audit logging) has an AWS counterpart. Knowing both gives you defense-in-depth across the full stack.

⏱️ Time Management — 120 Minutes, 15-20 Questions

CKS gives you 120 minutes. Each question has a weight (shown on screen). Weight = time budget. A 4% question deserves ~5 minutes. An 8% question deserves ~10 minutes. Do NOT spend 20 minutes on a 4% question.

60 min
PRIORITY 1: High-weight questions (8%+)
Do these FIRST while fresh
40 min
PRIORITY 2: Medium-weight (4-7%)
Steady pace, don't rush
20 min
PRIORITY 3: Low-weight + flagged
Review + partial answers

🔴 Pitfall 1: Wrong Cluster Context

Running commands on the wrong cluster is the #1 reason for zero scores. Every question specifies a context. Switch FIRST, verify SECOND, then work.

✅ Fix: kubectl config use-context <given-context> → verify with kctx

🔴 Pitfall 2: Not Reading the Whole Question

CKS questions often have hidden requirements in the last sentence: "Ensure the solution survives node failure" or "Do NOT modify existing resources." Read to the end.

✅ Fix: Read the last 2 sentences FIRST, then read top-to-bottom

🟠 Pitfall 3: Forgetting to Save YAML Files

You edit a YAML, apply it, it works. But the exam requires the saved file for grading. If you didn't save, you get zero — even if it worked.

✅ Fix: Always save as /home/candidate/<question-file.yaml> when instructed

🟠 Pitfall 4: SSH Timeout = Lost Work

SSH sessions to nodes can time out. Work done in an SSH session is lost if the session dies. Write files, don't just run commands.

✅ Fix: Use ssh node "command" for one-liners. For longer work, edit files directly.

🟡 Pitfall 5: kubectl --dry-run Not Saving

--dry-run=client -o yaml prints YAML but doesn't create the resource. If you forget to actually create it, nothing exists.

✅ Fix: kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml > file.yaml && kubectl apply -f file.yaml

🟡 Pitfall 6: Spending Too Long on One Question

You get stuck on Question 3 for 25 minutes. Now you have 95 minutes for 12 more questions. Flag and move on.

✅ Fix: After 8 minutes on a single question, flag it, write what you have, MOVE ON. Come back if time remains.

✅ Before You Click "End Exam" — Final 5-Minute Checklist
  • Every YAML file saved? Check ls -la /home/candidate/*.yaml. Each question tells you what filename to use.
  • Every context verified? Run kubectl config get-contexts — confirm you used the correct context for each question.
  • Every namespace created? kubectl get ns | grep -E 'anihpj|prod|dev|staging' — verify your namespaces exist.
  • Cluster left clean? Don't leave test pods running. Delete temporary resources you created for testing.
  • Flagged questions revisited? If you have time, re-read flagged questions. Sometimes the answer becomes obvious on second read.
  • Scoring: Partial = Points? Every partial answer earns points. Never leave a question completely blank. Even creating the namespace + YAML file earns something.
  • Take a deep breath. You've prepared for weeks. You've run 100 lab scenarios. You know the 20 command patterns cold. You are ready. Click "End Exam" with confidence.

🏆 The CKS Mindset — What The Exam Really Tests

The CKS is not a memory test — it's a security engineering test. They don't care if you memorized every CIS benchmark check number. They care if you can look at a cluster, identify what's insecure, and fix it. Think like a security engineer: scan → diagnose → harden → verify. Follow the pattern. Trust your training. You've got this.

🐳 Appendix I: anihpj/jobpost — Secure DockerfileDOCKERFILE

The complete, production-hardened, multi-stage Dockerfile for the anihpj/jobpost Django application — with every security decision annotated and explained. Use this as your reference for CKS supply chain security tasks.

2.1 GB
Before Hardening
198 MB
After Hardening
−91%
Size Reduction
340+
CVEs Before
12
CVEs After
2
Build Stages
📄 Dockerfile multi-stage production 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# ANIHPJ/JOBPOST — PRODUCTION DOCKERFILE (Multi-Stage, Distroless)
# Django 5.0 + Gunicorn + PostgreSQL + Redis
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# ═══ STAGE 1: BUILDER ═══
# Purpose: Compile deps, collect static files. This stage is DISCARDED.
# Security: Pinned digest prevents base image drift/tampering
FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:a1b2c3d4e5f6... AS builder

# Pin system deps to specific versions (reproducible builds)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc=4:12.2.0-3 \
    libpq-dev=15.5-0+deb12u1 \
    # ↑ libpq-dev needed to compile psycopg2 (PostgreSQL driver)
    && apt-get clean \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*  # ← Reduce layer size, remove package cache

# Copy ONLY dependency files first (layer caching optimization)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --user -r requirements.txt \
    && pip check  # ← Verify no broken dependencies

# ═══ STAGE 2: FINAL (DISTROLESS) ═══
# Purpose: Minimal runtime image — no shell, no package manager, no compilers
# Security: Distroless = 80% fewer CVEs, no shell for attackers to exploit
FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12:nonroot@sha256:f6e5d4c3b2a1...

# Copy Python packages from builder stage
COPY --from=builder /root/.local/lib/python3.12/site-packages /usr/lib/python3.12/
COPY --from=builder /root/.local/bin /usr/local/bin/

# Copy application code
COPY anihpj/ /app/
WORKDIR /app

# ═══ SECURITY HARDENING ═══
USER 65532  # ← Distroless nonroot user (NOT root, NOT 1000)

# Expose port (documentation only — does NOT publish the port)
EXPOSE 8000

# Use exec form (NO shell, PID 1 = gunicorn, handles signals correctly)
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "4", \
     "--worker-class", "sync", \
     "--max-requests", "1000", \
     "--max-requests-jitter", "100", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", \
     "--error-logfile", "-", \
     "anihpj.wsgi:application"]
🙈 .dockerignore prevents secret leaks 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# .DOCKERIGNORE — NEVER include these in the build context
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════

# GIT — contains commit history, might include old secrets
.git
.gitignore
.gitattributes

# PYTHON — bytecode, virtualenvs, caches
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*$py.class
venv/

.venv/

# ENVIRONMENT — CONTAINS SECRETS, NEVER COPY
.env
.env.*
*.pem
*.key
*.crt
credentials.json
service-account.json

# IDE + OS
.vscode/
.idea/
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# DOCKER
Dockerfile
docker-compose*.yml
.dockerignore

# TESTS + DOCS
tests/
*.md
docs/
🔨 Build & Push Commands secure build pipeline 
# ═══ BUILD (with security flags) ═══
docker build \
  --no-cache \                          # ← Prevent cache poisoning
  --build-arg BASE=python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc... \  # ← Pin base digest
  --label org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost \
  --label org.opencontainers.image.revision=$(git rev-parse HEAD) \
  -t 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj-api:v2.1 \
  -t anihpj-api:latest \
  .

# ═══ SCAN FOR VULNERABILITIES ═══
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 \
  anihpj-api:v2.1  # ← Block push if CRITICAL CVEs found

# ═══ GENERATE SBOM ═══
syft anihpj-api:v2.1 -o spdx-json > anihpj-api-sbom.spdx.json

# ═══ SIGN IMAGE ═══
cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj-api:v2.1

# ═══ PUSH TO PRIVATE REGISTRY ═══
aws ecr get-login-password | \
  docker login --username AWS --password-stdin \
  123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj-api:v2.1

# ═══ VERIFY IN REGISTRY ═══
cosign verify --key cosign.pub \
  123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj-api:v2.1

❌ Naive Dockerfile (Anti-Pattern)

FROM python:latest
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y gcc libpq-dev
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
USER root
CMD python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000

PROBLEMS:
• :latest tag — non-deterministic builds
• Single stage — includes compilers
• COPY . — secrets in .env copied
• USER root — container = root
• runserver — dev server in prod
• No layer caching — slow builds
• No .dockerignore

✅ Hardened Dockerfile (Best Practice)

FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc... AS builder
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc=4:12.2.0-3 libpq-dev=15.5-0 \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --user -r requirements.txt

FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12:nonroot@sha256:def...
COPY --from=builder /root/.local/ /usr/
COPY anihpj/ /app/
WORKDIR /app
USER 65532
CMD ["gunicorn","--bind","0.0.0.0:8000","anihpj.wsgi"]

FIXES:
✓ Pinned digest — reproducible builds
✓ Multi-stage — drops build tools
✓ COPY only what's needed
✓ Non-root USER 65532
✓ Production server (gunicorn)
✓ Layer caching optimized
✓ .dockerignore blocks secrets
✅ Dockerfile Security Checklist — 15 Rules
  • 1. Pin base image to digest: FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc... — never :latest. Protects against tag mutation and supply chain attacks.
  • 2. Multi-stage builds: Builder stage (compilers) → Final stage (distroless, no build tools). Reduces CVEs by 80%+.
  • 3. Distroless or scratch base: No shell, no package manager, no curl/wget. Attacker can't install tools if they breach the container.
  • 4. Non-root USER: USER 65532 or USER 1000. Container escape → non-root on host = limited damage.
  • 5. .dockerignore file: Exclude .env, *.pem, *.key, .git, credentials. The #1 source of leaked secrets is COPY . in Dockerfiles.
  • 6. COPY specific files, not entire directory: COPY requirements.txt . not COPY . .. Minimizes what's in the image.
  • 7. Pin OS packages to versions: gcc=4:12.2.0-3 not gcc. Ensures reproducible builds across time.
  • 8. Clean package cache: rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*. Removes 50-100MB of unnecessary data from the layer.
  • 9. --no-install-recommends: Installs only required packages, not suggested/recommended extras. Saves ~30% package size.
  • 10. pip --no-cache-dir: Don't cache downloaded packages in the image. Saves 100-200MB for Python projects.
  • 11. Exec form CMD: CMD ["gunicorn", "..."] not CMD gunicorn .... Ensures PID 1 = your app (proper signal handling).
  • 12. --no-cache build: docker build --no-cache. Prevents cache poisoning in CI/CD pipelines.
  • 13. OCI labels for provenance: --label org.opencontainers.image.source=.... Enables SLSA provenance tracking.
  • 14. Scan before push: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL. Block on CRITICAL CVEs. Never push unscanned images.
  • 15. Sign every image: cosign sign --key cosign.key. Enable ImagePolicyWebhook verification at deploy time.

🏆 Why This Dockerfile Matters for CKS

The CKS exam tests your ability to identify and fix insecure Dockerfiles. Common exam tasks: "The Dockerfile uses a vulnerable base image — fix it" or "The image contains secrets in layer 3 — rebuild securely." Memorize these 15 rules. They apply to every Dockerfile you'll encounter on the exam and in production.
