🔴 Top 20 Most Commonly Failed CIS Checks on CKS

These are the checks almost every CKS candidate's cluster FAILS. Run kube-bench, find these, fix them first. They're the highest-value points on the Cluster Setup domain.

#1kubelet anonymous-auth enabled — anyone can query pods via :10250/pods→ Set authentication.anonymous.enabled: false
#2kubelet authorization mode not Webhook — no RBAC check on kubelet API→ Set authorization.mode: Webhook
#3API server --anonymous-auth not disabled — anonymous API calls allowed→ Set --anonymous-auth=false in kube-apiserver.yaml
#4API server --profiling enabled — debug endpoints expose memory/goroutines→ Remove --profiling or set --profiling=false
#5Audit logging not configured — no API call logging at all→ Create audit policy + configure --audit-log-path
#6etcd encryption not enabled — Secrets stored as plaintext base64→ Create EncryptionConfiguration + --encryption-provider-config
#7PKI private key permissions too open — world-readable .key files→ chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.key
#8Controller Manager --profiling enabled→ Set --profiling=false in kube-controller-manager.yaml
#9Scheduler --profiling enabled→ Set --profiling=false in kube-scheduler.yaml
#10kubelet readOnlyPort not 0 — unauthenticated metrics exposed→ Set readOnlyPort: 0
#11kubelet protectKernelDefaults not true→ Set protectKernelDefaults: true
#12RBAC — wildcard * verbs on ClusterRoles for secrets/configmaps→ Audit + restrict: replace * with specific verbs
#13ServiceAccount tokens auto-mounted on pods that don't need them→ automountServiceAccountToken: false
#14No NetworkPolicy — full east-west traffic between all pods→ Create default-deny NetworkPolicy per namespace
#15PSA labels missing on production namespaces→ kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
#16Secrets as env vars — visible in /proc/*/environ→ Mount Secrets as volumes instead
#17securityContext missing — pods run as root with all capabilities→ Add runAsNonRoot + drop ALL + roRootFS + noPrivEsc
#18hostPath volumes mounted — pods access host filesystem→ Replace hostPath with PVC or emptyDir
#19privileged: true pods — full node access→ Replace with minimal capabilities + non-root
#20Docker socket mounted (/var/run/docker.sock) — container escape path→ Remove hostPath mount, use external monitoring
🔧 kube-bench Quick Command Reference
  • Full master scan: kube-bench run --targets master — checks API server, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd, PKI
  • Full worker scan: kube-bench run --targets node — checks kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime
  • Filter FAIL only: kube-bench run --json | jq '.Controls[].groups[].checks[] | select(.state=="FAIL") | {id, desc:.description}'
  • Check single item: kube-bench run --targets master --check 1.1.12 (anonymous-auth check)
  • Export JSON report: kube-bench run --json --outputfile cis-report.json
  • Fix + verify cycle: Fix config → restart service → kube-bench run --check X.Y.Z → confirm PASS

🏆 CIS Benchmark CKS Strategy

On the CKS exam: run kube-bench first for any cluster setup task. Identify the FAIL items. Fix the highest-severity ones (anonymous-auth, profiling, encryption, audit logging). Re-scan to verify. The exam doesn't require 100% CIS compliance — it requires you to demonstrate you can use kube-bench to identify and fix the critical security gaps. Focus on the Top 20 above.

📋 How to Present K8s Security to an Auditor

When an auditor asks "How do you secure your Kubernetes clusters?" — don't talk about kubectl commands. Talk about controls mapped to their framework:

1
PREVENT
"We enforce least-privilege RBAC, PSA restricted, and OPA policies at admission"
2
DETECT
"Falco monitors all runtime activity. Audit logs capture every API call at RequestResponse level"
3
RESPOND
"Falcosidekick routes critical alerts to PagerDuty. IR playbook isolates pods within 60 seconds"
4
PROVE
"Here's our kube-bench CIS report, Trivy scan results, and Cosign verification logs from the last 90 days"
✅ Compliance Evidence — What Auditors Want to See
  • Access Control Evidence: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml — show no wildcard cluster-admin bindings. RBAC audit report from kubectl auth can-i --list.
  • Encryption Evidence: EncryptionConfiguration YAML + etcdctl get /registry/secrets/... | hexdump showing k8s:enc:aescbc prefix.
  • Scan Evidence: kube-bench JSON report (weekly), Trivy JSON report (per build), dated and signed.
  • Incident Response Evidence: Falco alert logs with timestamps, IR playbook execution records, post-mortem documents.
  • Change Management Evidence: Git commit history with Cosign signatures, SLSA provenance attestations, PR approval records.
  • Continuous Compliance: AWS Config / OPA audit results showing no drift from CIS baseline over time.

🏆 Beyond CKS — The Security Engineer's Compliance Mindset

The CKS exam teaches you HOW to secure Kubernetes. Compliance frameworks tell you WHY. Every CKS control — RBAC, NetworkPolicy, encryption, audit logging, Falco — exists because a compliance framework requires it. When you present security to leadership or auditors, speak their language: map your K8s controls to PCI-DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA, or GDPR requirements. This transforms you from a "K8s admin" to a Security Engineer who speaks business risk.

🔗 Appendix L: CKA ↔ CKS CrossoverCROSSOVER

If you've passed the CKA (or are preparing for it), you already know a lot of what's on the CKS. This appendix shows exactly what carries over, what's new, and where the mindset shifts from operations to security. You're not starting from zero — you're building on a foundation.

1
Reinforce CKA
kubectl, RBAC, NetworkPolicy, etcd, certs — these are your CKS foundation
2

✅ CKA → CKS Quick Wins — 5 Things You Can Apply Today
  • 1. Add securityContext to every pod: You already write Deployments. Now add runAsNonRoot: true, drop: ["ALL"], readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. Same YAML, just 10 more lines.
  • 2. Create default-deny NetworkPolicies: You already understand podSelectors. Now apply a deny-all policy to every namespace. You've just cut your attack surface by 80%.
  • 3. Run kube-bench on your cluster: You already have a working cluster. kube-bench run --targets master takes 30 seconds. Fix the FAIL items — you're now CIS-compliant.
  • 4. Scan your images with Trivy: You already build images. trivy image myapp:tag shows you every CVE. Fix the CRITICAL ones — you've just added supply chain security.
  • 5. Install Falco: You already run Helm. helm install falco falcosecurity/falco. Now you have runtime threat detection. Exec into a pod and watch the alert fire.

🏆 The Bottom Line

If you have CKA knowledge, you're 40-50% of the way to CKS. The remaining 50-60% is the security-specific tooling (Falco, Trivy, Cosign, OPA, kube-bench) and the security mindset (assume breach, defense-in-depth, least privilege). Every CKA command has a CKS security layer. Master the crossover and you master the exam.

⚡ Appendix M: CKS Exam Day — 20 Security Command PatternsCRAM SHEET

Your last-30-minutes-before-exam cram sheet. Every pattern is a one-liner you can type from memory. Organized by CKS domain weight — start with Monitoring/Runtime (20%) and Supply Chain (20%) first. Read twice. Type from memory. Take the exam.

M.1
Trivy Scan → Identify CVE → Fix → Re-scan
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH anihpj-api:v2
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL anihpj-api:v2
Use --skip-dirs to exclude clean pip deps from scan scope
M.2
Falco Install → Custom Rule → Verify Alert
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace --set driver.kind=ebpf
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -- whoami
kubectl logs -l app=falco -n falco | grep shell
falco --list shows all loaded rules; falco --support shows driver info
M.3
etcd Encryption — Enable + Verify at Rest
Create EncryptionConfiguration (aescbc) → mount in kube-apiserver.yaml
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/ns/name | hexdump -C | head
Rewrite existing: kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
M.4
NetworkPolicy — Default-Deny + Allow + Verify
kubectl apply -f deny-all.yaml
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -O- --timeout=2 svc:port
NetworkPolicy is ADDITIVE. Test BOTH ingress AND egress directions.
M.5
RBAC — auth can-i + Role + RoleBinding
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:sa -n ns
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods -n ns
kubectl create rolebinding rb --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=ns:sa
Use --list to audit ALL permissions; imperative create is FASTER than YAML
M.6
securityContext — Full Hardening Recipe
runAsNonRoot:true, runAsUser:1000, capabilities:{drop:[ALL],add:[NET_BIND_SERVICE]}, allowPrivilegeEscalation:false, readOnlyRootFilesystem:true, seccompProfile:{type:RuntimeDefault}
Apply at Pod level for ALL containers; override per-container if needed
M.7
kube-bench — Run + Fix CIS Failures
kube-bench run --targets master
kube-bench run --json | jq '.Controls[].groups[].checks[] | select(.state=="FAIL")'
Focus on FAIL items only. WARN and INFO are lower priority on exam.
M.8
Audit Policy — Create + Verify Logging
Create audit-policy.yaml (RequestResponse for Secrets)
Mount: --audit-policy-file + --audit-log-path in kube-apiserver.yaml
tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq .
RequestResponse for Secrets captures the DATA; Metadata for everything else
M.9
OPA/Gatekeeper — ConstraintTemplate + Test
kubectl apply -f constrainttemplate.yaml
kubectl apply -f constraint.yaml
kubectl describe constrainttemplate → check Status.Ready
Test locally first: opa test policy.rego; use --dry-run=server on cluster
M.10
Kyverno — Validate + Mutate Pattern
kubectl apply -f kyverno-policy.yaml
kubectl run test --image=nginx → get pod -o yaml | grep securityContext
Kyverno mutate shows patches in resource annotation; check with grep kyverno
M.11
Cosign — Keyless Sign + Verify
cosign sign anihpj-api:v2.1
cosign verify --certificate-oidc-issuer https://accounts.google.com anihpj-api:v2.1
cosign verify-attestation checks SBOM/provenance; cosign download sbom dumps it
M.12
SBOM — Generate + CVE Impact Check
syft anihpj-api:v2.1 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
grype sbom:sbom.json
syft anihpj-api:v2.1 -o json | jq '.artifacts[] | select(.name|test("openssl"))'
syft + grype = Trivy (Trivy does both in one tool — use what's available)
M.13
ImagePolicyWebhook — Configure + Test
Create webhook kubeconfig → mount in kube-apiserver → --enable-admission-plugins=ImagePolicyWebhook
Deploy pod with untrusted image → should DENY
Set failurePolicy: Ignore during testing; Fail only when webhook is verified stable
M.14
cert-manager + Let's Encrypt + TLS Ingress
kubectl apply -f cert-manager.yaml → Create ClusterIssuer → Certificate → Ingress with TLS
kubectl get certificate -o yaml | grep -A5 'status:'
Use staging issuer first (acme-staging) to avoid rate limits during testing
M.15
PSA — Label Namespace + Enforce Restricted
kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label ns prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted
kubectl run test --image=nginx --privileged -n prod --dry-run=server
Apply warn FIRST, check logs, THEN enforce. Audit mode monitors without breaking.
M.16
AppArmor — Profile Create + Apply + Debug
Profile in /etc/apparmor.d/ → apparmor_parser -r → aa-enforce
Pod annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/*: localhost/profile
dmesg | grep -i apparmor
Start in complain mode (aa-complain), check logs, then switch to enforce (aa-enforce)
M.17
seccomp — Profile Create + Apply
{"defaultAction":"SCMP_ACT_ERRNO","syscalls":[{"names":[...],"action":"SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"}]}
Place in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ → seccompProfile:{type:Localhost,localhostProfile:"..."}
Use strace -c gunicorn to see which syscalls your app actually needs
M.18
RuntimeClass — gVisor/Kata Create + Apply
kubectl apply -f runtimeclass.yaml (handler: runsc for gVisor)
Pod spec: runtimeClassName: gvisor
kubectl exec pod -- dmesg | grep -i gvisor
gVisor doesn't support all syscalls — if pod fails, check gVisor compatibility first
M.19
Falco — Custom Rule Write + Test + Alert
Rule in /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml → falco --validate
Trigger: kubectl exec pod -- /bin/sh -c "curl evil.com"
Check: kubectl logs -l app=falco -n falco | grep CRITICAL
Use falco --list to see all loaded rules; --verbose for detailed event output
M.20
Full CIS Benchmark — Scan + Remediation Report
kube-bench run --targets master,node,etcd,policies --outputfile report.txt
grep FAIL report.txt | awk '{print NR": "$0}'
Fix top 10 → re-run → iterate until <5 FAILs
Master+Etcd checks run on CP; Node checks on workers; Policies cluster-wide

💡 Key Differences From CKA

CKA
Operations
Deploy, scale, troubleshoot, upgrade — RUN Kubernetes
CKS
Security
Harden, detect, prevent, respond, audit, comply — SECURE Kubernetes

CKA teaches you to RUN Kubernetes. CKS teaches you to SECURE it — a different mindset entirely. The CKA document is your operations manual. This document is your security playbook. Together, they cover the full spectrum of Kubernetes engineering.

This document is BOTH an exam prep guide AND a career-long reference. The CKS certification opens the door — the knowledge in this document builds the career behind it. Return to it whenever you face a security challenge in production. The answer is probably here.

☁️ AWS-Specific Security PatternsCLOUD

These patterns show how AWS services map to CKS security concepts. Used for illustration where cloud-native patterns apply — not tested directly on CKS, but essential knowledge for production.

AWS.1 — IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts)

Pod-level AWS identity via OIDC federation. No static IAM keys in Secrets. SA annotation → OIDC provider → IAM Role trust policy → Pod gets temporary STS credentials auto-rotated every hour.

Used in: CH9 (External Secrets), SC12 (ECR pull), SC19 (CI/CD auth)

AWS.2 — ECR Security (Elastic Container Registry)

Image scanning on push (Inspector-based), immutable image tags, repository policies, lifecycle policies, cross-account replication.

Used in: CH10 (ImagePullSecret), SC1-SC20 (supply chain), Appendix I

AWS.3 — Secrets Manager + External Secrets Operator

Secrets stored encrypted in AWS (never in etcd). Automatic rotation via Lambda. ExternalSecret CRD maps AWS Secret → Kubernetes Secret. IRSA ensures only authorized pods can read.

Used in: CH9, Q48 (external secrets), S19 (ExternalSecret sync)

AWS.4 — KMS for etcd Encryption

Instead of storing encryption keys on control plane nodes, use AWS KMS plugin. All encrypt/decrypt operations go to KMS. CloudTrail logs every operation. Automatic key rotation.

Used in: CH5, Q46 (EncryptionConfiguration)

AWS.5 — Signer + Container Image Signing

AWS Signer: managed signing service (alternative to self-hosted Cosign). Signing profiles define who can sign. Integration with ECR marks images as "verified."

Used in: SC4, SC16, SC18 (image signing and provenance)

AWS.6 — GuardDuty + EKS Runtime Monitoring

Managed equivalent of Falco. Detects crypto mining, privilege escalation, suspicious API calls in EKS. Integrates with AWS Security Hub for unified view.

Used in: ML1-ML20 (runtime detection), Q169-Q178 (Falco)

AWS.7 — Network Firewall + Security Groups

Defense layers: Security Group (node) → NetworkPolicy (pod) → Network Firewall (VPC). Multi-layer defense-in-depth for network security.

Used in: CS4 (NodePort), CS7 (egress), SH13 (etcd access restriction)

AWS.8 — CloudTrail + Audit Logs (Compliance)

CloudTrail: all AWS API calls logged. Combined with K8s audit logs: "who accessed the Secret?" → K8s audit log; "who assumed the IAM role?" → CloudTrail. CloudTrail Lake enables SQL queries over audit history.

Used in: ML2, ML9, ML14, Q161-Q168 (audit logging)

These AWS patterns are not tested on the CKS exam, but understanding them makes you a better security engineer by showing how cloud-native services implement the same security controls you learn in CKS.
